file: 5 NEW WORKS JOIN COOKING BOOKSHELF.txt
text:
ï»¿
AN ECLECTIC quintet of recent cookbooks might be just what is needed for that last-minute Christmas gift. 
In addition, they contain ideas for food gifts to make and for elegant holiday-entertaining dishes.
All the books are by New Jersey authors. 
Three are from the kitchens of popular cooking teachers; the two others are compilations of recipes from a mixed bag of contributors, and the proceeds from their sale will benefit the Paper Mill Playhouse in Millburn and the Newark Museum.
Subjects range from festive Chinese banquets to homey Italian casseroles and from sophisticated international dishes to favorite recipes of actors.
In ''Cooking at Cooktique'' by Silvia Lehrer (Doubleday & Co. 
Inc., $19.95), ''The Chinese Banquet Cookbook'' by Eileen Yin-Fei Lo (Crown Publishers Inc., $17.95) and Anne Casale's ''Italian Family Cooking'' (Ballantine Books, $9.95), the recipes, with their clear, step-by-step instructions, reflect these authors' many years of teaching the culinary ropes in their kitchen-classrooms. 
Questions that might be posed by inexperienced cooks are often anticipated and procedures are well spelled out.
Mrs. Lehrer, whose Tenafly cooking school, Cooktique, often is host to well-known guest chef-instructors, has compiled more than 200 recipes, several of them classics with a contemporary twist. 
Any do-ahead steps are pointed out and, in the lead to each chapter, Mrs. Lehrer provides tips on the best ingredients and techniques.
Herbed squash bisque, a salad of goat cheese, green beans and pine nuts, grilled chicken with two mustards, steamed red snapper with ginger Hollandaise and chocolate-coated pears in raspberry sauce are a few of the cosmopolitan offerings.
One cavil, however, is with the skewered sesame shrimp, which should be marinated for a shorter time in light, rather than dark, soy sauce so as not to be puckeringly salty.
In ''The Chinese Banquet Cookbook,'' Miss Lo has compiled 10 complete banquets from China's regions and more than 100 recipes, many preceded by personal anecdotes about the author's childhood in Canton.
Besides banquets from Canton, Peking, Shanghai, Szechuan and Hunan (including a delicious version of orange beef), there are also dishes from the nomads called the Hakka, as well as vegetarian and traditional New Year celebration recipes.
A teacher at the China Institute in Manhattan and at her Montclair home, Miss Lo's instructions are straightforward. 
Techniques are illustrated with dozens of line drawings.
The subtitle of ''Italian Family Cooking'' is ''Like Mama Used to Make,'' and for Mrs. Casale, a resident of Watchung, it could also read ''Like Father and Father-in-Law Used to Make.''
Both men were professional cooks whose influence on Mrs. Casale was strong.
Proprietor of Annie's Kitchen Cooking School in North Plainfield for several years, Mrs. Casale manages to convey in her writing the cozy enthusiasm and wealth of helpful hints that she has brought to her students.
A fan of the food processor, the author has adapted many of her 250-odd recipes from Northern and Southern Italy, as well as Italian America, to take advantage of shortcuts. 
For example, the pasta chapter gives detailed instructions for both machine and hand methods of preparation.
Desserts are particularly appealing, from the glazed orange cake and the ricotta mousse with raspberry sauce to the espresso cream pie.
The glossy cover of ''The Newark Museum Cookbook'' displays an elegantly set table (actually the opulent Victorian dining room of the museum's Ballantine House).
The comb-bound cookbook - it was edited by a museum trustee, Mrs. Theron L. Marsh of Bernardsville -is a collection of more than 300 recipes contributed by curators, trustees, members and staff of the museum. 
Appropriately, the book is liberally illustrated with black and white pictures of many of the museum's food-related art and objects.
As one would expect from such a communal effort, the originality of the recipes is as diverse as the contributors. 
But with some careful perusing, a number of choice dishes turn up, from Swiss onion soup and honey-curried bay scallops to Greek ragout of lamb and cheesecake with fresh lemon glaze.
The book is available at the museum for $10.95 ($9.95 for members) or by mail from the Publications Department, Newark Museum, 49 Washington Street, P.O. 
Box 540, Newark, N.J. 
07101. Add $2 for postage, handling and, if requested, gift wrapping.
The newest and also most lighthearted of the cookbooks is the comb-bound paperback called ''Cookbook of the Stars,'' a collection of about 116 recipes, some tongue-in-cheek but most serious, contributed by actors and actresses who have appeared at the Paper Mill Playhouse over the years. 
Photographs from the plays are scattered through the book.
Phyllis Diller sent Red and Yellow Catch-a-Fellow squash, Julie Harris contributed lettuce bread (which tastes much like it sounds), Eva Gabor sent a cookie recipe called Kisses of the Officer and there is a marinara sauce from Dom DeLuise. 
(President Reagan's macaroni and cheese recipe shows up in both this and the Newark Museum cookbook.) King's Supermarkets Inc. supplied a grant for the cookbook, and some of the most sophisticated recipes are those in a special section contributed by Joanna Pruess, director of the store's cooking school.
Available at the Paper Mill Playhouse gift shop before performances and at King's Supermarkets, ''Cookbook of the Stars'' is $10.
Often served as an appetizer or garnish for cold meats at Chinese banquets, these habit-forming glazed nuts make an equally tasty nibble with cocktails or, with additional sugar, with after-dinner coffee. 
Honey Walnuts #4 to 5 cups water #12 ounces walnuts, preferably freshly shelled #1 1/2 ounces sugar (about 3 to 4 tablespoons or more, if desired) #6 tablespoons water (to make sugar glaze) #3 to 4 cups peanut oil. 
1.
* Bring four to five cups of water to a boil in a wok. 
Place walnuts in boiling water for five minutes to remove bitter taste. 
Remove from water and drain, then run cold water over the walnuts. 
Drain again, then place back in the wok with another four cups of water. 
Bring to a boil and cook for another five minutes. 
Repeat draining process. 
Set aside and let drain. 
2.
* Wash wok. 
Add 6 tablespoons of water and bring to a boil. 
Then add sugar, constantly stirring. 
Let boil for 1 minute and add walnuts. 
Stir until the nuts are coated with glaze and remaining liquid in wok has evaporated. 
2.
* Remove walnuts and set aside. 
Wash wok with extremely hot water to remove sugar and dry. 
3. Place peanut oil in wok. 
Bring to a boil (look for a wisp of white smoke), then add walnuts. 
Fry for 4 to 5 minutes, or until walnuts turn light golden brown.
Note: Honey walnuts can be frozen for 3 to 4 weeks.
From ''The Chinese Banquet Cookbook.''
Â 
Green Bean, Chevre
And Pignoli Nut Salad 1/2 pound firm, crisp green beans, stems trimmed 1/4 pound chevre (goat cheese), preferably aged domestic 1/4 cup pignoli nuts, lightly toasted Vinaigrette: #1 large shallot, minced #2 teaspoons Dijon mustard #1 tablespoon raspberry vinegar #3 tablespoons light, fruity olive oil Freshly ground pepper. 
1.
* Bring 2 quarts of water to a boil, add salt, then beans. 
Cover and cook in briskly simmering water for 2 to 3 minutes. 
Drain in a collander and quickly refresh under cold running water. 
Pat dry, place in a mixing bowl and set aside. 
2.
* In a small bowl, combine the shallot, mustard and vinegar. 
Whisk in the oil in a thin, steady stream until mixture is thoroughly blended. 
Season to taste with pepper. 
3.
* Pour the vinaigrette over the beans and toss to mix. 
Transfer green beans to a salad bowl, crumble the chevre into bite-size pieces and scatter over the beans. 
Top with a sprinkle of toasted pignoli nuts and serve. 
Serves 4 to 6. 
From ''Cooking at Cooktique.''
Pasta With Salmon #4 ounces sweet butter 1/2 medium onion, chopped #1 1/2 cups heavy cream 1/4 cup Cognac or white wine 1/2 cup grated Romano cheese #5 sun-dried tomatoes (available at specialty food shops) or 2 plum tomatoes, cut in julienne slices 1/2 pound Nova Scotia salmon, cut into 1-inch pieces Salt and pepper to taste #1 pound linguine or fettuccine Fresh dill, optional. 
1.
* In 9-inch frying pan, melt the butter and saute the onions over low heat until tender but not brown. 
Stir in cream, increase heat to medium-high and simmer 5 minutes to reduce cream. 
2.
* Stir in Cognac or wine, grated cheese and sun-dried tomatoes. 
Mix in salmon, and season to taste with salt and pepper. 
Simmer for 2 minutes more and set aside. 
3.
* Cook pasta in plenty of boiling salted water with 1 teaspoon of salad oil, according to package directions; if fresh pasta is used, cook for 3 minutes. 
4.
* Drain pasta and toss with salmon sauce in a bowl. 
Sprinkle chopped fresh dill on each serving, if desired. 
Serves 5 to 6. 
Adapted from Sylvia Syms' contribution to ''Cookbook of the Stars.''

file: A CHINESE NEW YEAR DINNER IS A SALUTE TO THE ELDERLY.txt
text:
ï»¿
''IVE never tried Chinese food,'' confessed Freda Gibson, poking at a mysterious- looking plate of meat-filled dumplings. 
''It has always seemed so, well, foreign.''
For Mrs. Gibson, a native New Zealander, and more than a dozen other older people, it was a night of many firsts.
Elderly New Yorkers representing a variety of the city's ethnic groups were invited to the Flower Drum Restaurant at Second Avenue and 46th Street Tuesday night for a ceremony ushering in the Chinese New Year, which begins today. 
Attending the traditional event honoring the elderly were blacks and people of Italian, Scottish, Irish, German Jewish, Polish, Puerto Rican and Chinese extraction.
Bryan Miller article on party at Flower Drum Restaurant, New York City, honoring elderly and ushering in Chinese New Year 4682, Year of the Rat; photos (M)
''I've been thinking about doing this for two or three years,'' said Pao Peter Lee, owner of the Flower Drum and the organizer of the event. 
''These people symbolically represent the various communities who live in New York. 
In China, older generations are honored this time of year. 
I hope this causes that tradition to spread in this country.''
Mr. Lee and his family celebrate a traditional Chinese New Year annually at the restaurant. 
However, this was the first time so many outsiders had been invited. 
The evening began with firecrackers popping in front of the restaurant and wishes for the best fortune in 4682, the Year of the Rat.
The guests, chosen from three centers for the aging with the cooperation of the New York City Department for the Aging, dined on a multicourse Chinese feast while watching an hourlong ceremony that began with the Dance of the Mouse. 
Two young girls, one wearing a mouse costume, lilted and swirled around the dining room accompanied, the narrator said, by ''elegant and ethereal music'' that transformed the mouse into a ''graceful, sensitive being.''
Sidney Kilpatrick, a wiry man of Scottish-Irish descent, said this was the first time he had been to Manhattan's East Side in at least seven years, even though he lives on West 10th Street near Fifth Avenue. 
Mr. Kilpatrick has been homebound for years because of poor eyesight and a muscle disorder. 
''This place is most marvelous,'' he said, gazing around the ornately decorated dining room.
After the mouse dance Mr. Lee and his family presented strings of longevity pearls, symbolizing prosperity and harmony, to the artist Dong Kingman, who is of Chinese descent. 
Family members then participated in a ceremony signifying respect for elders in Chinese culture: Three generations kowtowed before their elders.
Later the elderly guests were presented with ''scrolls of wisdom,'' signifying the knowledge and judgment that come with age. 
A special citation was presented to Janet Sainer, Commissioner of the Department for the Aging, who was called a ''compassionate and caring pioneer'' in social services for the elderly.
''I think the Chinese have a good tradition dealing with the elderly,'' Commissioner Sainer said. 
''Respect for the family is frequently lost in our society. 
I hope this event can help bring some of it back.''
For Fred Robinson, a 74-year-old great-grandfather, the party evoked his boyhood in Georgia, where he had playmates who were Chinese. 
Mr. Robinson and the other guests said they admired the cohesiveness and love demonstrated by the Lee family. 
''There is nothing better than a family that can stay together these days, nothing better,'' he said.
Mr. Lee's strong sense of family and reverence for tradition are partly rooted in his escape from China after the Communist revolution. 
It took nearly a decade for him arrange for his wife, Tsen Yee Lee, to leave her homeland and come to America. 
Out of gratitude for his good fortune in the United States, Mr. Lee founded the Chee Yue Community Association, which helps Chinese immigrants learn English and find jobs. 
The association's headquarters are around the corner from his restaurant.
The festivities concluded with a chef demonstrating how to make silk- hair-fine ''longevity noodles'' by hand. 
They were served as part of a ginseng firepot soup.
Mrs. Gibson, still rather new to Chinese cuisine, finished her last dumpling, placed the chopsticks beside her plate and remarked: ''It really is very tasty I think, more so than New Zealand food. 
But it is a bit on the greasy side, don't you think?''

file: A CHINESE PLEA_ BRING BACK THE GREAT WALL.txt
text:
ï»¿
Farmers outside Peking are being asked to return any pieces of the Great Wall that they carried off to build houses and pigpens.
The request is part of a campaign begun this month to restore the section of the ancient wall that runs through the mountainous northern rim of the municipality of Peking.
The drive, organized by four Peking- based newspapers, is concentrating initially on Badaling, a section 50 miles north of Peking frequented by tourists. 
But the organizers hope that enough money will be raised to extend the restoration to other parts of the world's most prominent landmark.
Wall Was Built in Sections
Construction of the Great Wall started about 2,500 years ago. 
It was intended to keep out the marauding northern nomads who lived in the regions that are now Mongolia and Manchuria. 
The wall was built across China in sections using slave labor and was finally linked in 214 B.C.
The Great Wall snakes more than 1,500 miles from Shanhaiguan on the Gulf of Bohai westward to Jiayuguan in the desert of Gansu Province. 
The Chinese called it the ''10,000 li wall,'' partly because it so twisted and turned that no one was quite sure of its length. 
Three Chinese li equal an English mile.
American astronauts said the Great Wall was the only man-made feature on Earth visible from the Moon. 
But extensive portions have crumbled away over the centuries. 
Some sections were damaged in a dozen years of war that began with Japan's invasion of China in 1937 and ended with the Communist defeat of the Nationalists in 1949. 
Other parts eroded through neglect.
Since 1950, the Government has allocated more than a million dollars to repair the wall, notably at Badaling, which was made a historical site in 1961. 
Beyond this showcase, whose visitors included President Reagan last April, the once formidable wall has been allowed to deteriorate.
Â 
'Only Dikes of Earth'
The current campaign was galvanized by a recent aerial survey that found only a sixth of the Great Wall north of Peking still intact; two-thirds was in virtual ruins. 
''In some areas, the damage is relatively great,'' said Peking Evening News last month. 
In one 12-mile section, it said, ''there are only dikes of earth amidst the wild grass.''
The survey did not include the remainder of the Great Wall.
Peking Evening News teamed up early this month with Peking Daily, Workers' Daily and Economic Daily to kick off the drive to renovate the Great Wall as a national heritage.
''The Great Wall is the symbol of the Chinese nation,'' said Zhang Zhihua, a Peking Evening News correspondent who is helping to run the campaign. 
''Loving and repairing the Great Wall will reflect the patriotic feelings of the Chinese people.''
Peking Evening News announced that about $240,000 was sent in by donors up to last Saturday. 
Mr. Zhang said that 80 percent of this came from organizations and 20 percent from individuals.
When China launched another fund- raising campaign earlier this year to save the endangered panda, Chinese companies using the panda as their brand name were urged to contribute. 
No such pressure has been put on companies using the Great Wall brand, which is almost as common in China.
But the Great Wall Hotel, a Chinese- American joint venture in Peking, and a factory manufacturing Great Wall raincoats have each sent in $4,350. 
Other contributors have included the state Cultural Relics Bureau, the Ministry of Nuclear Energy, the China Travel Service and the state-run airline C.A.A.C. 
Mr. Zhang said a few foreign donations had come in, but so far ''not very much.''
The vandalism of the Great Wall north of Peking occurred during the 1966-1976 Cultural Revolution, when the anarchy created by leftist policies ''made people have no sense of discipline,'' Mr. Zhang said.
Â 
Offer of Substitute Materials
''For example, some peasants dismantled sections of the Great Wall to repair their houses,'' Mr. Zhang said. 
''One of the points of the present drive is to tell the residents living around the Great Wall to bring back the bricks they took away.''
The authorities in Huairou County, northeast of Peking, have pledged to get the local farmers to turn in the chunks of wall by offering to supply substitute building material to thosewho cannot afford to buy their own.
The drive to restore the Great Wall has focused around Peking, but Su Weiyang, another Peking Daily journalist, said donations and letters had come in from all over China. 
After the Badaling section has been renovated, the work will continue at Mutianyu, another section northeast of Peking that is scheduled to open in late autumn to alleviate the tourist congestion at Badaling.
No other cities in northern China have announced similar drives in their areas. 
The problem has been handled so far by putting the worst parts of the Great Wall off limits to foreign tourists so the extent of damage will not become known.

file: A COMING ATTRACTION ON CHINA_S TELEVISION_ _SESAME STREET_ SHOW.txt
text:
ï»¿
At the China Central Television station in Peking, a purple creature with a big pink nose appears on television monitors and says: ''Hello there boys and girls. 
This is your cute furry little pal Grover, and today I am going to demonstrate the difference between up and down.''
Television workers here are busily preparing Grover, Kermit the Frog, Cookie Monster, Big Bird and all the other Muppets of the Children's Television Workshop program ''Sesame Street'' for June debuts on Chinese television.
Children's television program "Sesame Street" is being prepared to be shown on Chinese television
The program has not yet been publicized, but translators have been dubbing ''Sesame Street'' into Chinese for several weeks, and workers at the station say there are plans to broadcast the program as many as four days a week in Chinese as a children's learning tool and in English for adult language training.
Given the popularity of studying English and of two American television series broadcast here, both Chinese and foreigners who have seen ''Sesame Street'' believe it may quickly become China's favorite program.
Â 
One Show Is Canceled
China introduced American programming two years ago with the series ''Man From Atlantis.''
Although the series was considered something of a dud in the United States, it became enormously popular in China, partly because Chinese programs have until recently been comparatively dull.
Another American series, a World War II commando saga called ''Garrison's Guerrillas,'' was suddenly taken off the air last week. 
The program was so popular that some Chinese believed street crime dropped every Saturday night when it was shown because all the hoodlums were watching it. 
Others, however, think it led local youth to imitate the violence on the screen.
At a recent national conference on broadcasting, a senior official said that the task of television in China was to ''integrate the universal truth of Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong thought with the accomplishment of the four modernizations, correctly publicize the party's line, principles and policies, carry out ideological and political education, popularize cultural and scientific knowledge, enrich people's cultural life, enhance socialist awareness and improve the cultural and scientific standards of the whole nation.''
Where Cookie Monster fits into this was not made clear.

The Greenwich Y.W.C.A. continues to offer a wide selection of moderately priced cooking classes. 
For specific information about each class, its instructor's culinary background and class content, it is advisable to call for specifics.
Â 
GUILFORD
Vickie Cohen's Chinese Cooking Classes, 122 Barker Hill Drive. 
453-0139.
Â 
Courses: Regional Chinese - basic, intermediate and advanced. 
Classes begin: October. 
Instructor: Vickie Canth Cohen. 
Maximum in class: 8 to 10 with full participation.
Â 
Cost: $50 to $65 for two to three sessions.
Vickie Canth Cohen, a native of Macao and Hong Kong, specializes in the cuisine of Peking. 
Classes are conducted in her home.
Â 
NEW FAIRFIELD
Milltown Gourmet, 9 Milltown Road. 
746-5518. Courses: Basic French Cuisine Techniques; French Cuisine for the Man of the House Classes begin: End of September. 
Time: 7 P.M. with dinner afterwards. 
Instructor: Jerry Huven. 
Class maximum: 12. 
Cost: $185 for six full sessions.
In a breezy, informal style, and working in slightly cramped counter areas, Jerry Huven manages to convey a sizable amount of specific cooking information to small classes in his home. 
Mr. Huven is offering his usual basic French course, plus a new one for male cooks or would-be masters of French cuisine. 
Classes include field trips to the Culinary Institute of America for dinner and to New York City markets.
Â 
NEW MILFORD
The Silo, Upland Road. 
355-0300. Courses: New England Country Cooking and Entertaining (five-day seminar, taught by Susan Purdy), Chinese Culinary Experience (five-day seminar), American Food with Classic Techniques (five-day seminar), Advanced Baking (one-day program), Puff Pastry, Chocolate, Festive American Game Dinner, Basic Skills, New American Cooking, Junior Chefs, Thanksgiving Desserts and Holiday Gifts, Christmas Gifts from Your Kitchen, Festive Christmas Desserts.
Â 
Classes begin: Sept. 
13, various dates all fall. 
Time: Various. 
Instructors: Susan Purdy, Kevin Reid, Ruedi Hauser, Mark McDermott, Jack Lirio, Jean Bernard Pautrat, Jean Jacques Dietrich, Libby Hillman, Norman Weinstein and Culinary Institute faculty members.
Â 
Maximum in class: Class size varies with course.
Â 
Cost: $250 to $300 for five-day seminars, four class hours day; $60 one day, $100 for two days of Advanced Baking (six hours a day); other fees for specific courses vary, begin at $18. 
Basic Skills (Oct. 
6, 13, 20) -three sessions, three hours each, cost $60.
This school, which opened in 1976, features a number of prominent guest instructors, demonstrating a wide variety of food preparation and technique. 
The work space is ample for some participation - the school quarters are the second floor of a handsome barn-culinary supply shop. 
This fall the ever-inventive proprietor, Ruth Henderson, is offering a series of three five-day seminars, with accommodations offered at nearby country inns. 
There will be daylong programs in advanced baking taught by faculty members of the Culinary Institute. 
Jean Bernard Pautrat will teach a course on fish preparation and one on birds. 
A wide variety of single-courses will be taught all fall and winter. 
Calling or writing for a detailed schedule is recommended.
Â 
OLD GREENWICH
Constance Quan Cooking Classes, P.O. 
Box 387. 
637-9302.
Â 
Courses: French and Chinese cuisine, Dim Sum, decorative fruit and vegetable carving. 
Classes begin: Year-round. 
Time: 10 A.M. to 12:30 P.M., 7:30 to 10 P.M. Instructor: Constance Quan. 
Maximum in class: 8. 
Cost: $160 for a series of four.
Whether teaching Chinese or French cooking, Constance Quan demonstrates an enthusiasm for her subject and the techniques at hand that seem contagious. 
Classes in her ample, excellently equipped kitchen are both demonstration and participation.
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Good Earth, 259 Sound Beach Ave. 
637-7774. Courses: All aspects of Chinese cooking. 
Classes begin: Sept. 
16. Time: 7:30 P.M. Instructor: Josephine Wong. 
Maximum in class: 10 Cost: $45 for four classes.
The Good Earth is a Chinese provision store, with foods and kitchen equipment, many imported from China, Hong Kong and Taiwan. 
Josephine Wong, who has taught for 10 years, claims her training began ''at my mother's wok.''
Â 
OLD LYME
Kah's Cupboard, R.F.D. 
1, Old Bridge Road. 
434-5956.
Â 
Courses: Basic Chinese cooking, learning to use a wok, cleaver and other implements, recipes demonstrating fundamentals; advanced Chinese cooking (open to students who have mastered the basic course), learning to make banquet recipes, such as birds nest soup, winter melon pond, Peking duck; Dim Sum.
Â 
Classes begin: Sept. 
8. Time: Usually 7 P.M.; occasional classes at 11 A.M.
Â 
Instructor: Kah Foo Batts. 
Maximum in class: 7 Cost: $75 - basic; $85 - advanced; $75 - Dim Sum (five lessons in each course, 2 1/2 hours each, tasting afterwards).
Kah Foo Batts, who studied in Hong Kong and Malaysia, demonstrates elements of Chinese cuisine in her kitchen. 
Good organizational ability makes it possible for her to work in rather limited space. 
She also has available tapes for students to buy and work with at home.
Â 
STAMFORD
Ronnie Fein School of Creative Cooking, 438 Hunting Ridge Road. 
322-7114.
Â 
Courses: Chinese - beginner and advanced; Dim Sum; French; elegant desserts; hors d'oeurves; basics; one-day workshops in Christmas baked goods, Jewish high holiday specialties, Thanksgiving dinner, New Orleans dinner, Easter breads, Passover specialties.
Â 
Classes begin: Sept. 
21. Time: 9:30 A.M. to 12 noon; 7:30 to 10 P.M. Instructor: Ronnie Fein. 
Maximum in class: 10. 
Cost: $100 for six lessons (basic Chinese); $55 for three lessons (advanced Chinese); $65 for four lessons (desserts); $75 for four lessons (French); $55 for three (Dim Sum and hors d'oeuvres); $90 for six (basics); $27.50 - for workshops (lunch included).
Home cooks interested in broadening skills in holiday specialties might find Ronnie Fein's wide repertory of courses of interest. 
The range runs from Chinese to French, Jewish and Christian festival dishes to a New Orleans dinner.
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Stamford/Greenwich Center for Higher Education, 6 Riverside Avenue, P.O. 
Box 88, Riverside. 
637-4563.
Â 
Courses: Introduction to Catering; Establishing Your Own Catering Company.
Â 
Classes begin: Oct. 
2. Time: 10 A.M. to 12 noon, 1 to 3 P.M. Instructor: Stephen Kennard. 
Maximum in class: Unlimited. 
Cost: $60 for a three-session course.
Two courses are being offered this fall conducted by Stephen Kennard, creator of a New York catering company. 
The first gives an overview of catering as a business and how to organize one, the prerequisites, planning techniques, pitfalls to avoid. 
The advanced course delves into the business requirements, how to set up a seated dinner for two to 200 or a buffet. 
These are courses geared toward cooks who have serious plans to make cooking a business.
Â 
WESTPORT
Cook's Corner of Westport. 
11 Sherwood Square. 
227-9554.
Â 
Courses: Italian, Regional Chinese, Dim Sum, Pasta, Gourmet Classes for Working Men and Women, Classic French, Cake Decorating and Baking, Food Processor.
Â 
Classes begin: Sept. 
26 Time: 10 A.M. and 7:30 P.M. Instructors: Robert MacKerroll, Ed Giobbi, Rose Chann Gray, Mary MacQuillan, Bari Cardiff.
Â 
Maximum in class: 20 - mostly demonstration, limited participation.
Â 
Cost: $30 to $110, depending on course and number of sessions.
In cheerful cooking-supply store setting, classes are held with some frequency. 
They feature guest instructors who demonstrate their specialties. 
The proprietor, Stanley Levy, has a wide acquaintance with food and food techniques and calls this the ''oldest continuing professional cooking school in Fairfield County.''
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Joanne Hush's Kitchen, The Greens Farm Store, 1254 East Post Road. 
227-4151.
Â 
Courses: Chinese, Japanese, Dim Sum, Food Processor, Hors D'oeuvres, French, Bread Baking, Children's Courses.
Â 
Classes begin: Sept. 
20. Time: Morning and evening. 
Instructors: Joanne Hush, staff members, Perla Meyers and other guest instructors.
Â 
Maximum in class: 12 in participation courses, 24 in demonstration courses.
Â 
Costs: $30 and up, depending on number of sessions.
An adequate-size kitchen (in the rear of a book and gourmet-supply store), equipped with overhead mirrors and a good range of supplies and tools, is the setting for lessons by Mrs. Hush in her Chinese specialties, and guest demonstration in a variety of food preparation. 
She stocks a variety of oriental foods in her store, as well as numerous gourmet takeout items.
Â 
WILTON
The Culinary Arts, Gateway Shopping Center. 
762-7575.
Â 
Courses: Simply Sensational, French, Italian, Croissants, Food Processor Hors D'oeuvres, Food Processor Breads, Food Processor Desserts, A Holiday Feast, Gifts from the Kitchen, Great Wine Seminar.
Â 
Classes begin: Sept. 
23. Time: 10 A.M. to 1 P.M.; 7 to 10 P.M. Instructors: Cecile Rivel, Albert Joarant, Melissa Sere.
Â 
Maximum in class: 12 for Simply Senational (full participation class), up to 24 for demonstrationparticipation classes.
Â 
Cost: $30 to $135, depending on the course and the number of sessions.
The proprietor, Cecile Rivel, has been combining her culinarysupply shop with cooking classes for 12 years. 
A large and superbly equipped kitchen in the rear of the store provides extensive viewing space (with the help of wide overhead mirrors) and counter space for observation and participation for considerable numbers. 
There are 12 different courses scheduled, including one called Simply Sensational, which is geared to first timers in the kitchen.
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Wilton Adult Education, Box 277. 
762-9046 or 762-2008.
Â 
Courses: Mondays - Food Processor, The Economy of Elegant Dining, Garnishes Galore, Uncanny Canned Cooking; Tuesdays - Microwave Cooking, Mexican, Cake Decorating for Beginners and Advanced; Wednesday - Perfect Pasta, Italian Cuisine; Thursdays - Hors D'oeuvres, Party Planning.
Â 
Classes begin: Sept. 
27.Time: 7:30 to 9:30 P.M. Instructors: Numerous. 
Maximum in class: 16 - combination demonstration and participation.
Â

file: A GUIDE TO CONNECTICUT_S FALL COOKING CLASSES.txt
text:
ï»¿
IT'S back-to-school time for adults as well as children. 
During the summer, many cooking school instructors - and their students - can't stand the heat, so they temporarily get out of the kitchen.
Now they are back, and fall and winter courses are beginning to be signed up for. 
Chinese, French and baking continue to be high on the list of Connecticut's cooking school offerings. 
But there are other appetizing courses available as well. 
New trends seem to be for pasta-making and for hors d'oeuvre courses, as well as elegant dining and dessert.
The following is a partial listing of schools and classes available and is not intended as an endorsement by this reviewer. 
Facilities that have been visited are noted in the description capsules under each specific heading. 
The classes are listed alphabetically by town, and then by class within each town.
Guide to Connecticut's fall cooking classesCOS COB
Cooking With Shiu-min, 8 Loughlin Avenue. 
629-2990 or 869-4448. 
Courses: The different regions of Chinese cooking - Sichuan, Hunan, Cantonese, Peking, Mandarin. 
Instructor: Shiu-min Lin Block. 
Cost: $90 for a three-lesson series. 
Starting date: Third week of September. 
Time: Morning or evening can be arranged. 
Type: Demonstration and participation. 
Maximum in class: 6.
Mrs. Block has an amiable, informal style, and emphasizes that she wants to make her students comfortable enough with various aspects of the Chinese cuisine to adapt it to their own home cooking. 
She keeps her classes small because her kitchen is small, with limited work space. 
Even so, students learn how to chop and arrange food, how to use Oriental spices and ''enjoy the process.''
A self-taught cook, former owner of a Chinese restaurant, and trained artist, Mrs. Block has been teaching Chinese cooking for 14 years.
Â 
DARIEN
The Complete Kitchen, 865 Boston Post Road. 
655-4055. Courses: Food processor, bread-making, hors d'oeuvres, Chinese, microwave cooking, pasta workshop, introduction to French sauces, Swedish coffee bread-making, autumn wine tasting. 
Also a series of three dinners with wine and cooking demonstrations (Sept. 
25 - Pasta Party; Oct. 
2 - French; Nov. 
13 - Mexican). 
Instructors: Mary Murray (proprietor ), Anne Brown; and special guest instructors : Abby Mandel, Karen Lee, others. 
Cost: $20 to $30 a class, $65 for the three-part Chinese series, $55 a couple fo r the dinner-demonstrations. 
Starting date : Sept. 
22. Time: Tuesday , Wednesday, Thursday, 10 A.M. to 12:30 P.M.; 7:30 to 10 P.M. Type: Demonst ration, but full participation in such classes as breador pastr y-making. 
Maximum in cl ass: 20 in demonstration classes, eight in participati on.
Classes are held in a large, airy, specially constructed kitchen in the rear of a well-equipped kitchenware shop. 
Although we did not see a class in session, we were impressed with the layout and space in the room and the quality of equipment. 
A long, large demonstration table with wide overhead mirror, good lighting and two skylights make observation easy. 
Mary Murray, who studied at La Varenne, has been conducting classes for one year. 
Anne Brown, who teaches bread-making, hors d'oeuvre and food processor cooking, has five years of teaching experience and formerly had a catering business. 
Special instructors teach particular courses from time to time.
Â 
FARMINGTON
The Ann Howard Cookery Ltd., Brick Walk Lane. 
678-9486. Courses: Seafood, French, breads, food processor, Northern Italian, French pastries, hors d'oeuvres, soups. 
Instructors: Ann Howard (proprietor) and guest lecturers - Guiliano Bugialli, Perla Meyers, Jacques Pepin, Martha Stewart. 
Cost: $18 to $20 for a single three-hour class by Mrs. Howard; $35 for a three-hour class taught by a guest instructor; $55 to $75 for a series of three classes. 
Starting date: Continuing courses, year-round. 
Time: 10 A.M. to 1 P.M.; 7 to 10 P.M. Type: Combination demonstration and participation. 
Maximum in class: 25.
Ann Howard, who studied at Cordon Bleu in Paris and London, at La Varenne and with Simone Beck, has been teaching cooking for five years. 
Informal in style, but informative and knowledgeable, she teaches on the second floor of a building that also houses her baker and gourmet cookware shop. 
An mirror over a long work table is an advantage during observation classes. 
A considerable range of threehour classes are taught throughout the year - useful for people who want to advance their skills or learn aspects of a new cuisine.
Â 
GREENWICH
Ron Buebendorf Chinese Cooking Classes, 44 West Putnam Avenue. 
869-7139. Courses: Chinese regional cooking - Cantonese, Sichuan, Fukien, Peking; canapes, dinners, desserts. 
Instructor: Ron Buebendorf. 
Cost: $200 for six lessons. 
Starting date: Mid-October. 
Time: Evenings. 
Type: Demonstration with limited participation. 
Maximum in class: 8.
A student of Virginia Lee in New York, Mr. Buebendorf has catered private and corporate dinners, and has been conducting classes for eight years. 
A sample menu at one leson might include instruction in preparing soy sauce chicken, bean curd casserole, Eight Precious Pudding; another menu - Shanghai duck, stir-fry vegetables, pancakes with apricot filling; a third - Sichuan shrimp, cucumber salad, walnut and date soup.
Cook's Corner Inc., 70 East Putnam Avenue. 
869-2653. Courses: French, Chinese, Japanese, Italian, food processor, hors d'oeuvres, Moroccan. 
Instructors: Nancy Mott (proprietor), Joanne Griffin, Elizabeth Andoh, Paula Wolfert. 
Cost: $30 to $125, depending on instructor and whether it is a single session or part of a series. 
Starting Date: Sept. 
27. Time: 10 A.M., 6 P.M. Type: Full particiption in Japanese and French courses, demonstration in others. 
Maximum in class: 8 for participation, 20 for demonstration.
Nancy Mott, who studied at La Varenne and Cordon Bleu (Paris), and with Giuliano Bugialli and John Clancy, has been teaching cooking for 12 years. 
In addition to the wide variety of cooking taught here, there are also walking tours of food-oriented stores in SoHo and Greenwich Village in New York. 
This school has not been visited, but the recipes used in various different classes - dilled cucumber soup, zucchini flan, caponata sesame lemon chicken, almond tart - are clearly presented, easy to follow, and should be of value to an intermediate-level cook.
Polly Fritch' s Cooking Class, 969 North Street. 
661-7742. Courses: Seas onal, do-ahead menus; international selection of recipes usi ng a wide variety of cooking techniques; food processor.Instructor: P olly Stewart Fritch. 
Cost: $25 a c lass. 
Starting date : Two three-part series - the first, Oct. 
20, 27 and Nov. 
3; the second, Oct. 
21, 28 and Nov. 
4. Time: First s eries, Tuesdays, 7 to 9:30 P.M.; second series, Wednesdays, 9:30 A.M. to noon. 
Type: Combina tion demonstration and participation. 
Maximum in cl ass: 8.
Mrs. Fritch, who has been teaching for 13 years, conducts small classes in her own home, in a large, well-equipped and easy-to-workin kitchen. 
Study at La Varenne, Cordon Bleu in Paris, with Marcella Hazan in Bologna and John Clancy in New York, as well as considerable international travel experience, have given Mrs.Fritch a wide repertory of dishes to draw upon. 
Careful and precise typed instructions for her students make the recipes easy for a beginner or intermediate cook to follow later at home. 
Her emphasis is on cooking techniques that are adaptable. 
Her step-by-step instruction is low-keyed and helpful, with much demonstration, but participation in dishes that demand ''knowing the field as they are being prepared'' - such as crepes, custards, omelets and sauces. 
Each class period is devoted to a full menu. 
In addition to conducting classes, Mrs. Fritch plans to conduct a food-oriented tour of Britain in May and September 1982.
Greenwich Board of Education, Continuing Education Program, Havemeyer Building, Greenwich Avenue. 
661-8236. Courses: Cake decorating (10 sessions); making pizza from scratch; nutrition from A to zinc (10 sessions); soup to nuts (six sessions). 
Instructors: Glee Miner (cake decorating), Dorothy McDonald (pizza), Meredith Sampson (nutrition), Mimi Bradley (soup to nuts). 
Cost: Cake decorating - $40; pizza - $10; nutrition - $35; soup - $35; $5 extra for non-Greenwich residents. 
Starting date: Week of Sept. 
21 and on. 
Time: 4 to 6 P.M., Tuesdays or Thursdays.Type: Demonstration and participation. 
Maximum in class: 12 for pizza making, 20 for other classes.
The facility at Greenwich High School, Hillside Road, where classes are held, is a goo d one, with overhead mirror s and ample work space. 
This fall's program represents an expansion i n cooking courses offered by the continuing education program, though all the teachers are known in the Greenwich area for their spe cial interests.
Greenwich Y.W.C.A., 259 East Putnam Avenue. 
869-6501.Courses: Bolognese, bread-making, microwave, vegetarian and classes for young people; also mini-courses - Indian, microwave, holiday cooking. 
Instructors: Debbie Krieger, Liz Guccione, Cathy Strachan, Chitra Ramcharandas, Jo Button, Tony and Helen Moore, Maria Lucia Perugini. 
Cost: From $45 for five-class vegetarian series to $66.50 for sevenclass Bolognese cuisine; $10 to $15 for one-session mini-courses. 
Starting date: Ongoing. 
Time: 9 A.M. to 10 P.M.; young people's classes held in late afternoon. 
Type: Combination demonstration and participation. 
Maximum in class: 14.
Classes vary in length from the numerous mini-courses offered from time to time to courses that might consist of 14 sessions each. 
Microwave courses are taught by Liz Guccione and by Debbie Krieger. 
The Indian courses by Chitra Ramcharandas, breads by Jo Button; vegetarian cooking by the Moores, and mini-courses by Cathy Strachan.
Â 
MANCHESTER
Margery Gussak, 97 Wyneding Hill Road. 
646-8852. Courses: Chinese cooking. 
Instructor: Margery Gussak. 
Cost: $115 for a four-class series. 
Starting date: Oct. 
12. Time: 10 A.M. or 6 P.M. Type: Full participation. 
Maximum in class: 6 to 8.
Margery Gussak has been teaching four years, specializing in the regional cooking of China: Mandarin, Peking, Cantonese, Sichuan. 
Her teachers include Virginia Lee, Florence Linn, Karen Lee and Sonya Whetston. 
Each class in the four-week series runs four to five hours and involves full class participation in the cooking process. 
There are three series taught, progressing from the simple to the more complex aspects of Chinese cooking. 
In Series I - Clas s II, for instance, the re will be recipes for poultry dishes representing each of four major provinces. 
Recipes include egg drop soup, Shanghai duck, chicken with vegetables, and Kung Pao chicken.
Â 
NEW CANAAN
Cook Nook, 90 Main Street. 
966-0178. Courses: Microwave, bread-making, food processor, pasta-making, children's classes, Chinese. 
Instructors: Joie Tauber; guest instructors: Ronnie Fein, Dorian Lee, Charles Wisniewski, Kristen Mountain. 
Cost: $20 for one class to $70 for a series of three. 
Starting date: End of October. 
Time: 10 A.M. to noon; 7 to 9 P.M. Type: Demonstration with some participation. 
Maximum in class: 8 to 30, depending on the type of class.
In the rear of one room in a two-room cookware supply store, a section has been turned into a kitchen area. 
There is a long Formicacovered work counter with built-in burners, and an overhead mirror for class observation. 
Classes run from one and a half hours to three hours, depending on the course. 
Children's classes, for ages 6 to 9 and 10 to 14, involve total participation; other classes, partial participation.
New Canaan Y.M.C.A., 564 South Avenue. 
966-4528. Courses: Food processor cooking, introduction to natural foods and nutrition, and holiday buffet. 
Instructors: Sandy Slaughter, Frances Sheridan Goulart, Susan Goodman. 
Cost: $30, $5 extra for non-Y.M.C.A. members, for four-week sessions each. 
Starting date: Sept. 
24 (food processor), Oct. 
5 (nutrition), Oct. 
28 (holiday buffet). 
Time: 10 A.M. to noon (food processor), 9:30 to 11:30 A.M. (nutrition), 9:15 A.M. to 12:30 P.M. (holiday buffet). 
Type: Demonstration, with participation, depending on the course. 
Maximum in class: 10.
Sandy Slaughter, who has taught at other adult education programs in Fairfield County and also conducts classes in her own home, encourages a small class to participate in the various things to be done with a food processor: bread-making, pasta, wok cookery, and ''entertaining with ease and elegance.''
The emphasis is on the technique of the food processor. 
Frances Goulart's teaching on natural foods and nutrition extends back 10 y ears, and she has written cookbooks on the subject. 
The holiday buffet course covers a range of festive party cooking, from menu pla nning to the end result.The class is small to enable full participati on in preparing each dish.
Â 
NEW FAIRFIELD
Milltown Gourmet, 9 Milltown Road. 
746-5518. Course: Basic French cuisine, with some nouvelle cuisine.Instructor: Jerry Huven. 
Cost: $170 for six-session course, with dinner and wine included. 
Starting date: Sept. 
22. Time: 7 P.M. Type: Full participation. 
Maximum in class: 12.
In a small kitchen in his home, Jerry Huven conducts perhaps the most informal classes we have watched. 
Barefoot, blue-jeaned, with a wine glass in hand, he conducts a chatty, but surprisingly authoritative class, in which students are encouraged to participate in each step of the process. 
Huven is a cooking hobbyist, with a background of lessons at La Varenne and Cordon Bleu in Paris and at the Culinary Institute of America in Hyde Park. 
He has traveled widely in his job and conducts cooking tours to France (the next one is Nov. 
1 and then again at Eastertime). 
He conveys tips and helpful hints to his students, as they all help in the preparation of a full dinner menu, using professionally prepared, typed instruction sheets for each recipe. 
The worktable in the center of the kitchen does not allow room enough for everyone to work at once, however, and the lighting would be improved if track lighting were installed overhead. 
But for a cook who understands the basics, the course can open the door to more complex dishes - and be enjoyable at the same time.
Â 
NEW MILFORD
The Silo Cooking School, Upland Road. 
354-3500. Courses: New Orleans luncheon, cooking with fresh fall herbs, economy and elegance, the supreme chicken, food Pocessor, junior chefs, others. 
Instructors: Mark McDermott, Barrie Kavasch, Kevin Reid, Sandy Slaughter, Ruedi Hauser, Tony and Gail Diminico, Susan Purdy, Barbara Patrick. 
Cost: From $20 to $35 a workshop, depending on the amount of participation; $18 for junior chef classes. 
Starting Date: Oct. 
7 with individu al or two-part workshops, continuing through Dec. 
13 for the fall season. 
Time: Varies, usually 11 A.M. to 2 P.M., or 7 to 10 P.M. Type: Demonst ration and participation. 
Maximum in cl ass: 16 for participation classes, 30 for demonstrati ons.
Students sit on high stools around an L-shaped butcher block table, behind which a guest instructor demonstrates each step of each recipe. 
Students are then urged to ask questions and participate in the cutting, chopping, mixing process. 
The kitchen is at the end of a large upstairs loft section of a barn, the rest of which contains a handsome culinary supply shop, and art galleries. 
Equipment used in the classes in new and first-rate. 
At the end of each session, students and teachers share the harvest of the dishes prepared, at a pleasantly-set table nearby in the loft. 
Many of the courses are onetime workshops, geared to helping new and experienced cooks deal with specific problems or develop new ideas - i.e., a session on economy and elegance called After The Game Supper, or a course called Understanding Stocks and Sauces. 
The Silo has a number of lively courses designed to make cooking interesting to children from ages 6 to 10 and up.
Â 
NORWALK
Classic French Cooking with Joan O'Connell, 1 Pine Hill Road. 
866-8951. Course: French-based cooking techniques. 
Instructor: Joan O'Connell. 
Cost: $30 a class, three-class session. 
Starting date: Mid-October. 
Time: 10 A.M., 6 P.M., each session four hours long. 
Type: Demonstration only, with a meal served at the end. 
Maximum in class: 8.
In a country kitchen, with fireplace, in her home, Joan O'Connell teaches ''French-based techniques that can be adapted to basic cooking methods and various combinations and adaptations.''
A student of Madelaine Kamman, Peter Kump, Jacques Pepin and Simone Beck, she also has the practical experience of cooking at Bon Appetit in Westport. 
She also conducts classes one day a week for high school and college students interested in pursuing a restaurant career.
Â 
OLD GREENWICH
Constance Quan Cooking School, P.O. 
Box 387. 
637-9302. Courses: French, Chinese, dim sum. 
Instructor: Constance Quan. 
Cost: $160 for a series of four classes. 
Starting date: Mid-November. 
Time: 10 A.M. to 12:30 P.M., 7:3 0 to 10 P.M. Type: Demonstration and participation. 
Maximum in class: 6.
Mrs. Quan's French cooking skills were acquired at Cordon Bleu in Paris. 
Her Chinese skills derive from being third-generation in the Chinese food business. 
She has taught both French and Chinese cooking for the past four years. 
In 1980, as a participant in the Culinary Olympics in Frankfurt, she won a bronze medal. 
Her classes, which are taught in the spacious kitchen facilities of the Complete Kitchen in Darien, combine an informal, but well-organized teaching style with a fair amount of class participation. 
The French classes emphasize techniques in meats, fish and pastries. 
The Chinese classes focus on meat, fish, vegetable, soup and salad preparation.
OLD LYME
Kah's Cupboard Inc., Old Bridge Road. 
434-5956. Course: Chinese cooking. 
Instructor: Kah Batts. 
Cost: $55 for a series of five classes. 
Starting date: Sept. 
15. Time: 7 P.M. to 9:30 P.M. Type: Combination demonstration and some participation. 
Maximum in class: 7.
In a tiny kitchen that adjoins a Chinese food and gift shop in her home, Kah Batts demonstrates elementary Chinese cooking techniques and invites class participation. 
Work space for both demonstration and participation is limited, but Mrs. Batts shows how to use Chinese cleavers, how to use the wok in stir-frying, steaming and other techniques. 
Step-by-step recipes help students follow the basic techniques when preparing the dishes by themselves later.
Â 
RIVERSIDE
The Good Earth, c/o University of Bridgeport, St. Catherine of Siena Church, Riverside Avenue. 
637-4563. Courses: Techniques of Chinese cooking. 
Instructor: Josephine Wong. 
Cost: $60 for a four-class series. 
Starting date: Sept. 
15 for Tuesday evening series, Sept. 
18 for Friday morning series. 
Time: 9:30 to 11:30 A.M., 7:30 to 9:30 P.M. Type: Demonstration and participation. 
Maximum in class: 14.
Â 
Over the co urse of four classes, students will learn how to preparesoup, dim sum , a seafood dish, vegetable dish, a beef or pork or chicken dish, dessert, a noodle dish, how to cook rice properly, the Chinese way. 
Some dishes Josephine Wong explains and demonstrates areexamples of C hinese family dishes, home cooking; others are more familiar rest aurant standards. 
These beginning series are designed toimpart the ba sics of Chinese cooking. 
Other series of four classes each will fol low throughout the year. 
A student who takes each graduated lev el will be able to progress in learning the more complexdishes of the Chinese cuisine.

13 - elegant desserts (four-part series); Oct.

227-4151. Courses: foods from Mainland China, Japanese (beginning and advanced), ''three-star French chefs,'' classic desserts, vegetarian cooking, children's cooking, holiday hors d'oeuvres, cocktail buffet, basic techniques, food processor, candy-making.

28. Time: 10 A.M. to 1 P.M., 7 P.M. to 10 P.M. Type: Some de monstration courses, others with full participation.

IT'S back-to-school time for students of cookery, too, and it is good news that Manhattan does not have a monopoly on the many interesting classes in varied cuisines.
Several schools in New Jersey are offering instruction in multilesson series or one-day workshops. 
Dishes taught range from homemade pasta in Plainfield to arroz con pollo in Teaneck. 
And the facilities are just as diverse, varying from snug home kitchens to sleek kitchen classrooms with visiting chefs.
Not only is there the convenience of not having to venture into the city, but, also, the fees for these schools are usually a good deal lower than those in Manhattan.
List of cooking schools in New Jersey
The three types of teaching methods are dem onstration, wherein the instructor lectures and performs techniques a nd the students merely observe; participation, in which the students prepare the dishes alone or in teams, and limited participation, in which the students do some of the hand tasks but the instructor completes the preparation.
Following is a list of cooking schools in the state that is by no means comprehensive. 
Classes have been visited whenever possible, and schools are listed alphabetically by town.
For more information and exact dates, you should call the school.

text:
ï»¿
TIRED AND DUSTY AFTER A DAY'S driving from the north, three men on a Yangtze River motorcycle pulled into the courtyard of the inn at Guanduping, a village in China's heartland province of Shaanxi. 
They stowed their helmets in the cycle's sidecar and moved toward a group of villagers seated at tables of hand-hewn slate.
An old man paused as he ferried bowls of steaming noodles to the bare-chested villagers. 
Although Tian Binggao, the innkeeper, had not seen a foreigner since Japanese troops passed through the village in 1938, he showed little surprise at finding an American and an Englishman outside his inn on a balmy evening last June, nearly 200 miles from the closest of the country's officially ''open'' cities.
He settled the foreigners and their Chinese companion at a table and listened attentively to the conversations that developed between them and the villagers. 
Later, after dusk settled on Shaanxi's dust-brown hills, he put the visitors to bed on his own k'ang, a traditional sleeping platform of stacked bricks.
The hospitality of that first night on the open road proved a fitting prologue for the experiences that the three travelers - Edward E. McNally, an American lawyer, Zhang Daxing, a Chinese recently returned from studies in the United States, and this writer, then The New York Times's correspondent in Beijing - had as we traveled unescorted across the mountains and plains of Central China, from the industrial city of Taiyuan to the semitropical bamboo forests along the border of Sichuan.
With this article, the story of that unauthorized 1,000-mile journey, and of my subsequent arrest, imprisonment and expulsion from China, is told publicly for the first time. 
As it happens, the six months since I was pulled from a prison cell in central Beijing and deported for having allegedly used the motorcycle journey for ''spying'' on military installations have also seen a dramatic swing in the political mood in China, one that may, in retrospect, help to explain why the authorities reacted to our trip as they did.
More important, if the conservative attack on the reforms in China gathers pace, our journey may serve as a bench mark of how things stood in a brief interlude of the mid-1980's, when the country seemed more relaxed than at any other time in its modern history. 
Just as our experiences provided us with a heady but elusive sense of freedom, so the Chinese people, once more facing a crackdown by Communist Party hardliners, may be in danger of losing their newfound liberty.
Our trip exposed us to a back-roads China that war and revolution have made inaccessible to foreigners since the 1930's, the China that has benefited most from the reforms initiated by the country's 82-year-old paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping.
Moving far beyond the ''open cities'' to which foreigners are normally restricted, we saw how Mr. Deng's reforms have fostered a well-being rural China has not known in generations. 
We saw a country where politics had virtually disappeared from everyday life, rural dwellers were exploiting the climate of broadening tolerance to make money, to laugh, to concentrate on family and personal contentment instead of the millenial social and political goals that were the dominating factors in rural life under Mao Zedong.
At a personal level, the journey was my most rewarding in more than six years of reporting from China, for The Globe and Mail of Toronto in the early 1970's and for The New York Times from 1984 to 1986. 
Until the night at Mr. Tian's inn, my China had been the one seen by the overwhelming majority of foreigners, one of polite but wary officials, of ever-watchful guides, of official guest houses and banquets and ''brief introductions'' at factories and hospitals that compensated in length for what they lacked in candor.
On our journey south, I felt for the first time that I was seeing an unrehearsed China, the one I had read about in the chronicles of earlier 20th-century travelers. 
Away from the planes and trains and buses that channel most visitors from one major center to another, aboard a motorcycle that gave us freedom to travel at will and to talk to whom we pleased. 
I felt an enormous fulfillment, as if all my years in the country had been but a preparation for this one extraordinary ride.
THE DECISION TO travel beyond the open areas without official permission evolved over several months. 
Like many Westerners living in China in recent years, I had become impatient with an official policy that proclaimed an ''openness'' toward foreigners while maintaining many of the constraints familiar from my earlier assignment.
My frustrations may have been greater than those of others seeing the country for the first time. 
On my return to Beijing in 1984, senior officials greeted me with intimate dinners in out-of-the-way restaurants, whispering apologies for our less-pleasant encounters during the Cultural Revolution and pledging that they would do all in their power to help.
The promises went unfulfilled. 
The working environment was more relaxed than a decade earlier, but few of my requests for assistance in obtaining interviews or trips were answered, much less granted. 
There were other unpalatable reminders of the suspicions that attach to Westerners. 
Staff members assigned to us by the Government rifled through our personal papers and reported regularly to their superiors on our private lives as well as on work-related matters.
Meanwhile, I was meeting more and more Western visitors, many of them Americans, who were venturing without permits into remote regions of the country and returning with accounts of a climate in which suspicion seemed absent. 
In every case I heard of, local authorities who stopped the travelers reacted to their presence in restricted areas either by asking them to move on to the closest ''open'' area or, at worst, by imposing a fine equivalent to $31.25.
The sense that it was time for me to test the possibilities was strengthened when a friend who works as a foreign correspondent for the French news magazine L'Express arrived in Beijing and regaled Foreign Ministry officials in my presence with accounts of a monthlong bus trip he had taken across southern China without a permit. 
The senior official present merely laughed and said, ''This is a new style of travel.''
The spirit of adventure was also encouraged by Mr. Deng, who repeatedly told visiting statesmen, investors and others that they should not take his word for the progress the country was making under the ''open door'' reforms. 
''You must go and see for yourselves,'' he said.
Mr. McNally and I had envisaged a journey that would begin in the central China city of Xi'an and traverse Sichuan province to reach the southern city of Kunming. 
But a Chinese friend whose father had worked in southern Sichuan warned us that the area was heavy with sensitive installations, including the rocket base at Xichang. 
Moving our starting point farther north, to the industrial city of Taiyuan, we plotted a course that would sweep southwestward across Shanxi province to the Yellow River boundary with Shaanxi, thence to the Communists' wartime sanctuary at Yanan, southward again to Xi'an, and from there up through the Qin Ling Mountains to Sichuan, where our last call was to have been at Mr. Deng's birthplace in Guangan county.
Our departure from Taiyuan coincided almost exactly with the 50th anniversary of the journey made by Edgar Snow, the Missouri-born journalist who left Beijing on his way to the encounters with Mao and Zhou Enlai that resulted in his classic account of the Communists' beginnings, ''Red Star Over China.''
For several hundred miles, we would be re-tracing Snow's footsteps. 
There was comfort in the thought that he, too, had set off without the Government's blessing.
FROM THE MOMENT we left the built-up area of Taiyuan, a steel city that sits in the lee of the Great Wall, we began experiencing the unscripted pleasures other unlicensed travelers had reported.
For one week, we spoke to whom we pleased. 
We slept in smoky inns, in truck-drivers' rest houses, in a mountain cave. 
We bathed in mountain rivers, ate in peasant restaurants and hauled our motorbike onto the flatbed of a truck to drive for hours through a summer storm. 
Time and again, we laughed with curious villagers who gathered about us as we repaired the bike's fragile spokes.
Whether it was a bed for the night, fuel for the motorbike, or an escorted journey into the hills to see an ancient Buddhist temple, no effort seemed too much for the villagers we met along the way.
The remoteness of many of the mountain villages we passed through was brought home to me when we stopped late one evening in a village in southern Shaanxi. 
As I crouched by the rear wheel of our cycle to repair some broken spokes, a hand from the crowd began running through my curly hair. 
''Excuse me,'' said the owner of the hand, ''with regard to your hair, did you suffer an electric shock?''
Elsewhere, peasants kneeled to measure my feet, marveling like Lilliputians at my size 11 shoes.
In the town of Zhenba, about 20 miles from the Sichuan border, the county party secretary dispatched the local historian to meet with us. 
He told us we were only the second foreign visitors in the town's 2,000-year history, the first being an American fighter pilot shot down by the Japanese in 1943. 
With no road out of the mountains at the time, the pilot was carried from the region in a sedan chair.
Among the ordinary people with whom Mr. Zhang and I conversed in Chinese, there was a widespread curiosity about the outside world. 
A truck driver encountered in a village south of Xi'an told us that he had seen an American film about trucking, ''Convoy,'' and wanted to know if American truckers really tangled so frequently with the police.
''Quite a bit, I suppose,'' I said.
''It's no different here,'' he replied.
Politics were not mentioned unless we raised the subject. 
More than once, we found villagers who could not name the local party boss. 
Outside the inn in Guanduping, I asked a group of young men who was in charge of matters in Beijing. 
''Who cares?'' one of them said, laughing. 
Mr. Tian told us that the decline in the power of the local party secretary, a petty tyrant under Mao, was the most important of all the changes under Mr. Deng. ''Nobody's looking over our shoulders now,'' he said.
A thriving spirit of enterprise greeted us wherever we went. 
Wheat fields and rice paddies were dotted with families working their private plots. 
From early morning to past dusk it was hard to find anybody of working age who was not busy, a contrast with the lethargy characteristic of the state-owned economy of the cities.
We traveled down an unbroken chain of entrepreneurship. 
From private inns to private restaurants, in private motorcycle shops and private coal mines, we saw how people indoctrinated against the evils of capitalism had turned their skills and energies to profit. 
What we observed in two provinces made nonsense of official figures that claim only 20 million people are self-employed, out of a population of 1.1 billion.
Mr. Tian, the innkeeper, had tilled the rocky hillsides near his home for more than half a century before the reforms spurred him to start gathering wild apples and pears to sell in a nearby town. 
It took him five years to amass the equivalent of $300, the first cash his family had ever had. 
With another $600 borrowed from relatives and friends, he built his three-room inn beside the main road to Yanan. 
With a general store selling grain, bicycle seats and shoelaces built onto the inn, his first year generated $750 in profit, more than he had earned in a lifetime of farming.
''We do not ask for much,'' he told us as his wife stir-fried noodles for our breakfast. 
''But if we can make a small profit, my children can do better. 
One day, they can each have a house of their own.''
Outside Yanan, blackened tunnel entrances began appearing in the hills. 
Turning down a side road, we came on a granite-lined shaft sunk 50 feet into the ground. 
This was our first look at the new industry of private coal-mining, which was to produce about 20 million of the output of 870 million tons China produced in 1986. 
An aging watchman told us that groups of men, sometimes 1 or 2, in the bigger mines 10 or 12, pool their labor and capital. 
After the local utilities bureau approves a site, they work 16 hours a day with hand shovels sinking shafts and digging tunnels. 
The coal is dug by hand, loaded onto tractors and hauled to neighboring power stations.
In a province in which millions of people were outside the cash economy until a few years ago, the miners are earning an average of $750 a year, three times the income of prosperous local peasants. 
Looking at a charcoal-stained flue through which deadly coal gas is burned off, we wondered how many men died in the process. 
''There are risks,'' the watchman said. 
''But this way a man can build a new life.''
Those forsaking the ''iron rice bowl'' of guaranteed employment run the risks of entrepreneurs everywhere. 
In Yanan, we befriended Zhang Yuanxin, a factory worker who had borrowed $2,250 to buy a battered, 20-year-old Liberation truck. 
Twice a week, he drives the 230 miles to Xi'an, ferrying freight. 
The journey, normally 12 hours, has been taking up to two days, because of breakdowns.
Over dinner at the Shanghai Restaurant in Yanan, other drivers laughed at his travails. 
''You're having a hard time now, admit it,'' the driver of a factory truck said. 
He drew an imaginary roof over his head and added: ''I like to keep things nice and safe. 
Why risk my head?''
Many of the simple joys and traditions of country life have been revived. 
In Fenyang, a market town in Shanxi, we saw a funeral procession of a kind proscribed by Mao, who condemned all ''superstition.''
A musical ensemble playing a dirge preceded a procession bearing a portrait of the deceased, an elderly lady. 
Behind, came trays of steamed dumplings, an offering for the afterlife. 
At the rear, a dozen young people were cloaked head to toe in the traditional funereal white, inscriptions of filial piety pinned to their backs.
Driving into the night in the Bashan Mountains near Sichuan, we passed lovers leaning against haystacks, youths using a remote stretch of road for motorcycle races, and three men who seemed to be busy stealing bags of road builders' concrete.
On our last night, in the Qin Ling Mountains, we came across a cave above a churning alpine river. 
Needing firewood, blankets and straw, we drove half a mile to a peasant's house, borrowed what we needed, then set up in the cave for the night. 
It was the eve of the Fourth of July, and Mr. McNally produced glasses for a toast. 
Mr. Zhang reached into his pack for a harmonica, then treated us to an impromptu concert of American ballads, including a rousing version of ''Oh!
Susanna.''
In the morning, the young peasant who had lent us the blankets, Yang Chaojin, took us on a hike into the mountains, to a village with a recently-restored Buddhist temple. 
The villagers' pride, and their religious commitment, were affecting. 
As we walked, Mr. Yang spoke of his sadness in having completed only a year of primary school. 
''When I dream at night,'' he said, ''it is of being in a classroom. 
I am an illiterate man. 
I have no skill.''
The incident made a strong impression on Mr. Zhang, only recently returned from four years of study at Middlebury College in Vermont. 
Disillusioned with his prospects when we left Beijing, he appeared to have found a new faith. 
''I wasn't sure there was a place for me in China,'' he said. 
''People have been telling me that I've been away too long, that I've picked up too many 'American' ways. 
Out here, I feel as though I belong.''
OUR ADVENTURE ENDED a few hours later, outside a guest house in Zhenba, in the small hours of the morning. 
Unaware that we were next door to the county police headquarters, we sounded the motorcycle horn in an attempt to rouse a napping desk clerk. 
Awakened by the noise, a policeman came out to admonish us, then asked for our travel permit.
Mr. McNally carried a letter from Beijing University, endorsing our journey. 
He had spent the 1985-86 academic year there, on leave from the United States Justice Department, teaching American constitutional law. 
But neither of us carried an official voucher for travel outside ''open'' areas - the 244 cities and towns that then constituted the tourists' China. 
After two days of back and forth with authorities in Beijing, the local police commander said that he had been instructed to have us write a ''self-criticism'' acknowledging our breach of the travel regulations, which we supplied, and to send us back to the capital by train. 
Back in Beijing, I had a brief session at the Foreign Ministry that concluded with officials assuring me that the matter had been resolved.
Ten days after our departure from Zhenba, on July 17, I drove to the Beijing airport with my wife, Jane, and two small children, en route to a vacation in the United States. 
In the customs hall, we were surrounded by uniformed officers from the Security Ministry, who led us into a small room off the departures hall, where a police videocamera crew awaited us. 
With my 5-year-old son clinging to my waist, the initial interrogation, which would last for 15 hours, began. 
Past midnight, long after the children had returned to the city with their nanny, Gen. Xilian Zhang, the officer in charge, returned to the terminal from a meeting in the city and told me that I was to be taken to my apartment for a search and from there to a prison. 
''You should prepare for the worst, and hope for the best,'' he said.
The first sight of Pao Ju jail was depressing. 
Situated off a busy residential lane about two miles from Beijing's Tian An Men Square, it is a maze of grimy red-brick buildings, windows gaping with broken glass, rusting bars and shades of rotting rattan. 
I was led to a cell in a section that appeared to be reserved for privileged prisoners. 
Downstairs, Chinese prisoners clustered 14 to a cell, with no furniture and a privy beneath a trapdoor. 
Upstairs, I had the same space - 8 feet by 14 - to myself, with a low cot. 
Heavy padding covered the walls. 
Ceiling lights burned 24 hours a day, a precaution against suicides.
The only book I was allowed to keep from the collection I had brought from home, a volume of Mr. Deng's collected works, gave me food for thought. 
Reading with an eye to my own situation, I found frequent reference to an old Chinese idiom, ''patting the tiger's backside,'' a reference to those who misjudge the tolerance of the powerful. 
It seemed well-tailored to my case.
After awhile, General Zhang relaxed the detention rules. 
My wife and I were allowed to exchange letters, and meetings were arranged with United States and British diplomats, with my wife, and with A. M. Rosenthal and Warren Hoge, the Times editors who had flown to Beijing. 
After I had eaten virtually nothing for the first two days, the prison cook was dispatched to ask me what I would like. 
Soon fresh vegetables were showing up in the tin bowls the guards brought to me three times a day.
General Zhang, an oval-faced man in his 50's with the manner of a country schoolmaster, told me that he had been an espionage investigator ''for many years,'' but there were anomalies in his technique. 
Facing me across a rough-hewn table in a dingy, cramped room at the rear of the jail complex, he took few notes and seemed to forget, or ignore, much that I told him. 
He was generally pleasant, even apologetic. 
''It is a legacy of the Cultural Revolution,'' he said when I complained of the bullying manner of one of his juniors. 
''The younger generation does not have any manners.''
When I rejected his offer of a peach during one post-midnight session, saying it seemed inappropriate for us to be friendly when I was being held on a capital charge, he flashed a smile. 
''No, no, not so serious, not so serious,'' he said. 
''We have many penalties for spying. 
For example, 20 years in prison. 
Do not fear to be shot.''
Under China's travel law, the three of us could have been punished with a warning or a fine. 
But because the State Security Bureau insisted throughout that the issue was not unauthorized travel, but espionage, we had to wonder whether we had inadvertently approached a sensitive military installation. 
If so, it was in innocence.
I challenged General Zhang to tell me what he meant by the ''classified military objects'' we were supposed to have photographed. 
''Think hard,'' he said. 
''did you not photograph a bridge?''
I remembered that we had - a 1,000-year-old marble structure in a village in southern Shaanxi. 
I had snapped Mr. McNally on the bridge, seated on the motorcycle and surrounded by local children. 
''Ah ha,'' the general said. 
''So you admit photographing strategic installations.''
In Beijing, some weeks later, Foreign Ministry officials told colleagues of mine privately that they opposed my arrest and subsequent expulsion but had been overruled by the security apparatus. 
The officials hinted that the affair was linked in some way to other problems that have dogged the Ministry of State Security in the last year, including the spying conviction of one of its agents, Larry Wu-Tai Chin, in a United States court, and the defection of a senior official of the ministry, Yu Zhenshan, to the United States.
Among United States and British diplomats involved in securing my release, there was a feeling that internal politics had played at least some part in the affair. 
One theory was that the State Security Ministry, institutionally wary of foreigners, had seized an opportunity to show how dangerous the broadening contacts with outsiders can be - and in so doing, to strike a blow against the policy of the ''open door.''
Whatever the motive, Mr. Zhang, our Chinese companion, who had been arrested 16 hours before me, briefly released, then re-arrested, was kept in jail for two months. 
When he was finally released, it was on the face-saving basis that his four years as a student in the United States had ''disoriented him'' and made him susceptible to the wiles of foreigners. 
Mr. McNally, who was in Hong Kong at the time of the arrests, canceled plans to return to Beijing.
At breakfast time on the sixth day of my imprisonment, one of General Zhang's aides came bounding up the stairs with a bag containing my clothes. 
I was given five minutes to dress and was then taken to the prison reception room. 
Inside, another officer awaited me with a written statement and a videocamera crew. 
The officer told me to stand at attention. 
I refused.
''John Fisher Burns, correspondent of The New York Times, born 1944, citizen of Great Britain, male, resident in Beijing, the State Security Bureau has investigated your activities. 
You have broken into restricted military areas and committed espionage. 
The facts are clear and proven. 
You have endangered the security of the People's Republic of China. 
You are ordered deported.''
I was marched outside to a security wagon. 
It passed slowly out of the steel gates, threaded its way through the early morning crush of bicyclists and onto the airport road. 
I gazed through the tinted windows at roadside vegetable sellers, horse-drawn carts and mud-walled homes, the commonplaces of everyday Chinese life that I might never see again. 
The wagon parked on the airport tarmac, beside a Chinese airliner.
A uniformed officer asked me to sign for my passport, handed me a ticket and a boarding card, and ordered me up the service stairs onto the covered ramp leading to the aircraft's forward door. 
The officer turned on his heel and descended the way he had come. 
I glanced at the ticket. 
The destination was Hong Kong.
