While the modern world has adopted a modified Gregorian calendar, introduced in 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII, many cultures retain ancient religious calendars. 
In the beginning, these were based on phases of the moon or other astronomical aspects. 
Life itself depended on the shifting sky, which told you when to plant and when to harvest, and so calendars took on spiritual significance.
''Calendars are arbitrary, and there are a wide variety,'' says William Gutsch, chairman of the American Museum-Hayden Planetarium in New York. 
''Lunar calendars can run from full moon to full moon or new moon to new moon. 
Since you get one each lunar month, you can start the year anywhere you want.''
Some solar calendars, too, begin when the sun is in a particular position, such as at the vernal or autumnal equinox, when it is directly over the equator. 
Through history, Mr. Gutsch says, calendars have became ''more and more out of whack versus the real calendar, which is the motions of objects through the heavens.''
Whatever its derivations or date, visitors can herald the New Year in a number of places. 
Following is a sampling.
Â 
JAPAN
Date Jan. 
1
Â 
Services The ancient New Year, in February, was pegged to spring (in early Japan, toshi, the word for year, was synonymous with the word for rice). 
Today Jan. 
1 is the national holiday and most significant in Japan. 
Many businesses close Dec. 
28 to Jan. 
4. Shops and restaurants usually reopen Jan. 
2, known as Hatsu-Ni, the first delivery day. 
Decorations come down Jan. 
7. During the holidays, transportation and hotels are tightly booked due to the mass exodus first from the city to the country and then in the opposite direction. 
Because of the Emperor's illness, some celebrations may be canceled.
Â 
Highlights At midnight New Year's Eve, Hatsu-Mode, the year's first visit to the shrine, begins. 
The best place to see traditional kimonos is the first three days of the year at the Meiji Shrine in Tokyo, the Daishi Temple in Kawasaki and at Shinshoji, a Buddhist temple in Narita. 
For the Gion Okera Festival, at the Yasaka-jinja Shrine in Kyoto, a sacred fire of the herb okera is lighted. 
Through the early hours of Jan. 
1, visitors take home a flame kindled on a short rope. 
Used to cook the first meal of the year, the fire is believed to prevent illness.
On Jan. 
2 the Emperor and Crown Prince usually make five appearances between 10 A.M. and 1 P.M. on the balcony of the Imperial Palace in Tokyo. 
Inner grounds are open to the public only on this day and the Emperor's birthday. 
The appearance may not take place this year.
At 1 P.M. Jan. 3, at the Yasaka-jinja Shrine in Kyoto, visitors can watch a traditional New Year's card game, karuta-hajime, played in costumes of ancient nobility. 
Kemari, a soccerlike sport favored by 10th-century aristocrats, is played 2 P.M. Jan. 4 at the Shimogamo-jinja Shrine in Kyoto.
On Jan. 
6, for the New Year's Parade of Firemen, Tokyo's firefighters perform acrobatics on bamboo ladder tops along Chuo-dori in Harumi.
Â 
CHINA
Date Feb. 
6
Â 
The New Year, a weeklong family festival of feasting and rituals, is the most important event of the Chinese lunar calendar. 
Sixty-year spans are divided into five 12-year cycles based on wild, domestic and mythical beasts; this year (the 4,687th of the Chinese calendar) hails out the dragon and in the snake.
The Lantern Festival, which falls on the 15th day of the first lunar month, ends the holiday. 
In ancient times, Chinese bore torches by which to see celestial spirits flying by the light of the first moon. 
Today the holiday is marked by colorful lantern processions and displays.
Â 
Services Public facilities, such as restaurants, remain open.
Â 
Highlights The daylong New Year's fair at Ditan Park, off Andingmen Road in northeast Beijing, features traditional acrobats, stiltwalkers and martial artists, with handicrafts and sweet dumplings for sale. 
To the south, in Dragon Lake Park, activities include stiltwalking, lion and dragon dancers, acrobats dressed in paper or cloth boats and dancing monkeys and horses. 
Lanterns light up the People's Cultural Palace near Tian An Men Square.
Â 
TAIWAN
Date Feb. 
6
Â 
Services Most businesses are closed until the third day, after which many shops reopen with a firecracker lighted to mark the occasion. 
Some, however, may be shuttered until Feb. 
11. Yuan Shiao, rice-flour dumplings symbolizing the first full moon of the lunar year, are available throughout the country.
Â 
Highlights The holiday's religious traditions can be viewed on New Year's Day at the Lungshan Temple on Kwang-Chou Street. 
Dragon and lion dances are held throughout the holiday in front of the Presidential Palace and the Chiang Kai-shek and Sun Yat-sen memorial halls.
The evening of the Lantern Festival, Feb. 
20, a procession is held at the Lungshan Temple. 
Major lantern displays can also be seen at the Cheng Huang Temple at Hsinchu on the northwest coast and at the Chao Tien Temple at Peikang in west-central Taiwan.
In Yen-Sheui, between Tainan and Peikang in southern Taiwan, about 200,000 people converge for the Lantern Festival. 
From 6 P.M. to 3 A.M. up to 20,000 rockets are ignited in enclosures in the shape of animals of the Chinese Zodiac and spew out indiscriminately. 
Goggles and helmets are recommended.

HONG KONG
Date Feb. 
6
Â 
Services Some businesses close for three days (the national holiday runs until Feb. 
8 this year), though tourist facilities remain open.
Since styled hair is expected for the holiday, salon and barber shop prices in Hong Kong and Taiwan double. 
Some shops refuse orders for custom-made clothes up to a week before the holiday. 
Firecrackers are illegal.
Â 
Highlights Shopping areas are decorated with banners and lights. 
Lion and dragon dances usually begin at 11:30 A.M. New Year's Day in Kowloon, at the Star Ferry Concourse, and proceed to the Ocean Terminal shopping center. 
Fireworks light up the harbor, usually on the second day of the New Year.
Winter flower markets, with peach and plum blossoms and chrysanthemums, crop up in city parks, the most popular being Victoria Park in Causeway Bay on Hong Kong Island, which begins Feb. 
4. The park is at its busiest midnight to 3 A.M. New Year's Eve.
The Lantern Festival, in Hong Kong called Chinese Valentine's Day, is Feb. 
20, with carnivals and lantern displays in Victoria Park and Tiger Balm Garden, both in Causeway Bay.
Traditional lanterns appear on market stalls and decorate homes, restaurants and temples.

SINGAPORE
Date Feb. 
6
Â 
Services The first two days are official holidays, with banks and businesses closed. 
Firecrackers are banned. 
Highlights Chinatown is the first area to be decorated and lit up; lights stay on from Jan. 
21 to Feb. 
20. The Hong Bao Special (Hong Bao refers to the red packets containing lucky money) is tentatively set for Jan. 
30, with floats and lighted boats on the Singapore River and a night market on the river bank. 
Cultural shows are planned for Feb. 
5 or 6 at Hong Kim Park in Chinatown.
Beginning at 9 A.M. Feb. 12, the Chingay procession proceeds from Scotts and Orchard Road to the Dhoby Ghaut Mass Rapid Transit station. 
The parade features decorated floats with acrobats, martial artists and stiltwalkers.

BALI
Date March 9
Â 
Services The Hindu solar calendar begins with Nyepi (quiet) New Year (there is also a 210-day Balinese calendar). 
Transportation to and from Ngurah Rai Airport and other essential services in Denpasar operate, and luxury resorts accommodate guests. 
Otherwise, everything is closed on New Year's Day.
Â 
Highlights The Melis ceremony, in which temple implements are cleansed, begins three days before the New Year, peaking on New Year's Eve. 
Informal processions can be seen headed for the beach or holy springs. 
In Ubud, processions lead to the Gunung Lebah Temple, at the Campuhan River. 
Ogoh-ogoh (demon) parades are at nightfall New Year's Eve in most communities, the largest in Denpasar. 
The parade is followed by 24 hours of quiet.
Â 
THAILAND
Date April 13
Â 
Services April 13 is the fixed date for Songkran, which is also marked in Laos, Kampuchea and Burma. 
As a national holiday, businesses are closed. 
Hotel reservations are necessary in the city of Chiang Mai.
Â 
Highlights When the plains were flooded during the rainy season in Siam, fish were trapped in ebbing pools. 
Farmers kept the fish until Songkran, when they were released into canals to gain spiritual merit, an essential element of a Thai festival. 
Today, birds and fish are bought in markets, then released.
The biggest festivals are in Phra Pradaeng, at the mouth of the Chao Phraya River, an hour's drive south of Bangkok, and in Chiang Mai. 
In Phra Pradaeng, also known as Paklat, young women of Mon origin parade with fishbowls to the river, where the fish are released. 
In Chiang Mai, Thais wade into the city's river, scooping up water in a free-for-all. 
Chiang Mai's festival runs April 12 to 14; for Songkran, the roads are alive with dancers, bands and floats, at the center of which is the city's favorite celebrity, a beauty-contest winner. 
This one is Nang Songkran (Queen of the Water).
As part of the celebration pedestrians are often showered with water by teen-agers passing in open trucks. 
It's meant in the spirit of fun, and Western tourists are not excluded.
Â 
NEPAL
Date April 13
Â 
Services Calendars, published in spring at the beginning of the Nepalese solar year, contain three different dates - solar, Gregorian and lunar (an extra month is added to the lunar calendar every three or four years, making 13 months for that year). 
There are many New Years in Nepal, including ones for the Newar calendar in the fall and Tibetan in February. 
The solar New Year (Nawabarsa) is a national holiday, with businesses closed. 
Festivals begin when the priest determines the most auspicious moment. 
Bhaktapur, nine miles east of Katmandu, can be reached by local bus, which run continuously after festivities end.
Â 
Highlights Bisket Jatra, the most important New Year festival in the Katmandu Valley, is held only in Bhaktapur, also known as Bhadgaon. 
Chariots of the gods are pulled through town four days before Nawabarsa and on Nawabarsa itself. 
Nights in between, dancers costumed to represent divinities perform by torchlight. 
A ceremonial pole is raised Nawabarsa eve and drops on Nawabarsa. 
Four days later, the pottery-making caste of Bhaktapur raises a smaller lingum.
Two miles west of Bhaktapur, the village of Thimi gathers all the deities, with the honored guest Bal Kumari, a consort of Lord Bhairab. 
Throughout the day and night of Nawabarsa, her pagoda temple is thronged with musicians and worshipers, holding aloft oil torches. 
At dawn on the second day of the new year, this year April 14, men from each village division shoulder canopied palanquins, with the idols within. 
A long-fringed umbrella whirls over each of the 32 khats, which converge at Bal Kumari's temple. 
Men throw red powder over everyone (blood is the favored color of mother goddesses). 
A parade is then held for the god Ganesh, with hundreds of men covered in red powder wielding torches.

file: A SPACE INVADER IN CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
I can't sleep. 
My mind's abuzz with the sound of bicycle bells - 1.2 billion of them. 
Partly I'm jet-lagging, but it's more than that: It's a question someone asked me a few hours ago when I got home from a month in the off-the-beaten province of Shandong, China - that peninsula sticking out like a hitchhiker's thumb through the Yellow Sea toward Korea. 
The question was whether I ever felt at home in China, and by it the questioner meant: Was there ever a moment when I felt my sensibility fused with the Chinese people, when we were brethren despite our astonishing barriers?
Briiiing, briiiing!
It being my third trip there in a year, I expected to feel pretty cozy. 
But things were both more and less exotic right from the gong: On the flight over the four of us in our group, sole Caucasians aboard, got to watch the eternally bellicose Sylvester Stallone, in ''First Blood,'' relive such terrifying flashes of Viet-era torture at the hands of inscrutably sadistic Orientals that our Chinese plane-mates (benign-looking, in that underbaked way people have at 30,000 feet) felt compelled to nod and send us bland reassuring smiles. 
The notion kept hitting me over the head that I was not only hobnobbing with former enemies but hobnobbing with them on the other side of the planet - it may as well have been the dark side of the moon.
I'm not talking about Shanghai, where in the last 12 months all sorts of cross-communications have evolved, making commonplace the sight of Chinese in Cardin jackets craning at stock quotations amid the ubiquitous year-round Christmas lights (a symptom of post-Mao jollity), and where it's possible to lounge in the splendor of your hotel room watching a TV rerun of ''Gone With the Wind.''
Nor am I talking about Peking, where there are now helicopter rides at the Ming Tombs, the Forbidden Palace has become Bullhorn City, with the inflections of central Texas seeming to fill the place, and the dusty junk store of yesterday is today's neon-flashing Antique Mall.
In both cities giant strides have been taken in the preparation of coffee, which is now distinguishable from ox broth; in towels, which are clean; in salad dressing, which is fresh. 
There's been a great leap forward in the proliferation of plastic laundry bags, pay toilets and the likelihood of bumping into people like Andy Young or Rod Stewart - just as in any other fancy world center. 
To be sure, you still feel the old totalitarianism in these places, when after a kung fu match, for instance, the entire stadium rises to leave in lock step. 
But generally you sense that the world's homogenization is furthered here. 
(Which is sad, in a way - China has been one of the last places on earth where you could still witness the breathtaking play of sunlight on bamboo without, at the same time, hearing the strains of ''Love Story.''
Two cheers for progress.) But no, I'm talking about the sticks, where Westerners are still regarded as space invaders, when they are regarded at all. 
This is where I spent my month this time, where the few cars drive in darkness and snap on their headlights flashbulb-style every six seconds to bleach the eyes of bicyclists like startled rabbits. 
Where kids swat at bats wheeling in the dusty gloom of remote roads, and there are rows and rows of poplars (''Let there be trees,'' Mao had said, and in these regions the trees had sprung forth); and no more flies as in the old days (''Let there be no flies,'' he'd said, and each peasant had killed 10 a day). 
Where the click of the abacus still mixes with the clack of the taps on everyone's shoes, and no one speaks English: If I picked up the phone, the operator on the other end would panic at one word and hang up. 
Out on the street schoolgirls giggled, babies burst into tears, grown men would catch one glimpse of me and fall off their bicycles. 
It took me three minutes to buy a pair of black slippers in a department store, and by the time the transaction was over I had attracted 200 people to study how I bagged my Topsiders.
For about two weeks, the four of us found ourselves sending each other the thumbs-up signal all the time, the way scuba divers do in potentially perilous situations to show everything's still O.K. 
But about the third week we began to split up to make our peace with the place individually - I went off by myself to mingle with the thin-suited men enplumed in serpentine columns of smoke (the Chinese look as though they learned to smoke watching ancient Belmondo flicks); and listen to a woman tearfully tell me the story of how she and her husband were separated three years during the Cultural Revolution and he traveled clear across China so he could speak with her for 10 minutes at a wintry train station (the Chinese ''Dr. 
Zhivago'' has yet to be written, but it will be a doozy); or put through a call to my two kids from my hotel room one evening before they were leaving for school.
That was nuts: talking to them about Crockett and Tubbs and then going back to the banquet room where another century was quietly taking place, the hot water bottles at each place setting along with the nib pens and ink pots and antimacassars on the chairs. 
There were my Americans without a care in the world, still gobbling down their scorpions and jellyfish and duck's feet and toasting our hosts a little cross-eyed from the maotais but otherwise not noticing how deeply bizarre we'd become. 
It was at that moment that I guessed we'd been made to feel at home. 
But rapport?
Communion?
That didn't happen till I was 1,200 feet above the pine tops in a cable car climbing Mount Tai Shan and busily extrapolating dire thoughts about the state of Chinese mechanics from my observation that no shower spill-off drain I'd yet encountered had been placed closer than completely across the bathroom floor. 
I exchanged eye contact with an old Manchu who was having similar dread. 
We kept contact throughout the eight-minute climb, hanging onto each other's irises for dear life, and when it was over I think if I wasn't his son at least we were nephew and honored uncle. 
(We didn't even look at each other as we climbed out, embarrassed the way close relatives would have been.) And there was one other moment, more brotherly, or generational, when I was homesick in Jinan, the capital of Shandong, and around twilight stumbled onto an amusement park filled with sedately screaming children and their parents, and I began to realize that they were my age; they were the Red Guards all mellowed out as we at home were the student activists of the 60's, all more or less discontentedly quiescent.
They were as tender with their children at the merry-go-round as I was wishing all month I was with mine, and two kids adopted me and waved to me each time they went around, in so loving and sensitive and ceremonial a way that for about 10 minutes I felt like one of the family. 
Of course I stuck out like a sore thumb, but the kids kept waving, the parents kept grinning; something took place in that drab and dusty park and for a moment in the twilight I swear we all felt related. 
We were no longer, remotely, at war.

The fifth annual Asian American International Film Festival opens today at New York University's Schimmel Auditorium with the premiere of a tragic love story made in China, Shui Hua's ''Regret for the Past.''
The festival, which will be held on two successive Friday and Saturday evenings, this weekend and next, is a showcase of works by Asian and Asian-American film makers.
This year the festival, which is sponsored by Asian Cine-Vision in cooperation with N.Y.U.'s School of Cinema Studies, will include two significant vintage works in Asian-American film history: Cecil B. De Mille's 1916 ''The Cheat,'' in which the Japanese-born Sessue Hayakawa established himself as Hollywood's first Asian star, and ''The Dragon Painter,'' a 1924 Hayakawa film.
Also scheduled is the highly acclaimed ''Chan Is Missing,'' directed, produced and in part written by Wayne Wang. 
The film, which concerns itself with Asian identity in the United States, will be shown next Friday.
The fifth annual Asian American International Film Festival opens today at New York University's Schimmel Auditorium with the premiere of a tragic love story made in China, Shui Hua's ''Regret for the Past.''
''We are trying to increase exposure and understanding of Asian and Asian-American films,'' said Michael Chu, the festival coordinator for Asian Cine-Vision, ''and we want to increase the exposure of the film makers.''
Â 
Resettling Refugees
In addition to the 1980 ''Regret for the Past,'' tonight's program includes ''Bittersweet Survival,'' a documentary by Christine Choy and J.T. 
Takagi about the resettlement of Southeast Asian refugees in fishing communities along the Texas Gulf Coast and California's Monterey Bay. 
Also to be shown this evening is ''Chiang Ching: A Dance Journey,'' Lana Pih Jokel's biography of a dancer who went from Hong Kong movies to New York's dance world and, triumphantly, back to China. 
The film was made in New York with added footage from Asia.
Tomorrow night's program is made up of films from India and China. 
''Akriet'' (''Misbegotten''), directed by and starring Amol Palekar, is a film dealing with an actual police investigation of village ritual murders. 
The work was banned in India. 
The other film is ''Return From Silence: China's Revolutionary Writers,'' which was made after the Cultural Revolution. 
Using historical footage and interviews, Chung-wen Shih produced this movie about the Chinese literary figures Cao Yu, Ding Ling and Mao Dun.
Mr. Chu said in an interview that many of the film makers would attend the festival to discuss their work. 
''A prime reason Asians are making films in this country,'' he explained, ''is to destroy stereotypes.''
He cited ''Chan Is Missing,'' now playing commercially at the Cinema Studio 1, as an example of a film that belies the image many non-Asians have of Chinese. 
''That film is the truth of what Chinatown is and what its people are all about,'' he said.
Â 
Experimental Shorts on the Bill
Two short experimental films will accompany ''Chan Is Missing'' next Friday: ''Commercial Eruption'' and ''School of Hard Knocks,'' both by Yoshiko Chuma, a Japanese woman who lives in New York. 
The first is a parody of television commercials. 
The second is described as an exploration of spatial and visual relationships. 
''Taiko: The Music of the Japanese Drums,'' by David Kimura, completes the evening's program.
Two early Hayakawa films will be shown on the festival's final night, Saturday, June 26. 
Hayakawa, who died at the age of 83 in Tokyo nine years ago, made more than 130 films and was nominated for an Academy Award for his role as the Japanese prison camp commander in ''Bridge on the River Kwai'' in 1958.
The festival sponsor, Asian Cine-Vision, with headquarters at 32 East Broadway, produces a nightly show in Chinese on Manhattan Cable television from 8 to 9, runs a workshop to instruct Chinatown residents in video-production techniques and publishes Bridge, a magazine primarily devoted to the arts.
The festival site, Schimmel Auditorium, is in Tisch Hall, 40 West Fourth Street. 
Programs begin at 7 P.M, with admission by a $3 donation.

file: A SWIRL OF CELEBRATIONS SWEEPS INTO CHINATOWN.txt
text:
ï»¿
FOR the rest of New York, winter, with snowy white trimmings, is still the order of the day, but in Chinatown, resplendent in rich reds and golds, it is the first weekend of the Spring Festival. 
Yesterday, the festival - which is the name for this celebratory season of the Chinese New Year - reached a climax with the customary frenzied Chinatown greeting of the first day of the year, but that is not the end of this joyous event.
Chinatown will continue to be a festival enclave for the remaining two weeks in which this most impressive of the 30 holidays on the Chinese calendar is observed. 
The welcome to the Year of the Rabbit still colors the streets of this ever-expanding and booming Lower East Side area of Chinese settlement. 
A walk along the crowded sidewalks, through Canal Street, down Mott Street, up the Bowery and East Broadway, brings to the discerning eye symbols of the celebration. 
In the buildings along the way, in those that house Chinatown institutions, there are music and dance programs this weekend that will make the assiduous stroller witness to even more of the New Year spirit.
Chinatown, holiday or not, is always an exciting walk-through, and it is even more so during these several weeks. 
As with most Where to eat in Chinatown, page C17. named areas in New York, Chinatown represents not so much geography as a texture of neighborhood, and nowadays East Side Chinatown extends north from Worth Street to Grand Street. 
One may approach Chinatown from any direction and become enmeshed in the spirit of the season, although it may be difficult at times to say whether the involvement is with the festival or the normally frantic swirl of everyday Chinatown. 
Chinese New Year is a time for home celebration, feasting and visiting, but the tradition of public performance has the holiday spilling over into streets and stores.
Canal Street, at the longitude of Centre Street, is a titillating point from which to start a walk eastward. 
The sidewalks are brimming with goods for sale, on building-side and on curbside. 
Live fish are a sidewalk-stall staple at all times, more so at New Year's. 
The Chinese word for fish, yu, is punningly akin to the word for abundance, and it is therefore lucky to have on the table when a year's outlook is in the programming stage; those without money to buy a real fish often have a symbolic wooden one at their hope-laden tables. 
Oranges are in profusion, a golden-hued fruit that hints of golden good fortune. 
Peanuts, pyramided in pretty gift-wrap packages, are the symbol of fertility. 
Dates and lotus seeds and special cakes are in demand, each of them sought for reasons of happy happenstance in nomenclature rather than for nutritional attraction. 
As the chef Kin Jing Mark, who teaches cuisine at the uptown China Institute in America, puts it: ''At New Year's, you don't eat the taste, you eat the meaning.''
Not everything on Canal Street is for the holiday. 
Much that meets the eye on these days meets the eye every day, from the splash of oddly shaped vegetables to the sidewalk Senegalese who was selling knives in what appeared to be a hopeless confusion of French and Cantonese. 
But at the southeast corner of Canal and Mulberry Streets, the florid front of a small store presents a vivid tableau to the passer-by. 
The wares on display are almost entirely for the New Year trade. 
Gold-colored objects, birds, pagodas and such are suspended from small red streamers, embodying two primary holiday colors. 
Some are little bells, others are merely eye-catchers, designed to do so from a friendly wall.
In an earthern dish, there are what appear to be bulbs, of the tulip type familiar to most of us. 
A knowledgeable onlooker allowed that they were sui xien, roots popular to take home at New Year's because they symbolize growth and ultimately sprout into angel-like yellow flowers. 
As with any folklore, interpretations are infinite, and one may make a choice of what is pure fact or charming fiction.
Â 
Joining in the Customs
A right turn onto Mott Street leads into what is Chinatown's main stem. 
Perhaps the bitter battlefield aroma of yesterday's firecracker orgy, which accompanied the fabled lion dance, still hovers over the pavement. 
The Year of the Rabbit is very much in evidence on this narrow, singularly Chinese New York thoroughfare that caters to visitor and inhabitant alike. 
At No. 74A Mott, the window of the Good Field Trading Company is ablaze with red-decor felicitations. 
Two of them, in Chinese, wish prosperity in business - whether on the four seas or, alternatively, on the three rivers. 
Chinese is a culture that bunches things, whether vices or virtues, advantages or disadvantages, in numbered slogans.
Inside, customers are buying hung bao, the little red envelopes, sold in packets, into which gift money, or perhaps certificates, are inserted before being passed on to children. 
There are hundreds of Chinese New Year's cards on sale and, if you want to take up the custom next year, this might be a choice time for a good buy. 
The man behind the counter said that New Year's greetings and general customs remain the same, although there are more regional variations noted these days with the influx of other Chinese into the basically Cantonese ingredient of Chinatown, whose largest element hails from the Taishan district.
Several doors south, at 62 Mott Street, is the home of the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association, Chinatown's most venerable community institution and operator of a school that trains American-born generations in the ways of the forefathers.
''Every year the celebration is about the same,'' observed Joseph P. C. Mei, president of the association, which sponsors some of the holiday's most public events. 
''This is a time, a cultural thing, for the benefit of all Chinese people, no matter what religion - I'm Christian, myself -they all come to celebrate.''
This weekend, the association's premises will be working overtime on celebrating with a schedule of events free and open to the public, almost all in the auditorium. 
The programs should more than slake a thirst for the music, song and dance of Old China. 
Today at 2:30 P.M., the New York Chinese School is to perform Chinese folk dance and modern songs and offer other entertainment. 
At 7 P.M., Project Open Door of the Chinatown Planning Council and the Chinese Music Club fill the house with Chinese melody.
Tomorrow at 2:30 P.M., that very specialized form of music, Chinese opera, is to take the platform under the ministrations of the Chinese Cultural and Recreation Association of New York. 
From 7 to 9 P.M., the Hsing Yin Chorus of New York raises its voice in song for the season. 
On Sunday at noon, the New York Chinese School's drum and bugle corps is parade on Mott, to be followed at 2 P.M. by the New York Institute of Cantonese program of Chinese music, southern style - southern Chinese, that is. 
At 7 P.M., the Kou-Lien Musical Association tops off the weekend with a final round of Chinese music.
Â 
The Felicitous Homonym
The eye of the visitor threading his way through Chinatown's network of restaurants, groceries, bakeries and gift shops, on Mott Street or any other, may spot pastries of various composition, such as the niangao, a rice cake whose name could also be confused with a phrase meaning ''exalted year.''
For sale, and going like hot cakes, are dumplings that also are filled with felicitous homonym significance.
Continuing on Mott Street, one can make a left U-turn onto the Bowery, where it widens into Chatham Square, with its statue of Confucius and monument to Chinatown's veterans of American wars. 
At 26 Bowery, in an undistinguished walk-up building opposite the southern end of the Confucius Plaza complex, is the Asian Arts Institute and the home of the Asian-American Dance Theater. 
Its quarters, up two steep flights, are dedicated to promoting dance and visual arts, contemporary often linked to traditional.
Tomorrow at 8 P.M. and again on Sunday at 3 P.M., the dance group enters the third season of a series that bears the distinctly un-Chinese double-entendre title of ''D'Asia Vu.''
The program of New Year's celebration will fill the small hall with a sword dance and a contemporary work performed by Kuang-yu Fong, schooled in Peking Opera. 
There is also to be Bell Yung playing Chinese classical music on the gugin, a seven-stringed zither, and the Chinese Music and Arts Hai Yuen Choir performing folk songs. 
All this against a backdrop of an art installation by an artist named Kwok. 
Admission: $7. 
Reservations: 233-2154, 233-8660.
Â 
Where Cultures Meet
If legs and spirit are willing, the pedestrian can cross Chatham Square and continue north along East Broadway, past the Chinatown branch of the New York Public Library, which is just beyond Catherine Street, and under the Manhattan Bridge, which hovers over the venerable Sin Sun movie house. 
East Broadway leads to Seward Park, where the old Jewish influence is still evident even as the tide of Chinatown flows around it. 
East of the park is the old Jewish Daily Forward building, now home to a Chinese organization. 
At Grand Street, turn left, for a walk of several blocks to the Henry Street Settlement Arts for Living Center, at 466 Grand, near Clinton Street, an institution that encapsulates the many cultures, including Hispanic, black, Chinese and Jewish, that flourish in these parts. 
Sunday afternoon belongs, appropriately, to the Chinese. 
At 1 and 3:30 P.M., two groups, Music from China and the Young People's Chinese Cultural Center, join in concert, traditional style.
In the center's modern hall, Music From China's 10 musicians are to join the other organization's 30 dancers, featuring community artists and visiting professionals from China representing regional companies and academies in Beijing, Shanghai and Tianjin. 
Among the highlights: excerpts from the modern Chinese ballet of the classic tale ''Dream of the Red Chamber'' and an eight-woman saber-sword dance choreographed by Pei-pei Gu of the Shanghai Dance Drama Company, as well as pipa solos by Tang Liang-xing, a virtuoso of this Chinese lute.
Admission at the door: $7; in advance, $5; over-65's and students, $3. 
Information: 962-5698.
Â 
An Island of Quiet
To complete the grand tour in an ambiance of quiet contemplation that contrasts with all of the celebratory turmoil, one might look in at one of Chinatown's traditional Buddhist sanctuaries. 
It is customary for Chinese who grew up in the Buddhist tradition to pray at temples during this holiday. 
Chinatown has several temple-like institutions, some geared for visits by other than believers, such as the one on Mott Street north of the Community Center and others squirreled away on side-street second floors. 
There is a particular sense of peace that pervades the ground-floor American Society of Buddhist Studies at 214 Centre Street, two blocks north of Canal Street, which can be reached from the northern boundary of Grand by walking west, past the Bowery, through Little Italy, and then turning south at Centre.
This is not a temple, a full temple, a shaven-headed monk explained through a translator, but for the visitor it might well be. 
It is a high-ceilinged spacious room dominated by a large golden Buddha. 
Worshipers, who come and go during the day, kneel on cushions in a milieu of red hangings, of walls lined with religious statues, of flowers, of incense and, above all, of a profound hush that contrasts with the pushy world at the door.
''It is not a religious day,'' the monk said, ''but people come to pray, for good luck and for peace. 
Some people don't eat meat for the whole month of the New Year celebration, some eat vegetables only maybe for a day or two. 
If you eat vegetables, it means that you didn't kill life, and that is good.''
Â 
An Uptown Briefing
Actually, the ideal briefing to brace oneself for the sights and sounds of Chinese New Year is to be found far uptown from Chinatown in an exhibition in the tasteful and small gallery of the China Institute in America, in a town house at 125 East 65th Street (744-8181). 
The show, sponsored by the institute's Women's Association, takes note of the usual effigy of the kitchen god who has watched the family's conduct all year and will have its godly lips smeared with honey before being sent off in a blaze of fire to the Jade Emperor. 
Hours are 10 A.M. to 5 P.M. Mondays to Fridays; 11 A.M. to 5 P.M. Saturdays and 2 to 5 P.M. Sundays; admission is $1. 
The exhibition runs through Feb. 
15.
There are carvings of food and feasting, examples of red gift envelopes (with Hong Kong coins), sets of games and informative displays, among them one that describes each of the 12 animals of the lunar calendar. 
Those born in the Year of the Rabbit are considered singularly lucky in money matters, are said to make good companions and are caring and sensitive and most compatible with people who entered the world in the Years of the Snake, the Monkey and the Horse. 
Year of the Rabbit people include Confucius, Martin Luther, Albert Einstein, Queen Victoria and Bob Hope. 
Rabbit people are also lively, full of movement and keep escape routes open, according to one Chinese lawyer who cited an old Chinese saying, ''Every rabbit has three dens.''
As you can see, there is more to a Chinese New Year than meets the eye or the mouth.

text:
ï»¿
Chi Zhongguo, the manager of the Yaxin Silk Weaving Factory, proudly showed off a copy of ''a very famous oil painting'' that his plant had started mass-producing for the American market.
There, in luminous hues more vivid than Leonardo da Vinci's original, was ''The Last Supper,'' being recreated on mechanized looms on 100,000 synthetic velveteen tapestries in a choice of large or small sizes.
The order, from an American importer, is a different one for the Yaxin factory: Eighty percent of its production consists of disposable artificial silk prayer rugs for Moslems, mostly in the Middle East. 
The plant turns out 3 million prayer rugs a year now, Mr. Chi said, virtually all for export.
Profile of Yaxin Silk Weaving Factory in China, which is currently producing tapestry of Leonardo da Vinci's "The Last Supper" for US marketFormer Elegance
When the factory opened as a workshop in 1954, it specialized in elegant yun jin, or cloud-fabric silk brocade, of a quality for which this eastern Chinese city was long renowned. 
It still makes a bit of the gold-threaded fabric for ethnic markets in Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang.
But in a kind of Gresham's Law of weaving, synthetic, machine-woven fabrics have been replacing the silk brocades that were painstakingly hand-loomed. 
As Mr. Chi explained, ''All the old-fashioned looms are now in the countryside because they are not used for production anymore.''
Certainly, no one who has seen the graceful ceramics and delicately patterned material of traditional Chinese design could accuse the Chinese of a lack of taste. 
Even Chinese toys can be found in stores today of a sturdy tin construction that went out in the West with World War II.
Â 
Competing With Hong Kong
But as Chinese industry develops export markets, it finds that its low labor costs let it compete in areas that Hong Kong and Taiwan have dominated with cheaply produced goods.
For example, having found that Westerners find pandas cuddly, Chinese manufacturers have been using the furry black-and-white animal as bait for everything from bamboo screens and bathroom rugs to Christmas tree lights. 
On a more traditional note, a procession of jolly plastic Santa Clauses has been making its way out of the industrial depths of China in time for the Christmas season, which the Chinese do not celebrate.
The Yaxin factory, having moved almost entirely to synthetics, still makes traditional Chinese tapestry scenes such as the pine trees and cranes that symbolize longevity. 
These go mostly to the Japanese market, but in modest quantity.
Â 
Shift to Prayer Rugs
The plant, which exports almost everything it makes, got into the prayer rug business in 1966. 
As output increased, the labor force grew to 1,700, compared with only 60 when it was making brocade in 1954.
By working around the clock on three shifts, the plant now nets 4 million yuan, or nearly $2.4 million, in annual profits, which is impressive by Chinese standards. 
The prayer rugs earned an award as an outstanding product from the Chinese Ministry of Light Industry two years ago.
Mr. Chi said that no Moslems advised the factory on the rugs, which were copied from a pattern supplied by a customer. 
Nor do any appear to go to the estimated 10 million Moslems that live in China; they are only for export.
Â 
Market of 400 Million
''We don't have a clear idea of the population of Moslems,'' Mr. Chi said of his export market. 
''Some say about 400 million. 
But there is a big demand for rugs like this. 
All Moslem people over 16 should have at least one of these.''
Other estimates put the number of Moslems worldwide somewhat higher. 
As part of the Five Pillars of Islam, devout Moslems are enjoined to pray five times a day.
Mr. Chi is a good enough businessman to recognize a market when he sees one. 
''When the rugs get dirty, they throw it away and get another one, like Chinese used to do with towels,'' he explained.
Though China competes with a dozen or so other countries, some Moslem, in making prayer rugs, Mr. Chi insisted that his were better because they had a high-quality cotton backing and an attractive glossy, silk-like pile.
The factory would manufacture more but the chemical fiber thread must be imported, generally from Japan. 
''We're facing a shortage of artificial silk because some people abroad say its production causes pollution,'' Mr. Chi said.
Â 
Exports Through Government
The products themselves are actually ordered and sold through China's foreign trade corporations. 
The prayer rugs, Mr. Chi said, cost about $4.20 apiece to make and are sold to the Government for about $5.40. 
The Government sells them to the importer at a higher wholesale price.
While ''The Last Supper'' is more expensive because of its size and many colors - the large model costs about $15 to make - Mr. Chi said that he would welcome more such Western orders.
''The prayer rug sells only in Moslem areas,'' Mr. Chi said. 
But there is a wider market in the United States and Canada and European countries for other designs, since everyone enjoys a piece of art.''

text:

DIM SUM, the inviting teahouse canapes of China, have inspired two recent cookbooks by New Jersey residents well versed on the subject. 
Jean Yueh of Summit, a skillful writer and a teacher of Chinese cuisine, has written ''Dim Sum & Chinese One-Dish Meals'' (Irena Chalmers Cookbooks, P.O. 
Box 988, Denton, N.C., $6.95, plus $1 postage).
''The feeling of sensuous well-being and deep satisfaction that dim sum bring'' is cited by Mrs. Yueh as another reason for trying to make these ''dainty morsels stuffed with savory ingredients in a matchless variety of tastes and textures.''
''The majority of the Chinese people still use charcoal for cooking,'' writes Mrs. Yueh, referring to a recent trip to China. 
She then points out how much easier Chinese cooking is ''in a modern American kitchen.''
DIM SUM, the inviting teahouse canapes of China, have inspired two recent cookbooks by New Jersey residents well-versed on the subject.
Her creative and thorough recipes - for use with or without the food processor - persuade us to begin learning. 
(Mrs. Yueh's ''The Great Tastes Of Chinese Cooking'' (Times Books, New York, $14.95; paper title: ''Great Chinese Cooking,'' $7.95) received the R.T. 
French Tastemaker Award. 
Perhaps because, as Mrs. Yueh writes, her cooking philosophy ''combines Western technology with classical Chinese recipes,'' this impressive cookbook should earn the gratitude of cooks of every inclination for its multitude of helpful tips.)
In ''The Dim Sum Book: Classic Recipes From the Chinese Teahouse'' by Eileen Yin-Fei Lo of Montclair (Crown Publishers, New York, $12.95), the author remembers her ''earliest memory of dim sum.''
When she was 4, she writes, her 18-year-old brother, joyful over winning a mah-jongg game, treated her to a visit to a Cantonese teahouse, where they both feasted on ''dim sum, the different and delicious small tea-house foods that we loved so much.''
No wonder, as Miss Lo tells us, that ''the misty rosiness that surrounds the history of tea'' has imbued the term dim sum with implications of romance.
Her exquisite account of the ''wondrous parade'' of filled miniature dumplings, scallion pancakes and half-moons of pastry - the leisurely served fare still offered in many corners of the world - makes dim sum's general definition (''A delight of the heart'') seem especially apt and enticing.
Look for the debut of more delicious foods from other lands to enrich the American menu - like adobo, a spicy stew, and pancit, a noodle dish - says Reynaldo Alejandro, author of ''The Philippine Cookbook'' (Coward-McCann, New York, $17.95).
''Because the Filipino people are in part Malay, Chinese and Spanish,'' explained Mr. Alejandro, a caterer and culinary lecturer, ''our cuisine combines the best elements of their cookery and displays a rich heritage.''
The cookbook's 12 chapters - from appetizer to dessert - include varied and tempting dishes that Mr. Alejandro learned, he writes, in his grandmother's kitchen in the Philippines.
''I was encouraged to write 'The Philippine Cookbook' by the Filipiniana Society of Jersey City, a group of Filipinos and Filipino-Americans active in promoting the Filipino culture in New Jersey,'' the author said.
With this opening challenge - ''I promise you will save between 30 percent and 50 percent off your family's meat bills'' - in ''Emilie Taylor's Inflation Fighter Meat Book'' (Warner Books, New York, $9.95), Mrs. Taylor, who lives in Paramus, instantly gets our attention.
The secret, she writes, is not in purchasing ''overwhelmingly large hunks,'' but in following the meat-buying and cutting guidelines (poultry included) that the ''Inflation Fighter'' clearly and fully illustrates.
If Mrs. Taylor's lessons on avoiding fraud seem especially credible, it's because she is a butcher herself and the daughter of one (her late father owned a public market on Washington Avenue, Bergenfield, for 32 years). 
She also operates Emilie Taylor's Meat School in Paramus.
Starting today, Mrs. Taylor added, a telephone call to the ''meat tip hotline,'' (201) 265-1024, between 9 A.M. and 5 P.M., will yield her tip of the week.
''Who cares whether you take the time to prepare yourself an appetizing meal?
I do,'' writes June Roth in the beginning of ''The On-Your-Own Cookbook'' (Dial, New York, $8.95). 
Mrs. Roth, of Teaneck, is a syndicated columnist and the author of 32 books on food and health.
The book's subtitle, ''Cooking for Yourself by Yourself,'' further explains its message, which makes the work an ideal gift for newcomers to the kitchen. 
Its information includes budgetwise shopping, easy but imaginative recipes and even advice on cleaning up.
Such appetizing dishes are found in ''Living Better With a Special Diet'' (Arco, New York, $12.95; paper, $7.95), also by Mrs. Roth, that it is hard to believe it was written, as the author intended, for people on restricted diets.
''People with digestive problems,'' she says, ''need not despair that they will never eat delicious foods again,'' and her descriptions of individually recommended diets and menu plans, along with lists of foods to omit or permit, include many recipes appealing to the entire family.
A distinguished book, ''Complete Fish and Game Cookery of North America'' (Winchester Press, 220 Old New Brunswick Road, Piscataway, N.J. 
08854, $29.95) by Frances MacIlquham, is especially appropriate for New Jersey readers, according to Charles R. Walther, president of the press and a resident of the Hunterdon County community of Pattenburg.
''Our excellent fishing, especially for shad at this time of year,'' said Mr. Walther, himself a fisherman, ''merits splendid recipes to match the quality of the catch.''
Besides offering instructions for dressing and storing fish and game and putting to use traditional skills like woodfire cooking and smoking, ''Complete Fish and Game Cookery,'' by including accounts of ancient cooking methods, unfolds a fascinating story of how the food preparation affected the social history of North America.
Find your images of homemade meals fashioned out of local produce, or haute cuisine served amid sparkling appointments, springing into reality in the pages of ''Country Inns of America Cookbook,'' (Holt, Rinehart and Winston, New York, $24.95), edited by Robert T. Reid.
This is a collection of ''recipes from America's leading inns,'' and for country inn cooking, New Jersey is represented by: Cheese strata (a souffle), strawberry crepes, deviled crabs and other dishes from the Mainstay Inn in Cape May; eggplant casserole and spoon bread from the Chalfonte Hotel, also in Cape May, and a luncheon buffet and hors d'oeuvres from the Old Mill Inn in Bernardsville.
After a glimpse at the scrumptious illustrations of delectable recipes in ''Country Inns,'' there's good excuse to opt for a visit to such an inn and leave the cooking for another day.

text:
ï»¿
Periodically one has to answer a summons from Hwa-Min Hsu, whose good offices are in Canal Street. 
Mr. Hsu knows practically all there is worth knowing about Chinatown, and so any day he is prepared to hold an inspection is a day of enlightenment, a gift. 
This one turned out to be the afternoon of the Chinese massage.
But first, some lunch and a ruminative discussion of various affairs. 
Mr. Hsu is building a hotel in Chatham Square, the first hotel in Chinatown - but it is too early to go into that, he said. 
Some tea and noodles showed up on the table, then some steamed asparagus, followed by a duck.
The Chinese movie theaters are slowly going under as a result of the popularity of video cassettes - but that is a subject for another time. 
Mr. Hsu slept only three hours the night before, a frequent occurrence for a businessman who deals by telephone with Asia. 
This produces stress and tension, and what reduces stress and tension?
Massage. We have arrived!
Mr. Hsu said that a few years back, change visited the barbershops of his native soil, Taiwan, as well as the mainland. 
Women infiltrated. 
What was more, the women offered massages. 
A man - or a woman, for that matter -could be shorn and kneaded into a stress-free puddle all in one stop. 
''We're not talking about porno massage parlors,'' Mr. Hsu cautioned. 
''No sex. 
This is for pressure, for tension. 
That's the job of the barbershop in China.''
One of these emporiums opened in Chinatown two years ago, and another came along soon after. 
Mr. Hsu is but one of many who are nuts about them. 
Even at $25 an hour, he said, it is a great service for the restaurant workers who stand all day, as well as the garment workers who sew for hours, getting themselves down in the back. 
He himself visits twice a week, sometimes forgetting he ought to get a haircut, too. 
As for the old style, all-male, lightless, basement barbershop-mah-jongg parlor of Chinatown days gone by, well, there are still a dozen around, Mr. Hsu pointed out on his after-lunch walk to modernity but they are mostly frequented by older men.
Up one flight of stairs, practically at the foot of the Brooklyn Bridge, Mr. Hsu entered the Ming Kai Barbershop, all chrome and high tech. 
''The male barbershop looks very sloppy,'' he pointed out. 
''This is decorated.''
He was greeted by several women who seemed to know him well. 
There was piped-in music and for a moment it sounded as if Patti Page had lost her mind, but soon it became clear it was the work of a Shanghai stylist.
''Women are better with massage,'' Mr. Hsu continued. 
''The female always does better than the male, always.''
Mr. Hsu then motioned to a darkened room off the well-lighted barbering room. 
In here were six well-padded reclining chairs and five of them were occupied by Chinese men who lay on their stomachs smoking cigarettes while five women in blue skirts and white blouses walked on their backs in their stocking feet, the women keeping their balance by holding on to chrome bars tracked across the ceiling.
It was just past noon, and Mr. Hsu was going to sit for a shampoo, haircut and a little massage tinkering about the head and shoulders. 
''You go in there,'' he said, insisting that ''you'' have the full treatment, soup to nuts, stem to stern. 
In a bit, a woman who would later become known as No. Seven came over and removed jacket, sweater and shoes and loosened the collar wide enough to let in a Shriner. 
Then she went to work.
This was Chinese acupressure, the fingers working down defined highways on the body. 
The trick is to release chi, or trapped energy. 
They begin at the head and don't miss a spot, down to the toe and fingertips.
Some time later, Mr. Hsu stuck his head in the door and said: ''I have to go. 
You stay. 
It's all taken care of. 
Just tip the girl.''
A good while later, from deep in slumber, there came the sound of unenthusiastic applause, thin clapping, that grew in stages so loud that it took ''you's'' breath away, until he put his hand to his lungs and realized someone was trying to beat the daylights out of his chest. 
A voice, ''Uh, the manager, she want to know how long you want the girl to massage?''
The next image that hove into view would have killed a heart patient. 
The vista was a dozen Chinese women, all leaning in close, only one of whom spoke English. 
No. 7 was wringing her sore hands. 
''You'' got up and scattered every greenback he possessed, like birdseed, gave effusive thanks and wobbled down the stairs to greet the night, shirttails flapping, a necktie so curlicued ''you'' could use it to uncork a new Beaujolais. 
''You'' was embarrassed but incredibly relaxed.

file: AMERICAN DREAM OF CHINESE FAMILY TURNS BITTERSWEET.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Tsoung Shing Coffee Shop - a little bit of China in the center of Queens - is a place of many beginnings. 
It officially opened three years ago, but its roots date back far longer - to the streets of Hong Kong and a man named Ming You, who left his home and pregnant wife to make a fortune in New York.
Mr. You never did make that fortune. 
In fact, it took 19 years before he earned enough money to send for his wife and the daughter he had never seen.
But it is that daughter, 35-year-old Tina Wong, who stands behind the counter these days at the Tsoung Shing - a combination coffee shop and Chinese restaurant where the cornflakes sit alongside the ginger hot sauce and scrambled eggs share plates with the pork fried rice. 
It is the kind of place that will never make a fortune for anyone, but that an entire family calls home.
Article in occasional series "A New Melting Pot" discusses experience of Chinese family in New YorkMore Work, Less Money
Family-run ethnic restaurants like the Tsoung Shing dot the streets of Elmhurst, a section of Queens that is among the city's newest ethnic outposts and where, according to immigration officials, 20,000 immigrants from 110 countries live. 
The restaurant is the kind of establishment where immigrants have struggled for generations.
''Work, work and more work,'' said Tina Wong, who begins her day at 8 A.M. and stays at the shop until well past midnight. 
''Less and less money.''
There are five tables and a counter in the Tsoung Shing Coffee Shop. 
There is never a line. 
But every morning Tina Wong is there, scrubbing the floor, polishing the counter, mixing the tea. 
Jimmy Wong, her 39-year-old husband, is there, too, washing the tables, chopping the onions, dicing the carrots. 
So is Linda Yim, 33, who also does many of these tasks and whose husband has known Mr. Wong since they were children.
Altogether, two sets of grandparents, two daughters, two husbands, one sister, one brother and one 10-year-old grandaughter work, eat and spend most of their time in this small restaurant with its white plastic counter tops and overhanging prints of Shanghai. 
It is an arduous existence that neither Mr. You nor anyone else in this extended family ever thought they would lead in America, a place where they expected life to be easy and wealth to abound.
''I thought America would be a good country, maybe it would be easy to make a living here,'' said Jimmy Wong, who now spends 12 hours a day over three smoldering woks. 
''But it's not so easy. 
Nobody gives you something.''
But so it is. 
The Tsoung Shing is neither gold mine nor stepping stone for this extended family. 
It is nothing more than a means to pay the rent, clothe the children, run the car. 
Although they live four blocks away, their homes are only places to sleep. 
The families eat all their meals at the restaurant. 
The grandchildren play there. 
The parents balance their checkbooks there. 
They have even conducted Thanksgiving Day dinners there under the smiling faces of the painted porcelain Buddhas.
Â 
Try at Free Enterprise
The beginning of the Tsoung Shing in some ways was the day Mr. Wong strung up the red, white and blue flags on the restaurant's outside facade -May 23, 1979 - a day that marked the family's first stab at free enterprise in this country. 
Since that time no one has taken a vacation. 
Those flags, now slightly frayed, still hang.
''We knew we could make it work,'' says Mr. Wong. ''And it has.''
Spend the day at the Tsoung Shing, which loosely translated means fortune and happiness, and the life of the extended immigrant family comes alive: Their responsibilities are shared, but their roles are sharply defined.
First there is Tina Wong, who limits her cooking to cheese omelets and sandwiches. 
All day she stands at the grill behind the counter, ladling the tea, filling the cooler with soda, trying to decipher the English that some other members of the family do not comprehend.
''Is there any salt in here?'' a customer asked the other day, digging into a plate of chop suey. 
''Yes,'' Mrs. Wong replied. 
''Lots of sauce. 
Lots.''
''I didn't want any salt. 
''Next time order the chow mein,'' she said pleasantly. 
''Not so much sauce.''
Linda Yim and Jimmy Wong are the cooks at the Tsoung Shing. 
Their days are spent in the hot, cramped kitchen where Shanghai specialties like orange-flavor beef, crispy fried bass and cold noodles are turned out with remarkable speed. 
She does all the chopping, mixing, dicing, stuffing, blending and scrambling, and he does the frying, basting, steaming, stirring and roasting. 
Mr. Wong also washes the pots.
Mrs. Yim and Mr. Wong are the owners of the Tsoung Shing, and because of this they are the only ones who are paid and allowed to give orders. 
Mrs. Wong, for example, is rarely welcome in the kitchen. 
It is already crowded - something that patrons can see for themselves since it contains the restaurant's only bathroom. 
But, she concedes, she is also not welcome in the kitchen because she does not know how to cook.
The other day, Mrs. Wong walked into the kitchen to help her husband at the height of lunch hour. 
Even when business is slow, things are hectic in this tiny kitchen. 
But when tables are filled, the scene could be plucked from a Charlie Chaplin movie.
This was one of those days. 
Mr. Wong was busy whipping up a portion of hot and sour soup in one wok, steamed dumplings in another and sweet and sour bean curd in a third. 
A plate of cold sesame noodles waited on the counter. 
There were several back orders for eggplant in garlic sauce, shrimp in chili sauce, Shanghai won-ton soup.
Mrs. Wong rushed in and announced that she was going to prepare an order of fried dumplings to go. 
She threw eight dumplings into a skillet and turned up the flames, but before she realized that she had not used enough oil, the dumplings burned. 
Mrs. Wong spent the rest of the afternoon out front, peeling potatoes at one of the restaurant's rear tables.
''I'm tired,'' she said, jumping up to serve tea to a customer.
Â 
Differing Recollections
How Tina Wong met her husband, Jimmy, is another of the Tsoung Shing's many beginnings. 
She says she met him years ago while he was a sailor on a cargo ship in Hong Kong. 
He says he first saw her on a street corner in Brooklyn.
Be that as it may, they were married 11 years ago and now have two children. 
After school, their oldest child, Jeannie, 10, washes dishes, peels the onions, fries the bacon and fills patrons' cups with tea. 
William, 5, stays at home with Mrs. Wong's parents, except when activity at the restaurant becomes so hectic that they are all called in to help.
''I hope business is slow,'' said Jeannie, who was born in the United States and is sometimes taunted by her friends because she cannot stay home to watch television.
When Mrs. Wong is not at the restaurant, she can probably be found somewhere in Chinatown shopping for food, scouring for bargains. 
She makes the trip there from Elmhurst, she says, because the prices are lower.
The other day, Mrs. Wong went to a fish store on Canal Street in Chinatown, where she walked past a tank of live turtles and picked out a collection of live crabs. 
One crab escaped and Mrs. Wong had to chase it across the store. 
She did all this quickly, confidently and with good humor, stopping to haggle over the price of shrimp, then racing three blocks away to pick up 10 pounds of pork.
Over the years Tina Wong has perfected her shopping. 
She knows where to buy the freshest noodles, how to squeeze the tripe, where to get the meatiest, least expensive spareribs. 
But what might particularly inspire awe among even the most exacting bargain hunter is that, when it comes to cucumbers, she makes a special trip to Essex Street on the Lower East Side and Gus's pickles.
''It's cheaper,'' she explains with authority. 
How Linda Yim decided to go into business with Jimmy Wong is yet another of the Tsoung Shing's many beginnings. 
Mr. Wong's godmother is Mrs. Yim's mother-in-law, a complicated connection that began in Shanghai, continued years ago in Hong Kong and ultimately resulted in their cooking together four years ago in a Chinatown restaurant. 
Neither really knew how to cook before that.
Mr. Wong and Mrs. Yim worked in the Chinatown restaurant for about a year. 
One day, Mrs. Yim's husband, David, who works in another restaurant in Queens, spotted an empty storefront at 86-32 Broadway in Elmhurst with all the fixtures needed for a coffee shop. 
The rent was $800 a month and it was near the subway. 
Several weeks later they moved in, leaving virtually everything intact, not even replacing the white plastic chicken that still sits incongruously in the front window.
If the Tsoung Shing were in Chinatown or SoHo, it might become chic. 
The service is friendly and attentive, the food inspired and prices unbelievably low. 
But in Elmhurst - a place that is often a contradictory fusion between a small town and an international metropolis - the Tsoung Ching Coffee Shop gets lost.
Those in the neighborhood who want a real coffee shop usually head to the Greek diner around the corner. 
Those who crave Chinese cuisine prefer places with dragon wallpaper and duck sauce.
No matter. 
The family works hard just the same - the kind of routine that Mr. You established years before when he got his first job as a short-order cook in Brooklyn. 
But unlike Linda Yim and Jimmy Wong, he never needed to master the art or the tedious preparation of Chinese cooking.
''His specialty was steak and hamburgers,'' Mrs. Wong explained. 
''That's better,'' said Jeannie, who prefers everything that is American. 
She said she would take a steak over orange-flavor beef any day.
