text:
ï»¿
SU ZHI and Qu Yongchun usually spend their days teaching advanced classes at the Academy of Chinese Opera in Peking, the central training school in China for performers of the Peking Opera. 
But for the last six weeks, their students have been Americans, in classes and lecture demonstrations held at the Eugene O'Neill Theater Center in Waterford, Conn., and throughout the area.
The two are in the United States in an arrangement worked out by George C. White, president of the O'Neill Center, with the Chinese Theater Association during his trip to Peking last year to direct a Chinese-language production of O'Neill's ''Anna Christie.''
If the notion of a Chinese ''Anna Christie'' is a novel one - and Mr. White may return to Peking next year to direct a Broadway musical in Chinese - the idea of imparting an ancient and complex Eastern theater technique to young Western actors is almost as unusual.
But Miss Su and Mr. Qu are more than master teachers with long experience as Peking Opera acrobats. 
It quickly became apparent in a recent conversation that they were possessed of a vivid sense of humor, practicality and warmth likely to bridge the largest of cultural differences.
Â 
Lecture at Brooklyn Theater
Speaking through an interpreter, Miss Su and Mr. Qu talked last week of their work and their impressions of their American students. 
They were preparing for a lecture-demonstration at the New Theater of Brooklyn, a center for new American theater founded in 1982 and directed by Deborah J. Pope and her associate, Stephen Stettler, who also teaches acting at the O'Neill Center's National Theater Institute.
''The American students have been very clever and very adorable,'' Mr. Qu said. 
''They make us feel very young.''
Miss Su nodded. 
''Perhaps we will cry when we leave,'' she added.
Like Mr. Qu, Miss Su began training in the Peking Opera technique at the age of 10. 
Now 46, she retired from performing in 1964 to begin a career as a teacher of stage-fighting at the Academy. 
Mr. Qu, 52, left the stage last year. 
''I have a 91-year-old mother and there was no one to take care of her,'' he said. 
His wife is an actress who is often on tour. 
''This way, I can go home at lunchtime,'' Mr. Qu explained. 
He grinned. 
''Frankly speaking, I would prefer to be acting. 
But China is still a filial country.''
Â 
Performers Must Specialize
Training for the Peking Opera is rigorous, for in addition to mastering a highly developed, stylized and intricate technique, the performer must specialize in one of many types of characters. 
And within the Peking Opera's specific acting styles there are differences, for example, in the way characters hold out their hands, depending on what age they are.
''The manner of speaking and tone of voice change depending on who the character is and who is addressed,'' Mr. Qu said. 
He imitated a child greeting a father, a father greeting a child, and that same father greeting ''someone he must respect.''
From the young applicants for the first level of training, about 40 or 50 students are chosen annually out of 1,000, a ratio that hasn't changed since Mr. Qu began his studies. 
''It is very competitive,'' he said. 
''You are tested on physique, facial characteristics, voice and acting ability. 
You must study for six years before graduating, and then prepare with advanced training for three years. 
After that, you may call yourself a performer. 
It's difficult. 
George White said that to study Peking Opera requires strength of steel.''
Â 
System of Selection
''It is different from the American system,'' Mr. Qu continued. 
''In China, the student wants to have to do it, but the teachers have to select the students. 
If you are too tall, too thin, too short, too fat, you're out. 
Here, the discipline seems to depend on the student's desire to study.''
To indicate the kind of talent the Academy seeks, Mr. Qu described several final exercises given the youngest applicants. 
''We give them something to act,'' he said. 
He mimed children pretending to grasp a cup of tea. 
The first takes hold of it carefully, the second grabs it clumsily. 
The first child, told to swat an imaginary fly, searches for the insect and hits at it. 
The second lunges immediately. 
''Then if that is O.K., the teacher will do gestures and see how well they follow,'' he said. 
He moved his arms in windmill turns, then imitated arms being thrown stiffly into space. 
The examination concludes with a crucial test on academic subjects.
Applicants for the second, or oldest, level of training must act a scene from the Peking Opera repertory. 
They also are tested on academics and ''politics,'' which Mr. Qu described as ''general social structure and social knowledge.''
The advanced-level exams are as competitive. 
''There are no back doors into the Peking Opera,'' Mr. Qu said.
Â 
'Character Teachers'
Teachers specialize in acrobatics, basic movements such as kicking and bending, floor work, the use of knives and swords, full body movement and ''character teaching,'' which is the most important. 
''It is like a bicycle,'' Mr. Qu said, adding that he and Miss Su are character teachers. 
''Some people make the wheels, some the bars, some the handles. 
But there must be someone to put the whole together.''
Given this high degree of specialization, what were the two able to teach to American acting students with no experience in the Peking Opera style?
''We taught the basic skills,'' Mr. Qu said. 
Method was stressed over theory. 
''Because it was the first time Chinese had come to teach, arrangements were very tight and the students were physically tired,'' Miss Su said.
''In the beginning,'' Mr. Qu said, ''there were some students at the O'Neill Center who thought studying Eastern art didn't make sense in the context of Western theater.''
To make those connections clearer, he said, he would tell his Brooklyn listeners a story. 
''George White took us to Washington, where we met Senator Dodd,'' he said, referring to Christopher J. Dodd, the Connecticut Democrat. 
'' 'Why is your performing different from a movie?'
Senator Dodd asked us. 
'Both are art,' we said. 
'But the techniques are different. 
Movies are closer to daily life. 
The Peking Opera shows ancient life in China. 
It is best compared with Western ballet. 
Does anyone walk on point, spinning around rapidly, in real life?
This is art. 
But film is also real life with art added.'
'' Mr. Qu said that Senator Dodd agreed, and even extended the analogy to politics. 
''His manner of speaking was very artistic,'' Mr. Qu observed. 
''He can also perform.''
And so Mr. Qu and Miss Su taught their American students, whom they will leave early next month, ways to open a door and call someone, to use swords and daggers, and to ride a horse. 
''Now, when they perform things from the past,'' Mr. Qu said, ''they can also use the Peking Opera style.''

file: AN OASIS OF PRIVILIGE IN CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
ORVILLE SCHELL is the author of ''Watch Out for the Foreign Guests!''
(Pantheon).
Each evening a middle-aged woman in a simple print dress sits down at a large grand piano set to one side of the hotel lobby and begins to play Mozart, Beethoven and Chopin from sheet music that is so aged that small pieces of yellowed paper break from the edges and drift down onto the keyboard every time she turns a page.
Hotel guests sit at surrounding tables, the murmur of their voices mixing with the sound of music and ice cubes clinking in glasses.
As dusk begins to fall, the chandeliers come on, and some of the guests begin to move toward the hotel's main restaurant, where they sit down at tables set with crisply ironed cloths and choose between such delicacies as salade de magret de canard au vinaigre framboise ($7), cr eme d'artichauts au caviar et filaments de betterave ($2.50), paillard de veau aux chanterelles ($19.50), paupiettes de sole Montrose sauce Nantua ($15), and a list of wines from Italy and Germany as well as France.
Out in front, where chauffeured limousines await their charges just beyond a large fountain, stands a silent phalanx of common people, staring transfixed through the plate- glass windows at the activity inside the brightly lit hotel lobby.
Orville Schell article on opulent Jianguo Hotel, Peking, China; photos (M)
''At night . . . where in hidden springs of electricity flooded the great dining room with light, it became as it were an immense and wonderful aquarium against whose wall of glass the working population of Balbec, the fishermen and also the tradesmen's families, clustering invisibly in the outer darkness, pressed their faces to watch, gently floating upon the golden eddies within, the luxurious life of its occupants, a thing as extraordinary to the poor as the life to strange fishes and mollusks,'' so wrote Marcel Proust at the turn of the century of the Grand Hotel in Normandy, where he used to summer on the coast with his grandmother.
But the scene unfolding around me here is not Balbec or even France before the Great War. 
It is Peking, the Peoples' Republic of China in 1983, a curious place to find the ghost of Marcel Proust, or even a mutation thereof. 
The hotel is the Jianguo (Build the Nation), the first Western-run inn to open in China in 35 years.
Instead of vacationing French aristocrats taking the sea air, the Jianguo is filled with businessmen, tourists and diplomats. 
And instead of Norman ''fishermen'' and ''tradesmen's families,'' it is Chinese workers and peasants who stare into the Jianguo's aquarium-like interior from outside.
The building itself, a sprawling four-story cream-colored structure, is actually an architectural replica of the Palo Alto Holiday Inn in California. 
It is situated on Jianguo- menwai Boulevard outside what used to be the old city wall before the Communists tore it down to build a highway. 
Its neon signs, eternally energetic fountains, extravagant lighting and California styling make it as noticeable among the frieze of gloomy buildings which flank it as one gleaming gold tooth in a mouth of otherwise neglected dentures.
Standing as it does in front of row upon row of dormitory-like housing for the families of Chinese Foreign Ministry employees (where there are usually not even any operable lights in the hallways), the Jianguo fairly sparkles with seductiveness. 
It is a living advertisement for the outside capitalist world with which the denizens of Peking have just begun to become reacquainted after three decades of socialist isolation.
Compared to the crowded, inefficient and noisy world of urban China, where there is literally no place for family members, lovers or friends to sit in quiet comfort and share a meal or conversation, life in the Jianguo Hotel appears like a fantasy incarnate. 
When one steps through these doors, China ends and another world begins. 
The rooms have wall-to-wall carpeting. 
The matching drapes and bedspreads are made of bright floral print fabric that seems as remote to China as tropical foliage in Greenland. 
The private bathrooms are finished with black and white Chinese marble, one of the few interior effects of local origin. 
The king-size beds are all imported from the United States. 
Every room has a color television set, its own air conditioner, a push-button phone and an American-style lamp hanging down from the ceiling on the end of a gold chain. 
Sliding doors open out onto little balconies which overlook an interior court where more fountains bubble away in reflecting pools.
Downstairs, one can dine on quite good Continental cuisine in a candle-lit restaurant staffed with a headwaiter in a dinner jacket, swim in an indoor pool, dance until 2 A.M. in a fully outfitted disco, imbibe a drink at a Western-style bar, knowing that a German and five Swiss hotel managers from the Peninsula Group (of the Peninsula Hotel fame in Hong Kong, which has contracted to run the Jianguo for 10 ears) hold a steady helm. 
No wonder the occupancy rate of the hotel has recently been 99 to 100 percent. 
Even though rooms cost two and three times more ($60 to $70) than Chinese-run hotels, and must be paid for with hard currency, foreign visitors are more than glad to incur the cost.
How did such an aberration ever come into being in a country once so dedicated to eradicating class distinctions and foreign privilege?
It is the brainchild of the Shanghai-born architect and hotel owner Clement Chen Jr., whose offices are in San Francisco, and who owns the Buffalo Hilton Hotel and Holiday Inns in San Francisco and Palo Alto.
Wanting to do something for his native land, and aware of Chinese interest in earning foreign exchange through an expanded tourist industry, he proposed constructing a first-class inn under foreign management in Peking. 
The Chinese, having embarked on their new ''open door policy'' to the West, accepted his plans to build a 480-room hotel, costing $22.6 million, which would be jointly owned, 51 percent by the China International Travel Service and 40 percent by Mr. Chen himself. 
After 20 months of construction, involving the shipment of 200 containers of building supplies from the United States, this curious hostel, which seems to defy the momentum of the whole Chinese Revolution, opened in 1982.
''Let's face it, we live in the 20th century,'' Mr. Chen told me when I called him at his San Francisco office to ask about his conception of the Jianguo. 
''People may enjoy visiting a country with an unfamiliar culture like China, but when they get back to their hotel from a tour in the afternoon, basically they want to be able to relax in a first-class place. 
What I mean to say is, that after the Peking duck, they may still feel a need for some bacon and eggs, a club sandwich or maybe a steak. 
I purposely designed my hotel with these needs in mind, so that once a guest gets inside, he will be able to forget where he is and feel as if he were back home.''
One obvious hurdle to Mr. Chen's notion of opening a hotel in China in which Westerners can ''forget'' where they are, is the ubiquity of the Chinese people themselves. 
No foreign guest would ever be able to imagine that he or she was ''back home'' if the hotel in Peking was open to the Chinese masses as well as foreign guests.
''This was a real problem,'' Mr. Chen acknowledged. 
''But let me tell you a little story. 
One time while we were building the hotel, I decided to go out to a public restaurant here in Peking to eat some jiaozi (steamed dumplings). 
Well, when I got to the restaurant, the first thing I discovered was that I had to get in line with everyone pushing and shoving. 
When I finally worked up to the head of the line, I found that everything was not just noisy and dirty, but that the restaurant didn't even provide bowls or chopsticks for their customers. 
I ended up eating my jiaozi on a piece of newspaper. 
Can you imagine that?
''So, I started thinking,'' Mr. Chen continued. 
''I asked myself whether I wanted to have the restaurants in my hotel look like this. 
And I decided that I didn't, that if I let all these people come in, I would have thousands of them arriving for a cup of tea, and then spending the rest of the day sitting around enjoying the air-conditioning. 
I knew that it would be impossible to run a first class hotel that way.''
As a result, all local Chinese, except the staff of 655, Chinese accompanied by foreigners or high ranking cadres attending official functions are excluded from the Jianguo. 
Security guards hover around the lobby and elevator just to make sure that no trespassers get through.
A hotel like the Jianguo serves its purpose well by providing the foreign community in Peking with an oasis of service and efficiency where there previously was none - the hotel will, for instance, take phone messages for guests, provides stenographic services, and will even accept reservations from independent travelers made abroad through the Peninsula Group (call 213-670-9450 or 312-263- 6069), unlike any other Chinese-run hotel. 
But its presence raises a number of questions about how official Chinese attitudes toward foreigners are evolving.
While understanding China's urgent need to earn foreign exchange and to open up to the outside in order to develop technologically, one still cannot help but wonder what has happened to that extreme sensitivity to flagrant displays of wealth and foreign privilege that so animated China only a few years ago.
Have Chinese Communism and the Chinese people now reconciled themselves to such social contradictions?
Or as more such hotels as the Jianguo open, will they evoke, at least for older people, an earlier and humiliating time when another generation of foreigners lived inside China, but protected by privilege in enclaves of splendid isolation?
Party officials, still sensitive to this humiliating past, are quick to point out the differences. 
The Chinese Government owns a controlling share of the hotel and will fully acquire it for one dollar in 1992. 
Foreigners no longer enjoy such privileges as extra- territoriality, which once made them inviolable to Chinese law, nor are they now allowed to indulge in the kinds of essentially unregulated commercial and evangelical activity which they once were. 
And it is also true, these officials point out, that most other developing countries provide luxury hotels as well as other facilities for those foreign visitors who can afford them.
While it is true that China has changed much over the past few years, and now even espouses such amazing slogans as ''To Get Rich is Glorious,'' somehow the Jianguo still occurs as an anomaly in downtown Peking. 
China is searching for a new identity. 
Just what that new identity will be, and how foreign-run luxury hotels for foreigners will fit into it, is not certain.

file: ANTIQUE VIEW_A CAPTAIN_S STORE OF CHINESE RICHES.txt
text:
ï»¿
Formidable collections of Chinese art have, in recent years, enriched the auction market with stunning offerings in a variety of categories - from snuff bottles to Sung and Ming porcelains. 
Two years ago, Edward T. Chow's spectacular Ming porcelains sold in three sessions of an auction at Sotheby Parke Bernet in Hong Kong and London that totaled $20.1 million, the most important public sale held in recent years of such material and the fourth highest total ever gaveled for a single owner sale of art at auction.
In that same season, the auction house sold Elva and Eugene Bernat's Sung and Tang pottery, a memorable assemblage that established a record price at auction in America for Chinese art and for Sung porcelains with the sale for $500,000 of a brown and white floral-decorated 11th-century vase. 
And Sotheby's three-session sale last season of the late Bob C. Stevens's 800 Chinese snuff bottles and related wares totaled $1.4 million, exceeding all other auctions of such material.
Formidable collections of Chinese art have, in recent years, enriched the auction market with stunning offerings in a variety of categories - from snuff bottles to Sung and Ming porcelains.
This season's prizes in Chinese art from a private collector include rare Shang and Chou bronzes, Tang tomb sculpture and Han Dynasty pottery figures. 
These art works were collected in China in the mid-1940's by Capt. Sergius N. Ferris Luboshez, a retired officer in the United States Navy who, at the close of World War II, was sent by the State Department to the Far East to serve as General Counsel to the Foreign Liquidation Commission and, later, as Central Field Commissioner.
During the four years he was stationed in China, staying primarily in Shanghai, Captain Luboshez acquired the 110 offerings that will be up for bidding Thursday at Sotheby Parke Bernet galleries. 
He was extremely fortunate, he recalled in a recent telephone interview, to be given opportunities by Chinese government officials to meet knowledgeable owners of Oriental art.
''They made a point of introducing me to the great Mandarin collectors and connoisseurs,'' he said. 
''I was the only Westerner invited to their gatherings. 
Their courtesy and gentleness were astounding. 
At that time, our people very often looked down their noses at the Chinese. 
These people welcomed me because I never assumed any airs with them. 
I trusted them and they trusted me.''
The finest ceramic offering in the Luboshez collection is a Tang tomb figure of a serene and graceful court lady, shown seated on an hourglass-shaped bamboo stool, holding a blossoming stalk in her right hand. 
Despite repairs to the neck and coiffure, and a replacement of a piece of the plant stalk, this extraordinary 6th-to 9th-century three-color glazed figure may rewrite the $250,000 record for a tomb figure, the price paid for a Tang horse at Sotheby's in London in 1978. 
According to Robert D. Mowry, curator of the Mr. and Mrs. John D. Rockefeller 3rd Collection at Asia Society, such repairs to damages of the kind this piece has suffered are not unusual. 
''In quality it compares favorably with a similar piece in the Idemitsu Museum, Tokyo, and with the superb piece in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, currently on display in their newly renovated Asiatic galleries,'' Mr. Mowry said.
Even more remarkable for its expressive energy, is the Han Dynasty watchdog, a brown-glazed tomb figure modeled 1,900 years ago in a seated position, its ears taut, its teeth bared, its whiskers bristling and its eyes bulging. 
Expectations are that it may sell for up to $90,000.
Other pottery wares of interest in the sale are a Tang owl-shaped pottery flask splashed with amber and green glazes (up to $75,000), an an early Tang straw-glazed torso of a fierce-faced warrier in armor (up to $6,000) and an impressive gray pottery storage jar, wide shouldered and ovoid in form (up to $50,000).
The Shang and Chou bronzes in the sale include several of interest: a covered Chou cauldron called a ding, dating to about 500 B.C. (up to $120,000); a covered Shang wine vessel or fanglei from the 11th or 12th century B.C., the cover of which may not be original to the work (up to $60,000) and an animal-shaped Shang wine vessel called a Guang (up to $70,000). 
Captain Luboshez said that the Guang - its spout in the shape of a tiger's head - was one of the most difficult pieces to find. 
''I was told over and over again that there aren't any, there are none in China,'' he said. 
''But, after three years of asking and looking, finally one appeared.''
Whatever damage the bronzes have suffered has more to do with age and what happened to these works in tombs than to anything else, Mr. Mowry points out, explaining that bronze vessels were not used for everyday use but were made as ritual works for use in burial ceremonies. 
Afterward they were put into the tomb.
In acquiring these wares, Captain Luboshez said that his meetings with collectors occurred over tea or dinner at which an art object - the court lady, for example - would be exhibited and then removed. 
''If you expressed admiration for the piece, that meant you were able and willing to buy it,'' he explained, adding that it would be impolite to ask to see an art work again. 
Two or three years after he had seen the court lady, he reported, he was told it might be available and an intermediary informed him of the price. 
''I was more or less committed to pay whatever they asked,'' he said. 
''It was high - but not by today's prices.''
The pottery dog came to him in a different way - in the middle of the night in a laundry basket, borne by a collector who was ''drenched to the skin'' and who needed the money.
Captain Luboshez spoke philosophically of his collection. 
The attraction of Chinese art lay in its view of man not as the Lord of nature, as in Western art, but as ''part of nature.''
He is selling, he added, because over the years ''an art object can become part of you.''
And once that happens, he noted, owning the object seems unnecessary.
James J. Lally, Sotheby's specialist in this material, will give a lecture on the Luboshez collection this afternoon at 2 at the auction house, York Avenue at 72d Street. 
The lecture is open to the public without charge.

file: ANTIQUES VIEW_THE LURE AND LORE OF BAMBOO.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese bamboo craftsmen, from the 16th century on, enriched scholars' desks with sculptures, writing tools, brush holders, wrist rests and other objects. 
Some excellent examples survive, as can be seen in ''Bamboo Carving of China,'' an exhibition of 85 selections at China House Gallery, 125 East 65th Street, on view through May 29. 
The show is believed to be the first in this country devoted to the craft.
Undeniably esoteric, these whittled figures and objects may seem unfamiliar to most Western viewers. 
Indeed, only a limited number are found in public and private collections in this country, and what does exist is rarely shown.
Chinese bamboo craftsmen, from the 16th century on, enriched scholars' desks with sculptures, writing tools, brush holders, wrist rests and other objects.
There are, on close examination, many similarities between these meticulously carved bamboo objects and those rendered in ivory, jade, rhinoceros horn, coral, amber and wood. 
Subjects that recur include gods and goddesses, legends and history. 
In many the emphasis is on nature, be it real or imagined. 
Dragons, frogs, crabs and phoenixes, squirrels climbing trees, birds in flight and insects resting on bamboo leaves enliven a score of selections.
The distinctive characteristics of bamboo - its tough texture, burnished coloring, cylindrical shape and root-like embellishments - contribute a great deal to the finished objects. 
Many carvers capitalized on the natural form of the plant or its imperfections, allowing them to dominate in the execution of a subject. 
Other artisans did the opposite - incising calligraphy on the sides of a vessel or cutting deeper into the bamboo surface to detail an exquisite landscape, effects that might appear on virtually any material.
Carved bamboo spearheads and flutes date to prehistoric times, according to Wan-go Weng, curator and designer of the show and author of its catalogue. 
It was not until the 16th century, however, that craftsmen turned their attention to carving desk accessories. 
Mr. Weng, who is the president of the China Institute in America, which is the China House Gallery's parent institution, explains the symbolic value of bamboo in his intelligently written text. 
''It is upright and sturdy, bending but never broken,'' he writes. 
''Its hollow cane reminds the scholar of humbleness, for there is room inside to receive knowledge and advice.''
Whatever their symbolic meaning, scholars must have also found these objects a pleasant distraction. 
Brush holders are the largest and usually the most intricately carved accessories of the scholar's desk. 
One in the shape of a pine stump is enhanced with cranes and pine branches. 
Another in the same shape dramatizes a fungus growth carved in high relief on the bark.
Life situations are captured in carved vignettes on several of these vessels. 
One shows a woman and an artisan polishing her mirror. 
Others depict lovers parting, a literary gathering in the garden, a prime minister playing a board game while he loses a war and an old man greeting a flying goose.
Far more amusing are some of the sculptures intended as decoration for the scholar's desk. 
There are, for example, imaginatively carved Ming toads - one, the size of a baseball, is a quizzical creature with bulging eyes and rough skin, and another, with two young ones on its back, stares blankly with its mouth wide open. 
An equally charming Lilliputian sculpture is a Ching crab with a shaft of grain. 
There are realisitic water chestnuts, a tangerine and a bunch of grapes. 
There is also a winning study of a water hyacinth and an arresting depiction of a mythological beast looking as if he is about to spit fire. 
The more elaborate works - an old man on a raft, a log boat on which eight gods are traveling - are of traditional tales but are fussily carved and less impressive.
Most, but not all of the wrist rests are half cylinders, the surfaces embellished with calligraphy or landscapes or both. 
An exception is an exuberantly carved work - a free-standing sculpture - depicting a scholar at the base of a gnarled pine tree with realistically rendered branches.
Bamboo carvings are seriously collected in the East, but less so in the West where collectors of Chinese art usually acquire only a few examples. 
Most auctions of Chinese art offer some bamboo carvings, which bring low to moderate prices. 
Brush pots of the 19th and 20th centuries are among the more common offerings in sales at Sotheby Parke Bernet, selling at from $200 to $600. 
Brush rests sell for as little as $300, and other carvings are usually less than $1,000. 
The highest price registered at auction was $6,800, the sum paid in Nov. 
1979 at Sotheby's in Hong Kong for a 19th-century bamboo scepter. 
The most expensive bamboo carving auctioned in New York was an 18thcentury bamboo vase, which sold in May 1981 at Sotheby's for $2,400.
This explains why most of the works on view in the China House show are from Hong Kong collections, including 36 from Dr. Ip Yee, a Hong Kong physician. 
In addition, there are 31 from the Julia Y. Cheng collection on loan at the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City, which also sent some selections of its own. 
The other museums represented are the Cleveland Museum of Art, Boston's Museum of Fine Arts, the Denver Art Museum, the Seattle Art Museum and the Asian Art Museum of San Francisco.
Exhibitions mounted by the China Institute in its tiny gallery have always been admired for their consummate sophistication both in subject matter and presentation. 
This exhibition of well-crafted, if less than exciting objects is pleasantly arranged and lighted in showcases framed by calligraphic cutouts, an obvious reference to the scholar's lettering skills. 
The show is funded in part by the New York State Council on the Arts. 
A generously illustrated 144-page catalogue is $12.50.

file: ANTIQUES_A Booming Market For Asian Art.txt
text:
ï»¿
Dealers in Asian art are increasing in number and becoming more visible in New York - opening new galleries and presenting specialty exhibitions. 
Last week, for example, a major gallery opened on 57th Street, a Madison Avenue dealer moved to larger quarters, two private dealers presented their first combined exhibition and several others initiated specialty shows.
All these activities were timed to occur while scores of collectors and dealers were in town from the Far East, Europe and throughout the United States, attending the sales of Oriental art at Sotheby's and Christie's. 
The increased momentum in this market comes in a season of booming art auctions that included last month's record-breaking dispersal by Sotheby's in Hong Kong of the first half of the Chinese ceramics and jade collection of Tsao Yee Chao, a Hong Kong ship owner.
At that sale, Seijiro Matsuoka, a 92-year-old Japanese industrialist and real-estate enterpreneur, purchased a 14th-century Ming porcelain dish, awash with flowers on a red ground. 
He paid $1.3 million, a record at auction for Oriental art.
The newest and most impressive addition to the Asian-art scene in New York is J. J. Lally & Company at 42 East 57th Street. 
James J. Lally, the 41-year-old former president of Sotheby's in New York, who headed its Chinese art department from 1974 to 1982, has assembled in this sensitively lighted, understated setting a splendid selection of works of ceramic, bronze, jade, lacquer, wood, silver and gold dating from the neolithic period to the 18th century. 
Ceramics dominate, and the choice works of early pottery, jade and bronze, from neolithic through Sung, reveal this dealer's preference for bold forms and highly expressive art. 
In size, these works range from monumental to miniature and include an arresting pair of 40-inch-tall ceramic Tang dignitaries from the eighth century and a postage-stamp sized third-century B.C. Han seal - a block of carved gold, topped by a tortoise, with neatly chiseled characters in the base.
Outstanding is a large red pottery Han horse, a powerful figure almost two feet tall from about 200 B.C., boasting admirable musculature, flaring nostrils and fully formed legs. 
The mottled red surface on this recently excavated sculpture still shows traces of encrusted earth. 
''He's quite rare,'' Mr. Lally said. 
''So many of the Han-period horses are without legs.''
Limbless ceramic horses, he said, were originally fitted with wood legs that have since disintegrated.
Among the more provocative of the archaic jade disks is a serenely simple icy white donut, almost six inches in diameter. 
Prices here range from $3,000 for a bronze Han seal to $180,000 for the pair of Tang dignitaries.
Later works are memorable for other reasons. 
There is, for example, an exquisitely detailed silver box of the 14th century with flowers in high relief decorating the lid. 
From the 16th century comes an aristocratic pair of yoke-back Ming chairs, and from the 18th century a large Imperial yellow dish, a ravishing example of the enameler's skill from the Chien Lung period.
''We are going back to a golden era,'' Mr. Lally said, observing that the works being offered collectors of Chinese art today are comparable to those available at the turn of the century. 
Then, as now, excavations uncovered a wealth of tomb material.
Susan B. Levinson and Donald J. Wineman, private dealers, are currently presenting their first exhibition of Oriental art works in her apartment, at 12 East 86th Street. 
The number of paintings, textiles, ceramics, lacquer wares and ivory works on view is somewhat limited, but the range is wide in both age and materials. 
The oldest of the Chinese, Japanese and Indian works in the stock on view is a bronze garment hook inlaid with gold, silver and turquoise, that dates from the Warring States period of the third century B.C. The most recent is a Bamboo brushpot carved in relief that dates to about 1800. 
It is also the least expensive work in the selection at $1,800. 
The most expensive is a Han court lady, standing more than 28 inches tall, at $35,000. 
The dealers may be visited by appointment.
At Ralph M. Chait Galleries, 12 East 56th Street, a collection of armorial porcelains made in China for export to the West is on view through Saturday. 
All of the 80 offerings are 18th-century selections and most of these teapots, dishes, cups, saucers and great rimmed platters called chargers were made for British clients. 
They range from about $1,500 for a dish to $20,000 for a set of 12 plates.
Michael B. Weisbrod, a Toronto dealer who relocated in New York 10 years ago, opened Monday in new quarters at the Carlyle Hotel, at 987 Madison Avenue. 
On view are highlights from his stock of neolithic through 19th-century Ch'ing ceramics, sculpture, bronzes, and paintings that range from about $5,000 to $250,000.

file: ANTIQUES_A Dragonish Display in New Haven.txt
text:
ï»¿
Bug-eyed dragons emblazoned on the Chinese ceramics exhibited at the Yale University Art Gallery are bound to spark more fantasy than fear in viewers. 
For the winged, horned reptiles whipping energetically around beach-ball-sized jars, breathing fire as they stretch clawed paws on basins and raging, fangs bared, on the center of great platters, are propitious symbols - not docile, but seemingly well disposed to all.
These mythical beasts dominate the images seen on the Yuan and Ming porcelains in this exhibition of works from the Idemitsu Museum of Arts in Tokyo, a privately owned institution of a Japanese petrochemical company. 
The show, ''In Pursuit of the Dragon: Traditions and Transitions in Ming Ceramics,'' includes 90 porcelains, of which 31 are decorated with the bewhiskered monsters. 
They are but a small part of the Idemitsu's holdings, which also include Japanese and Middle Eastern ceramics, as well as European and American 20th-century art. 
Organized by the Seattle Art Museum, which produced the excellent catalogue ($19.95), the show will remain at Yale through Jan. 
15.
What could be more appropriate in this the Chinese year of the dragon than an exhibition of some of the world's most spectacular crockery on which these beasts play a starring role?
Ming blue-and-white wares are embellished with blue dragons or white ones. 
Polychromed vessels are splashed with green, red, orange, yellow or brown beasts. 
Dragons crown the lids of boxes, slither around the necks of ewers, rim basins and dramatize otherwise understated dishes. 
The animals are depicted in the traditional Chinese manner with a camel's head, deer's horns, cow's ears, snake's neck, hawk's claws and tiger's paws.
The show's most majestic Ming monster is a marvelous blue dragon with bulging eyes and a scaly body wrapped around a massive blue-and-white jar about 20 inches in diameter. 
The vessel, made between 1425 and 1436, is a rarity, one of only two known. 
The other one was donated in 1937 to the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
The Idemitsu's porcelains, decorated with dragons, flowers, leaves, butterflies, landscapes or glorious washes of color, trace the evolution of ceramics in the Yuan and Ming periods, from 1260 to 1644. 
Porcelains flowered in China during a period of great artistic ferment more than 200 years before this technology reached the West. 
Among the earliest major achievements are monochrome porcelains that include elegantly shaped stem cups - a white one with straight sides, and a red one with a flared mouth - and a sturdy meiping jar dipped in a rich cobalt glaze that accentuates the boldy rounded form.
Seeing the development of color and decoration on these vessels, one suspects that ceramists experimented with colored glazes - cobalt blue, celadon, blood red, turquoise and egg-yolk yellow - the way bakers learn to ice cakes. 
First they frosted the surfaces without a whisper of decoration. 
Then, after glassy coatings were mastered, they moved on to more complex techniques, such as carving images in the surface.
Two outsized 15th-century celadon platters, larger than Hula-Hoops, illustrate these developments. 
On one of these vessels, 27 inches in diameter, the surface is a glowing lime-green glaze. 
On the other, the shimmering green coating is carved with fruits and flowers.
Painterly ceramics abound in this exhibition, and three shallow dishes show how images were modified over a century in the hands of different artists. 
These plates - one blue and white, the others blue and yellow - are decorated at the center with a flowering branch and on the rim with sprays of peaches, litchis, cherries, persimmons and pomegranates. 
The blue-and-white version, made between 1426 and 1435, is the freest and most realistic botanical rendering. 
A yellow-and-blue dish decorated a half century later in the same tradition is strongly expressionistic. 
Although beautifully drawn, the motifs on the third dish, which dates from 1506 to 1521, are predictable.
Chinese ceramics have commanded an increasingly enthusiastic international following since the early 1970's. 
Many of the finest porcelains in the collection of the Idemitsu, which was founded in 1966, were acquired over the last 16 years. 
In this period, prices for great rarities rose from well under $100,000 to $1 million or more.
James J. Lally, a New York Oriental art dealer, was a Chinese art specialist at Sotheby's and its president in New York during the period when the Idemitsu bought many treasures from Sotheby's and Christie's in London. 
''The Idemitsu's ceramics collection far outdistances anything done earlier in this century by the Morgans or Rockefellers,'' he said. 
''They choose masterpieces of each form - there are no compromises.''
Among many of the works in the exhibition found at Sotheby's auctions in London was the massive dragon jar, which was bought in 1981 for $1.5 million, then a record at auction for Chinese art. 
In 1983, the museum bought a large 14th-century blue-and-white foliate dish, awash with lacy flowers, for $117,986. 
In 1976 a bowl with a molded and incised dragon-and-cloud design, glazed blue on the outside and red on the interior, was bought there for $102,960. 
The Idemitsu also shopped at Christie's in London, where in 1982 it paid $618,624 for the 15th-century blue-and-white dish decorated with a pomegranate branch bordered by fruit sprays.
Money for the exhibition is from the National Endowment for the Arts, Kyoto's Metropolitan Center for Far Eastern Art Studies, the Asian Cultural Council and the Federal Council on the Arts and the Humanities. 
The exhibition is to travel through January 1990, visiting the Detroit Institute of the Arts, Pittsburgh's Carnegie Museum of Art, the Birmingham Museum of Art, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and the Honolulu Academy of the Arts.

file: ANTIQUES_CHINESE PUPPETS WITH ANCIENT LINEAGE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese puppets date back more than 2,000 years and are probably rooted in ancient religious rituals.
Western knowledge of these hand, string and rod dolls is, however, relatively recent, according to Roberta Helmer Stalberg, guest curator of ''Puppetry of China,'' at the China House Gallery, 125 East 65th Street, through June 29.
The exhibition of about 50 examples is described by the gallery as the first comprehensive presentation of the subject in this country. 
The puppets shown are on loan from public and private collections in the United States and from two professional puppet troupes in China. 
They constitute more than 30 period examples, dating from the late 19th century to about 1940, and a number of performance-quality contemporary puppets, some of which are as skillfully carved and seem as aged through wear as the period specimens. 
An additional group of six lavishly dressed hand puppets adorn an elaborately carved miniature stage that dates, as do the hand figures, to the turn of the century.
Many of these figures are superbly crafted and the variety of characters and styles of costumes represented is impressive. 
Most of the three-dimensional puppets are glorious theatrical conceptions - fierce-faced or elaborately mustached and wearing embroidered robes, crowned by feathered helmets and winged hats. 
The rod-operated shadow puppets are exquisitely delicate two-dimensional creatures, fashioned of leather, that appear to waltz on stilts. 
The characters represented are legendary rulers, warriors, gods, demons and heroines that were devised to bring alive on miniature stages the same dramas that are depicted in plays and operas by human actors.
Unfortunately, this magical material is displayed unimaginatively in showcases and behind or against lighted panels that convey little of the wonder and charm of puppet shows. 
It is a pedantic presentation following, more or less, the equally uninspired groupings that appear in the catalogue of this traveling show.
Dr. Stalberg recalled in an interview that she was surprised to discover at the outset of her research how little had been written in English on Chinese puppets. 
She became interested in the subject, she said, after she was introduced to the puppeteers of the Longxi Hand Puppet Troupe of China during its 1980 tour of this country. 
Later, she learned that in China, as here, most puppets are seldom exhibited, and that very little has been written about their origins and history.
''I went to China four times to do research,'' she reported. 
Her findings have been recorded in an informative book, ''China's Puppets,'' published in 1984 by China Books of San Francisco ($29.95), and in the less detailed catalogue of the show ($7), both of which are available at China House gallery.
Dr. Stalberg notes in the catalogue that written records of puppets are rare before the 12th century A.D., and the few that exist, she writes, are tantalizingly vague. 
''One popular legend ascribes the invention of puppetry to a craftsman named Master Yan, said to have lived about 1000 B.C.,'' she continues, adding that the articulated figures he constructed were supposedly so perfect, they could dance and sing realistically. 
However, no details survive about how early craftsmen accomplished these feats.
Puppets probably originated in religious ceremonies, according to Dr. Stalberg. She says that early written accounts survive describing lifelike funerary figures, images of deities animated by shamans for spiritual guidance, protection or to bring good fortune. 
A recent discovery appears to support this thesis. 
In 1979, a man-sized jointed figure, measuring 6 feet 2 inches tall, was unearthed in a tomb dating to 107 B.C., in Liaxi County, Shandong Province. 
The solemn-faced puppet, constructed of wood strips to permit the figure to sit, kneel or stand, has many holes drilled in the abdomen and legs used, no doubt, either to attach costumes or the strings used to move the marionette.
Dr. Stalberg relates that the first shadow puppets may well be explained by a legend from the second century B.C. in which the heartbroken widower Emperor Wu of the Han Dynasty sought ways to bring his wife back to life. 
To please him, one of his subjects devised an image of the Emperor's wife and, lighting it by a lantern, showed it behind a gauze curtain.
The puppets that Dr. Stalberg and others have purchased or inherited, she said, were acquired for the most part in China, some in the early decades of this century. 
Scarce though these dolls may be, they are not necessarily costly and probably never were. 
Missionaries and travelers to China between 1900 and World War II are responsible for the few that one finds changing hands today or in museum collections in the West.
Berthold Laufer, an ethnologist, went to China for the American Museum of Natural History in 1901 and bought the entire holdings of a shadow puppet troupe that was disbanding, a group he thought incorrectly was the last in Peking. 
That acquisition, which included musical instruments, stage curtains, dramatic texts and more than 500 shadow figures, cost $600.
This traveling exhibition was originated in 1984 by Atlanta's Center for Puppetry Arts, and has visited cities in the United States and Canada on the tour. 
Dr. Stalberg found many of the examples shown in the Lutz Collection of the University of Richmond, which was assembled in the 1920's, and in private collections of those who have lived in China or traveled there in recent years.
The exhibition is aided by the National Endowment for the Humanities through the Georgia Endowment for the Humanities, the National Endowment for the Arts and the New York State Council on the Arts.

file: ANTIQUES_COLLECTIBLES THAT PACKED A CHARGE.txt
text:
ï»¿
The bang that Kenneth Legunn and hundreds of other collectors get out of firecrackers lasts long past the Fourth of July.
''The best day to find and swap firecracker labels is the fifth of July,'' Dr. Legunn, a periodontist from Pleasantville, N.Y., said. 
''That's the real collecting day. 
But it goes on throughout the year.''
When Dr. Legunn began his search for these offbeat graphics 21 years ago, he recalled, he was 9 years old and never dreamed he would still be pursuing these labels two decades later. 
He also had no idea that there were 19th- and early 20th-century examples extant and that his quest would one day take him to Hong Kong, Macao and China.
What he and other enthusiasts realized when he was a boy in Bellerose, Queens, was that the debris left by Independence Day celebrants represented a gold mine of colorful ephemera. 
They left no paper scrap unturned in their search through rubbish piles in which occasionally one label lurked. 
The boldly lettered labels on the red, white and blue paper wrappings showed such images as a ferocious-looking black cat, a snarling tiger, soldiers advancing or the Stars and Stripes.
But today, Dr. Legunn explained, firecracker labels are far less imaginative, so collectors no longer poke around in the trash on the day after the Fourth. 
Instead, he said, they mark that day with a post-holiday ritual - meeting fellow collectors to swap or sell vintage labels.
For centuries, firecrackers have been a staple in Chinese New Year's celebrations. 
''The first firecrackers were used to frighten away the evil spirits during festive occasions,'' Dr. Legunn said, adding that the Chinese, who probably invented these noisemakers, believed that lots of confetti chased demons away. 
This explains, he noted, why the Chinese did not remove the labels from the packages before they lighted them.
Firecracker labels have been made throughout China, Hong Kong and Macao for the American market since the turn of the century. 
It is these designs, Dr. Legunn said, that he and about 300 other Americans collect. 
Like Dr. Legunn, many of these enthusiasts are members of the Pyrotechnics Guild International, an organization whose members make or collect fireworks, related artifacts and firecracker labels.
Period firecracker wrappers look like anything but what they are, which is one reason people collect them, he said. 
The pictures on the packaging of 19th- and early 20th-century Chinese firecrackers depict such images as a Boy Scout, an Indian chief, United States Marines or characters from the ''Wizard of Oz.''
The brand names are often puzzling, too, especially those such as Home Run, Touch Down, Bo-Peep, Captain Kid and Alligator, which seemingly have nothing to do with the product.
''The old ones are very deceiving, and that's an attraction,'' Dr. Legunn explained, as he flipped through a huge scrapbook that contained some of his 800 labels. 
What originally interested him about these graphics was the sense of adventure they sparked.
''Firecrackers were forbidden, but kids always got a hold of them,'' he said. 
''Parents never liked them because they are dangerous. 
There was something else that made them special - I thought I had found something no one else collected.''
Now Dr. Legunn is happy that he is not alone in this pursuit because acquiring labels from other collectors and thus meeting people who share his interest is part of the fun. 
''There are collectors who have been at it since the 1920's,'' he said. 
He has already acquired many of the most important examples of these graphics, the finest of which date back to the 1920's and 30's, when typography and graphic design reached perhaps their highest level.
Dr. Legunn stopped collecting once - when he went to college - but resumed again in 1983 after he had completed his post-doctoral studies. 
He can be found on the telephone several nights a week talking with other collectors throughout the United States and Canada. 
He also trades with a collector in Hong Kong and one in India.
There are finds to be made at paper shows and in bookstores. 
Dr. Legunn recalled fingering through a 1920's diary written by a boy from the Middle West in which he discovered three 1920's firecracker labels, stuck in the pages. 
What did they cost?
''A dollar,'' he said.
But most of what he has tracked down involved greater effort and expense. 
One way he seeks out labels is by advertising in many paper collectible and suburban newspapers. 
One ad brought a response from a woman in Newburgh, N.Y., who had 50 excellent examples that her son had collected a half century ago. 
The price of $125 was worth it, he said.
His most exciting experience took place on a trip to the Far East last September, where he met a retired firecracker manufacturer. 
''In Macao I hired a guide and spent hours going to the old addresses of firecracker factories - they are all jeans factories now,'' he said. 
He located one of the owners of the Kwong Hing Tai company, who had kept samples of all the old labels, and sold him 75.
The prices for labels range from about $10 to hundreds of dollars, he said, adding that collectors have offered him $500 to $600 for some of his best pieces, which are not for sale. 
The most he has paid, he added, was $250, for a rare Golliwog label dating to 1908.
Spelling mistakes on labels are another category sought by collectors, Dr. Legunn said, adding that two of the favorites in his collection are Yan Kee Boy and Atta Boy. 
The latter was supposed to say That-a-Boy, and it was corrected later. 
It is the incorrect one that collectors seek, he said.

TIMED TO COINCIDE with the impressive presentation of art works from the Shanghai Museum on view in ''The Chinese Scholar's Studio: Artistic Life in the Late Ming Period,'' at the Asia Society, is a dealer's exhibition organized by James J. Lally that expresses in a generous assortment of art and objects the traditional taste of the educated elite in China over a thousand years.
In ''Chinese Works of Art for the Scholar's Studio,'' at the J. J.Lally gallery, 42 East 57th Street, the material - 106 art works dating from the 11th-century B.C. Shang dynasty through the mid-19th century - covers the full spectrum of what today's Western collectors most admire in period Oriental art. 
There are Shang bronze vessels from the 11th century B.C.; Han animal figures and seals from the first century A.D.; Sung ceramics from the 13th century; Ming jades of the 16th century and Ching porcelains and wood boxes of the 19th century.
Mr. Lally's selection includes many objects associated with the scholar's studio that were made much later than the late Ming dynasty - the focus of the Asia Society exhibition. 
He has included these post-Ming works to show how objects admired by the educated class were produced until quite recently. 
From the 18th century come a turquoise porcelain rock, a fussily carved jade water pot and a molded stemmed gourd object. 
Notable objects from the 19th century include a small, shapely wood bud vase and a superb, austerely crafted pair of melon-shaped lidded wood boxes for game pieces.
Outstanding among earlier works are an Imperial blue and white cylindrical porcelain brush pot of the Ching period that is decorated with calligraphy; Han seals in the form of snarling chimeras and a Ming document box with brass mounts. 
The realistic and mythical Han and Sung animals seen throughout this show engage the mind with a sense of wonder at the importance of symbolism to the Chinese. 
Notable examples include a bronze tortoise water dropper, a stone water pot in the shape of a ram, a lacquered bronze deer-unicorn figure and a bull-shaped - or is it a tapir?
- silvered and gilded bronze water dropper.
''A scholar always had a sense of participation in the past,'' Mr. Lally said, adding that the scholars demonstrated this in a variety of ways that included collecting ancient works and altering works of an earlier period to a practical use centuries later, an honored tradition in China. 
One of the most memorable objects in the show, a regal first- or second-century Han duck of gilded bronze, standing less than four inches tall, was transformed into a seal in the Sung or Ming period.
''The tradition of art collecting has a longer history in China than anywhere else in the world,'' Mr. Lally said. 
''Collecting and connoisseurship were already essential attributes of an accomplished gentleman by the time of Confucius, in the fifth century B.C.''
The prices of the objects, furnishings, paintings and calligraphies shown by Mr. Lally range from $1,200 for a bamboo wristrest to $35,000 for a pair of Ming chairs. 
These selections cover so many periods and art styles that they show the broad range of works from which scholars were able to select pieces for their studios, thereby retaining a strong sense of individuality in the highly personal environments where they worked, studied and spent long hours in meditation. 
Virtually every work in the show seems chosen as an object worthy of extended inspection - be it the tripod Shang bronze vessel with flattened scrolls decorating the entire surface or the shapely, gold-washed, 18th-century bronze censer.
A fuller understanding of the reason these art works were made and collected in China over the centuries can be gained by visiting the Asia Society exhibition, which remains through Jan. 
3, and by consulting its generously illustrated catalogue (clothbound, $45; paperback, $35).
The physical re-creation of a scholar's studio in the Asia Society show, although smaller and less sumptuous than it would have been in the late Ming period, which ended in 1644, gives collectors for the first time in memory an opportunity to see the elements of a scholar's studio as it might have been. 
The materials in this setting are on loan from the Metropolitan Museum of Art, private collectors and Robert H. Ellsworth, a New York dealer. 
Dr. James C. Y. Watt, senior consultant for Chinese antiquities and decorative arts at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, said that the scholar's studio which existed from the 11th century on ''was never so formalized that the individual could not express his own personality in the art works and objects selected.''
Dr. Watt, one of the four curators from the United States who worked with the curatorial staff of the Shanghai museum on the show, explained that although there were some general rules governing what an educated gentleman should choose for his study, ''the rules applied more to those who were not sure of themselves than to the true scholar, who was an arbiter of taste and did not go by the rules.''
His one disappointment, he said, was the limited space accorded the re-creation of the scholar's studio, which was all that was possible in the society's exhibition space. 
''It should have been spread into an area five times the size,'' he said. 
''The window would have been much larger and the chair would have been covered with very colorful brocades and velvets.''
Even so, the setting is rich in exquisite detail, reflecting the delight that an educated gentleman of the Ming period must have experienced in collecting objects alive with shimmer, painted detail or carving. 
Most of the items placed on or near the mother-of-pearl inlaid and lacquered desktop - stone seals, a fluted wood scroll pot, jasper rocks, a jade brush rest, five bamboo brushes, carved boxes, a bronze vessel, albums of paper and the inevitable qin, or zither - are wonderful to touch and study.
However difficult the symbolism and traditions of the literati may be for 20th-century viewers, the objects that represent them are not, because most of them - including the fly whisk hung over the back of the aristocratic yoke-back armchair - bear a resemblance to the tools and artifacts common in our libraries and offices today.

IT is only within the last 15 or 20 years that collectors have rediscovered Chinese Export silver, says Robert Egleston, curator of the New Haven Historical Society Museum, adding, ''It's important to understanding our own late 18th- and 19th-century society.''
An exhibition of Chinese Export silver is now on display at the New Haven Museum, with pieces on loan from the Yale University Art Gallery, the Proctor Institute in Utica, N.Y., and private collections in Connecticut, Massachusetts, New York and Pennsylvania. 
The exhibit will continue through Dec. 
1.
Because of the way it often was marked, most Chinese Export silver is not easy for the average collector to identify. 
This is especially true for those who have inherited silver. 
Unless there is a family record that describes the pieces as having been made in China, many may believe they own silver made in England or early 19th-century America.
When Western examples were shown to Chinese silversmiths for them to copy, that is exactly what they did, down to the hallmark, changing, sometimes, only the letter that indicated the year it was made. 
This was done by substituting the Chinese maker's own initial. 
Some Chinese silversmiths stamped their own initials in English on pieces made for export. 
This has led dealers and buyers to believe they have discovered a piece that had been made by a heretofore unidentified American smith. 
As a result, there are probably more pieces of Chinese Export silver on dining room sideboards, displayed in corner cupboards or tucked away in silver drawers than their owners may realize.
There were silver mines throughout China and all of Asia, but much of the silver used to make Chinese Export pieces was transported from America and England to Canton, trunk after trunk full of silver coins. 
There they were melted down and, as one earlier traveler wrote, soon ''converted into articles of luxury or convenience.''
Between 1784, when American merchants first began to trade with China, to 1854 more than $1 million in coins was shipped to China to be transformed into goblets and mugs, tea services, flatware, cream pots, sugar dishes and other holloware.
In the 18th century and early 19th century, pieces of silverware - cups, tankards and plates - were used as money. 
These also were exported to China not only to be made into ''new-fashioned'' silver but to pay for cargoes of exotic silks and teas. 
In 1789, a ship out of Salem, Mass., took to Canton $30,000 in coins, as well as 23 pieces of silver that had been fashioned by colonial silversmiths.
Whether American or English coins, old silver pieces or Chinese silver was used, apparently little attention was given to the amount of silver in each new piece made by the Chinese. 
Silver that has been assayed shows a variance from 78 to as much as 97 parts of silver to copper, the alloy used.
Chinese silversmiths were paid so much less than their Western counterparts that in spite of the cost of transporting the silver and the payment of export and customs duties, the finished pieces brought back to the United States were much less expensive than if they had been made here.
Without a knowledge of English hallmarks or of American touchmarks, the only way most Americans can recognize old Chinese silver made, as the Chinese said, ''in the English manner,'' is to take it to a museum such as the New Haven Colony Historical Society and ask for help.
One indication of Canton workmanship is that in many instances, Chinese-made examples differ only in weight. 
Many are somewhat heavier than American and English pieces.
It was not until 1842, when Western merchants were permitted to take their wives and families to China, that more silver pieces were brought back to the United States. 
One reason was that rather than take all of their own silver flatware and serving pieces with them, merchants' wives packed ''samples'' to take with them and ordered new silver made for them in China. 
Sometimes these pieces were kept separate from their American prototypes. 
More often, they eventually ended up in the same silver drawer as the originals.
Chinese silver has been found in Ireland, Canada and Australia, as well. 
In this country, most examples have been discovered in Connecticut, Massachusetts and Rhode Island, due to the fact that so many merchant traders were from this area. 
More pieces have been found in New Haven and in the Boston area than in any other principal early trading center, including Philadelphia.
But discoveries are made where there is interest and knowledge. 
One principal reason for New Haven's eminence in this particular field may be the influence of a local collector and authority on American and English silver, John D. Kernan. His curiosity was aroused when he found a pair of sugar tongs in a New York antiques shop with the puzzling mark, CUT. 
A year later, in 1959, he discovered a snuff box with a similar mark in another shop. 
Two snuff boxes, purchased in Connecticut, one marked W and one KHC plus an unidentified Chinese character, confirmed his guess that all of the oddly marked pieces were Chinese.
His curiosity and research led to correspondence with museums and silver experts. 
In 1975, under the imprint of the Museum of the American China Trade, an excellent explanation of Chinese Export silver and its makers was published, written by Mr. Kernan, H. A. Crosby Forbes and Ruth S. Wilkins.
The New Haven Colony Historical Society Museum at 114 Whitney Avenue is open without charge Tuesday through Friday from 10 A.M. to 4:45 P.M. and on Saturday and Sunday from 1 to 4:45 P.M.

China welcomed the Year of the Pig today with firecrackers, mass weddings, calls for frugality and reminders not to forget family planning.
PEKING, Feb. 
13 (AP) - China welcomed the Year of the Pig today with firecrackers, mass weddings, calls for frugality and reminders not to forget family planning.
Peking television showed crowds in Fujian Province launching two orange rubber rafts toward Taiwan, 100 miles east. 
They stocked the boats with mao-tai liquor, food and fruits and topped them with banners reading ''Wishing You Happy New Year'' and ''Reunification Is Everyone's Sacred Duty.''
In Tian An Men Square in Peking, thousands of lights and red lanterns decorated major buildings. 
Crowds of merrymakers milled in the square.
The holiday is the traditional time for weddings, and China has therefore stepped up its family-planning campaign to remind newlyweds they are permitted to have only one child.

BY AUDREY TOPPING
Visitors to the Metropolitan Museum beginning April 3 will have an opportunity to walk through a simulated Buddhist cave temple and see original fragments from ancient wall frescoes, painted temple hangings and exquisite clay sculptures that were excavated from the desert sands of Central Asia after being buried for almost a thousand years. 
This loan exhibition will continue through June 20.
These rare religious treasures will be shown for the first time in the United States. 
The exhibition, called ''Along the Ancient Silk Routes: Central Asian Art From the West Berlin State Museums,'' will offer the viewer a unique insight into the exotic art of a virtually unknown chapter of Central Asian history.
Visitors to the Metropolitan Museum beginning April 3 will have an opportunity to walk through a simulated Buddhist cave temple and see original fragments from ancient wall frescoes, painted temple hangings and exquisite clay sculptures that were excavated from the desert sands of Central Asia after being buried for almost a thousand years.
The exhibition, made possible by a grant from I.B.M., displays 152 works of art that once adorned the Buddhist caves, temples and palaces that graced the oasis centers in the Taklamakan and Gobi Deserts, where camel caravans laden with silk and spices stopped to rest during their journey across the fabled old silk routes that joined Imperial China to the Holy Roman Empire.
All the art dates from the fifth to 10th century A.D., when Buddhism was at its height in Central Asia. 
After flourishing for over 500 years as both a religion and a culture, Buddhism in this area came to an inglorious end after the Uighur ruler of Kashgar converted to Mohammadism. 
It was not long before Arab Muslim armies swept through Central Asia on a holy mission, destroying and desecrating all Buddhist temples and edifices they could find. 
Whole cities were flattened. 
Remote temple caves that escaped destruction were soon blocked with sand drifts. 
The people became Muslims and have remained so to this day. 
So complete was the devastation that all traces of the rich Buddhist culture were lost to civilization.
Over the next 10 centuries stories about hundreds of fabled cities swallowed by the sands of the Gobi and legends of buried treasures abounded. 
But no serious interest was taken until 1873 when the Englishman Sir Douglas Forsyth returned with two Buddhist figures, some gold jewelry and coins, from a sand-entombed city near Khotan that had disppeared some 800 years before. 
The European nations were soon competing in an archeological gold rush to retrieve the precious antiquities and carry them off. 
China was so involved in interior turmoil that it made no effort to stop the foreign expeditions, which it later criticized.
The lost and found art works coming to the Met were all recovered by German archeologists in a dramatic series of four scientific expeditions that took place in the first few decades of this century, led by Orientalists Albert Grunwedel and Albert Van Coq, both scholars of Indo-Tibetan Buddhism. 
The art was discovered in sites along the northern silk route in Chinese Turkestan. 
Today it is known as the Sinkiang-Uighur Autonomous Region and includes the province of Gansu in China.
Most of the pieces were found around Turfan, the temple caves of Bezeklik and the ancient city of Karakhoja in the eastern part of the silk route. 
Others were discovered at Kizil near the city of Kucha in the West.
The first expedition, which lasted from December 1902 to April 1903 yielded 44 crates of clay and wooden figures, painted frescoes and manuscripts in many languages and scripts, including Mongolian, Sanskrit, Chinese, Tibetan, Uighurian and ancient Turkish. 
They were retrieved from ruined temples at Karakhoja, also known as Khocho. 
The rarest finds, however, were not Buddhist but some manuscript pages from the original writings of the Manicheans, a now lost religion which originated in Persia around the third century A.D. and later spread to Central Asia. 
The archeologists also found some sacred texts and a faded wall painting from the remains of a Nestorian Christian temple, thus confirming reports that the Christian missionaries as well as Buddhists had brought their religions along the old silk road. 
Examples of these texts are on display.
When the relics of these vanished ancient cultures were excavated, they were packed for the long trip by camel caravan and then boat to St. Petersburgh in Russia and then to Germany where they were finally displayed at the Museum of Indian Art in Berlin. 
All of the art on exhibit at the Metropolitan was lent on an exchange agreement with this museum.
Published in connection with the exhibit is a catalogue with an introduction by Professor Herbert Hartel, director of the Museum of Indian Art in Berlin, who tells the exciting story of the recovery of this lost art. 
A poignant passage is a quote from one of Gruenwedel's letters after he had first seen the ruins of Khocho: ''The city serves as a quarry for materials to build the modern houses, as a gold mine for those who dig treasure, as a place of amusement where one can smash frescoes and statutes of Buddha to the glory of Allah - not to mention the practical benefit of being able to use the fragments (of frescoes) to fertilize the sugar cane, cotton and sorghum fields.''
That these fragile works were found at all is a wonder, but that they could survive the desert, Muslim armies, local pillagers, foreign treasure hunters, excavators and finally the trek across the world's deadliest deserts to Germany, where they were almost blown up by Allied bombs, is nothing short of miraculous.
However, when one walks through the cavelike exhibit at the Met, the violent past is soon forgotten and one is filled with a peaceful tranquility that seems to emanate from the painted scenes of the legendary events in the life of Buddha and his various incarnations that line the dark crimson walls of the simulated cave.
Jeffrey Daly, chief designer of the Metropolitan, has sought to create a cave atmosphere by lighting. 
Frescoes are lit at eye level while the ceiling is shrouded in darkness.
The man responsible for the concept of bringing the lost Central Asian art to the Metropolitan is Martin Lerner, curator of the Indian and Southeast Asian art, who came to the museum in 1972 after working for six years with Sherman Lee at the Cleveland Museum of Art. 
He is a tall, bearded man whose intense gray eyes betray his fascination for the art he personally selected to be shown.
''What we have done,'' he explained during a walk through the exhibition, ''is to arrange the material both chronologically and geographically so you are really starting on a pilgrimage going from West to East. 
You see, we are working our way to China.''
The earliest works of art date from about 500 to 700 A.D. and are known as the Western School. 
They show a definite Indian and Persian influence.
''The early material comes from the temple cave sites at Kizil,'' explained Mr. Lerner, ''the style is called Indian-Iranian. 
It does not show any Chinese style yet.''
The later artifacts, dating from 650 to 950 A.D., come from the Turfan Oasis area and are known as the Eastern School. 
In color and style, the frescoes show a strong Chinese influence, with some ancient Turkish elements.
Mr. Lerner, a scholar of Chinese Buddhist art, is also familiar with all the stories behind the paintings and sculptures. 
He pointed out a particularly well preserved fragment of a fresco from the Cave of Statues in Kizil which typifies the Indian-Iranian style. 
It depicts the cowherd Nanda, listening to the preaching of Buddha. 
''The cowherd is so wrapped up in what he is hearing that he doesn't realize that he is resting his gnarled stick on the back of this frog. 
But the frog does not want to disturb Nanda's attention by running away. 
According to the legend, the frog will be rewarded in a future life by being reborn as a god, and the cowherd will become a Buddhist monk.''
Not all the artwork is so optimistic. 
One painting from the Cave of Devils is a chilling freize showing scenes from the 10 hells of Mahayana Buddhism. 
''This explains exactly what you are going to suffer if you have not lived a proper existence,'' said Mr. Lerner with an enigmatic smile.
In the first hell the damned are hanging upside-down while being hacked to pieces with axes. 
Those that escape fall into other hells where they are beaten incessantly, flayed alive, devoured by vultures, burned in pools of acid, dismembered, crushed between walls, forced to eat molten iron and boiled before being transformed into pillars of fire.
The ancient artists were extraordinarily creative in the painting of monsters (infernal watchmen of King Yama) who inflicted the tortures. 
Some resemble modern depictions of creatures from outer space.
About halfway through the exhibit the wall color effectively turns to dark green. 
The murals that begin this section reveal the origins of the inhabitants of Central Asia. 
These are portraits of wealthy patrons and aristocrats who donated art to the temples to gain religious merits. 
They show the striking difference between the people from Western and Eastern areas of the northern silk route.
One large fragment (number 107), found in the cave of 16 swordbearers at Kizil in the western section, dated 600-650 A.D., shows four Tocharian knights of obvious Indo-European descent dressed in Persian-style apparel. 
They have light-colored eyes and reddishbrown hair. 
In contrast, a ninth-century grouping of Uighurian princes from Bezeklik Temple in the eastern part show definite East Asian characteristics with black hair and Oriental eyes.
Both types of people can be seen in Sinkiang today. 
It is still a melting pot of cultures and inhabited by 12 national minorities as well as Han Chinese. 
On a trip to this area in 1979 I was surprised to meet a fair, blue-eyed man, a leader of the East Wind commune near Urumchi, who said he was Chinese. 
The people of the Turfan Oasis are still known as Uighurs and are still Muslins but they have retained the features of their Buddhist ancestors that were depicted in the frescoes. 
They have now planted millions of Lombardy poplar trees to protect their towns from the desert sandstorms, but until recently they paid little heed to their cultural heritage lost in the cave temples and buried cities.
Although the Chinese stopped all foreign expeditions in the 1930's, the Buddhist sites were left in a state of neglect until the 1970's, when the Peking Government, in an effort to preserve its ancient monuments, began to restore the temple caves and guard the ruins of the old cities.
A few of these caves are now open. 
To reach the cave temples one must pass along the foot of the legendary Mountain of Flames where the first Buddhist pilgrim Xuan Zhuang journeyed west in 630 A.D. to bring the teaching of Buddha from India. 
Legend says that he was accompanied by a white monkey who cooled the flaming mountain with a palm-leaf fan so they could pass. 
The red tertiary sandstone of the naked mountain still scintillates like fire in the blazing sun.
The only part of the original Old Silk Route which can still be seen is a gray brick path that leads to the ancient city of Khocho - where libraries of old manuscripts, frescoes and sculptures were found and shipped to Europe. 
Today it is a haunted city, with crumbling city walls and misshapen temple ruins revealing empty vestibules still showing faint outlines of the Buddha.
Restoration of the Bezeklik Temple caves is proceeding slowly. 
The sand has been shoveled out but the caves stand empty and desolate. 
The keeper was more interested in showing us the pelts of the foxes he had trapped in the caves than in the remains of the Buddhist art. 
The few frescoes that remained on the walls had been defaced. 
The eyes of Buddha's disciples had been scratched out by local Muslims who believed the figures would come alive at night. 
The pedestals where gods once resided stood vacant. 
And most of the walls were blank except for the deep scars of crowbars where the paintings had been hacked off and taken away by Europeans. 
No wonder, as the writer Eric Teichman wrote in ''Journey to Turkistan,'' it made the Chinese ''boil with indignation.''
