FOR the second time this year, the Metropolitan Museum of Art has inaugurated galleries, and for the second time, the museum cannot adequately fill them. 
The Sackler Galleries for Asian Art that open to the public tomorrow are much smaller and more modest than the Lila Acheson Wallace Wing for 20th-century art, and the art in them, being from one country, is more of a piece. 
But, here, too, there is not enough first-rate art. 
The Met continues to reinforce its reputation as an encyclopedic institution, at the expense of its reputation as a defender of the highest artistic standards.
This is not to say that the new galleries are not important. 
Barbara B. Ford, an associate curator of Asian art and, with Wen Fong, Yasuko Betchaku and Kakichi Suzuki, a prime mover in the installation, said the ''assignment was to write a book on Japanese art.''
The installation may not be a book, but it outlines many key chapters. 
It begins with prehistory and essentially ends with the 19th century, moving from ceramic figurines with squat bodies and embryonic eyes, to the inventive and irreverent narratives of Utamaro, Hiroshige and Hokusai, which helped trigger the explosion of interest in Japanese art in the West.
Perhaps most important, there is now a place in New York where the public can begin to orient itself to Japanese art. 
The installation provides several points of reference. 
One is that there is little or no distinction between the fine and decorative arts. 
All arts in Japan are interrelated, and it was common for artists to work in several media. 
Another is that the Japanese have a very particular sense of appropriateness and place. 
Objects, even suits of armor, were made for a specific occasion. 
Presentation has always been crucial.
There are fine and instructive works. 
In the 17th-century screen ''Su Tung-po's Visit to the Wind and Water Cave,'' precisely delineated figures share a gold background with foliage that rises and falls and follows its own laws. 
The painting helps define the tension between formality and freedom, human beings and nature, that plays a decisive role in Japanese art. 
In a work like this, the gold background seems like an alternative space in which the conventions of human life and unconventional nature have a chance to coexist.
Ogata Korin's celebrated early-18th-century screen painting ''Rough Waves'' is just as revealing. 
A hissing wave in the foreground struggles to ward off other hissing waves that seem to be baring their teeth and rearing up like marauding cats. 
There is humor in the painting. 
There is also something of the awe before a wild sea. 
The painting is so stylized that it becomes decorative, but decorative in a way that gives the word a good name. 
As the imagery becomes ornate, it becomes unknown.
The one contemporary work in the installation - the work intended to bridge Japan and the United States - is Isamu Noguchi's ''Water Stone.''
It consists of a block of deep red and black basalt resting on a bed of stones taken from the Ise River, the site of one of Japan's most sacred Shinto shrines. 
Water rises from within the stone and forms a sheet on top before spilling down the sides; after this work, the glass tops of Mr. Noguchi's tables will not be seen in the same way. 
The work suggests not only the hard, earthy aspects of Japanese rock gardens, but a symbolic dimension as well.
If all the arts in Japan are interrelated, however, not all are of equal interest. 
The precious objects, such as teaware, lacquerware, writing boxes, incense boxes and porcelain, may be superbly crafted, but there are too many of them, and they break the spell of paintings that have the power to involve us in a more imaginative and total way. 
The effect of this blend of ''high'' and ''low'' art is an unresolved tension between objects to which we are expected to respond in terms of spiritual aspiration and objects that appeal largely to luxury taste. 
If the installation cannot begin to clarify this tension, which seems so essential to Japanese art, it is no wonder. 
The unresolved tension between high purpose and high luxury is now part of the fabric of the Metropolitan Museum.
Although the installation is filled with information, it is intellectually flat. 
There is no sense of a passion for ideas - of an urgent engagement with issues raised by the art. 
We can recognize but not participate in the artistic dialogue between nature and style, otherworldly spirituality and courtly refinement. 
What does ''decorative'' mean in Japanese art?
Or nature?
The constant struggle both to respect its otherness and tame it suggests an ambivalence toward nature that is not present in Chinese art.
It is hard to understand from the installation why Japanese art has become such a key player on the stage of world art that the Met has now given it its own pocket of the museum. 
It is just as difficult to understand from the installation why contemporary American artists as different as Sonia Gechtoff, Yvonne Jacquette, Robert Kushner and Judy Pfaff have been drawn to Japanese art and culture. 
And can an installation that does more than enough justice to the refinement of Japanese art while avoiding its erotic dimension give an appropriate sense of Japanese culture?
There are 10 galleries in all, together providing 11,000 square feet of space. 
Of the 15,000 Japanese objects in the museum collection, 280 are now on display. 
The museum hopes eventually to be able to change the installation four times a year. 
The galleries mark the second major step in the development of the Met's department of Asian Art: the Astor Court and the Douglas Dillon Galleries for Chinese paintings, which are adjacent to the Japanese galleries, opened in 1981. 
The next step will be galleries for ancient Chinese art, which are expected to open next year.
The absence of more first-rate works is not entirely the fault of the museum, which formed its department of Asian art in 1915. 
Tradition is being rapidly destroyed in Japan, but there are many Japanese who are determined to preserve it. 
Japan is very strict about allowing its art to leave the country. 
In addition, there is currently a museum boom there that appears to be the equal of the boom in Europe and the United States. 
Although acquisitions are still possible - one of the screens featured in the installation was bought only a couple of weeks ago - it will be hard for any American institution to make a dramatic improvement over the Japanese collection it now has.
The installation is roughly chronological. 
The first gallery, with its pre-Buddhist material, is one of the best. 
The six pots in one display case have an easy perfection and understated feeling for shape and pattern that are characteristic of Japanese ceramics. 
There is a steatite bracelet that seems as elastic as a Japanese lamp. 
A ceremonial bell is shaped like a tower, and the decorative patterns make this heavy object, like the bracelet, seem light. 
In this gallery, refinement, expressiveness and toughness exist together.
Given that Japanese art was made for particular occasions, it is logical that the museum would try to place objects in some kind of architectural context. 
There is a replica of a 12th-century altar and a replica of a shoin, or study. 
But placing different kinds of architecture close together, as well as covering thousands of years with relatively few objects, makes the installation schematic. 
We can recognize the religious authority of the altar and the delicate proportions of the study, but we can not participate in either.
One of the centerpieces of the installation is the 12th-century sculpture of a Buddha seated on a lotus pedestal on the altar. 
Its privileged position makes a point about the importance of Buddhism to Japanese culture. 
Everything in this serenely proportioned sculpture, from the hairdo, to the position of the fingers and knees, to the expression of the face, has a particular meaning. 
In the gallery around this Buddha, there are informative but less compelling sculptures representing different aspects of Buddhism.
The installation moves through the development of narrative painting. 
There are several works on the four seasons, a recurring Japanese theme. 
We get some sense of the development and importance of screens. 
The installation suggests ways in which Japan alternately opened itself up to and closed itself off from the outside world, particularly China. 
Some Japanese painting, particularly during the Muromachi period, is very Chinese. 
In Kano Sansetsu's early-17th-century ''Ancient Plum,'' installed in the shoin, the artist takes a Chinese theme, the flowering plum, paints it on gold leaf and weaves it into a grand decorative pattern that is not Chinese at all.
In another large screen painting, ''Bamboo in the Four Seasons,'' the absence of linearity and the way bamboo shoots seem to be standing on, not rooted in the ground, seem particularly Japanese. 
So does Ogata Korin's famous ''Irises and Bridge,'' the focus of the gallery of the Edo period (1615-1868) and almost the keystone of the installation, with its pure colors and blend of gestural sweep and architectural stylization.
There is one section on Japanese porcelain and another on ''Samurai Splendor,'' which includes a suit of armor that is described in the caption as the ''most important example of Japanese armor in the West.''
Japanese armor can be stylish and seemingly impractical. 
The way soldiers looked and presented themselves mattered profoundly. 
''When you read accounts of battles,'' Ms. Ford said, ''one-quarter may be about the battle, one-half about the pedigree of those who fought in it, and one-quarter a loving account of what people wore.''
The installation essentially ends with 18th- and 19th-century scrolls and wood-block prints. 
In Hokusai's ''Poet Li Po Viewing a Waterfall,'' the drunken poet is being held up by two aides as he tries to contemplate the water he is in danger of toppling into. 
The waterfall is reduced to blue and white vertical streaks that resemble strips in a Morris Louis painting.
There are a few 20th-century objects in the collection, mostly crafts. 
Collecting contemporary Japanese art is difficult, Ms. Ford said. 
It is in considerable demand in Japan. 
Furthermore, many contemporary Japanese artists are searching for an international style.
The galleries were designed by a team made up of Cleo Nichols of Cleo Nichols Inc.; the architectural firm of Kevin Roche, John Dinkeloo & Associates, and Kyotaro Nishikawa, the deputy director of the Tokyo National Museum. 
Most of the roughly $4 million cost was raised in Japan, starting with $1 million given by the Japanese Government in 1979. 
All the Japanese grants were received through the Japan Foundation.

text:
ï»¿
ANKOKU DOJI was an aide to the kings of Hell, and Mr. Nice Guy he wasn't. 
Sporting a tiny hat with propellerlike projections, holding a brush and a plank to take notes, his face screwed up in a knowing scowl, he served as a clerk of the court where the kings tried each sinner for his misdeeds on earth. 
A dramatic, larger-than-life-size image of this most uncelestial deity, carved of Japanese cypress in the 13th century, is one of the many stunning surprises in ''Japanese Buddhist Sculpture: A.D. 600-1300,'' a marvelous exhibition at the Japan Society Gallery, 333 East 47th Street (through Jan. 
16).
Grace Glueck reviews exhibit at Japan Society Gallery on Japanese Buddist Sculpture
The show, organized by the Japan Society and the Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth, is the first exhibition of classic Japanese sculpture to tour the United States. 
Its 52 key objects, all borrowed from active temples and important museum collections, track the Buddhist era in Japan. 
Seven of the sculptures are classified as national treasures, no less, and 37 more, including the Ankoku Doji, are considered important cultural properties. 
They were chosen to cover the full range of Buddhist expression, from the enlightened serenity of Amida, the Buddha who reigns over the heavenly pure land of a previous existence, to the fierceness of the Myoo divinities, who symbolize Buddha's wrath against evil. 
The idea is also to show how - from an initial reliance on the forms and techniques of Chinese art -Japanese sculpture developed along more native lines.
Born in India, Buddhism arrived in Japan from China and Korea in the sixth century, and by the seventh had firmly settled in, with a full-blown religious hierarchy. 
It flourished for more than 600 years, changing with the Chinese theological winds, and in the process making rich contributions to Japanese architecture, sculpture and painting. 
As might be expected, the first images in the show are naive and stiff, small seventh-century representations in gilt bronze of two bodhisattvas, deities who have refused Buddhahood in order to help others find salvation.
By the next century, things had livened up. 
The Japanese got more deeply into Buddhism, and the sculpture, taking cues from the art of Tang China, became more sophisticated, as we see in life-size images of Komokuten and Tamonten, two of the four guardian kings who in Indian legend ruled over the North, South, East and West. 
Both, dressed in armor and taking very assertive stances, are of carved wood, a material for which the Japanese had a special sensibility. 
In the ninth century, as Emily J. Sano, curator of Asian art at the Kimbell, points out in her catalogue introduction, wood replaced everything else as the sculptural medium, and its working by skilled carvers had a great effect on style. 
A small but powerful ninthcentury ''Miroku,'' or Buddha of the Future, a corpulent figure carved from a single block of wood, exemplifies in its ''wave'' pattern of deeply incised drapery folds the influential way in which early Heian sculptors explored the wood-block surface.
Also in the ninth century, a more esoteric, intense Buddhism appeared, producing all manner of exotic divinities, such as Fudo, one of the Five Great Myoo who ruled the world of wisdom. 
A 10thcentury, life-size image of Fudo depicts this dour deity, bug-eyed and fang-toothed, seated in the lotus position and holding a lariat with which to catch offenders. 
Farther along, in the late Heian period, calmer imagery reflects a change in the emotional pressure of the religion. 
Eleventh-century examples include three delicate ''Bodhisattvas on Clouds,'' so Baroque in feeling they could almost have come from a 16th-century German church; and a sybaritic-looking Nyoirin Kannon, the six-armed bodhisattva who grants desires, reclining in a drowsy posture of royal ease.
The coming of realism to Japanese sculpture in the late 12th and 13th centuries - credited by Miss Sano to a revival of eighth-century classical styles and the influence of Sung Dynasty China - is exemplified here by, among other images, two powerful, life-size 13th-century portraits of priests. 
One in bronze-finished wood, with inserted crystal eyes and thought to depict Enji Benen, the first abbot of the Zen temple Tofuku-ji, is so startlingly modern it might be a 20th-century work.
Unfortunately, the Kimbell installation has been shoehorned into the small Japan House Gallery, and the lighting of individual works leaves something to be desired. 
But at that, it's the most fascinating show in town. 
It's accompanied by a beautiful, full-color catalogue - $26 and well worth it - written by Dr. Sano and Dr. Kyotaro Nishikawa of the Fine Arts Bureau of Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs. 
The show has been made possible in part by grants from the Tandy Foundation and the Tandy Corporation-Radio Shack of Fort Worth, and the Friends of Japan House Gallery.
Other shows of interest this week: Miriam Schapiro (Barbara Gladstone Gallery, 41 West 57th Street): Two big paintings are the set pieces of this show, in which Miriam Schapiro combines fabric collage and paint in dense, decorative surfaces that also incorporate reworkings of her past imagery. 
In ''Invitation,'' she celebrates the American quilt, laying down on a rich painted ground a schematic pattern of such motifs as stenciled, painted and cut-out fabric teapots, cups, simplified houses, blossoms, crocheted potholders, doilies and a tiny apron. 
In and out of a large central rectangle snakes a broad band of patchwork fabrics, actually made by cutting up, unraveling and reforming a ''Friendship Ring'' quilt.
In ''Presentation,'' the other large work, a central proscenium structure, whose border of painted diagonal stripes is inflected by gold fabric roses, contains a ''scene'' of multicolor painted and collaged abstract forms in a kind of tumultuous ballet. 
To make a wild, contrasting border for the proscenium, Miss Schapiro raided her previous ''fan'' paintings, dissecting them for zig-zag motifs that she layered on a motley painted ground. 
The play back and forth between painting and collage, defying the viewer's ability to differentiate, strengthens the interest of these lively paintings, which, however, lack the elegance of Miss Schapiro's best work. 
(Through Dec. 
4.)
John Willenbecher (Hamilton Gallery, 20 West 57th Street): Marble graining has appeared in John Willenbecher's work for the last two years or so, and in this show, titled ''Scenes From Ovid,'' it burgeons. 
Against plywood panels skillfully grained to simulate various marble species, he places found objects of abstract form covered with gold leaf, each work as a whole evoking a mythological theme. 
In ''Olympus,'' for example, two vertical panels in a rich green grain bear on their surface a gold template, pierced with round holes and a rectangular slit that has a startlingly anthropomorphic appearance; in ''Zeus,'' one of the show's stars, a gilded iron reinforcement bar, bent like a branch, inflects a sumptuous black ''marble'' surface, veined in light blue.
The stagiest metaphor is ''Echo,'' two skulls, cast in bronze and then marble-painted, resting on velvet cushions on a white table. 
There are also a number of arched-window devices, a familiar form to those who follow Mr. Willenbecher's art, which encase found objects on shelves, such as ''Olenus and Lethea,'' a comradely pair of - male and female?
- gilded rocks. 
This is risky work. 
At its most restrained, as in ''Zeus'' and ''Olympus,'' there's poetry to it, but certain combinations of gold leaf and flashy graining look - well, tacky. 
(Through Dec. 
11.)
Ralph Mayer (Sid Deutsch Gallery, 20 West 57th Street): The late Ralph Mayer (1896-1979), a leading authority on paint technology and author of the classic ''Artists' Handbook of Materials and Techniques,'' was a painter himself, but he was rarely exhibited during his lifetime. 
The small body of work that he left, ranging over some 50 years, has a kind of naive Precisionist approach, depicting factory buildings, urban streetscapes and industrial waterways in spare, quasigeometric compositions that have a good deal of charm. 
They are light on people and heavy on architectural structures, such as ''The Bridge'' (1927), in which the looming understructure of a bridge frames a group of pink brick buildings and an empty street. 
Nevertheless, it succeeds in capturing the mood of a city place.
A flaw in these works is the irresolution of certain compositions, such as ''Brooklyn Bridge, Red City,'' in which the East River doesn't too readily separate itself from the roof of a frontally placed building. 
Oddly enough, that only adds to their appeal. 
(Through Dec. 
4.)

text:
ï»¿
THE Chinese do not see stone the way Westerners do. 
Rocks for them are concentrations of energy and life, objects of contemplation and worship, models for human character, microcosms of heaven and earth. 
In his foreword to the catalogue of ''Kernels of Energy, Bones of Earth: The Rock in Chinese Art,'' at the China House Gallery, 125 East 65th Street, through Jan. 
26, Wan-go H. C. Weng, the gallery president, writes that ''if, according to William Blake, a world could be seen in a grain of sand, then the Chinese universe can also be comprehended in a piece of rock.''
Despite the show's modest size - it contains 50 works, many of them small - it seems big. 
Through his selection of sculptures and paintings and his invaluable catalogue, John Hay of New York University's Institute of Fine Arts sets out to survey the rock in Chinese culture. 
Since for the Chinese everything in the natural world was interrelated and filled with religious and philosophical meaning, a serious handling of the rock throws open the doors to just about everything.
A rock could be from a few inches to 50 feet high. 
The Chinese had a clear sense where to look for it, what to do with it and what made a rock desirable. 
In a 19th-century text by Liang Jiutu, who called himself the ''man of the 12-rock studio,'' the quality of a rock was determined by ''leanness, surface texture and a pierced interior.''
The preferred identified with vapor, which the Chinese saw as released energy, and clouds.
Rocks were also seen as the root of precious metals, including gold and therefore indispensable to alchemists, who were trying to bring cosmic forces under control. 
They were equally indispensable to scholars and monks, for whom they could be objects of inspiration and meditation. 
Scholars saw inkstones and brush rests as anything but indifferent resting places for their pens and brushes. 
When they put pen and brush down, it was to enable them to re-establish contact with basic sources of energy and knowledge.
Rocks could be talismanic. 
At different times, they were thought to cure illness and even drunkenness. 
They could also be friends. 
One of the key figures in Chinese ''stone lore'' is the eccentric 11th-century magistrate and rock connoisseur Mi Fu. 
When ''he entered the official precinct for the first time,'' Mr. Hay writes, ''he saw a large and bizarre rock set up there. 
At once he called for his robe and tablet of office, and bowed deeply to the stone. 
Subsequently he always addressed it as ''Shixiong,'' ''Elder Brother Stone.''
From all this, it is also easy to see why there may have been rock cults in Chinese culture; why the sixth-century Indian monk Bodhidharma, later considered the first patriarch of Chan Buddhism, apparently spent nine years meditating upon a rock; why caves and cliffs had such sacred meaning, and why some reknowned Chinese scholars, from the Middle Ages on, have been known as petrophiles. 
Because of his obsession with rocks, the Emperor Huizong was called a ''petromaniac.''
The place of rocks in Chinese culture can probably be most strongly felt in Chinese gardens, where, in Mr. Hay's words, rocks were ''both the frame'' and the ''foci of visual attention.''
In Wu Zhen's 14th-century scroll, ''Poetic Feeling in a Thatched Pavilion,'' a literati's retreat seems to have been organized around a huge, upright rock that seems like a distant ancestor of the stone heads from Easter Island.
In Yuan Jiang's 18th-century handscroll ''The Gazing Garden,'' the massive rock garden seems enchanted. 
The stones resemble coral and skulls and bones, and they seem to crawl, rumble and howl through and around the landscape and architecture, which appears totally reassured by their otherworldly presence. 
The stone is by far the most powerful force there.
Visitors to this exhibition who still have trouble understanding what the fuss is all about should look for the ''Penjing'' in another room. 
To the Chinese, ''penjing'' means a ''a thousand-mile vista, on a single tray.''
This miniature distillation of mountains consists of three stones, the largest about a foot high, resting in a shallow basin. 
The stone is cavernous, striated and worn. 
It seems open and closed, both in the process of regenerating itself and frozen. 
The largest stone suggests a mesa, but also the sea. 
The work brings to mind groups of figures by many modern sculptors, including Medardo Rosso, Henry Moore and Alberto Giacometti. 
It is possible to pull up a chair and watch it, as if it were a living theater. 
Also of interest this week: Michael Steiner (Andre Emmerich Gallery, 41 East 57th Street): Michael Steiner's recent bronze sculptures are transitional, provocative and intelligent. 
These free-flowing sculptural compositions are crammed with references to Classical culture, landscapes and sculptural history. 
The challenge Steiner seems to have set himself is to create substantial sculptural and thematic complexity while at the same time draining his works of any physical and emotional weight.
The material helps. 
The strips of wax from which the bronze is cast are light. 
Along with the blue-black patina, they make it hard to distinguish the sculpture's actual supports. 
The works depend on a play between forms that have thematic meaning and others that don't, between forms that have a clear sense of sculptural necessity and others that do not, between forms that are essential to the structure and others that seem to be but aren't. 
It is an odd game, not always played with the same amount of interest, but filled with surprises.
There are a lot of sculptors who move in and out of these works - not just David Smith and Anthony Caro, but also Henri Laurens, Mark di Suvero and Giacometti. 
In ''Babel'' we also run into Umberto Boccioni, Vladimir Tatlin and Picasso. 
Steiner tries both to make everybody welcome and to clear everybody out so that all that remains is the language of sculpture and a feeling of fresh possibility. 
The tension generates energy and gives these works consistent visual interest. 
(Through tomorrow.) Henry Finkelstein (Prince Street Gallery, 121 Wooster Street): Henry Finkelstein is a young, essentially expressionist painter recently out of art school who is having his first one-man show in New York. 
His subject matter is traditional - still lifes and landscapes of Maine, New Jersey and Umbria. 
What is engaging is the artist's willingness to jump in with both feet. 
When a mood, instinct or compositional idea hits him, he goes with it.
Paint is the artist's means of fixing contact with the world around him. 
In most of these paintings, we never lose sight either of him or his subject. 
The Umbrian hills may have the colors of Bonnard, but we still roll right through the familiar, undulating land. 
We recognize the Maine coast immediately, but the colors can be hot and the rocks and land seem barely able to restrain the wild sea. 
In the painting of a New Jersey farm, everything is predictably quiet, except for the vegetable garden, which seems to be erupting with paint and light. 
(Through Jan. 
15.) Joseph Szilva (Eastman-Wahmendorf Gallery, 216 East 10th Street): Joseph Szilva was born in Hungary, raised in Canada and now lives in New York. 
His paintings and copper wall sculptures have the sweetness, small-scale and calculated awkwardness that are characteristic of a large body of East Village work. 
As his prints indicate, however, there is a visionary ambition behind Szilva's style. 
He seems to have gone back to mosaics, medieval miniatures and Romanesque and Gothic painting in order to find a language that can express both his feeling about New York City and his almost religious feeling for the natural world.
The sculptures, installed high up on the gallery walls, consist of sheets of copper, cut and then hammered. 
With titles like ''Mantis'' and ''Cobra,'' they suggest essential gestures and movements reduced to a quirky essence. 
Some paintings contain patterns of glass pellets laid on with cement. 
In others, one form, with three leaves that suggest both a plant and a human with outstretched arms, seems almost autobiographical. 
We watch it in different landscape situations and in the midst of a seascape in which sea and sky run together. 
These works have a distinct, warmth, integrity and sense of place. 
(Through Sunday.)

text:
ï»¿
IN New Jersey, Franc Palaia has
been blessed with the gift of
ubiquity. His photographs seem
to have appeared everywhere in the last 10 years, including:
Mercer County Community College, the Princeton University Art Museum, Jersey City State College, the Jersey City Museum, the Morris Museum of Arts and Sciences, Monmouth Museum, Glassboro State College, Fairleigh Dickinson University, Kean College and Brookdale Community College.
Mr. Palaia, who lives in Elizabeth, is also well on his way to establishing his omnipresence in New York City. 
After a spate of shows there, he is currently having not one, but two, exhibitions in Manhattan.
Works by photographer Franc Palaia are on display at Metropolitan Museum of Art and at Trompe L'Oeil Gallery in Manhattan; photo (M)
One is at the Trompe L'Oeil Gallery, 24 East 81st Street, through Saturday, and the other is part of a group show at the Metropolitan Museum of Art through Nov. 
30. Both are results of a trip Mr. Palaia made to China in 1981.
Most people go to China and try to see, among other things, the Great Wall. 
Mr. Palaia seems to have seen every wall there that he possibly could. 
At least that's the impression one gets at the Trompe L'Oeil, where 11 works celebrate the wall art of signs, billboards, broadsides, manifestos, graffiti and murals.
Mr. Palaia not only paints images that he saw on walls (these are done from photographs he took), but also constructs his own versions of walls. 
Almost life size, they appear to have been rescued from demolished or bombed buildings, and both they and their overpainted images look authentic.
Although the synthetic polystyrene used to make the walls has the surface and material consistency of an actual wall, the tempera on plaster superimposed on them has the faded appearance of something that has weathered and deteriorated with time.
There are political icons of Mao and Mao's wife, Jiang Quing, after she was sentenced for her participation in the Cultural Revolution.
There also are messages and advertisements on Mr. Palaia's walls, and they are quite amusing for their seeming incongruity: argyle socks, Marlboro cigarettes, a warning about safe bicycling, a buoyant portrait of a young woman selling flowers, a '' Democracy Wall'' (a busy collage of notices and announcements) and a fresco in which we see an automobile parked at what appears to be a gasoline station.
One must not look at these works as only fascinating paintings for their imagery and for the accuracy of the imagery, but also as constructions or sculptures. 
As a combination of the two art forms, they are strikingly persuasive.
The figures and all of the pictorial activities, including the calligraphy, which has been executed with impressive precision, are assertive in their broad boldness and simple poster-like monumentality. 
The painting, with its simulated blemishes and chips and its flat modeling in stark, tonal modulation and color, has a beguiling directness.
The images are made all the more effective - maybe in the same romantic way that the Parthenon and other buildings of the past are - by their partial destruction.
One of Mao's eyes is missing, as well as part of his ear, and his face is pock-marked with white spots caused by missing plaster. 
The young woman in the safe-bicycling message has barely survived, and the girl selling flowers is a phantom of her former self.
They make us feel as if we must preserve the vanishing image of a disappearing civilization.
The rough configurations of the fragmented pieces, which must be seen as sculptural slabs, contrast with and complement nicely the imagery.
While they seem to be of different eras, as if the painting were a relatively recent superimposition on an older building, they both seem to be doomed to disappearance, two disparate elements that have been united by different cultures and linked into a similar destiny.
They have the same haunting quality that Italian frescos might have were they disembodied from the context of their walls.
Mr. Palaia's work in gold illumination is discussed in the crafts column.

text:
ï»¿
The exhibition of Japanese art opening today at the National Gallery of Art in Washington is unprecedented in the scope, quality and numbers of treasures (close to 500 works of art) gathered from more than 100 collections all over Japan. 
''Japan: The Shaping of Daimyo Culture 1185-1868'' represents the outcome of years of collaborative effort among Japanese and American officials and scholars following a meeting of the minds at the Tokyo Summit in 1983.
Conceived by guest curator Yoshiaki Shimizu, a professor of art history at Princeton University, the theme is that of the art and values of the powerful warrior elite known as daimyo who ruled Japan for seven centuries, from the late 12th to the mid-19th century. 
A group of anywhere from 50 to 250 regional feudal lords commanding armies of samurai and owing allegiance to the shogun, daimyo had the wealth, status and power to commission the finest artists and the best craftsmen.
In short, while the arts of the courtier and the commoner, at opposing ends of the spectrum, may not be emphasized in this exhibition, it is safe to say that the essence of Japanese culture is presented here by many of its greatest masterpieces, including sculpture, painting, calligraphy, textiles, lacquer, ceramics, and arms and armor, an extraordinary gesture of good will on the part of the people and Government of Japan. 
Screen paintings that have not left the homes of their owners in generations, even to travel from Tokyo to Kyoto, have been made available to the National Gallery.
The key to this exhibition is the warrior ideal of the fusion of the arts of war and the arts of peace. 
Suspicious, brutal, ruthless men who often spent their entire adult lives in battle, intrigue and the pursuit of power, the daimyo were also deeply religious students of Zen Buddhism, as well as poets, painters and voracious collectors. 
These complex, contradictory personalities are at the heart of the exhibition; they are brought to life through a stunning and somewhat eerie array of portraiture and by subtle juxtapositions of the lethal weapons of their trade - glistening steel blades, for example - together with elegant scrolls of calligraphy.
Where else but in Japan would poetry be a matter of utmost concern in the heat of battle?
When the castle of the daimyo Hosokawa Yusai was besieged in the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, the emperor, fearing the worst, sent a messenger begging him to hand over knowledge that only he possessed, interpretations of poems in a venerated 10th-century poetry anthology, transmitted secretly from generation to generation. 
Yusai survived the battle, but his ''document of transmission,'' still preserved in the Hosokawa family collection, is on display in Washington.
Throughout the 9th to the 12th centuries in Japan the ruling class was a hereditary court aristocracy centered in Kyoto, the ancient capital. 
Loath to relinquish the luxuries and civilities of palace life, a halcyon world of poetry and romance, courtiers delegated responsibility for managing and policing their distant estates to local warlords, who gradually became rich landowners in their own right. 
An efficient and tightly knit system of lord-vassal relationships had evolved with small military bands in the provinces. 
Warrior leaders established a power base and mode of organization that gave them a significant advantage over the increasingly ineffectual courtier.
Needless to say, these military officials were despised and ridiculed as a crude and unsophisticated lot by the snobbish elite in the capital. 
And yet, because of a universal respect for the cultural attainments of the nobility, the supposedly uncouth military men were deeply aware of their esthetic shortcomings and were committed to the conservative, courtly tradition of the men and women whom they were displacing.
This is at once apparent in the dazzling suits of multicolored armor worn by mounted daimyo chieftains. 
Beautiful armor laced with colorful silk threads enhanced the warrior's self-esteem - it was his weapon of culture - even though it may have been oppressively heavy and evil-smelling when soaked with water and teeming with lice during long campaigns in the rainy season. 
The courtly arts infected the warrior class and it is not unusual to read in medieval battle epics that a flute wrapped in a brocade bag was tucked into the sash around a young soldier's waist.
It is an indication of Japanese concern for social status that more often than not the portraits of military rulers show them wearing the tall lacquered hats and starched silk pantaloons generally reserved for titled nobility. 
Hideyoshi, a small, homely man notorious for his ''monkey face,'' started life in the late 16th century as the son of a peasant farmer and rose through the ranks to become the despot who not only unified the country after decades of civil war but also dared to attempt imperialist expansion onto the mainland. 
He nonetheless found it necessary to legitimize his role as ruler of Japan by fabricating an aristocratic lineage and acquiring a high court office, and his portraits in the exhibition show him in the robes of a courtier.
It may be for similar reasons of self-esteem and innate reticence that imagery of violence, bloodshed, decapitation and the like are scarce in Japanese art. 
The occasional pictorialization of man's inhumanity to man issued primarily from Buddhist temples. 
Warriors preferred to focus on the positive virtues of loyalty, courage and martial skills.
Of course, the daimyo and their samurai vassals were enterprising, self-made men with great confidence in their own abilities. 
They patronized new art forms - ink painting foremost among them - imbued with a pragmatism, realism and ascetic sensitivity that owed a great deal to Zen, the new religion introduced to Japan from the continent in the 13th century. 
There were many warrior-artists over the centuries; some were inspired amateurs in the style of Winston Churchill at his easel, others, the famed Musashi among them, were accomplished painters who wielded their brushes with the skill of samurai swordsmen.
To compete with the esoteric skills of the courtiers (poetry competitions and the sniffing of incense, for example), and to acquire cultural prestige of their own, daimyo took up the tea ceremony and sponsored troupes of No actors. 
Increased trade with China gave the military elite an alternative cultural model. 
They sponsored Chinese priests who came to Japan, helped found Zen monasteries and mimicked Chinese customs such as tea drinking. 
Medieval daimyo assembled large collections of Chinese art works to be displayed at tea events for important visitors. 
These expensive imports symbolized, through their link with an advanced culture, intellectual superiority and, ultimately, the political power of their owner. 
High-quality utensils were essential for entertaining superiors.
Among the most unprepossessing tea utensils in this exhibition is a fat little 13th-century Chinese ceramic tea caddy with an outer glaze like a thin coating of molasses. 
It was owned by Hideyoshi's tea master, Rikyu. 
The daimyo Hosokawa Sansai is said to have so coveted this caddy that he declared he would trade one entire province for it. 
After Rikyu's death (Hideyoshi had forced him to commit suicide) the caddy passed into the collection of the first Tokugawa shogun, Ieyasu. 
After the important Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, Ieyasu invited Sansai to a banquet and presented the treasured caddy to his vassal as a reward for his loyal support. 
(The ivory lid of the caddy is lined with gold foil that served as a device to signal any obvious tampering with the tea: the foil would change color if poison were present. 
In the world of the warrior, even a tea gathering could be dangerous.) Daimyo culture was chiefly a man's world. 
Woman's role was that of obedient wife and mother. 
Both Budddhism and Confucianism relegated her to an inferior status. 
Wives put up with infidelity but were themselves executed for adultery. 
Samurai daughters became hostages in daimyo warrior contracts, and were often forced to commit suicide at a young age as an expression of loyalty to their husbands when their castles were under siege. 
The organizers of the exhibition have nonetheless gone out of their way to include arts associated with the women of the samurai and daimyo aristocracy - their robes and sumptuous bridal trousseaus, for example. 
Most telling is the suit of red armor complete with fierce face mask for the daughter of the daimyo Ii Naosuke.
Conflicting values are a conspicuous feature of Japan's feudal age. 
The feminine sensibility and good taste of the old imperial court - the preciousness of a beauty soon faded, the unspoken overtones of a casual remark, the melancholy of a rainy evening - became the heritage not only of a handful of Kyoto aristocrats but of the entire Japanese people.
The importance of the transition from courtly to military ethos in the 13th century, however, may be that contemporary Japan is much closer in spirit to the esthetics of the warrior class, who ruled Japan with great success for 700 years, than it is to the world of Prince Genji and Lady Murasaki. 
Even after their special privileges of swords and stipends were abolished after the Meiji Restoration in 1868, former daimyo and samurai were recognized as the intellectuals and men of action who helped lead Japan into the modern age.
The primary sponsors to whom we are indebted for this exhibition are the R.J.

The authoritative full-color catalogue edited by Professor Shimizu is a product of joint Japanese and American scholarship and should be read cover to cover. 
''Japan: The Shaping of Daimyo Culture 1185-1868'' will be shown exclusively at the National Gallery in Washington until Jan.

A Tang Dynasty court lady, a richly glazed pottery study of a serene aristocrat seated on a bamboo stool, may rewrite the $660,000 record at auction for Tang art when it comes up for sale next week at Sotheby's. 
The gracefully modeled eighth-century tomb figure, owned in recent years by three major collectors of Chinese art, is one of several major Oriental works to be offered at Sotheby's and Christie's next week. 
The presale exhibitions this weekend were timed by the two houses to coincide with the long-awaited opening tomorrow of the Charlotte C. and John C. Weber Galleries of ancient Chinese art at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
The sale at Sotheby's at 2 P.M. Wednesday is to present the Tang court lady for the second time in six years at a Sotheby's auction. 
The sculpture was acquired in the mid-1940's in China by Capt. Sergius N. Ferris Luboshez, a retired United States Navy officer who was sent to the Far East by the State Department at the close of World War II to serve as general counsel to the Foreign Liquidation Commission; the work remained in his collection until it was auctioned for $198,000 at Sotheby's in 1982. 
The buyer, Giuseppe Eskenazi, a London dealer, sold it to C. C. Wang, a Chinese artist living in the United States. 
Last year the court lady changed hands again when Earl Morse, a retired food executive and a major collector of tomb sculpture, acquired it as a present to himself for his 80th birthday. 
The work is being sold from Mr. Morse's estate; he died in February.
''The market is very strong and for something of this rarity, prices are very high,'' said Carol Conover, Sotheby's specialist in Chinese art. 
She said the figure may even exceed her estimate of $450,000 to $650,000, despite repairs to the neck and coiffure, and a replacement of a piece of the blossoming plant stalk in the figure's right hand. 
Ms. Conover said she was optimistic because the prices paid for several major Chinese ceramics at Sotheby's in Hong Kong last week were double the house estimates and most pieces sold for more than Sotheby's expected.
An uncommon 19th-century set of 12 Japanese lacquered zodiac carrying cases, called inro, is one of the highlights of Sotheby's auction of Japanese art at 2 P.M. Wednesday and 10:15 A.M. and 2 P.M. Thursday. Happy Rockefeller is the consignor of these three and four-section small gilded and lacquered silver boxes, the Japanese solution to no pockets in a man's robe.
The set comes in a handsome black lacquer box that has silver mounts, gilded edges, an illustration on the front and four drawers inside for storing the inro, each of which is decorated with one of the 12 signs of the Oriental zodiac - the rat, ox, tiger, hare, dragon, snake, horse, goat, monkey, rooster, dog and boar. 
Although each case is signed by Koma Kansai 2d, a major Edo artist who retired in 1824, its black lacquer box is not signed. 
Peter J. Bufton, Sotheby's specialist in Japanese works of art, said only four zodiac inro have been offered at auction in the West in the last decade.

text:

GOOD MASSAGE is a potent tonic for mind and body. 
It can help relieve tension, stress and strain; temporarily aid blood circulation; make joints more supple, and act as a natural tranquilizer to induce pleasurable sedation. 
Medically, when performed by a physician or physical therapist, it can ease the pain of backaches, arthritis, bursitis, whiplash, sciatica and migraines. 
Massage, as a passive form of exercise, is also a valuable substitute for those who are incapable of activity.
Yet massage does not build muscle strength, burn up calories or break up fat cells. 
Unlike physical exercise, the effects are shortlived. 
And some people should not be massaged: those with infections, malignancies, blood clots, redness or contusions, impaired sensation, phlebitis or skin disease. 
In addition, skin that is thin due to injury or burn should not be massaged.
GOOD MASSAGE is a potent tonic for mind and body.
But if one can afford a massage -an hour usually ranges in price from $25 to $50 and up - it can play a useful role in a health program. 
Aside from the heightened sense of well-being it arouses, it relaxes muscles in preparation for physical activity - the reason massage is often used by athletes. 
After a vigorous workout, it may also help relieve muscle tightness and, with the temporary increase in blood circulation, aid the body in removing wastes - such as lactic acid - generated by physical exercise.
In general, the success of any type of massage therapy is linked to the skill of the therapist. 
''Massage has lost a lot of its potential value because it's being done by everyone and everybody,'' says Jack Hofkosh, director of the department of physical therapy at New York University's Institute of Rehabilitation Medicine. 
''There is no reason why somebody who needs a relaxation massage can't go and have a masseur work with him as long as it's understood that it's only going to have a relaxation effect. 
But if it's massage that has to be medically prescribed for a particular condition, you need a physician who is trained to prescribe it properly.''
In New York State, massage therapists must be licensed. 
To be eligible for the examination, an applicant must have graduated from an approved school and have completed 500 hours of rigorous study. 
Fewer than half the states now have licensing requirements, however.
Massage methodology is usually categorized as Eastern (from Japan and China) or Western (from Sweden). 
Offshoots of these range from medical massages to intensive body-working techniques.
The principles of Swedish massage were organized in the early 1800's by Pehr Henrik Ling, a Swedish fencing master and gymnastics instructor who used massage and exercise to treat his own rheumatism.
The French brought massage to the West, and French terminology is often still used. 
The basic movements of Swedish massage are effleurage or gliding strokes; petrissage or kneading;tapotement or stimulating strokes; friction or movements that compress the skin, and vibrating or shaking movements. 
All are done on bare skin that has been lubricated with cream, oil or powder to reduce friction.
Shiatsu massage from Japan (shi meaning finger; atsu, pressure) is sometimes called acupressure, which it resembles and which originated in China nearly 5,000 years ago.
''The ancient Chinese became aware of an increased sensitivity of certain skin areas (called points) when a body organ or function was impaired,'' writes Frances M. Tappan in ''Healing Massage Techniques'' (Reston Publishing Company, Reston, Va., 1978). 
''Consequently some of the relationships between various internal organs and their functions were established.''
In the shiatsu system, pressure can be from hand, elbow or knee and is used upon strategic points - known as tsubos - located along pathways called meridians. 
Improving ''energy flow'' along these paths is said to benefit the health of the internal organs. 
One caution: Having someone walk on your back and apply pressure with the toes is not part of traditional shiatsu; the heavy and inexacting pressure may cause back injury.
Shiatsu usually lasts from 30 minutes to an hour. 
Clothing is worn and no lubricants are used. 
The treatment may be uncomfortable, but should not be painful - it has been referred to as ''hurting good.''
In the area of medical massage, connective tissue and friction massage are both used on specific areas of the body. 
Connective-tissue massage helps to loosen fibrous tissue around muscles and to ease various disorders. 
Friction massage involves intermittent pressure on the body's soft tissues and is often used in treating tendon injuries.
Reflexology is based on the ancient Chinese method of using thumb pressure on specific areas of the feet that correspond to different body organs in an effort to improve their functioning.
In some cases, notably Rolfing and the polarity method, the therapy may be as uncomfortable as the disorder. 
Both systems use heavy and painful pressure purportedly to bring the body into vertical alignment; practitioners claim that normal posture may have become distorted due to stress, injury, illness or even the force of gravity. 
Polarity therapy works on reflex points, like those along the meridians, attempting to free ''energy flow.''
Rolfing manipulates the fasciae, or membranes supporting and sheathing the muscles. 
The premises and outcomes of both types of treatment are in dispute by experts.
Massage is generally thought of as an art form, and massage therapists all have their own styles of operating. 
For instance, at the Helena Rubinstein Beaute salon in Manhattan, Evelina Cardenas, a registered therapist with 35 years of experience, borrows from various disciplines. 
She also uses magnets to ''energize the body,'' tiger balm for sore muscles, a suction machine to ''help cellulite'' and a Chinese technique that gently hammers the soles of the feet ''for alignment.''
The massage therapist William Weslow, with a client list that reads like a Who's Who in dance and theater, is a former soloist with the New York City Ballet and a practitioner of massage for 25 years. 
He has developed a technique that combines strong relaxing strokes, deep muscular pressure and some needed probing - occasionally painful - of tight troubled areas. 
A high point of his treatment is an invigorating scalp massage, which one famed client has described as ''a mild earthquake.''
Between treatments, he advises clients who have upper back and neck problems to take hot baths, use heating pads, rub light balms on the affected areas and sleep with a warm covering to keep the body temperature up at night, which also keeps muscles relaxed.
The aim of his therapy is to increase circulation and bring about relaxation. 
''The biggest compliment someone can give me is falling asleep,'' says Weslow. 
''I know they're totally relaxed.''

text:
ï»¿
In 1947, Daisy Wang walked away with Shanghai's last beauty crown.
Then came Communism, proletarian morality and the conviction that in the workers' and peasants' paradise, beauty was bourgeois. 
Mao suits, in a choice of blue or gray, became the fashion. 
For women, lipstick and nail polish were decadent extravagances.
Perfume, makeup and coiffures have been back for a while, and this year, it appeared, so were beauty pageants. 
But the beast ideological purity, that treacherous ground of uncertainty in Chinese life, has resurfaced and beauty is on the run.
Last month, a local television station announced a contest to crown a Shanghai Maiden. 
A Beijing television station followed suit, declaring a Girls of Youth and Elegance pageant.
Now, the Shanghai event has been canceled while the Beijing affair has retreated from public view. 
Political puritanism, it seems, is back.
Â 
Picking a Beijing Flower
Three weeks ago, wobbling uncertainly on new high heels, 800 young women crowded into the Chongwenmen Cultural Palace to compete for the title of Beijing Flower in the capital's first beauty pageant in more than four decades.
''This is the first such contest in the capital similar to beauty contests in other countries,'' said Long Xinmin, the head of the Beijing television studio. 
''But ours puts as much emphasis on the participants' knowledge, performing technique and moral character as on their appearance and dress.''
Pageant officials printed up score sheets to evaluate the contestants, with categories ranging from ''teeth'' to ''length of legs,'' from ''color of skin'' to ''demeanor,'' from ''makeup'' to ''sense of humor.''
''Such contests are necessary to raise Chinese girls' awareness of grooming and deportment as a whole,'' Lan Guang, one of the eight judges, told the China Daily. 
''Esthetic education and training are also urgently needed in this country. 
The level of the contestant's grooming as a whole is rather low. 
A large number of them don't know what beauty is or how to use makeup or clothes to show off their natural beauty.''
Â 
Now a Closed Affair
Nervous young women were required to show off their talents by singing, dancing, reading aloud and expounding on their knowledge of Chinese culture. 
The finals of the Beijing Flower pageant, an extravaganza of music, color and fashion, was to have been broadcast by Beijing television, with the top 30 women offered modeling jobs.
In any case, those were the plans. 
Now, the Shanghai contest has been scuttled and the Beijing pageant has been reduced to a secret affair in a room somewhere in the city, closed to Chinese and foreign reporters alike and banned from television.
Â 
'Conditions Are Not Yet Ripe'
Shanghai's Communist Party chief, Jiang Zemin, was quoted by the official press agency as saying ''conditions are not yet ripe'' for a beauty pageant. 
An unnamed official was also quoted as saying that the city's economic problems require ''leaders and the 12 million city residents to be of one heart and one mind and to quietly immerse themselves in hard work.''
''It is premature to spend 450,000 yuan'' - about $126,000 - ''on a beauty pageant,'' the official said.
In Beijing, there was more mystery about what had happened, more rumors.
One story has it that the propaganda department of the Communist Party Central Committee frowned on the notion of picking a Beijing Flower and decreed that the show would not go on. 
Another rumor was that Hu Qili, a member of the Standing Committee of the Politburo, the most powerful body in the country, ordered the pageant scrapped.
Â 
'Not Good for the Girls'
Zhu Hansheng, a pageant organizer and a man of irrepressible good humor, deflected suggestions that politics had torpedoed his project. 
But he admitted that the grandiose schemes of last month had evaporated.
''Our way of doing things now is not quite the same as we originally planned,'' Mr. Zhu said, spreading his hands as if dropping a watermelon.
''We don't need to broadcast it on television,'' said Mr. Zhu, a director of the China Television Artists Association. 
''It's not good for the girls.''
No, Mr. Zhu insisted, there had not been any explicit instruction to tone things down.
''If Hu Qili had said stop, we would have had to stop immediately and I wouldn't have agreed to see you,'' he said. 
''China's not too rich. 
Some people don't eat. 
Some people say how can you hold a beauty contest if some people can't eat or dress properly?''
A collaborator in the pageant's organization, Zhang Andong, interrupted, ''We haven't received any directives directly from the authorities, but we can feel the atmosphere.''
''Feeling the atmosphere'' is a talent most Chinese have cultivated with care, for a loss of touch usually means trouble from above.
Mr. Zhu said the Beijing pageant would now be a private affair between the judges and the contestants. 
Previously announced prizes, including a piano, have been withdrawn. 
Instead, he said, the winners will receive ''Olympic-style medals.''
Across the Formosa Strait, Taiwan, which banned such beauty contests until last year, reveled in the attention it attracted by staging the Miss Universe Pageant, which ended today. 
''This kind of publicity is something our Government cannot possibly buy,'' Yao Ying-chi, an official of the ruling Nationalist Party, told The Associated Press in Taipei.
But Mr. Zhu, foreshadowing a sobering of Communist attitudes toward parading female pulchritude, said, ''If the whole country started to do this, it wouldn't be good.''

text:
ï»¿
When Christian Bale auditioned for Steven Spielberg's ''Empire of the Sun'' a year and a half ago, he had never been in a feature film and was but one of 4,000 teen-age boys vying for the role of Jim Graham, a pampered, cocky schoolboy in pre-World War II Shanghai who is transformed by four terrifying years of war into a gaunt yet courageous young man. 
In fact, the 13-year-old English boy had never really considered acting professionally until three years ago, when his sister Louise was cast in a musical in London's West End. 
''I thought it was really good fun, and it looked easy,'' said Mr. Bale, whose critically acclaimed performance in Mr. Spielberg's new $30 million movie has made him an odds-on favorite to join the very select group of child actors ever to be nominated for an Academy Award.
The film, which is based on J. G. Ballard's autobiographical account of his childhood in a Japanese prisoner-of-war camp in China, follows Jim through a remarkable emotional landscape of fear and pathos, bewilderment and bravery as he is separated from his parents during the Japanese invasion, befriended by an American drifter named Basie (played by John Malkovich) and herded into the Soochow Creek internment camp, where he learns the skills of survival and the art of compassion.
A Tough Span of Years
''At the beginning, Jim's a spoiled kid who wants his own way,'' said Mr. Bale in a recent telephone interview. 
''But he grows up really quickly. 
By the end, he's not as selfish or pigheaded.''
Although Jim loses his choirboy innocence, his energy never flags. 
As he tirelessly runs errands for Basie, helps the camp's physician, barters with other prisoners and stands up to the often brutal Japanese guards, this leather-jacketed waif begins to look and act like a young Harrison Ford.
''We realized that it's extrememly difficult for an actor who is 13 to carry a film, and that the span of years from about 10 to 15 is a very tough time for a child to be able to convincingly portray a character,'' said Kathleen Kennedy, who produced ''Empire of the Sun'' with Mr. Spielberg and Frank Marshall. 
''But Christian was remarkable. 
He showed a real, natural spontaneity as well as many levels of concentration and a great deal of attention to detail.''
The young actor was born in Wales and now lives with his family in Bournemouth, an English seaside town where Robert Louis Stevenson once lived. 
His father is a financial adviser and former pilot, and his mother is a former circus dancer, while one sister is a 20-year-old aspiring musician and the other is a 15-year-old actress. 
Barely a year after he began taking acting lessons, Mr. Bale got a part in a London stage production of ''The Nerd,'' playing what he described as ''a really obnoxious American kid who shouted his head off.''
He appeared in several television commercials and BBC productions as well as the 1986 NBC mini-series, ''Anastasia: The Mystery of Anna,'' before he began the long process of auditioning for ''Empire of the Sun.''
Â 
'Nothing to Do' in China
During 16 weeks of filming this year, Mr. Bale shuttled from England to Spain to China for a production that was monumental even by Steven Spielberg's standards. 
The streets of Shanghai were cordoned off for several days of shooting, and more than 15,000 extras and 500 crew members were recruited for the film, which is the first major Hollywood feature to be shot in China since the 1949 revolution. 
Despite the historic, larger-than-life scale of this undertaking, the young actor was nonplused by China. 
''There was nothing to do, and everything is very dusty and crowded,'' he recalled. 
''There's no color anywhere and the Chinese are always coughing.''
California, however, was another story. 
Like Jim, who finagles his way into living in the American barracks in the internment camp and is ecstatic at the appearance of an American bomber squadron, Mr. Bale was very much taken by the United States. 
''I really like working in America, especially California,'' he said. 
''I like the weather and the beaches, and the people are more friendly than in England.''
''I enjoyed doing film more than the stage,'' he added. 
''Ideally, I'd like to do a couple of films and a TV series over the next few years.''
He said he had received several film offers, and Ms. Kennedy confirmed that Mr. Spielberg ''would very much like to cast him in another film,'' but because of British child-labor laws, he cannot work again until the spring. 
In the meantime, he returned to Bournemouth this weekend, just another schoolboy back from his first gala Hollywood opening.

text:
ï»¿
It was the practice of the very earliest Chinese emperors, such as those of the Shang Dynasty from around 1,500 to 1,000 B.C., to have a group of slaves slaughtered at the time of their own deaths, so that the souls of the slaves could continue to serve the emperor's soul in the afterlife.
Around 200 B.C., however, these killings gave way to a more civilized practice that eventually developed into one of China's oldest and most refined artistic traditions: ceramic funerary art. 
Under this practice, life-size ceramic sculptures of slaves would be interred with the royal figure.
An exhibit now at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, which continues through May 24, provides the first major museum survey of the tradition of Chinese ceramic funerary art. 
With its 157 sculptures, the exhibition demonstrates that not only human figures, but ceramic sculptures representing the full range of Chinese life, were also made for burial.
In this show are sculptures of cows and cats, of horses and houses, of musicians and dancers, of soldiers and stable boys. 
Many funerary sculptures were made not for emperors but for wealthy landowners, who re-created their entire estates in miniature ceramic form for burial, complete with small models of granaries, rice hulling machinery and irrigation systems of which they were especially proud.
Â 
Four Terra Cotta Sculptures
The centerpiece of the exhibition is a group of four of the famous life-size terra cotta sculptures - a horse and three soldiers - made for the first emperor of the Qin Dynasty, whose tomb in Shaanxi Province has been excavated in recent years and found to hold some 7,000 such sculptures.
''For the imperial tombs, there was a vast bureacracy just getting ready for the burial of the next emperor,'' said Felice Fischer, a curator of Far Eastern art at the Philadelphia Museum who installed the present exhibition. 
''There were workshops and bureaucrats in charge of making sculpture, and they put out edicts regularly on the proper number and size of ceramic figures to be made for persons of given rank.''
The present exhibition is organized chronologically, beginning with funerary sculpture taken from Neolithic burial mounds dating from between 8,000 B.C. and 2,000 B.C. There are a handful of small pieces from the slave-based Shang and Zhou Dynasties, leading up to the life-size Qin sculptures.
It is during the Han Dynasty - a period of national unification, internal peace and economic development that lasted about 400 years around the time of Christ - that Chinese ceramic funerary art flowered. 
Some of the best examples are represented in this show.
Â 
Scenes of Farm and Home Life
In the Han period, work made for wealthy landowners appears, and figures depart from the strict military style of the Qin period into agricultural and domestic tableaux, as well as scenes of music, dance and entertainment.
From the Han Dynasty onward, further technical innovations - such as the use of glazes and paints - appear in the work, which reached its height in the famous three-color glazes of the Tang Dynasty, whose ''tomb guardian'' figures are among this show's most elaborate and impressive pieces.
Among the exhibition's most recent pieces are Ming funerary figures from between A.D. 1368 and 1644, made of the distinctive colorful glazed porcelain that is best-known from the vases of the same period.
Important trends in the cultural history of China can be read in the stylistic evolution of the sculptures in this show. 
In works from the Wei Period, for instance, between A.D. 386 and 556, the soldiers, servants and other figures depicted increasingly come to resemble the staid, impassive image of Buddha, reflecting the increasing contact and trade between China and India at that time.
Â 
Sculpted Camels Also Appear
Later, brilliantly glazed Tang-period sculptures of dromedaries -some with bolts of silk lashed to elaborate saddles - depict the animals used by traders plying the silk route between China and the West. 
The fierce faces and the often stylized, dancing poses of the tomb guardian spirits of the Tang period also reflect an influence from Hindu sculptures depicting that religion's variously warlike and ecstatic deities.
The present exhibition, organized by George Kuwayama, senior curator of Far Eastern Art at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, opened to the public at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and not in Los Angeles, because the Los Angeles museum's exhibition schedule did not permit.
The show will travel to the Museum of Fine Arts in Houston from June 28 to Sept. 
6; to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art from Oct. 
15 to Jan. 
3, 1988, and to the Cleveland Museum of Art from Feb. 
7 to April 10, 1988.

THE China Institute of America, long the territory of those who supported Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek and the Kuomintang Party that ruled Nationalist China before Mao Zedong's Communist takeover, finally opened its arms to the People's Republic, and its diplomats were on hand the other night at a black-tie dinner honoring C. Douglas Dillon.
The gathering at the Helmsley Palace began with drinks, during which 400 guests stood nibbling hors d'oeuvres and studying one another. 
Some Caucasians were either born in China or had ties going back before World War II, and several women wore Chinese attire. 
But it was the Chinese- American women in their embroidered silks and impressive jewels who stole the show, gathering around Grace Chu, whom Millie Chan, a teacher of Chinese cooking who knows not a word of Chinese, introduced as ''the Julia Child of Chinese cuisine.''
Charlotte Curtis article on dinner honoring C Douglas Dillon at Helmsley Palace (M)
Across the room, Liang Yufan, China's chief delegate to the United Nations, was deep in conversation with Morley Cho, the shipping executive. 
The representative, true to People's Republic protocol, wore his immaculately tailored if austere gray uniform with its Mandarin collar. 
He said he was having a nice time.
Several years ago, this political mixture would not have been possible. 
When Chiang and his followers fled to Taiwan, the cultural institute's affection and sympathy went with him. 
Thus was born a segment of the so-called China lobby, which opposed American recognition of Mao's regime. 
But times do change.
In 1979, in step with President Jimmy Carter's normalization agreement, members began to include the occasional Chinese mainlander. 
And last fall, 10 years after President Richard M. Nixon's celebrated rapprochement, the institute officially invited Beijing's diplomats and trade executives.
''This is one of the few organizations I'm for,'' said Shanghai-born Richard King, an associate of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, the accounting concern. 
''It's apolitical.''
''The old wounds are healing,'' said Mrs. Wan-go H.C. 
Weng, the American-born daughter of a leading Kuomintang official. 
''Whether you love Taiwan or the mainland, there's only one China. 
The sooner we all realize that, the better off we'll be.''
Mrs. Weng was in midsentence when Kitty Carlisle Hart, chairman of the State Council of the Arts, arrived clutching the script for her part of the program and practicing her 12 words of Mandarin. 
''She's very good,'' Mrs. Weng said, adding that Bi Jilong, the Under Secretary of the United Nations, was expected.
At that point, Nathan Pusey, former president of Harvard and the dinner chairman, borrowed a taxi whistle from Robert L. Houguet, the banker, and blew a shrill blast. 
''That ought to get them moving,'' Dr. Pusey said, though it did not. 
So he blew it again, and the guests gradually trooped off to dinner. 
They had reached dessert when Dr. Pusey announced that he'd never before been what he called the lead-off man. 
''I gather I'm supposed to calm you down and say a word of welcome,'' he said. 
And when guests went right on talking, he said there was no point in his being there. 
That quieted everyone.
Dr. Pusey said the assembly marked ''our shared love of things Chinese and beyond that our love for Doug,'' a reference to Mr. Dillon. He said, too, that he detected ''a kind of crimson atmosphere,'' a reference not to communism but the dozens, including Mr. Dillon, who went to Harvard. 
He introduced the diplomats. 
He discussed Mr. Dillon's affection for things French, including art, wine and middle-size poodles, and handed the podium on to Mr. Weng, the institute president, who introduced Thomas Lawton of the Freer Gallery of Art, who spoke on the study of Chinese art.
Then came Mrs. Hart, describing eight Chinese paintings Mr. Dillon had given the Metropolitan Museum. 
Finally, Mr. Hoguet, the institute chairman, extolled Mr. Dillon's accomplishments as longtime chairman of the Metropolitan and presented him with a calligraphy scroll. 
Mr. Dillon appeared genuinely touched.
He said he became interested in Chinese, Japanese and East Asian art 15 years ago when he discovered that the museum's holdings ''were so lamentably weak.''
He said, ''The only way we could acquire what we needed was to get it in very large gobs,'' which he did. 
His first gift was 25 major paintings.
''When I began to see these treasures,'' he said, ''it changed my life. 
I fell in love. 
There is no other way to describe it. 
Other people contributed. 
We were then able to acquire other things that interested the museum. 
We're coming along. 
Now, we have 250 paintings.''
The Dillon Galleries also contain porcelains and bronzes from the 11th to the 18th centuries, thereby explaining the choice of words on the honoree's new scroll. 
Translated, it says: ''Looking at the ancient to develop the present.''
What it means, of course, is that you can't understand the present without knowing what went before.
Correction
The Charlotte Curtis column yesterday, on a dinner in honor of C. Douglas Dillon, misidentified the firm of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. 
It is an investment banking house.

It took a Chinese-language petition signed by 3,000 immigrant seamstresses to get it started, and today it will be opened formally: the Garment Industry Day Care Center of Chinatown.
The dedication of the little red- brick schoolhouse in the heart of Chinatown culminates a cooperative effort by government and private business that the city would like to see duplicated, officials said.
Mayor Koch and Matilda Cuomo, the Governor's wife, will be at the opening, and the children, most of whom speak only Chinese, plan to serenade them with their favorite song in English: ''Jingle Bells.''
The cost of the center is being borne, in small part, by the parents of the children themselves. 
The idea for the center, however, came totally from the people involved, immigrant women who labor long hours as they struggle to make their way in their new country.
Garment Industry Day Care Center to open in Chinatown, NYC, after much petitioning by local residents who work small garment shops; children illustrated; Mayor Edward Koch and Mrs Matilda Cuomo to visit; NYC, factory owners' group and parents to share costs (S)Day Care Common in China
''In China, any unit that you belong to has a day-care center as a matter of course,'' said Katie Kwan, a union activist who helped lead a campaign to open the center.
She said the immigrant mothers ''can't believe it when they get here and there's nobody to take care of their kids.''
Because most of the husbands work in restaurants while their wives sew piecework, she said, the children were often taken along to work or left in groups with untrained babysitters for lack of an alternative.
Mrs. Kwan and other members of Local 23-25 of the International Ladies Garment Workers Union drew up a petition and spent their lunch hours carrying it up and down the narrow stairs of many of Chinatown's 500 small garment factories to gather the signatures. 
There were delays, she said, but in the end the union championed their cause.
Â 
Costs Are Subsidized
The center, at 115 Chrystie Street, opened its first classes last Nov. 
28. It now cares for 70 pre-kindergarten children of union members.
The Agency for Child Development of the city's Human Services Administration will be paying about half the operating costs, with funds from the Federal Emergency Jobs Act.
Private assistance comes from the Greater Blouse, Skirt and Undergarment Association Inc., which is made up of owners of the small factories for whom the immigrant seamstresses work. 
The association will pay $32 of the weekly cost of $82 per child.
To cover the rest of the cost, parents will be assessed by the city on a sliding scale pegged to income. 
The cost will range from $2 to $8 a week for each child.
''We would like to be able to market similar services to other employers,'' said Irene Greim, a spokesman for the Agency for Child Development. 
The city benefits by sharing day-care costs, and employers benefit by having the city handle administration, she said.
Â 
Rosh ha-Shanah Observed
The center also provides a service in helping the children adapt to the language and culture of their new home. 
Each of its four classes has at least one teacher who speaks Chinese, said the director, Mee Ling Chin. 
But after the first month or so, once the children get used to school, English will be the order of the day.
There are few signs of China in the decor or curriculum. 
The older children are already beginning to study the alphabet in English, not Chinese characters.
In Alice Leong's classroom, 3- and 4-year-olds are preparing a cardboard dragon for Chinese New Year Feb. 
2. But at Christmas, she said, they learned about Santa Claus, and they will also observe Rosh ha- Shanah, the Jewish New Year.
''We'll celebrate all the holidays,'' she said.

Tucked along the back wall of a battered refrigerator on the third floor of the chemistry building at Beijing University are two beetle-brown laboratory bottles, their caps sealed with white tape. 
They contain what is very likely to be the oldest wine on earth.
''We believe it is about 3,000 years old,'' said Lin Zuming, an assistant professor of chemistry at the university. 
''It is the oldest ever found here.''
For six years, the wine has sat undisturbed, undiscussed in Professor Lin's refrigerator.

text:
