China's participation in a world's fair for the first time since 1904 has produced a dramatic exhibit that grew out of difficult negotiations that came within a breath of failure.
Visitors to the China pavilion at the World's Fair here seem unanimously fascinated with the artifacts and handicrafts, the hundreds of elaborate carvings in jade and ivory, the hand-painted porcelain, the tapestries and silks and carpets.
In the views both of the Chinese and world's fair officials, it is just that fascination that placed paramount importance on China's participation in the 1982 international exposition.
''What the presence of the People's Republic of China did was to position us as a world class event,'' S.H. 
Roberts Jr., the president of the fair, said in an interview today.
KNOXVILLE, Tenn., May 4 -China's participation in a world's fair for the first time since 1904 has produced a dramatic exhibit that grew out of difficult negotiations that came within a breath of failure.
The pavilion is easily the most heavily visited one at the fair. 
The Chinese estimate that at least half of the quarter-million people who have turned out for the first four days of the fair have been through the China pavilion.
Virtually everything inside the pavilion is available for purchase, even the most intricate and expensive objets d'art. 
''That Chinese exhibit is fantastic,'' said Ed Shoch, a 72-year-old Pennsylvanian. 
''It's beautiful and the prices are very reasonable.''
Rhonda Higgins, of Three Rivers Mich, said, ''I was interested because they have people doing the Chinese needlework without a pattern. 
I couldn't believe it.''
Mr. Roberts and other fair officials decided at least four years ago that the involvement of either China or the Soviet Union was crucial to the fair's success. 
Although the Soviet Union was invited, it chose not to participate.
Â 
Need for Major Exhibition
In a report on the financial feasibility of the fair, Economics Research Corportion, a consulting concern, had concluded that ''a major exhibition provided by a foreign world power,'' was crucial to the fair's success.The consultants said attendance would be greatly enhanced ''if the exhibition is from a nation with which we have only limited cultural exchange,'' and added, ''The U.@S.@S.@R. and the People's Republic of China fit this description.''
For China's part, said Lu Fengchun, commissioner general of the pavilion, the exposition was an opportunity for his country to expand its ''policy of open-door economics'' that began in 1979 when diplomatic relations with the United States were established after 30 years without such ties.
''We need to have many experiences from foreign countries,'' he said through an interpreter in an interview. 
''We have much to learn from other countries, especially in economic matters.''
He stressed the ''progress of relations'' between China and the United States since the initiation of friendship in 1972, and said, ''This world's fair is a good place to introduce China to the American people.''
Â 
Hope for Future Exchanges
''A bridge of friendship between China and the United States was connected in 1979,'' he said, ''and we hope that through this bridge the two countries will strengthen the friendship and continue to have an exchange of economics, technology, culture and trade.''
A bridge to other nations is also on the minds of the Chinese. 
''This fair is called a world's fair, so a lot of countries are participating,'' Mr. Lu said. 
''They will display their contributions and technologies here and we would like to share ours for the benefit of mankind.''
Apparently, it was a fear that their exhibit might not compare favorably with those of other nations that caused the Chinese almost to reject the invitation to participate.
According to Mr. Roberts, the initial video presentation to the officials in Peking in the fall of 1980 led them to say that ''it involved more than they had thought and that they would need help in order to participate.''
Â 
'Negative Signs' From Chinese
What Mr. Roberts described as ''difficulties in communication'' plagued the prospect of Chinese participation for much of last year. 
Not only did the fair send a team to Peking a second time, but the Chinese sent a delegation to Knoxville in February 1981 to review the fair site. 
Still, for much of the year, ''we would get negative signs from time to time,'' Mr. Roberts said.
President Carter brought up the subject of the fair with Chinese officials on his visit to China after his election defeat. 
Howard H.Baker Jr. of Tennessee, the Senate majority leader, discussed the subject repeatedly with officials in the Chinese Embassy in Washington.
One fair official said that the Chinese three times declined the offer to participate in the fair, but Mr. Roberts disagreed. 
''We got awfully close to being turned down a few times, but it never got to be official,'' he said. 
''One time, Senator Baker had a meeting with the Chinese Ambassador and prevailed on him to hold off a denial.''
Â 
Agreement Is Reached
Finally, after three days of negotiations again in Peking, the Chinese agreed to come to Knoxville. 
The fair officials agreed to pay for shipping the large exhibit to the fair, to pay for some basic construction changes in the pavilion and to provide technical assistance in preparing the exhibit. 
The cost to the fair was more than $1 million.
''They had concerns about how they would present themselves in a show this large and lasting this long,'' Mr. Roberts said of the Chinese officials. 
''We think we made a great investment.''

text:

When even the banana sellers take a break the fever of the Lunar New Year has indubitably gripped Peking.
As the festivities celebrated by Chinese throughout the world began here Tuesday amid a blowing snowstorm, young merchants with bicycles were missing from their usual stations outside foreigners' compounds and hotels. 
The bananas are a cover for black- market currency dealings, which have boomed along with the rest of the economy here in recent years.
The closing of the ''banana bank'' was one measure of how the Lunar New Year has changed. 
A decade ago it was deemed reactionary to call it by its traditional name, so it was called the Spring Festival. 
Workers got three days off, as now, but they were well advised to keep their revelries away from neighbors' prying eyes.
Lunar New Year festivities celebrated by Chinese throughout world begin in Peking; workers get three days off to hail year of the ox (M)
Now, Maoist austerity is treated as a bad memory, and the traditional festivities are back in vogue. 
For weeks people have been hanging silk lanterns and laying in food, firecrackers and gifts. 
By 3 P.M. Tuesday, nine hours before the Year of the Rat gave way to the Year of the Ox, everybody who could was slipping out of the plant or office and pointing his bicycle toward home.
Â 
Snow Slows the Traffic
It was a murky day, made duller by an unusually heavy snowstorm. 
By afternoon the sun was a limpid orange ball amid the smog, and the Forbidden City's fluted roofs hung mysteriously in the gloom. 
Everywhere bicyclists were skidding on the snow, and motorized traffic slowed to a crawl. 
Yet through it all there was a zest unmatched here at this season in years.
While Mao Zedong was alive the new year stole in silently, but at midnight all Peking and the region beyond, home to nine million people, erupted in a joyous cacophony. 
As the year 4683 on the old Chinese calendar began, spectators in a high-rise building looking toward the imperial palaces were treated to half an hour of booming firecrackers that lit up the maze of hutungs, or alleyways, that make up much of the city.
The official New China News Agency called it ''the most prosperous New Year ever.''
Along the city's main shopping street of Wangfujing, always crowded, sidewalks were thicker still with urban couples and peasants in from the country struggling out of stores with ''the four new big things'' - color television sets, washing machines, refrigerators and stereos.
Years ago, it was the ''eight treasures,'' less expensive things such as sewing machines and radios, that were most eagerly sought. 
But incomes have risen sharply under market-oriented economic changes, and the problem for many is not cash but supply.
At the One Hundred Varieties Big Building, Peking's principal department store, the newly appointed manager said recently that he could sell 10 times his quota of Japanese television sets, at $650 each, 18 months' income for a factory worker.
Â 
Leader Shuns the Limelight
On the whole the man behind the changes, Deng Xiaoping, has inverted the old personality cult, preferring to shun the limelight. 
But as the holiday began the association between Mr. Deng and the new prosperity showed through in some official quarters. 
A typical New China News Agency dispatch quoted a peasant woman aboard a train outside Peking as having credited Mr. Deng's ''flexible economic policy'' for her holiday well-being.
The woman was one of 600 million travelers expected to take advantage of the break, more than half the population. 
At Peking station, where officials were reprimanded for unannounced train cancellations that stranded 10,000 passengers overnight on Jan. 
1, workers were bracing for a surge of six million holidaymakers. 
Many of these will be peasants heading into town for festivities that have been revived for the first time in several decades.
Officials are expecting 800,000 people at an open-air ''temple fair'' at Ditan Park, site of the Ming dynasty's Temple of the Earth. 
The centerpiece of the Lunar New Year for centuries, temple fairs were proscribed in the 1950's. 
This year, the park has been opened to hundreds of merchants and entertainers offering things not seen in the lifetimes of the majority of people now living.
There are bird-singing contests and fashion shows and beauty parlors and stalls selling ingeniously fashioned paper windmills and kites. 
There are consultants to advise on medical problems, traffic regulations and family planning, and magicians, comedians, wrestlers and bare-chested men competing in a nearly forgotten sport that involves tossing and catching a 30-foot bamboo pole topped with lanterns and bells.
Â 
Sales of Firecrackers Up
As always in China, food is at the heart of the celebrations. 
At the temple fair and from stalls all over Peking, entrepreneurs taking advantage of Mr. Deng's encouragement of private enterprise are hawking dishes of baodu, a delicacy made from sheep's stomachs, as well as sweet potatoes roasted on coal-fired braziers and sticks with hawthorn berries dipped in sugar.
At 1.3 billion, sales of firecrackers in the city have been up 75 percent on last year and it has sounded like it. 
For a few cents children can buy rockets with such innocent-sounding names as ''Heavenly Maiden Walking Through Flowers'' that have a report like a three-inch mortar. 
Among Chinese the bang counts for more than an array of color in the sky, so there have been several noisy nights. 
Fires set by the embers last year caused damage estimated at $25 million and wounded 27 people, three of whom were permanently blinded. 
The country's top leaders saw in the New Year in a hectic round of factory visits and receptions. 
Mr. Deng, who is 80 years old, was at a hotel in the southern city of Canton, where he attended a party with the widow of Prime Minister Zhou Enlai, Deng Yingchao, and with the armed forces' commander, Yang Dezhi.
As with other aspects of Mr. Deng's policies of relaxation, quite a number of people have taken the revival of the old traditions as an excuse for ''dipping into the big pot,'' using public funds for private gratification. 
The Communist Party's principal newspaper, People's Daily, hit out last week at officials in various regions who have taken advantage of the festivities to give lavish banquets, accept gifts and pass out unearned bonuses.
In one case chronicled by Economic Daily, managers of a glass factory in the northern province of Liaoning spent 4,400 yuan - $1,565 - on a 16-course feast of chicken, prawns, fish and sea slugs, ''creating a bad impact on the masses.''
People's Daily demanded that the culprits ''study the three do- nots: do not stretch out your hands for gifts, do not accept them and do not use public money for big banquets.''
Exceptions have been permitted for Government officials in Peking, who have held a series of receptions. 
When foreign reporters took the floor at one with a satirical song poking fun at the Foreign Ministry, officials joined in the laughter with everyone else.
American diplomats went one better, offering their Foreign Ministry hosts instruction in disco dancing. 
Some of the senior Chinese diplomats responded enthusiastically, doffing their Mao tunics and taking the floor.

text:

FEI LO is the author of ''The Dim Sum Book: Classic Recipes from the Chinese Teahouse.''
Â 
By EILEEN YIN-FEI LO
V egetarianism in China is as old as Buddha. 
And the Chinese co ncept of elaborately arranged artistic banquets of many courses is as old as Confucius. 
Somewhere in time, felicitously and naturally, th e ideas came together. 
These days the vegetarian banquet, with beancu rd, vegetables and doughs artfully dressed to appear as something th ey are not, is common to such disparate parts of the country as Ca nton, Peking or Shanghai, whose cuisines are quite different.
One traditional center of vegetarianism is Hangzhou, whose name means ''City Across the Stream.''
Hangzhou is built surrounding the beautiful West Lake with its pavilions and palaces, its boats, its tree-shaded paths and gardens and its thickets of magnolias, camellias and azaleas.
Eileen Yin-Fei Lo discusses cooking vegetables the Chinese way
In the days when Hangzhou was a warm-weather resort for the wealthy of Shanghai, it had a tradition of specialty restaurants, a tradition that continues in a small way today, for it is in Hangzhou that one finds restaurants of many regions of China, including several fine Moslem eating places. 
It is in that city that the arts of carving melons and gourds into table decorations and arranging sliced foods on plates so that they resemble butterflies, roosters and birds flourish.
Hangzhou is also known for its restaurants serving temple food, the food of the Buddhist temples, vegetarian foods such as vegetables, soybean products and breads of grain.
One of these, more than 30 years old and perhaps its best, is the Spring Vegetable, on Yanan Street, just one short street away from the eastern rim of West Lake. 
On a recent trip to China I had the experience of eating in that restaurant a banquet that was as much an art exhibit as it was a meal. 
There were slices of beef that were actually kneaded dough, a fish constructed of mashed taro root, duck of bean curd and meatballs of minced vegetables. 
It was an artful feast, and a delicious one.
The Spring Vegetable is not the only vegetarian outpost in the resort city. 
Others include Kui Yuan Guan on Jiefang Road, justly famous for its vegetables and noodles; the Hangzhou Hotel Restaurant, perhaps the most sophisticated in the city; San Wai San inside the Hangzhou Botanical Garden, where the specialty is soup made with the vegetable called shuen chai, native to Hangzhou. 
But we were the first Westerners to come to the Spring Vegetable, we were told, and the restaurant wanted our banquet to be very special. 
And it was.
Much of the $30-per-person banquet was based on the soybean, one of China's most important staples. 
In most of the country it replaces the need for dairy products, providing more protein an acre, nutritionists tell us, than any livestock could produce. 
It is also quite versatile. 
The beans are seldom eaten as grown, they can be fermented, they can be ground into flour, they can be sprouted and those bean sprouts used as a vegetable accompaniment, they can be milled. 
When they are milled wet they form a spongy mass that when pressed dry and cooked become those bean curd cakes (called dau-fu by the Chinese, tofu by the Japanese) that are so popular these days. 
The bean curd skins are really a byproduct of boiling the soybeans, and are skimmed and dried and used often in soups.
The Spring Vegetable, just across the street from the Islam Food Shop, is a rather small restaurant, two floors high, and, like the majority of the restaurants in China, is somewhat short on decoration. 
It was obvious that the restaurant's effort goes into its food, which is as it should be.
We sat down around large round tables and after a sip of plum wine the first course came out. 
Actually it was a series of three cold platters of ''duck,'' ''chicken,'' and ''beef.''
Th e first was dried bean curd ski n rolled tightly and sliced across, dressed with sesame oil and quick ly deep-fried. 
It did indeed taste like pressed duck. 
The chicken w as likewise of bean curd skin, but skin that was rolled flat and then sliced so that it resembled slices of breast of chicken. 
The beef was a dough, kneaded, allowed to ferment, rinsed incold water, f lavored with anise and sugar and colored with dark soy sauce before frying. 
All the frying, by the way, was in peanut oil.
The second course was ''scallops,'' again made of fermented dough, flavored with garlic, vegetable stock and sugar and cut to resemble scallops. 
They were stir-fried with bok choy, the green stalk vegetable so widely used by the Chinese.
Three vegetable courses followed. 
First there were fresh bamboo shoots with soaked black mushrooms in a light soy sauce. 
Then came a chicken soup made of vegetable stock into which was put sliced bamboo shoots; then the soup was garnished with fresh roasted sesame seeds. 
Mushrooms and fresh water chestnuts in a thick sauce of soy and water-chestnut powder came next.
The sixth course was a platter of fresh bean curd cakes, their centers opened and filled with minced vegetables, and vegetarian spring rolls, filled with shredded bamboo shoots, mushrooms, water chestnuts and carrots. 
The skins of the spring rolls were made of dried bean curd.
The next dish was an imitation Chinese sausage, made of bean curd skins, tightly rolled, deep-fried, c olored wi th soy sauce and sliced diagonally. 
These were mixed with choy sum, a small stalk green vegetable, with sliced black mushrooms and fr esh tiny straw mushrooms.
Our palates were refreshed and sweetened with courses eight and nine. 
First came fresh sweet red dates coated with tapioca flour, then a sweet soup concocted of fresh water chestnuts cooked to tenderness, sweetened with rock candy and thickened with waterchestnut powder.
The highlight of the banquet was the 10th course: Our ''fish'' was presented. 
Its body consisted of taro root, (the poi of Hawaii) cooked until soft and seasoned with salt, pepper, sesame oil and sugar, then mashed. 
This was shaped like a fish. 
The head and gills were shaped out of fresh bean curd cakes. 
The tail and fins were finely cut dried bean curd skins. 
The aroma of the fish was nutlike (from the sesame oil dressing) and the platter was garnished with fresh, green coriander. 
It was a triumph.
The last two courses were almost anticlimactic, and would have been had they not been so good. 
There was a sub gum, which means a mixture of 10 ingredients, and it was sort of a reprise of stir-fried dried bean curd skins, slices of dough, vegetables and nuts. 
The finale consisted of a soup of fresh bean curd cut into small cubes, of vegetarian meatballs, chopped vegetables, bok choy and tiny fresh mushrooms.
That was to settle our stomachs, we were told, as were the cups of hot, steaming green tea, the Dragon Well tea for which Hangzhou is equally famous. 
It was altogether a splendid memory to take with us as we left on the train for Shanghai a couple of hours later.
Â 
Hong Kong
Two of Hong Kong's monasteries serve meatless, fishless meals. 
One is the Po Lin Monastery on Lan Tau Island, a day trip by boat from Hong Kong proper, where Buddhist monks will prepare lunch (with advance notice). 
The second is the Chang Chung Koon Monastery in Castle Peak, the New Territories, outside of Kowloon, where Taoist monks do the same. 
Arrangements are made through the Hong Kong Tourist Association.

text:
ï»¿
The Great Wall Hotel borrowed its name from China's ancient landmark and there the similarity ends. 
The operators of the new 22-story building, its exterior sheathed in reflective glass, say it is China's most modern hotel, which is hardly an exaggeration considering the state of hotels in this country.
The Great Wall Hotel, which opened the first 40 of its 1,007 rooms on Dec. 
10, is the biggest Chinese- American joint venture so far, involving an investment of $75 million and setting a new standard in the hotel boom in China.
The Westerners who descended on China after it opened its doors to foreign trade and tourism placed a strain on facilities that has yet to be resolved. 
Peking's Tourist Department reported last May that 456,000 tourists visited the capital in 1982, 2.4 times more than in 1978. 
Over the same period, Peking's hotel accommodations expanded by only 70 percent, to about 5,100 rooms.
Â 
Service Is Often Poor
At the height of the autumn season, tourists have been bused to other cities as much as 75 miles from Peking, or left sitting in airport lounges for lack of hotel space. 
Those who get into a hotel may confront bleak rooms, broken toilets, spasmodic hot water and indifferent service.
The reservation system is so chaotic that travelers seldom know where they will be billeted, and the hotel staff cannot tell callers who is registered. 
Restaurants and other facilities usually shut down early.
The dearth of comfort and courtesy has left a vacuum for foreign investors to fill. 
The pacesetter has been Peking's new Jianguo Hotel, a joint venture built by Clement Chen, a San Francisco businessman, for $22 million. 
The Jianguo, which looks like the Holiday Inn in Palo Alto, Calif., opened in 1982 and earned $1 million in its first 10 months.
Â 
Boom Spreads in China
A half-dozen other quality hotels, including the 2,000-room Lidu, are now under construction in Peking, and the demand has spread to other major Chinese cities.
Nanjing has the newly opened 37- story Jinling Hotel, with a revolving restaurant at the top. 
Canton's White Swan Hotel opened last February and a Hong Kong joint venture, the China Hotel, is expected to be completed shortly.
The Great Wall Hotel has tried to eclipse them with such novelties as an indoor swimming pool, a nightclub and a 24-hour coffee shop, as well as China's first computerized reservations system. 
The hotel's shiny steel pillars are reinforced to withstand earthquakes, and there is even a bomb shelter in the basement.
The Chinese employees wear sleek uniforms instead of the usual soiled white jackets. 
Their training program stresses knife-and-fork etiquette and the pronunciation of English tongue-twisters like cauliflower.
Â 
Ex-Bendix Official's Idea
The hotel was the idea of C. B. Sung, a Shanghai-born American businessman who was vice president of engineering and research for the Bendix Corporation until he resigned in 1974 and went into trade with China.
Through his California-based company, Unison International, Mr. Sung has advised or represented American clients like the American Motors Corporation, which has a $51 million joint venture to manufacture cross-country vehicles in Peking, and Parker- Hannifin of Cleveland, which invested $1 million to make rubber seals in China.
Mr. Sung, who has degrees from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Harvard Business School, conceded, ''I know nothing about hotels, except for having stayed in them.''
But he saw the potential for a luxury hotel in China.
He joined with the Becket Investment Corporation, based in California, to create the E-S Pacific Development and Construction Company. 
As its chairman, he signed China's first joint-venture agreement, in October 1979, to construct the hotel in partnership with the Peking branch of the China International Travel service. 
The $75 million cost was financed through a consortium of Western banks led by the Nordic Bank of Scandinavia.
Â 
Dispute Over Construction
Problems developed after the ground was broken in March 1981. 
The American side favored a fast approach, in which construction pushed ahead while the detailed drawings were completed and materials purchased and shipped. 
This upset the Chinese side, which wanted the project to move in tidier stages.
Because of what was euphemistically called an incompatibility between Chinese and American construction practices, the American engineers were dismissed and the Chinese took over.
Mr. Sung declined to discuss the infighting. 
''This project has many problems like any pioneering project, so I don't need to rehash them, but I think we have learned a lot from them,'' he said.
The hotel met the Dec. 
10 deadline by opening the coffee shop and part of three guest floors while construction continued on the rest of the building.
The prices are the highest of any hotel in Peking. 
A double room ranges from $110 to $160 a day - three times what some other major hotels charge. 
A small pizza in the coffee shop costs up to $7, and a premium Scotch in the bar, up to $5. 
The customers pay because such treats are generally unavailable in China.
Â 
'Top People Are Spoiled'
Mr. Sung felt that the comparatively high prices would not deter Western businessmen. 
''Frankly, America's top people are spoiled,'' he said. 
''How can you ask them to stay in a hotel where they don't feel comfortable?''
In any case, the limited rooms are already full.
The secret of success in the hotel joint ventures lies in efficiency. 
The Jianguo Hotel, thanks to its smooth management by the Hong Kong Peninsula Group, has become the most popular with Peking's Western expatriate community.
By contrast, the more elegant Fragrant Hills Hotel, which was designed by I M. Pei, has deteriorated only 14 months after its opening. 
Its marble floors are scuffed and dirty, glass panels are smudged, and bathroom fixtures are broken or missing.
Mr. Sung felt that the emphasis on staff training would help the Great Wall Hotel avoid such pitfalls.

text:
ï»¿
The river forms a green gauze belt, the mountains are like jade hairpins.Â Â Â -Â Â Han Yu, a Tang dynasty poet
Â 
I'D timed my visit to coincide with the flowering of the osmanthus trees. 
So when I arrived in Guilin on a moonless night in early October after a one-hour flight from Hong Kong, I smelled the city of my forebears before I saw it. 
Even as I stepped off the plane, the pervasive sweet-orange scent made me shut my eyes both in reverie and in anticipation of what daylight would bring. 
The next morning, and every morning thereafter, I threw open my bedroom window to intoxicate myself, first with the delicate fragrance that suggested that I was in the Forest of Osmanthus Trees, as Guilin is translated, then with the unearthly scenery that convinced me that I was.
I was staying in my grandmother's house, a dignified half-timbered two-story brick and stucco house - sort of Chinese Tudor - that she had built in 1941 as a wedding present for my parents. 
Around the house ran a high, thick wall into which was built a row of small rooms that traditionally had no place in a Chinese house: a storage room for coal, a privy, a washroom with new shower, a kitchen and a larder. 
With the advent of modern plumbing, two bathrooms were installed inside the house, and my grandmother's home had the distinction of being the first in Guilin to possess Western-style toilets. 
Above and beyond the wall lay Guilin's totally improbable, impetuous mountains, some of them right in the middle of the city. 
I could see two of them from my bedroom terrace: to the left, Folded Brocade Mountain rose in layers of soft greens, grays and violets, like so many quilts piled one on top of the other; to the right, set on the river bank, the straight, proud shaft of Wave Restraining Hill was more than sufficient to contain the tranquil Li River, almost at a standstill now that it was the dry season. 
My grandmother had her house built close to and equidistant from the two mountains, not only for esthetic reasons but also for practical purposes: both contained caves that were natural air-raid shelters when the Japanese bombed Guilin during the Sino-Japanese War and World War II.
As I was a member of the four generations of Lis who lived under her roof, there was always a cousin, aunt or uncle to accompany me up some of the more famous limestone towers thrust up from their seabed 300 million years ago and carved to their present-day configurations by centuries of erosion. 
Luckily, the most famous had steps, requiring walking rather than scaling. 
So after a substantial breakfast of mi fen (rice noodles, a Guilin specialty), a cousin and I joined the crush of visitors - mostly Chinese from other provinces and several Americans and Japanese - who poured out of their tour buses to partake of the forces of nature from the pinnacle of Folded Brocade Mountain.
FROM its pergola-topped summit, Guilin's shan-shui - its otherworldly mountains, lakes and rivers - seemed straight out of a Chinese landscape painting. 
Scores of rocky crags and peaks soar straight up without warning from the verdant plain. 
The jade-green Li River meanders among them, dotted with rickety houseboats and the narrow bamboo rafts of fishermen using cormorants rather than nets to catch fish, looking like floating matchsticks from such a height. 
Gardens, walkways and pergolas embroider the edges of Banyan and Fir Lakes, all reasons why Guilin has for centuries been the destination of Chinese painter-poets in quest of immortalizing on silk, paper or stone the ''fragment of eternity'' to be found here.
Based on its dreamlike karst scenery, an abundance of myths and legends have grown up over Guilin's 2,000-year history, examples of which my cousin took pleasure in pointing out. 
Brooding yet indomitable, Old Man Hill sat facing away from the city in the direction of the sea, awaiting the return of his unfilial son. 
Piercing Rock's gaping hole was the result of a general's arrow shot in a contest of strength that re-established the allegiance of a rebellious tribe to the emperor. 
A kindly elephant who deserted the emperor's ranks to help Guilinese plow their fields during a time of famine dipped his trunk into the Li River to quench his thirst and is commemorated as Elephant Trunk Hill. 
I climbed Elephant Trunk Hill alone one morning, passing by the small Buddhist reliquary tower on its summit, the hilt of the sword thrust into the elephant's neck by a vengeful general. 
Taken altogether, the mountains of Guilin, one of China's major tourist cities, were once stones carried from central China by conscripted laborers to fill up the South China Sea. 
The laborers got only as far as Guilin, and the ''stones'' have remained here ever since, making Guilin the epitome of Chinese landscape when in reality it is a landscape unique to Guilin.
Guilin's importance as a commercial and cultural center began in 214 B.C., when the first Qin emperor built the nearby Lin Canal - one of the longest canals in the world and used today as an irrigation aqueduct - to connect the Yangtze and the Pearl Rivers, thereby establishing a north-south route for military transport and trade. 
From the Ming Dynasty (A.D. 1368-1644) to the 1950's, Guilin served as the capital of Guangxi Province, which, in southwestern China, was far from Beijing's administrative authority and cultural influence. 
Headquarters of an American Air Force unit in World War II, Guilin was described by Theodore White, then a foreign correspondent, as ''the most lovable and abandoned city in the Orient. 
For intellectual Americans there was always good conversation; for Americans of a more earthly sort there were women.''
For a group of Chinese liberals who took advantage of the province's reputation as a traditional thorn in authority's side, Guilin was a shelter from which to irritate Chiang Kai-shek's central government. 
For most of its history, Guangxi has been known for four things: its extreme poverty, its aversion to authority, the quality of its fighting men, and as a way station for opium shipments passing from India to neighboring Guangdong Province. 
Given the rebellious nature of Guangxi, it is not surprising that the Taiping Rebellion, which hastened the downfall of the decadent Qing Dynasty, began here, nor that the Northern Expedition, which my grandfather helped lead, had its starting point in the then capital of Guilin.
Even after the success of the Northern Expedition, which ostensibly stamped out warlordism and unified the nation, Guangxi, dissatisfied with the policies of Chiang's Kuomintang government, threatened more than once to secede. 
Even today the independent-minded province, a great many of whose inhabitants are members of several ethnic minorities, the largest of which is the Zhuang, is officially known as the Guangxi-Zhuang Autonomous Region.
IF Guilin's shan-shui as seen from its mountaintops seems straight out of a landscape painting, by riverboat it is a slowly unfurling horizontal scroll. 
The Li River cruise should not be missed, even though the return bus ride is long, bumpy and positively noxious with diesel oil fumes. 
It starts in Guilin, whose ''landscape is the best under heaven,'' and wends its way to Yangshuo, 50 miles downstream, a town that vies with Guilin for this accolade. 
Because it was the dry season, our boat didn't dock under Elephant Trunk Hill, the usual site, but at Yangdi, an hour away by bus. 
Here, where the hillocks resemble the horns of a goat, we threaded our way past vendors on the shore selling Mao caps and coolie hats, pomelos and panda bear pins, then past those on the river, their slender rafts loaded down with little bags of mandarin oranges or woven bamboo handbags, to reach our awaiting vessel, revving its engine and jockeying for position with a dozen other boats, all impatient to be on their way.
Once we had weighed anchor, river life flowed past like scenes from time gone by. 
Tiny villages of several houses apiece dotted the shoreline at distant intervals. 
A fisherman in a graceful bamboo boat sat motionless in the shade of a tall cliff waiting for a bite or more likely just to pass the time. 
A woman washed clothes by slapping them on the pebbly shore, while a throng of children played in the water, slicing it with their hands to see if the spray would reach our boat. 
A more serious youngster guided the family water buffalo into the river to give it a refreshing bath and a meal of duckweed from the river bottom.
The Chinese imagination takes pantheistic pleasure in giving a life and spirit to inanimate things, so our boat was fairly buzzing with botanical and zoological comparisons. 
Each twist and turn of the river, each new vista that appeared around the next bend, besides evoking sighs of delight or amazement, elicited a game that peopled the ''stone forest'' on our flanks with geological flora and fauna: here a mountain shaped like an apple, there a rock that looked like a turtle basking in the sun, and directly ahead Mural Hill - nine horses that nature had painted on the sheer face of a cliff, each in a different pose, though I could see only three with certainty.
BY midday, exercising our imaginations had whetted our appetites, and we scrambled down from the deck for lunch. 
Guangxi Province is renowned for the unusual animals - scaly anteater, bamboo rat, masked civet - that make their home in this hinterland and find their way onto restaurant tables here and in cuisine-conscious Guangdong. 
The highlight of our meal, however, was a quite commonplace though unquestionably fresh fish I had seen thrashing about in a net dropped over the side, hauled aboard just as our river safari got underway, and cooked in the tiny al fresco kitchen at the stern.
Green Lotus Peak, looking exactly like its namesake, announced our arrival in Yangshuo, a small but growing town that capitalizes on its proximity and resemblance to Guilin. 
Shaking out our sea legs, we followed winding paths lined with shops selling the usual scrolls and paintings, crocheted sweaters from Shanghai and embroidered nappery, ceramics and curios. 
Evidence of ''spiritual pollution'' abounded. 
Joanne's, a restaurant whose sign was written in English, invited us to try their ''best Irish coffee,'' while another establishment offered, also in English, a ''feast of menus - aren't you lucky!''
But the most interesting sign in our wanderings through Yangshuo, and certainly the most beautiful, was the single bold Chinese character emblazoned onto the side of a cliff: dai, which can mean many things, including bring and wear. 
The calligraphy is exquisite, a combination of painting and writing. 
Chinese calligraphy is, in fact, abstract painting, composed of structure, composition, rhythm, movement and balance and requiring of the calligrapher both tranquillity of mind and spontaneity of execution. 
''The artist must nourish in his heart gentleness and cheerfulness,'' a classic on Chinese calligraphy reads, ''the ideas must be harmonious. 
The heart should be quiet, honest, and sincere to the utmost, then the various aspects of human gladness and sorrow and every other thing, be it pointed, oblique, bent or inclined, will appear naturally in the mind and be spontaneously brought out by the brush.''
Some say the dai of Yangshuo comprises eight strokes; some say as many as 14. 
No one knows who put it there, or when. 
It was the attraction of these ambiguities - particularly after the straightforwardness of Yangshuo's appeal to the tourist dollar - that lent the huge ideogram a good part of its charm.
But it is not from Guilin's unearthly peaks or on the Li River's blue-green waters that one gathers a sense of the region or comes to feel the city's rhythm, but on the streets of the city. 
One morning at dawn, I walked along the Li River Promenade on my way to watch Guilin's elders practice the ancient art of tai chi in the small acacia-shaded park midway up Wave Restraining Hill. 
In the still-blue light of early morning, Guilin was alive with other forms of athleticism: people jogging, skipping rope, playing badminton, pedaling bicycles or huge tricycles that pulled wagonloads of people, produce, coal, bamboo or scrap iron. 
The trickle of cyclists became a steady stream as I entered the campus of Guangxi Teachers College, which in the 14th century was the palace of the emperor's nephew.
In the center of the campus, in the center of town, solitary Single Beauty Peak rose 306 knee-bending steps above Guilin, offering the sheerest climb, highest point, broadest and, after Folded Brocade Mountain, most breathtaking view. 
By midmorning I found myself on Zhongshan Street, the main thoroughfare and shopping street, where I bought a stone seal incised with my Chinese name, following the Chinese custom, albeit belatedly, of choosing one's mingzi, or first name, at the threshhold of adulthood according to one's own philosophy or experience. 
Still following the bicycle traffic, I crossed Floral Bridge, the tile-roofed and many-arched Song Dynasty beauty that leads to Seven Star Park. 
Inside the park are caves whose walls are lined with stelae that look like stone newspapers but really are poems carved in rock by visitors, dynastic and contemporary, inspired by Guilin's beauty. 
Deeper inside Seven Star Cave, stalactites and stalagmites re-enact the drama of Guilin's karst scenery above. 
The theatrical effect of colored lights ''coaching'' the rock formations to appear to be what they already resembled seemed melodramatic, besides robbing the imagination of a different interpretation. 
The same was true for Reed Flute Cave, a 15-minute motor scooter ride into the lush paddy fields and even higher peaks outside Guilin. 
According to legend, this technicolored grotto is a fragment of a heavenly crystal palace built at the beginning of time and hidden so that mortal eyes might one day gaze on it.
But after Seven Star Cave and the Li River cruise, I'd had enough of comparisons and associations, however apt, and wanted to see things as they were. 
The streets of Guilin were the place to find them. 
By late morning every thoroughfare wide enough for the simplest conveyance was a cacophony of bleating truck horns and ringing bicycle bells, a swollen river of cyclists unperturbed by close encounters with heavier transport and oblivious of pedestrians who ventured out into each intersection and managed each street as though it were a dare and an obstacle course combined. 
Such maneuvers would have been even more hazardous had the women's feet been bound, a former northern practice that the women of Guilin never had to tolerate.
I HAVE never seen, not even in Sicily, life lived so openly, so completely in the public eye as Guilin lives its daily life. 
For lack of adequate living space, personal life spills into the street in an almost Bruegelesque intensity. 
It is on the street that many Guilinese cook their midday meal and eat it as well, that they wash their dishes as well as their clothes, hanging clothes on ropes strung between trees to dry. 
Seamstresses hunched over treadle sewing machines make or repair clothing on the street; cobblers affix heels and soles on the street; bed quilts are sewn and shown to clients there; mattresses are dragged out of doors for a thorough wash and rinse there. 
Even the storefronts have no fronts: open barber shops, restaurants, pharmacies, shops of all kinds abound, testament to China's infatuation with private enterprise.
Toward dinnertime, the roads become passable; the populace retires indoors; the tinkle of bicycle bells sounds like music rather than a threat, and the mountains again predominate. 
For all the people who spill out of their Lilliputian dwellings onto the sidewalks and streets in daylight hours, Guilin seems smaller than its 400,000 population would suggest. 
Despite the influx of visitors and continuing construction of new buildings and repair of old ones, Guilin remains curiously rural. 
Even the several hotels, the three-stage 800-room Ramada Renaissance Hotel being the newest of the lot, do nothing to alter this impression. 
It is as if the primeval mountains that surround the city and rise right in its midst, like sentries, guard it against the march of progress elsewhere, preserving its aura of timelessness.
Â 
FLIGHTS, LODGING AND DINING
Â 
Getting There
Â 
C.A.A.C., the national airline, has direct daily flights to Guilin from major Chinese cities, such as Beijing, Shanghai and Canton. 
From Hong Kong there are daily flights via Canton on C.A.A.C., direct charter flights, and direct flights three days a week on Dragonair. 
There are also rail connections to Guilin from Beijing, Shanghai, Kunming, Zhanjiang and Nanning, as well as boat and bus service from Canton and Hong Kong.
Â 
Where to Stay
Â 
Several first-class hotels have been built in the last two years to help cope with the enormous influx of foreign visitors.
Ramada Renaissance Riverside, Yuanjiang Road; telephone 2611. 
Opened late last year, this 334-room hotel on the Li River will have 800 rooms and a shopping arcade when its two remaining phases of development are completed this year. 
The hotel has a heated indoor swimming pool, health club and Chinese, Continental and Japanese restaurants. 
A room with two double beds for double occupancy costs from $95 to $105; for single occupancy the rates are from $83 to $95. 
Reservations through Ramada Worldwide, 800-272-6232.
Holiday Inn Guilin, 14 South Ronghu Road; 3950. 
Situated in the center of town on Banyan Lake, this 259-room hotel has a ballroom, health club, banquet hall and telex. 
A double room, double occupancy, costs from $80 to $90; single occupancy is $75. 
For reservations call 800-465-4329.
Guilin Riverside Resort, Anjiazhou Road; 2291. 
This 236-room hotel with a river view from every room has both Western and Chinese restaurants, a swimming pool, tennis courts and a shopping arcade. 
A double room, double occupancy, costs $65 to $75. 
Direct reservations or through a travel agent.
Li River Hotel, 1 Shanhu Bei Road; 2881. 
Remodeled in 1986, this 360-room hotel is in the center of town on Fir Lake. 
At 14 stories one of the highest buildings in Guilin, it provides spectacular views of the surrounding landscape and has been the city's major tourist hotel for years. 
The price of a double room is $65 to $75. 
Direct reservations or through a travel agent.
Â 
Where to Eat
Â 
The best restaurants in Guilin are to be found in the best hotels, many of which serve both Western and Chinese (mostly Cantonese) cuisine. 
While not noted for the excellence of its cuisine, Guilin is nonetheless famous for the unusual nature of its regional offerings. 
Visitors who would like to try wild game dishes should specify their order a day in advance. 
There are also a number of good bakeries and noodle stands along Zhongshan Road, the main shopping street. 
For those who want to venture out on their own, two suggestions:
Yueyalou Restaurant, in Seven Star Park; 3622. 
Here you can have a vegetarian meal, or one of wild game, after visiting the park's six caves, bonsai garden and small zoo complete with panda.
Tonglai Guan Restaurant, Zhongshan Zhong Road; 3449. 
For the adventurous palate only. 
This restaurant just north of the Hotel Osmanthus Guilin is famous for its wild game, live examples of which are displayed in cages outside, and include pangolin (scaly anteater), bamboo rat, masked civet, snake and turtle.Â Â Â Â L.

text:

Beijing may be a long way from River City, but on May 8 the members of an all-Chinese cast are to buckle their tap shoes, uncrate the trombones and mount a full-scale production of ''The Music Man.''
In what are to be the first performances of an American musical in China by a Chinese cast, the ''Music Man'' is to be done in Beijing simultaneously with the run of another well-known American musical, ''The Fantasticks.''
Both productions are to be directed by Americans, and are to be performed in Mandarin in a collaboration by the Eugene O'Neill Theater Center of Waterford, Conn., the Chinese Theater Association, the Central Opera Theater of Beijing and the Center for U.S.-China Arts Exchange. 
The production of ''The Fantasticks'' is eventually to tour China's provinces.
''The Chinese have a great desire to learn about the form,'' said Chou Wen-Chung, director of the Center for U.S.-China Arts Exchange, a nonprofit organization established in 1978 at Columbia University. 
''The Chinese are keen to learn modern techniques of lighting, set design and stagecraft. 
They're also looking for freer manners of expression.''
The founder and chairman of the Eugene O'Neill Theater Center, George C. White, is to direct the production of ''The Music Man,'' Meredith Willson's 1957 hit musical, which features such tunes as ''76 Trombones'' and ''Trouble in River City.''
In 1984, Mr. White staged and directed a Chinese cast in O'Neill's ''Anna Christie'' in China.
Â 
'Fantasticks' Will Tour
An associate artistic director of the Circle Repertory Company in New York, Rodney Marriott, is to direct the production of ''Fantasticks,'' the long-running musical by Tom Jones and Harvey Schmidt. 
After an initial run in Beijing, it will go on to Nanjing with hopes of eventual performances in Shanghai, Canton and Hong Kong.
Susan Rose of the arts exchange, which helped arrange the venture, said that it was exciting for the Chinese performers to have to work in an entirely inhabitual manner.
Performances in China usually contain only one discipline, according to Ms. Rose. An opera singer sings opera, a ballet dancer dances ballet, an actor acts and so on.
''The American musical forces all three to collaborate,'' Ms. Rose said.
The project, which is being produced by Edward Corn and Gayle Ritchie, is being partially financed by the American Express Company, which will provide all expenses for the American professionals traveling to China, as well as royalties and nominal fees for the small group of Americans supervising the undertaking. 
The Central Opera Theater is paying for the sets, costumes, Chinese performers and scenery. 
The Chinese Theater Association is paying for the Americans' housing, meals and local transportation in China.
Â 
Lessons in Marketing
Mr. Corn said he had been asked to conduct workshops in China about marketing and promotion -areas, he said, in which the Chinese have become increasingly interested. 
Printed posters are to be displayed around Beijing to advertise the musical - a totally novel practice for the Chinese. 
Usually in China, where cultural events are almost always sold out, performances are not advertised, but merely mentioned in local newspapers.
There are no playbills in China; only mimeographed lists of performers. 
For the production of ''The Music Man,'' a program is being prepared. 
Usually it costs one yuan (about 27 cents) to attend a production. 
''The Music Man'' will cost the Chinese, who take home anywhere from 70 to 90 yuan a month, slightly more than two yuan, Mr. Corn said.
Mr. White, who cast the productions in China last October, said that he had initially wanted to do ''Oklahoma!'' but that the Chinese thought their performers would be unable to dance to Agnes de Mille's choreography and sing simultaneously.
The Chinese, he said, countered his proposal with ''Fiddler on the Roof.''
Mr. White said he resisted, because he thought it was not typically American. 
He then briefly considered ''Man of La Mancha,'' but decided the rape scene in the play would be deemed inappropriate for Chinese audiences. 
It was then that ''The Music Man'' came to mind.
''Once I thought about it,'' said Mr. White of the show, which is set in Iowa in 1912, ''it was obvious.''
Mr. White said the Chinese at first wanted to know if they needed 76 trombones to mount the production. 
Mr. White told them they did not. 
Then they began to worry whether Prof. Harold Hill, the play's protagonist, was a bad man.
''I told them that love makes him a good man,'' Mr. White said.
Â 
Retaining American Aspect
The next decision was whether the cast should appear Chinese or American. 
Unlike his production of ''Anna Christie,'' in which Mr. White tried to tap the universality of the play and to set it in China, he decided that the performers should try to match the classically American content.
''It's no different than Renata Scotto wearing a Kabuki wig,'' Mr. White said.
The 32-member chorus, 24-member ballet, 17 principals, a children's brass band of 15 and an orchestra of 60 are to begin rehearsing on Monday, with the artistic director of the annual O'Neill Music Theater, Paulette Haupt, conducting. 
The choreographer is Lynn Britt, also of the O'Neill. 
Pearl Somner has designed the costumes, and the scenery is based on original designs by Howard Bay, who died in November shortly before a planned trip to China to supervise initial work.
Mr. White said he did not foresee any problems with the translation. 
Musically, he said, he thought the Chinese would be totally at home with the piece, given their training in Western opera. 
The only new undertaking, he said, was the jazz and tap dancing, but he said their training in classical ballet should adequately prepare them.
''What I really want to do is teach the Chinese the basic form,'' Mr. White said. 
''What I would love is for the Chinese eventually to do to us what the British have been doing: come over here with their own style of musical that will knock our socks off.''

text:
ï»¿
THEY say it was the women of ancient China who created the anonymous art form of embroidery called paintings in thread. 
The Chinese still excell at hand embroidery, but as the role of women changes, the art is gradually becoming industrialized.
At the same time, the Chinese have given a whole new dimension to the American table linen industry, providing hand embroidery, crochet work and laces previously imported from Europe at extravagant prices.
''China is the last bastion of fine quality hand embroidery for reasonable prices,'' says Ruth Nesi, co-author of the book ''China's Crafts.''
Mrs. Nesi, a stylist for the Sunweave Linen Corporation, a New York table linen manufacturer, has worked with Chinese embroiderers for five years.
In Shanghai, Liu Jinqi, director of the China National Embroidery Factory, speaks with satisfaction about the American connection. 
The factory is the largest of its kind in China and last year ''graduated'' from the arts and crafts corporation to the category of light industry.
The factory's production has doubled in the last five years to two million pieces, Mrs. Liu said, with 80 percent going to the American market, mostly tablecloths, tablemats, curtains, aprons, pillowcases and cushion covers.
American buyers discovered modern Chinese handwork in the mid-1970's at the Canton Fair, and importers moved in aggressively, according to Mrs. Nesi.
But it wasn't easy, she says; there were basic cultural differences. 
How could young rural Chinese women produce designs for Americans when they hadn't seen American movies, knew nothing about American life and ''didn't have the foggiest notion what a place mat is or where knives and forks and spoons go?''
At that time, some enterprising New York importers decided that the best way to familiarize the Chinese with contemporary tastes in hand embroidery was to take them examples of work from Madeira. 
That Portuguese island used to be an international center for hand embroidery until the young women started to work in the tourism industry.
In 1980, Mrs. Nesi began working with designers of what was then called the No. 1 Embroidery Factory in Shanghai, suggesting designs and colors that would appeal to the American market. 
Until then, the factory had been exporting classic table linen to Europe and Hong Kong.
Sunweave reached an agreement with the Shanghai factory in 1981 and since then, most of its production has been for the American market. 
No problems of protectionism have arisen because there is no hand embroidery industry in the United States to be threatened, according to Mrs. Nesi. The agreement could be affected if new laws set quotas for piecework.
''What is so wonderful about the Chinese is their understanding of the old art form, which has enabled them to create good contemporary commercial products,'' Mrs. Nesi said. 
''Ten years ago American consumers had good solid color and prints made in U.S.A. but had to pay a fortune for imported embroidery work from Switzerland, Italy, Belgium or Madeira or else do it themselves.''
The Chinese have adapted fast. 
Mrs. Nesi recalls that five years ago Mrs. Liu was head designer and has risen through the ranks to become vice manager, working with new products and new machinery. 
Last spring, the Chinese designer, who speaks no English, was invited by Sunweave to work with designers in New York. 
She visited Lord & Taylor and Macy's and ''took it all in her stride,'' Mrs. Nesi said.
''Our production is half and half, half machine, half by hand,'' Mrs. Liu said as she escorted visitors through the Shanghai factory. 
Some of the 1,024 workers were operating old Singer sewing machines, some were making intricate stitches by hand and others were using new Japanese machinery bought in 1984.
Factory workers earn an average of 63 yuan ($21) a month for an eight-hour day plus bonuses, according to Mrs. Liu. A branch factory for making only curtains in a Shanghai suburb employs 600 more people.
Most of the workers, however, are peasant women living in Shanghai's outlying rural districts and do piecework for the factory. 
About 10,500 regular employees work at home for 3 yuan ($1) for a day's work.
Mrs. Liu stressed that it wasn't easy to keep up with the changing American market and said the factory wouldn't be able to do it if American buyers didn't bring them new designs several times a year.
''Chinese don't always like the American designs,'' the factory's technical director said. 
They prefer traditional designs like peacocks and princesses, she said, and are enthusiastic about polyesters - which they call nylon - because they are thin, washable and no-iron. 
They can't understand why Americans love natural fibers, she added.
There are these main types of Chinese embroidery, Mrs. Liu said:
* Suzhou, appliques with flat surface, tight stitches, even thickness and harmonious colors.
* Hunan, with soft shaded hair-thin stitches used in landscapes.
* Guangdon, the ornate style with gold or silver thread and seed-pearls or other embellishments.
* Sichuan, mainly large stitched squares used as wall hangings or for quilts.
Although they seem to prefer machines, some skilled workers demonstrated that they could still make ''invisible'' stitches by splitting one thread 60 times. 
In the old days, the light was so bad that working with this thread ruined the eyes. 
Early this century, the Government is said to have banned the Peking knot, which was so tiny it caused blindness. 
Now, with better working conditions, there is no longer a ''forbidden stitch.''
Mrs. Liu believes hand embroidery will never disappear altogether but predicts that in time most work will be done by machine. 
''Women are getting tired of handwork,'' she said. 
''Particularly now with the one-child family, people don't want their child to stay home and sew. 
Everyone wants to go to the university.''

Archeologists have excavated the huge tomb of a rich, slave-owning duke who lived 2,600 years ago, the biggest ancient burial chamber found in China this century, a leading newspaper said today.
As deep as an eight-story building and large enough to hold 200 dump trucks, the tomb is in the shape of an inverted pyramid and contains the bodies of 180 male and female slaves, said the report in The Guangming Daily.
The report said the duke's coffin would be opened this week, climaxing 10 years of work on the site in Shaanxi province.
The tomb was discovered in 1976, and the report said the dig had been the longest and most elaborate in Chinese archeological history.
Experts think the tomb was built for Duke Jing of the state of Chin during the Spring and Autumn Period (770-476 B.C.) of the Chou Dynasty.

WHETHER New Year's Day is celebrated on Jan. 
1 according to the Gregorian calendar, in September or October as the Jews' Rosh ha-Shanah or in midwinter by Asians, foods serve as edible talismans to assure luck, happiness or prosperity in the coming year.
The notion, for example, that eating gold-colored food will put money in your pocket is common in Peru, where papas a la huancaina, a potato dish tinted with tumeric or with a saffron-colored spice called tadillo, is served on New Year's Eve. 
In China, dumplings made from golden egg pancakes, crisply gilded spring rolls and oranges are the aureate foods appropriate for the Chinese New Year's celebrations in midwinter.
The Chinese also value fish. 
A whole one is preferred, suggesting that prosperity has favored you with more than you can eat.
Pork is on the New Year's table in many cultures, connoting riches because at one time having a pig to slaughter guaranteed food for the coming year.
In Italy and the southern parts of the United States, pork is eaten in the form of sausage, stuffed pig's trotters (zampone), ham hocks or pig's knuckles, invariably accompanied by a dish of dried beans. 
The Italians eat lentils, or lenticchie, which since Roman times have represented coins. 
According to the cookbook author and cooking instructor, Anna Teresa Callen (''Anna Teresa Callen's Menus for Pasta,'' Crown, 1985 ), parsley decorates the dish because it was thought to ward off evil spirits. 
In the American South, greens are added to black-eyed peas or hoppin' John (black-eyed peas with rice). 
The symbolism is straightforward: the greens represented dollars and the black-eyed peas coins. 
Dried beans, garnished or plain, represent the changing over of years, for they can be stored through the winter and then be planted to create the harvest.
Sometimes a silver coin or trinket is buried in a dish of black-eyed peas or hoppin' John, providing an extra measure of good luck to the person finding it. 
The Twelfth Night cake or king's cake served on Epiphany in France will have coins or fava beans tucked inside. 
Similarly, the Spanish roscon de Reyes, a bread, is baked with a coin or small ceramic animal inside for luck. 
The Mexican version, a king's bread with nuts and raisins, is baked with a clay doll inside. 
These breads and cakes are round, symbolizing a whole year, much like the hallah baked for Rosh ha-Shanah.
When it comes time to ring in the New Year, you lift a glass - of Champagne, punch, eggnog or whatever -and propose a toast. 
Why toast?
The tradition in England and Wales was for slices of toasted bread to be soaked in the hot spiced ale called wassail and served with it.
In Spain, according to Penelope Casas, author of ''Tapas'' (Knopf, 1985), 12 grapes are eaten just before midnight on New Year's Eve, one for each chime of the clock. 
Good luck will come to those who finish the grapes before the final stroke.

text:
ï»¿
The goods ranged from goat-hair scarves (khati) and yak-butter lamps (choekung) to dharma buttons and copies of the official Dalai Lama comic book.
They all sold well as the fourth annual Tibet Fair opened near the United Nations yesterday. 
It attracted those with considerable knowledge of the Himalayan land - a man from Virginia showed up to buy a study book for third-year Tibetan - as well as those with only a passing curiosity about the ''roof of the world.''
Strung along walls and piled on tables in a crowded room in the Eastside International Community Center, at 330 East 45th Street, exotic items beckoned buyers, many of whom said they were looking for Christmas ideas. 
Jewelry, dresses, sweaters, boots, hats, silver teapots, ornamental knives, scrolls, books, Buddha statues and ''I Love Tibet'' T-shirts all vied for a spot under the tree.
Many of the items were made by Tibetans, but many were not.
Â 
'Hey, Don't Buy That'
''Don't you just love this?'' said Helen Brill, holding up a red scroll with Chinese characters on it. 
''I don't know whether it's Tibetan, but it sure is beautiful.''
''Hey, don't buy that,'' a man whispered conspiratorially to his wife, who was admiring a silk scarf that had a ''Made in Beijing'' tag on the back. 
''The Tibetans don't like the Chinese.''
China annexed Tibet in the early 1950's and has run it as an administrative unit since a crackdown in 1959 that prompted the Dalai Lama - the Tibetan spiritual and temporal leader - to flee on horseback over the Himalayas into India.
The fair involved an odd mix of Tibetan serenity and American hustle. 
''Now wait a minute,'' hissed a woman who believed she had been overcharged. 
''I thought the Dalai Lama postcards were a quarter each and five for a dollar.''
The seller started to explain no, those were 50 cents each.
Â 
'A Sort of Uneasiness'
Then he shrugged and sold them, placidly, five for a dollar.
''The feeling is something different from a normal feeling for me,'' explained Jigme Sampho, who with his wife, Dechen, was selling hats and boots made by Tibetans living in exile in India. 
''There is a sort of uneasiness.''
But Mr. Sampho, who works for the Parks Department as a maintenance man in Central Park, added that the fair does come only once a year. 
And he said he was glad that people could come and learn something about the land where he was born.
Many said they did appreciate that chance. 
''I'm fascinated about Tibet,'' one woman said, ''but I've pretty well decided I'll never go there because of the altitude.''
Tenzing Chhodak sat selling posters, books and calendars underneath a large print of the Tibetan Wheel of Life, depicting what are believed to be the six stages into which human beings are continually reincarnated and from which, in order to attain enlightenment, they must escape.
These cycles are the realm of false gods; of titans vainly trying to battle their way into heaven; hell dwellers being administered hot-and-cold tortures; preta, or hungry ghosts, that symbolize greedy people; animals, guilty of ignorance, and humans, who alone among those in the six cycles are offered the chance to study and practice religion.
The fair, proceeds of which are contributed to Tibetan refugees in India, continues today from 11 A.M. to 6 P.M., and also Saturday, Dec. 
20.
Tibetans hold the fair both to raise money and to educate people about their land, said Tinley Nyandak, president of the New York-based Tibetan Association.
Mr. Nyandak said the region's Tibetan community, numbering about 160, is one of the smallest ethnic groups in the metropolitan area. 
Not quite the smallest, he noted: ''You know the Manchus?
There are only two Manchus in the whole Northeast, so far as I know.''

TUNG'S dances work their way along with a thoughtfulness and conviction that persuade one to follow. 
Such was the case Friday at the La Mama Annex, when Chen & Dancers presented Mr. Chen's new ''Longmen Mountain,'' one in a series of modern-dance pieces on old China.
Set to wonderfully primeval clangor and chants composed by Li Tai-Shaing, ''Longmen Mountain'' takes its title from the name of a Chinese grotto of the fifth century, a cave-temple that served Silk Route travelers and Buddhist pilgrims. 
Mr. Chen blends the elasticity and bold attack of Western modern dance with the flexed fingers and hands, for example, of ancient Chinese dance forms in work that is as much dance as drama.
Jennifer Dunning reviews "Longmen Mountain" by Chen & Dancers at La Mama Annex
A lone pilgrim enters the stage space, which comes to seem remarkably like a cave. 
He pays intent homage to religious hangings along the walls, probing the ground before him with his walking stick. 
Six travelers follow in a group, exploring the cave in an orderly fashion that looks, nonetheless, almost rambunctious beside his stillness.
The dance grows more frenzied as the six young men and women move in juxtaposed groups or break, one at a time, from the crowd. 
But by the end of ''Longmen Mountain,'' they are moving in unison, reverent creatures who have taken on something of the single pilgrim's gravity. 
Changes have occurred inside the cave, for them, at least.
Such changes seem to be a subject of interest to the Shanghai-born choreographer, a product of dance education in Taiwan and at New York's Juilliard School and New York University. 
The previously reviewed ''Voices of Yellow Dust,'' which completed the program, took a group of the dead on their journey into the afterlife, accompanied by a guide from whom life ebbs as they awaken. 
That dance unfolds at as measured a pace as ''Longmen Mountain,'' but is a neater piece of choreography.
The likable company includes Bambi Anderson, Wei Chen, Lynn Frielinghaus, Mr. Chen, Dian Dong, Kristin Jackson and Long Phi Nguyen.
