text:
ï»¿
IN THE ETHNIC COMMUNITIES that spawned them, artists who manage to cross over into the mainstream from Harlem or Watts or Chinatown east or west call the journey ''riding on the hyphen.''
Pop musicians like Mexican-American Ricardo Valenzuela, who as Ritchie Valens topped the charts in the 1950's with ''La Bamba,'' were among the first. 
Today's crossover stars include the black American film maker Spike Lee, whose vaguely anarchist dispatches from the city (''She's Gotta Have It'') and the campus (''School Daze'') are propelled by a savvy populist energy.
David Henry Hwang - barely 30 and haunted by spirits often of his own invention - is riding on the hyphen into mainstream American theater as few Asian-Americans have before him. 
For the young playwright, the Broadway opening next Sunday of his ''M. 
Butterfly'' represents a breathtaking leap. 
With its scandalous and incredible plot, its flourishes of Chinese opera and flashes of nudity, its Western soliloquizing and reflections on East-West politics, its original music (by Lucia Hwong) interwoven with Puccini's ''Madama Butterfly,'' Hwang's play breaches just about every convention of the commercial theater.
Of the five new American dramas to open on Broadway in the 1987-88 season (a figure that baldly expresses many producers' hostility to the category), Hwang's is the only one to arrive without the benefit of development in the noncommercial sector. 
Moreover, the $1.5 million production, staged by the British director John Dexter and starring John Lithgow, is one of the most opulent ever given a nonmusical play on Broadway.
The source of ''M. 
Butterfly'' is a story that itself defies belief. 
Under the headline ''France Jails 2 in Odd Case of Espionage,'' a dispatch from Paris in The New York Times of May 11, 1986, told of Bernard Boursicot, a former French diplomat, and his lover, Shi Peipu, a star of the Beijing Opera, who had each been sentenced by a French court to six years in jail for spying for China. 
(Shi was subsequently expelled from France.) Their affair had begun in 1964 in Beijing, where Boursicot was stationed. 
It ended two decades later, after the opera star, accompanied by a child who had purportedly been fathered by the diplomat, moved into the Frenchman's Paris home and attracted the attention of the French counterespionage service. 
During the trial, the opera star was revealed to be a man.
The diplomat testified that this was shocking news to him. 
Paris buzzed.
So did the young playwright. 
''The story enabled me to pull together various concerns that I have about racism, sexism and imperialism,'' says Hwang. 
''The story was like a perfect little jar that could hold all these different subjects.
''I only knew Madame Butterfly as a cultural stereotype,'' he continues. 
''Like, sometimes you would say, 'Oh, she's pulling a Butterfly' - which meant someone trying to do a submissive-Oriental number. 
I was trying to think of a hook, a way to break the back of this spy story. 
One day it popped into my head: What did Boursicot think he was getting?
Well, he probably thought he was getting Madame Butterfly.''
Hwang, who lives in Los Angeles with his wife, Ophelia, would fit nobody's stereotype of the submissive Asian. 
He tends to augment his slight frame with the padded contours of Armani suits and speaks with considered precision, though his voice has a childlike pitch and often cracks when he is engaged by a subject.
In ''M. 
Butterfly,'' Hwang spins a complex yarn from the 1986 news report. 
His fantasy includes a slangy precis of the Puccini opera from an Asian point of view and an attempt to pair the story of the affair with a meditation on what might well have been going on within a French mission in China in the late 1950's and early 60's.
The spying gave the playwright a route into political issues he wanted to deal with. 
''It has real implications for the choices that were made,'' Hwang says of the affair. 
''People went to war, died, made political decisions through these personal things. 
We didn't consider Orientals to be our equals. 
We didn't figure after the Second World War that they'd come back and beat us at our own game. 
That sort of miscalculation also led us to believe that if we bombed Vietnam enough, they would all give in.''
''M. Butterfly'' begins a few years earlier than the true story. 
The diplomat, renamed Gallimard, meets the opera star, called Soong (played by B. D. Wong), at an embassy function where the singer performs Madame Butterfly's death scene. 
In a conversation over drinks, Soong scoffs at Gallimard's sentimental response to the opera. 
''Consider it this way,'' the singer says. 
''What would you say if a blonde homecoming queen fell in love with a short Japanese businessman?
He treats her cruelly, then goes home for three years, during which time she prays to his picture and turns down marriage from a young Kennedy. 
Then, when she learns he has remarried, she kills herself. 
Now, I believe you would consider this girl to be a deranged idiot, correct?
But because it's an Oriental who kills herself for an American - ah!
- you find it beautiful.''
Jack Viertel - one of the principal figures in bringing ''M. 
Butterfly'' to New York - was a dramaturge, working with playwrights on scripts, at the Mark Taper Forum in Los Angeles when he read the accounts of the French spy trial. 
Soon after, he called Hwang to suggest that the newspaper account had dramatic possibilities; the playwright told Viertel he'd already written the play, with the encouragement of Stuart Ostrow, an independent producer.
''It's one of the few plays that present a fascinating event - as in e Met a the blinding of the horses in 'Equus' - and then explain it in a way that's up to the fascination of the event, that isn't ultimately a disappointment,'' says Viertel.
Ostrow sent Hwang's script to John Dexter last year. 
The director's response was immediate and positive. 
Dexter - who had staged Peter Shaffer's ''Equus'' on Broadway in 1974, as well as such modern operas as Francis Poulenc's ''Dialogues of the Carmelites'' at the Metropolitan Opera - instantly recognized in David Hwang a powerful new theatrical voice.
''The language and the freedom with which he uses the stage, playing across time, space, geography - I suppose that was the appeal,'' says Dexter, whose staging of Alban Berg's ''Lulu'' will open at the Met a few days after ''M. 
Butterfly.''
''But mainly the language, which is extraordinarily funny and touching, never striking a false note. 
He has a great instinct for creating situa-tions in which theatrical magic can happen.''
DAVID HENRY HWANG, the son of a Shanghai-born banker and a Chinese pianist raised in the Philippines, began riding on the hyphen to mainstream prominence from the unlikely ''ghetto'' of San Gabriel, Calif., a middle-class enclave south of Pasadena.
''I knew I was Chinese,'' he says, ''but growing up, it never occurred to me that that had any particular implication or that it should differentiate me in any way. 
I thought it was a minor detail, like having red hair. 
I never got a lot in school to contradict that. 
My parents brought us up with a rather nice sense of self.''
Nothing in his past propelled him toward the theater; indeed, he assumed he would go into law when he went to Stanford University in the mid-1970's. 
But when he got there, he found himself searching for the meaning of ''Chinese-American.''
His parents' diverse histories didn't make the task easy.
''My father has always been interested in discarding the past,'' says Hwang. 
''He's never much liked China, or the whole idea behind China or Chinese ways of thinking. 
He's always been much more attracted to American ways of thinking. 
He feels Americans are more open - they tell you what they think - and he's very much that way himself.''
Hwang's mother brought to the family a tradition of Protestant fundamentalism. 
Her grandparents, who lived in the seaside village of Amoy, in Fujian Province, were converted by missionaries; her grandmother, Hwang says, was an exorcist. 
His mother's family migrated to the Philippines and there became wealthy merchants before coming to the United States in the late 1960's. 
Hwang's parents met at a foreign-students' dance at the University of Southern California and fell in love, but they couldn't marry until his father converted to Protestantism.
While at Stanford, Hwang started going to the theater, particularly San Francisco's Magic Theater, where Sam Shepard was bringing out his new work. 
On a lark, in 1978, Hwang attended the first Padua Hills Playwrights Festival in Claremont, Calif. 
- a workshop that has become a major playwrights' retreat - where Shepard, Maria Irene Fornes and others worked with fledgling writers.
There, Hwang began writing ''FOB'' (''fresh off the boat''). 
The play tells the story of a young, rich newcomer to California and his visit with Chinese-American cousins. 
But, in the kind of twist that was to characterize much of Hwang's subsequent work, that story is interwoven with one about Fa Mu Lan, the legendary heroine who figures in Maxine Hong Kingston's novel ''Woman Warrior,'' and Gwan Gung, the Chinese god of war introduced to American audiences by another Chinese-American playwright, Frank Chin.
''I read Maxine's book,'' Hwang says, ''and felt immediately excited by the possibility that you could interweave the hyperrealistic details of contemporary American life with the larger, mythical ghost story in the background.''
The naive in ''FOB,'' the son of a Hong Kong businessman, is treated with contempt by the kin who know what the future holds for him. 
''Coming to America, you're gonna jump the boat,'' an assimilated Chinese-American hisses. 
''You're gonna decide you like us. 
Yeah - you're gonna like having 15 theaters in three blocks, you're gonna like West Hollywood and Newport Beach. 
You're gonna decide to become an American. 
. . . You won't even know it's coming before it has you. 
Before you're trying real hard to be just like the rest of us - go dinner, go movie, go motel, bang-bang. 
And when your father writes you that do-it-yourself acupuncture sales are down, you'll throw that letter in the basket and burn it in your brain. 
And you'll write that you're gonna live in Monterey Park a few years before going back home - and you'll get your green card - and you'll build up a nice little stockbroker's business and have a few American kids before your dad realizes what's happened and dies, his hopes reduced to a few chattering teeth and a pack of pornographic playing cards. 
Yeah - great things come to the U.S. out of Hong Kong.''
No one who read ''FOB'' in its first drafts could fail to be moved by the blend of slice-of-life realism and yearning spiritualism - scattershot anger mixed with a sense of fathomless loss. 
It wasn't Hwang's first play, but John L'Heureux, his writing coach at Stanford and author of the novel ''A Woman Run Mad,'' was stunned by it.
''He came in and said he wanted me to give him a tutorial in play writing,'' L'Heureux recalls. 
''He showed me some of his first attempts; they were palpably bad. 
I told him to read Sam Shepard and to get some education. 
In the middle of the second week, he handed in a play. 
I couldn't believe it was by the same person.''
''FOB'' was first performed by students in Hwang's Stanford dormito-ry - part of the spring rites on cam-pus - under the young playwright's direction. 
At the same time, he sent it off to the National Playwrights' Conference of the Eugene O'Neill Theater Center in Waterford, Conn. 
- one of the country's most prestigious launching sites for new plays. 
In the spring of 1979, just weeks before he graduated from Stanford, he got the call: the O'Neill wanted the play. 
''Of all the moments in my career so far,'' says Hwang, ''just on a visceral level, that's probably been the most exciting.''
''The main thing I learned there,'' he says of that summer at the O'Neill, ''was how to filter criticism. 
You do this play and then everyone sits around and tells you how they would write your play if they were you. 
. . . I tended to take the bulk of the comments and do rewrites based on those lines, and I eventually threw them all out, because, yeah, there's a certain value in all this criticism, but you can't just swallow it all.''
HWANG FILLED A VAC-uum in New York, where productions of Asian-American plays were mostly limited to Tisa Chang's Pan Asian Repertory Theater and Wynn Handman's American Place Theater. 
In the early and mid-70's, the latter had produced Frank Chin's ''Chickencoop Chinaman'' and ''Year of the Dragon'' - angry plays by an angry young playwright. 
In Hwang, the producer Joseph Papp -on the prowl for new Asian-American work - found a different but no less compelling and personal voice.
'' 'FOB' reminded me of the 'greenhorns,' the Jews who came from Eastern Europe,'' says Papp. 
''Even though the cultures were strikingly different, it was the same notion. 
The principle of someone coming from the old country who didn't know how to behave himself was very much part of my own tradition. 
But this went further than that. 
'FOB' went into the traditions by suddenly moving into a more abstract, poetic existence in the context of a very naturalistic play.
''So I met him and liked him immediately,'' Papp continues. 
''He was trying to maintain his connection with his roots. 
I met his parents in Los Angeles. 
We went out for dinner. 
Naturally, his father selected a French restaurant. 
There was the son, holding on to tradition, and the father, very Westernized. 
David was looking for his past. 
That was very refreshing to me, because usually it's lost into the American culture or nobody can articulate it properly.''
''FOB'' opened at New York's Public Theater on June 9, 1980, directed by Mako, who had acted in the original Broadway production of Stephen Sondheim's ''Pacific Overtures.''
Starring in Hwang's play was John Lone, a Chinese actor trained in Asian opera techniques, with whom the playwright would be associated through several subsequent productions, and who would himself ride on the hyphen to stardom in Bernardo Bertolucci's ''The Last Emperor.''
Frank Rich wrote in The New York Times: ''Surely 'FOB' is the first show that has ever attempted to marry the conventional well-made play to Oriental theater and to mix the sensibilities of Maxine Hong Kingston and Norman Lear.''
Though ''FOB'' won Obie awards for both Hwang and Lone, the playwright found that not everyone was comfortable with his unboosterish portrayal of assimilation.
''My work has always been controversial within certain segments of the Asian-American community,'' says Hwang. 
''This is a community that is generally not represented well at all on the stage, in the media, etc. 
So on those few occasions when something comes along, everybody feels obligated to make sure that it represents his own point of view. 
And of course no artist can do that. 
. . . I find that sort of political criticism much more difficult and substantial than the esthetic criticism that I received at the O'Neill - that's nothing compared with being told that you've set the Asian-American back 10 years.''
Maxine Hong Kingston saw the Public Theater production of ''FOB.''
''The main question he asks is, What is a Chinese-American?'' says the novelist. 
''Is there a separate identity?
In 'FOB' there's a little bit of borrowing from Chinese theater, but it's not Chinese theater. 
He's searching, and he hasn't found it yet.''
Hwang achieved greater recognition with his next work, ''The Dance and the Railroad,'' which was commissioned by the Off Off Broadway New Federal Theater and moved to the Public in 1981. 
That play, set in 1867 during the construction of the transcontinental railroad, featured John Lone as a Chinese laborer more concerned with maintaining his operatic skills than with serving the white man, and Tzi Ma as another laborer whose heart is set on learning how to perform the role of a heroic warrior. 
While continuing to combine past and present, the playwright was also revealing another trait: a packed literary style that is never turgid.
Confident in Hwang's development as a playwright, Papp followed ''Dance'' almost immediately with a full-scale production of an audacious new work, ''Family Devotions.''
Mixing unembarrassed family portraits with a searching into the past, ''Family Devotions'' is a big, messy farce with a bleak, surreal coda. 
The centerpiece of the set is a pulpit, embellished with a neon cross, that is brought out daily for family prayer meetings. 
Here was Hwang skewering the Christian tradition that had obstructed his journey into the past.
''In this country, Christianity provides both a means of assimilation and a source of community,'' says the playwright. 
''Community for obvious reasons, because you have these Chinese churches and Korean churches. 
But you're also taking on what is perceived to be the religion of the society, doing something that's very acceptable by American standards -that is, you're buying into the great American cultural myth, and everybody's very happy. 
Except for your own soul, everybody wins.''
''Family Devotions'' is set in a home much like the one the playwright came from and revolves around a visit from a family elder who runs afoul of his sisters' efforts to convert him to Christianity. 
It also tells the stories of a wealthy father -a bank president who has found notoriety as a victim of a kidnapping -and his son (a thinly disguised stand-in for the author), who is leaving the family to go east and play the violin for the Boston Symphony.
''Chinese culture in general is not very religious,'' Hwang observes. 
''Confucianism is more a code of ethics than a religion, and ancestor worship is a way for parents to control you even after they're dead.''
The playwright's parents, Henry and Dorothy Hwang, were in the audience on the opening night of ''Family Devotions.''
''When he was a sophomore in college, he showed me a play and I said, 'Well, I send you to this expensive school and you write trashy stuff like this?'
'' recalls Henry Hwang, who was himself kidnapped in a bizarre incident about 10 years ago. 
''Two weeks later, he said it was going to be done in the dormitory. 
We went to see it, and I was moved to tears. 
But I felt dizzy after 'Family Devotions.'
I felt as if my life had been turned upside down. 
Of course, if the material is useful to him, he's welcome to it.''
With fame came a strong dose of self-doubt. 
''I was being put in a position for which I was not prepared,'' says the playwright. 
''At 23 or 24, I was asked to be some sort of spokesperson for Asian-Americans on various issues which I hadn't really thought out that well consciously. 
On the one hand, it was flattering. 
But on the other hand, growing up as a person of color, you're always ambivalent to a certain degree about your own ethnicity. 
You think it's great, but there is necessarily a certain amount of self-hatred, or confusion at least, which results from the fact that there's a role model in this society which is basically a Caucasian man, and you don't measure up to that.
''What was happening to me,'' he continues, ''was that that quality about which I was ambivalent was being thrust into the forefront. 
. . . It was no longer that I was a playwright per se, but that I was an Asian-American playwright, and my Asian-Americanness became the quality which defined me to the public.''
Hwang spent the next few years living a life of modest celebrity in New York - in 1983, the Public produced a pair of one-act plays of his under the collective title ''Sound and Beauty'' that were received with qualified praise - and traveling in Asia, Europe and Canada. 
In Toronto, he met Ophelia Chong, a Chinese-Canadian; they were married in Los Angeles and have lived there since 1985 with an aging Welsh corgi named Victor.
''Rich Relations'' was written during Hwang's Canadian sojourn, after a long bout with writer's block, and produced Off Broadway by the Second Stage in the spring of 1986. 
It was his first non-Asian play. 
It was also his first flop. 
Critics complained that he was rehashing old themes, and the playwright didn't disagree with the charge.
'' 'Rich Relations' was another attempt to write a spiritual farce,'' says Hwang, ''and it's about my family -except that they're not Asians. 
It was also an attempt to talk about resurrection, which was what I felt had just happened to me. 
Ethnic writers still have a kind of second-class cultural citizenship. 
. . . I've gotten a lot of mileage out of writing about Chinese-Americans. 
Whether that's good for my career in the long run is debatable.''
Hwang began writing for the movies and television as well as for the theater. 
He recently completed ''My American Son,'' about the Iran-contra affair, for Home Box Office and is at work on ''Seven Years in Tibet,'' a feature film set in India and Asia during World War II. 
All-out failure, he says, was the most liberating thing that had happened to him since the first strong flush of success with ''FOB.''
IT IS EASY TO SEE ALL OF Hwang's work as leading up to ''M. 
Butterfly,'' a play that is, at its root, a meditation on the ways the West misperceives the East and vice versa.
The composer Philip Glass, with whom Hwang was working on another project, recommended the playwright to Stuart Ostrow, who funded the research for ''M. 
Butterfly.''
By the time the play was ready to go into production, Jack Viertel had moved to New York to become a creative director for the Jujamcyn Theaters organization, which owns five Broadway theater houses. 
Viertel persuaded the company to invest in ''M. 
Butterfly'' and Ostrow to house it in a Jujamcyn theater when it came to Broadway. 
David Geffen signed on as co-producer. 
For a hugely risky work, ''M. 
Butterfly'' had garnered an extraordinary amount of mainstream support.
''This is a leap for a number of reasons,'' says Viertel. 
''One, it's a big play. 
It's the first play David's written that deals with history in a way that isn't totally imaginary or imagined; he's using the real world in a highly theatrical way. 
It's a much larger version of what he was doing in 'The Dance and the Railroad' -take an event and find the underlying social and political meaning of it.''
In ''M. 
Butterfly,'' as in all of his plays, Hwang searches in some of the darker corners of his own psyche. 
''As an Asian, I identify with Soong,'' he says. 
''As a man, I identify with Gallimard. 
That willful self-delusion is something I know I've experienced as a man; I've been good at self-delusion when I've wanted to be. 
The really sexist things Gallimard says are things that I know on some level work in my own soul and color my relationships with women. 
Pleasure in giving pain to a woman is not that far removed, I think, from a lot of male experiences.''
He recognizes the risks in moving into the political arena with so personal and stylized a work as ''M. 
Butterfly.''
During its pre-Broadway run in Washington, Hwang sweated out some negative criticism, reworking a few scenes and adding others to clarify the play without compromising his iconoclastic history lesson.
''The play might be seen as anti-Western, in the sense that it's saying that the West just hasn't looked at these issues,'' he says. 
''That's partly true, but it's very pro-American, too. 
It's saying, 'These are the facts of the situation, and if you would like to get along better in the world, then you had better look at the world more clearly. 
The East isn't going to go away.'
''

text:
ï»¿
Xiang-Dong Kong
Xiang-dong Kong, a pianist, was born in Shanghai in 1968, and was one of the young musicians featured in Isaac Stern's 1979 film, ''From Mao to Mozart.''
Since then, he has completed his studies in his homeland and enrolled at Brigham Young University, in Utah. 
Earlier this year, he won the gold medal at the Gina Bachauer International Piano Competition, which sponsored his New York debut recital Oct. 
15 at Alice Tully Hall.
Mr. Kong proved especially impressive in works that demand outgoing, bravura playing - Liszt's ''Rhapsodie Espagnole,'' Grainger's wild-eyed paraphrase on Tchaikovsky's ''Waltz of the Flowers,'' and the sober, incisive and fiery Second Sonata by Robert Muczynski.
In these, he played with great energy, and a sense of rhythmic liquidity. 
Yet, even in the densest, loudest passages, every strand of the musical texture was clear and well-placed, and matters of phrasing and coloration appeared carefully considered.
This deliberation worked less well in a Haydn Sonata (Hob. 
XVI:50), Chopin's Polonaise-Fantaisie (Op. 61) and a Rachmaninoff Etude-Tableau (Op. 33, No. 8), all of which he played more gently. 
His sound was delicate and lovely in these, and there were some fine coloristic ideas. 
But there was also a tendency toward rhythmic squareness - the opposite of what made the brighter works so successful.
Â 
Arax Davtian
Arax Davtian, a soprano from Armenia who has been singing at the Bolshoi Opera in recent seasons, made her way easily through a demanding debut program last Sunday afternoon at Weill Recital Hall.
Ms. Davtian has a large, powerful, rich-toned voice and a commanding presence. 
She was most striking in arias by Verdi (''Pace, Pace'' from ''La Forza del Destino,'' and ''Ecco l'Orrido Campo'' from ''Un Ballo in Maschera'') and Bellini (''O Quante Volte'' from ''I Capuletti e i Montecchi''), and her renderings of contemporary songs by Tigran Mansurian and Edward Mirzoyan were quite moving.
She was also an effective Mozart singer, after a fashion. 
To this listener's taste, her heavy but well-controlled vibrato is better suited to music of later vintage; yet, once one got used to the dimension of her voice, her renderings of ''Come Scoglio'' from ''Cosi Fan Tutte'' and a pair of Mozart songs turned out to be fairly persuasive.
Also on the program were songs and arias by Beethoven and Glinka. 
Diana Mkrtchian was the excellent accompanist. 
Her handling of the operatic reductions were particularly pleasing.
Â 
Edith Murano
Edith Murano, a pianist from Argentina, favors a dry, lightly pedaled sound, and an approach to phrasing that can seem clipped and edgy. 
But her ideas are often original enough that one can overlook the more quirky aspects of her style - as well as the fact that her renderings are not always note-perfect.
At her North American debut, on Thursday evening at Weill Recital Hall, she played Beethoven's ''Pastorale'' Sonata and Prokofiev's Sonata No. 3 daringly, with razor-like rhythms and a tempestuous energy that often threatened to careen out of control, but never did. 
She also offered the United States premiere of Virgilio Mortari's Serenata, an attractive, neo-Baroque suite, which she played with clarity and incisiveness. 
Her opening pair of Bach Preludes and Fugues was less impressive. 
And her closing Chopin group was a mixed success. 
A Barcarolle (Op. 60) and an Impromptu (Op.51) were nightmarishly overwrought, but the Andante Spianato and Grande Polonaise Brillante (Op. 22) was played with a soulful, almost improvisatory approach that offset the frequent wrong notes in exposed places.

file: DISCOVERIES_1. Once-Over Easy.txt
text:
ï»¿
With many clothes again made of natural fibers, which wrinkle more than synthetics, travelers are packing irons. 
Sanyo makes a travel iron with several attractive features. 
For one thing, it's a steam iron, more effective against wrinkles than a dry iron. 
It has adjustable settings and dual voltage (120 and 220) and comes with two converter plugs for foreign outlets. 
Best of all, it folds flat, measures 6 by 1 by 2 3/4 inches folded and weighs a pound. 
It's priced at $40 in the Lee Bailey section at Bendel's.
Angela Taylor highlights various interesting finds in area retail stores2. 
Robes From China
China's fashion industry is perking up, adapting some of its classic styles for Western taste. 
Take the Eastern dress called the cheongsam, which is usually made of silk or rayon, with a rather close fit and short sleeves. 
By translating it into cotton and making it looser, the manufacturers have achieved an attractive short robe that can be worn right through summer. 
The same updating has been given to the full-length kung pao, or palace robe. 
It comes in such shades as sky blue, has a diagonal fastening banded in pale pink and is appliqued with large flowers. 
The short robe comes in pink, red, pale or deep blue with a Jacquard weave and has sprigs of flowers embroidered at the top. 
Since the robes are made of cotton and polyester, they are washable. 
The Sino-American Commodities Center, 29 West 23d Street, will have them later this month priced at $25 to $30.
Â 
3. Vacation for the Eyes
A vacationer heading southward might check a clever new sunshade idea: a visor attached to sunglasses so that eyes get double protection. 
The Valley Visor comes in bright shades of rigid plastic. 
It has elastic loops that slip over the ear pieces of sunglasses framed in the same color as the visor. 
You'll find it in red, blue, yellow, black, white and bubblegum pink for $18 at Bloomingdale's hat bar.
Â 
4. To Protect Laps
They are really dish towels, but at the Wolfman-Gold shop in SoHo they are sold as oversized napkins, particularly to protect buffet diners from food spilled in their laps. 
The dish towel napkins are made of white cotton printed with ''Eat,'' ''Dine'' or a trio of tray-carrying waiters. 
They're $4 each at Wolfman-Gold & Good Company, 484 Broome Street.
Â 
5. Bard Sends Greetings
Shakespearean scholars know that the Bard wrote quotations that can be used for just about any situation. 
Michael LaPlaca, a young artist, has done greeting cards based on Shakespeare's characters and used the quotations amusingly. 
For instance: ''The lady doth protest too much, methinks'' (''Hamlet'') shows a rather rattled Elizabethan woman and reads ''Happy Birthday'' inside. 
''O, my offence is rank, it smells to heaven,'' also from ''Hamlet,'' apologizes for having forgotten a birthday. 
And ''Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em'' (''Twelfth Night'') impudently asks, ''But what's your excuse?''
The cards are $1 each at Under Attack, 187 Columbus Avenue (68th Street) and Wendell's, 20 Eighth Avenue (West 12th Street).
Â 
Advance Warning
You've promised to knit a sweater for someone you're fond of, but you've put it off too long. 
Unless you're a lightning-fast knitter, you'll probably not get it finished in time. 
How about an I.O.U.?
A yarn shop has come up with a clever thought: When you purchase the yarn for a full-size sweater, it will give you instructions for knitting a tiny version of it that can be done in an hour, plus a gift box to put it in. 
You'll find a large selection of yarns and the instructions for miniature sweaters at Dariff Design Associates, 80 Fifth Avenue (13th Street).

Discoveries column surveys a variety of products2.

The set is $25 at Penny Whistle, 1281 Madison Avenue (between 91st and 92d Streets).

An array of ingenious and attractive makeup cases has just arrived from Italy from a company called Pupa (it means doll in Italian).

file: Distinctions Blur as Deaf Actors Share a Stage.txt
text:
ï»¿
As soon as the powerful-looking Akahira Yonaiyama moves across the stage, speaking in Japanese sign language as he goes, the blur of simultaneous translations begins.
Mr. Yonaiyama is a star of the Japan Theater of the Deaf; as he plays his part in a rehearsal, a speaking member of the cast interprets the sign language into spoken Japanese. 
At the same time, Mr. Yonaiyama's lines are being spoken by another actor in English - and immediately translated into American sign language. 
In the actual performances, though, the only spoken words are in Japanese.
When Mr. Yonaiyama's American co-actors from the National Theater of the Deaf in Chester, Conn., speak or sign their roles in the Tokyo International Theater Festival here, the whole process is reversed. 
The festival continues through Wednesday; the theaters of the deaf will perform in Osaka for one night.
Â 
'Somehow, It All Works'
''When you think about it, it should all be a confusing mess,'' the American group's artistic director, David Hays, said during a rehearsal. 
''But somehow, it all works.''
In fact, it does, and the success of this largely deaf cast from India, Japan, China and the United States seems to prove that sign language is less of a barrier on stage than the spoken word.
Although spoken Japanese and English have about as much in common as sashimi and hot dogs, American and Japanese sign languages share fundamental concepts.
''I think it must be easier to understand English sign language than English itself,'' the 36-year-old Mr. Yonaiyama said through a sign-language translator.
The deaf actors in the American and Japanese acting companies were soon chatting, and by late afternoon during one recent rehearsal it became clear they were already on each other's wavelengths.
Â 
Festival Is in Ikebukuro
The festival is in the Seibu Theater in Ikebukuro, a jammed commuter hub and shopping area in northwest Tokyo. 
The Japan Theater of the Deaf, a small company founded eight years ago, opens its part of the program with a Kyogen, a traditional Japanese comedy often performed during the intermission of Noh, or dramatic, plays.
The American actors perform improvisations based on spoken and sign-language suggestions from the audience, with Mr. Yonaiyama and another deaf Japanese actor, Tetsuya Izaki. 
Both trained with the American group in Connecticut.
The highlight of the program is ''In a Grove'' by Ryunosuke Akutagawa, a tale of rape, betrayal and suicide that was the basis of Akira Kurosawa's film ''Rashomon.''
The story is told through the testimony of a woodcutter, a priest, a policeman, a bandit and others involved in a bizarre encounter in the woods. 
The one-at-a-time nature of the testimony - in which each of the participants gives a different version of the truth - helps to simplify the problem of multiple translations.
Â 
Selecting the Play
''I chose the play because the testimonies are individual, and the parts can be developed,'' said Mr. Hays, a former set designer for George Balanchine who first came to Japan in 1960 as a technical adviser to the Kabuki theater.
But Kabuki is one thing to the Japanese, and deaf actors are another. 
It is rare to see physically disabled people on the subways and buses in Tokyo; physical handicaps are viewed here as a family stigma, and the disabled are often kept at home.
That is changing slowly in Japan, and Mr. Hays and his troupe are trying to speed the process. 
''When we first planned to come here, agents told me that Japanese would not come to the theater to see deaf actors,'' Mr. Hays said. 
''They would be afraid that if they were seen, people would assume their families had someone at home in the closet.''
Â 
Popular Actress Appears
So far, the crowds have been encouraging. 
And this performance has an added drawing card: Tetsuko Kuroyanagi, an immensely popular actress and talk-show host, who has become a major force behind the Japan Theater of the Deaf. 
She appears in one of the few speaking roles.
Along with her are a few actors and actresses from theaters of the deaf struggling to begin elsewhere in Asia. 
Among them is Wang Ling, a young business school graduate from Beijing who is fulfilling the dream of his late father, Wang Zhentai.
When the National Theater of the Deaf went to China in 1986, Wang Zhentai spoke in Mandarin as the company performed in sign language. 
He then started a theater of the deaf in China and brought several Chinese performers to the National Theater's summer school in Connecticut. 
He died last August, shortly after returning to China, and his son picked up the effort as a tribute to him.
Â 
Winning Recognition
''The Chinese bureaucracy is so huge, and they had never heard of a theater for the deaf before,'' Wang Ling said. 
But he has begun to win recognition for the group, and he persuaded the Chinese authorities to allow a young deaf factory worker, Yang Ling, to join in the Ikebukuro festival.
An actor and an artistic director from India, which uses the American sign-language system, are also involved.
''I've never seen anything quite like this,'' said the artistic director of the Indian group, Zarin Chaudhuri, an actress from Bombay.
''Yesterday it looked impossible,'' she said. 
''Today it is all coming together.''

text:
ï»¿
Christopher S. Wren is The New York Times Peking bureau chief. 
By Christopher S. Wren ANY WORTHY undertaking in China starts with a meeting, and a voyage aboard the East Is Red No. 46 was no exception. 
Once the river steamer had pulled away from the dock at Chongqing in the early morning drizzle and swung into the cocoa-colored waters of the Yangtze, the ship's loudspeaker asked passengers in each cluster of cabins to dispatch a representative to the small dining room on the second deck.
Because it was my first trip down the Yangtze, I asked if I could sit in. 
''There's nothing secret about it,'' shrugged Hu Yuchun, the chief steward. 
So I joined 14 other passengers around the table. 
Tea was poured. 
''We need the help of the passengers to make this trip smooth and peaceful,'' said Mr. Hu, a tall, earnest young man in a white jacket and horn-rimmed spectacles. 
Everyone nodded at being asked to do his part to get the vessel to Wuhan, 851 miles downriver.
Mr. Hu rattled off the statistics in the flat drawl of his native Sichuan province. 
The East Is Red No. 46 was 252 feet long and 50 feet wide. 
Its mighty twin diesel engines propelled it at a speed of 16 miles an hour, but the Yangtze's current was so swift that it sailed downstream at 21 miles an hour and back upstream at only about 10 miles an hour. 
It was carrying 850 passengers, not quite full capacity, and Mr. Hu asked that they not leave watches and other valuables lying about, throw trash overboard or sit on the railings; he also cautioned against shining flashlights at night because it would confuse the helmsman.
This was not just any boat excursion. 
A voyage down the Yangtze offered a look at a China in the midst of what may be the most massive peaceful transformation of the 20th century. 
The agricultural communes we would pass were being dismantled to encourage greater peasant initiative on a household basis. 
In the countryside and towns, private enterprise, once prohibited, now burgeoned. 
Our ship was a microcosm of this changing China. 
An increasing minority of the passengers who take this river trip travel for pleasure, and many of the rest are traveling to enrich themselves, taking advantage of a relaxation of restrictions that accompanied the de-mythification of the late Chairman Mao Zedong.
The upper reaches of the Yangtze remained closed to foreigners, no doubt because the Government was embarrassed at the persisting pockets of rural poverty. 
But between Chongqing and Wuhan, the country was moving from a spartan garrison society toward a more dynamic mixed economy. 
A traveler who changed boats at Wuhan to continue down the lower Yangtze to Nanjing or Shanghai would see signs of China's doors opening anew to foreign investment and commerce.
The Yangtze, at the heart of this transition, is to the Chinese, who call it the ''Long River,'' what the Mississippi is to Americans - and more. 
Like the Mississippi, the Yangtze courses through the nation's heartland, delineating distinct regions, customs and dialects. 
Geographically, it runs from west to east, dividing northern from southern China. 
Historically, it was a cradle of Chinese culture and later became the prominent route by which the Western colonial powers pried open the decaying empire of the ineffectual Ching Dynasty in the 19th century. 
Today, a third of China's one billion people live in the fertile basin watered by the Yangtze.
Nearly 4,000 miles in length, one of the world's longest rivers, the Yangtze begins as a clear mountain stream fed by the glaciers of the Tibetan plateau in western Qinghai province. 
But as it drops more than 17,000 feet and cuts eastward past eight more provinces to join the East China Sea, its clear waters turn muddy with silt, some 500 million tons a year, that gives the Yangtze its distinctive brown hue.
By the time it meets the Jialing River at Chongqing in southeast Sichuan, the Yangtze is also fast becoming a sewer. 
Less than a third of the 100 million tons of industrial waste dumped annually from Chongqing into the Yangtze gets treated. 
No sooner had we boarded the East Is Red No. 46 than my fellow travelers began flinging the dregs of their teacups over the side of the boat. 
As we churned downriver, some backwaters frothed with the suds of unabsorbed detergents and other effluents.
Â 
HE EAST IS RED No. 46 was one of 110 steamers dubbed with the same revolutionary motto that have plied the Yangtze. 
Other reminders of the old Maoist fervor lingered. 
A sign atop the boat ticket office in Chongqing proclaimed in fat red characters, ''Long Live Mao Zedong's Thoughts,'' which in the revised ideological exegesis now means the collective wisdom of the Communist Party and not really Mao Zedong's thoughts.
Deng Xiaoping, the man behind the new reforms in China, was born in the Sichuan countryside 100 or so miles from Chongqing. 
The wooden, hand-lettered sign he made to hang over the entrance to the Chongqing Youth Palace of Culture has been a weathervane of his political career. 
Twice, when Mr. Deng was demoted into official disgrace for his reformist notions, the leftists pulled down his calligraphy. 
Twice, it has been hung back up.
Mr. Deng's impact has been more obvious along the steep winding streets of Chongqing, which was the capital of the Nationalist Government during World War II. 
The air-raid shelters tunneled into the embankments to provide protection from the heavy Japanese wartime bombing have been converted into workshops. 
On the sidewalks, small private businesses repaired shoes, sewed clothes, served up steaming noodles laced with fiery peppers and rented out comic books for a penny apiece. 
Peasants in rough denims noisily hawked juicy oranges, wriggling river eels, and fresh vegetables still moist with the morning dew. 
Such farmers' markets were suppressed as the ''tail of capitalism'' under Chairman Mao. 
Now they provide Chongqing with nearly a third of its pork and half of its vegetables.
Chongqing's gray industrial skyline overlooking the river, which tempted comparisons with less prosperous Pittsburgh, soon gave way to a view of snug farmhouses with tiled roofs and terraced fields diligently exploiting every inch of soil. 
Navigational lights anchored in small gray dinghies churned against the river current. 
The river banks were scarred at intervals by the detritus of small mines and factories that splattered ugliness across an otherwise pastoral landscape.
From our steamer's wheelhouse, the foghorn blasted and a loudspeaker squawked at slower barges and sampans to pull over and yield way.
''The Yangtze River is more complicated than the Mississippi,'' declared Xu Guilin, the ship's captain, though he had never seen the big American river himself. 
''We have memorized everything - the light signals, the rocks.''
Before receiving me in his cabin on the bridge, Mr. Xu took the trouble to change from the customary sailor's garb of shorts and sandals into a new gray pinstripe suit with dark shirt and maroon tie. 
He had slicked back his thick black hair and thrust his feet, without socks, into leather shoes without laces.
Mr. Xu grew up on the river. 
At 13, he shipped out as a cabin boy. 
He became a river sailor at 18 and captain of a ship at 41. 
Now he was 49 and sailed four round trips a month between Chongqing and Wuhan, which left him little time at home. 
Snapshots of his family were tucked under the glass top of his desk, along with a large magazine picture of Deng Xiaoping in an army uniform.
The most treacherous shoals were dynamited out of the Yangtze in the 1950's, but the muddy water has remained unpredictable, particularly as the river swells with the accumulation of melting snow in spring and heavy rain in summer. 
''When there are high tides and floods, it is difficult to navigate,'' said Mr. Xu. The trickiest section, he reported, was the Yangtze Gorges, a spectacular 120-mile stretch of sheer canyons and small ragged peaks that attracts tourists to the Yangtze. 
''I steer the boat myself in the most difficult sections,'' Mr. Xu said.
By mid-afternoon, the passengers, many of whom were bound on business great and small, had acquiesced to the ship's routine. 
Some lay on their narrow bunks reading or sleeping. 
Others leaned over the railing, played cards on the bleached deck or gobbled rice with chopsticks from enameled bowls. 
One man washed his white shirt and hung it out in the passageway where it flapped wetly against passers-by. 
Curiously, the airy top deck was reserved for the crew; the paying passengers were billeted in the gloomier quarters below.
The accommodations ranged from second class, which cost $44 for a bed in a small cabin for two, with a fluorescent bulb overhead and hot water in thermos flasks, down to fifth class where a bunk for $10 came with 23 roommates. 
The boat had no first class, whether because it was deemed inappropriate for a society marching toward Communism or because none of the quarters could be called deluxe. 
Sleeping space on the deck for the 2 1/2-day journey to Wuhan cost only $8.50.
Some Tibetans camped in one of the passageways: six men and a shy woman, all with heavy coats, necklaces of coral and turquoise and cheeks ruddy from exposure to the sun. 
One said that they came from western Sichuan and were going to Wuhan, but he didn't know enough Chinese to explain why. 
They kept sullenly to themselves for the entire trip.
The second-class cabins were filled mostly with a delegation of elderly cadres, or party and Government functionaries, who were getting a free trip down the Yangtze as one of the rewards for agreeing to retire and let the middle-age generation move ahead. 
They wore drab garments, of the kind preferred under Mao, and the women wore their graying hair bobbed severely short.
The crowd seemed livelier down below. 
(One can move from second down to lower classes, but not the other way around.) A young man with glasses was returning to Wanxian, a town 200 miles down the river. 
The ship cost more than the bus from Chongqing and took the same time, 11 hours, he said, but here you could walk around.
A gaunt, unshaved cadre named Lu was attending a family-planning conference in Nanjing, on the Yangtze. 
It was his second visit. 
The first had been 35 years ago, as a young soldier in the Communist forces that captured Nanjing from the Nationalists. 
He extended a twisted hand to show where shrapnel had torn it. 
''But I couldn't sightsee because we were too busy fighting and we went through too fast,'' he said. 
This time, Mr. Lu planned a more leisurely look around.
I asked if he was satisfied with how China had turned out. 
''There have been great changes so far, but it is still not enough,'' Mr. Lu said. 
''The reforms are correct and the policy is correct. 
The cadres at the top understand the reforms and the grass roots understand them. 
But there is no direct link, because the middle-level cadres still don't fully understand them.''
A squad of soldiers lugging dirty-looking rifles filed aboard the ship at Peiling, the first of half a dozen stops down to Wuhan. 
For most Chinese, traveling down the Yangtze is purely business. 
At Peiling and elsewhere, a few officials got on carrying small black vinyl portfolios that are as much a status symbol for cadres as the metal fountain pens in their breast pockets. 
But China's broad masses, as ordinary folks get called, staggered under the weight of canvas bags, gunnysacks, cardboard cartons, bedding and the odd slab of raw meat, sometimes all swinging together from bamboo shoulder poles.
At Wanxian, a county seat west of the great gorges, the East Is Red No. 46 was scheduled to tie up for the night rather than run the worst stretch of river in the darkness. 
Wanxian, perched on a bluff atop a wide stone staircase, had been one of the treaty ports forced open a century or so ago, when Western colonialists vied with one another to control the Yangtze. 
Many years ago, a British gunboat shelled the town to retaliate for some local resistance, a fellow traveler told me. 
During the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution, Wanxian saw new violence when rival Red Guard factions shot it out with guns stolen from Sichuan's armament factories. 
NOW WANXIAN, LIKE most of rural China, was succumbing to Peking's new mandate to ''get rich through labor; getting rich is glorious.''
As the passengers disembarked to wander up the winding streets, they were beset by local sellers of homemade baskets and wicker chairs. 
The chief steward, Mr. Hu, passed the word that any passenger coming back loaded with wicker furniture would pay a freight charge.
Most of Wanxian's shops had closed by 7:30 P.M., but a score of young men hung around a hardware store, wistfully watching a romantic movie on one of the small black-and-white television sets for sale. 
The lilting song of the heroine, who kept fluttering her eyelids as she leaned against a tree trunk, echoed down the dark street into the dingy Beautiful Taste Spring Restaurant, where patrons were wolfing down the last of the fried fish and rice.
A display of large propaganda cartoons across the street told passers-by that they, too, could own a television set and even a refrigerator if they worked harder and saved. 
There were cartoons warning about extravagance, notably in weddings. 
In one, a greedy young woman informed her dispirited fiance, ''I want everything but your mother.''
In another, a bride- to-be with her mother sat at a negotiating table presenting a young man and his father with a set of demands: color television set, electric fan, bicycle and wedding banquet. 
A sort of dowry system, previously condemned as feudalistic, was clearly still a problem in Wanxian.
Passengers straggling back to the ship before the midnight curfew had to wait while seven peasants in patched denims lurched aboard with large flat wicker baskets containing scores of baby chicks intended for the market in Fengjie, downriver. 
They arranged the baskets in the passageway and hunkered down beside them for the night. 
Using the boats for private enterprise was not permitted under Chairman Mao. 
Besides, most peasants were too poor to buy a boat ticket.
Mr. Hu said that the peasants were most numerous in the autumn, when oranges and tangerines ripened along the Yangtze. 
The farmers got a high price for their fruit down in Shashi, Wuhan and even Shanghai - because they moved it faster than the state transportation network. 
Peasants were permitted to bring aboard chickens, ducks and live fish; but reasons of sanitation, Mr. Hu said, ruled out pigs or sheep.
At Fengjie, the tired peasants got off. 
Each man slid his bamboo pole under two baskets and, as if balancing on eggs, slowly climbed the long steps to the city gate. 
Wanxian's vaguely European architecture, introduced by colonial merchants in the 19th century, had looked romantic after dark. 
By cold daylight, the buildings seemed worn and gritty in the old river town near the entrance to Qutang, the first of the great gorges.
The sheer canyons loomed abruptly overhead on either side like high-rise apartment buildings, leaving a channel for the ship barely 100 yards wide. 
For the next few hours, we rode the quickening brown river past cliffs capped with lush foliage and rock spires shrouded in clouds. 
Their bizarre shapes had given rise to centuries of fanciful interpretations. 
We sailed past Fairy Maiden Peak, the Lion Wearing a Silver Medal and the Peak of the Jade Screen. 
Shafts of sunlight penetrated the morning mist.
Between gorges, isolated farmhouses were perched on the hillsides. 
Some were striped red and white like barber poles to mark the shoreline when fog hung over the river. 
The steep slopes held rows of citrus trees. 
A sharp valley at the Wu Gorge defined where Sichuan ended and Hubei Province began.
Small sampans with sails moved slowly upstream, the boatmen sometimes standing and rowing with their long oars. 
The trail worn by the trackers, men who once labored like draft animals hauling barges through the gorges, disappeared underwater when the Gezhouba Dam was thrown across the Yangtze a few years ago. 
Still, we passed other men pulling their sampans upstream with long ropes from the rocky shore as if nothing had changed.
In the second-class lounge, a grizzled, retired Red Army veteran named Liu sat in a fat armchair by the window, taking in the scenery. 
He needed little encouragement to reminisce about how he had joined the Communist guerrillas in North China's Shanxi province in 1935. 
His family was so poor that ''I had no other choice.''
He was 15 when he went off to war, Mr. Liu recalled. 
''It was hardest against the Japanese in the early 1940's. 
We never had enough to eat and we were always fighting. 
We would take some millet and potatoes and black beans and cook them together. 
Those were bitter years.
''I never expected to live this long. 
We always thought that we would die in the next 24 hours.
''We captured our weapons from the Japanese. 
Later we used them against the Kuomintang,'' he said, referring to Chiang Kai-Shek's Nationalist Government. 
''The Japanese were much harder to fight. 
When we fired, the Kuomintang troops would run away.''
He returned home after 15 years. 
''My mother and father were very happy to see me. 
They had no letters from me, and thought I was dead. 
Neighbors came from miles around.''
After the Communist victory in 1949, Mr. Liu said, the leadership ''Put me in a factory and make me a leader.''
He retired recently and, as an old party man, receives his full salary plus a bonus and other perquisites.
Mr. Liu went on: ''My three sons said to me, 'Your life hasn't been so easy, so we want you to enjoy your remaining years. 
Travel and see the country. 
You deserve it.'
''
The veteran party man was too old to be coy about Mao Zedong: ''Chairman Mao had the right idea when he launched the Cultural Revolution. 
He did it to combat revisionism, but it became confused because of the Gang of Four.''
Mr. Liu employed the approved epithet for Mao's widow, Jiang Qing, and three other imprisoned leftists, who have been blamed for all the ills that befell China during Mao's final decade.
''Everybody makes mistakes, and Mao Zedong was no exception,'' Mr. Liu said. 
''Later, he made some wrong decisions. 
But without Mao, there wouldn't be any Communist Party. 
And without the Communist Party, we wouldn't be here today.''
AFTER XILING, THE last of the three great gorges at Nanjinguan, the landscape flattened out. 
The river widened from a few hundred yards to more than a mile and a half. 
The boat headed for the locks of Gezhouba, China's largest hydroelectric dam and the first built to harness the powerful Yangtze.
The Gezhouba was conceived by Chairman Mao in the 1950's to solve both China's energy shortage and the Yangtze's seasonal flooding. 
Construction began in 1970, when it was considered better to be Red than expert, and the revolutionary amateurs made such a mess that the project was halted two years later.
The Yangtze was finally dammed in 1981, after China's experts were summoned back from tending pigs and cleaning toilets. 
When the dam is fully completed, in four years, it will generate 14.1 billion kilowatt hours a year of electricity and transmit it as far as Shanghai, Peking and Canton.
It took an hour for the boat to be lowered 65 feet to float through the lock. 
The Gezhouba will have cost about $2.4 billion by the time it is finished, but no tolls are charged, on the principle that the dam belongs to the people.
To further solve the country's shortage of energy, a hydroelectric power dam four to five times bigger than Gezhouba has been proposed 25 miles upriver in the Xiling Gorge. 
Its construction would not only impair the beauty of the three Yangtze Gorges by raising the water level farther; it would also mean relocating up to 1.4 million Chinese, whose ancestral roots in the Upper Yangtze Valley go back centuries. 
The Government has been nervous about ordering such a massive displacement of its citizens. 
WITH THE MOST exciting part of the voyage over, a few frictions surfaced. 
Most of the staff spoke Sichuanese, a dialect that other Chinese passengers had trouble understanding. 
One man asked an attendant for glue to put stamps on a letter. 
She thought he wanted ink, and snapped back that there wasn't any.
Complaints about the poor food were more numerous. 
As waibin, or foreign guests, my wife and I were in a separate dining room where for $7 a day, 5 to 10 times what ordinary Chinese might pay, we were served a plethora of undistinguished dishes of meats, vegetables and rice. 
In the mess hall below, less coddled travelers had to buy meal coupons and then line up, sometimes for 45 minutes, before getting rice, bean noodles and vegetables.
Some passengers seemed content. 
A tall young army officer from Peking remarked later that his eight- bunk cabin was like home - better - because a hot shower and toilet were just down the passageway. 
He reminded me that most Chinese still make do without the luxury of indoor plumbing and hot-water taps.
With dusk, the tree line on the wide flood plain faded into the horizon. 
A fisherman effortlessly cast his weighted net. 
Lights twinkled on the buoys marking a channel on the broad river. 
A cool wind blew up, drawing the travelers out of their stuffy cabins.
A trio of salesmen from Chengdu leaned against the railing. 
They were traveling to Wuhan, then to a foreign trade exhibition in Canton. 
''It's fun to travel around when you are young, but when you get older, you want to settle down and raise a family,'' one of them said. 
He was already 30, with a wife in Chengdu. 
''I've been traveling for five years, but next year I hope to stop.''
He complained that he couldn't live on his travel allowance, which amounted to barely $1.30 a day. 
''Our leaders know that life is hard for us, so sometimes they try to give us a little more. 
It still doesn't cover the expenses, so I have to pay out of my own pocket sometimes.''
I asked why he didn't set up his own business, as the Peking Government is encouraging young Chinese to do in order to alleviate unemployment and provide more consumer services. 
''Oh no, then you don't have a work unit,'' he objected, referring to the state enterprises providing lifetime tenure and womblike welfare benefits, however badly an employee works. 
''And besides,'' he added, ''you can't quit your work unit without permission.''
The next morning, the passenger delegates were summoned to a last meeting. 
''Give us your opinions and suggestions in order to help us improve our work, in order to meet the demands of the broad masses,'' implored Mr. Hu.
A man with glasses and a graying crew cut stood up. 
''The guiding ideology of the boat's crew is correct,'' he announced. 
''They have acted according to the promises they made at the start of the journey, including maintaining sanitation, delivering drinking water and being responsible in their service work.''
This man knew his way around a criticism session.
''However,'' he said, only then going into complaints about the food, ''I know that it is impossible to satisfy everybody's tastes since we come from all over the country. 
But it seems there is not a suitable taste for people from the north, and the quality of the food should be improved.''
Others took up the litany, a few opening compliments followed by danshi, meaning ''however.''
Danshi, the staff should learn standard Chinese. 
Danshi, there should be a television set on board. 
Danshi, the meal coupons were too flimsy and easy to lose. 
Danshi, the boat's store should sell film and better souvenirs.
Another speaker complained that his cabin loudspeaker was broken, so that his group missed the announcements, light music, Peking opera and comedy patter that were broadcast from dawn till dark.
Mr. Hu explained that the boat had a wireless operator, but that perhaps he didn't know how to repair the loudspeaker. 
If he's happy, he may be willing to try. 
If he's not, he may refuse.
With a glance toward me, Mr. Hu plunged to the crux of the problem: foreigners sometimes ripped out the wires when the loudspeaker began blaring at 6:30 A.M. Mr. Hu pointed out that trains didn't suffer this vandalism because their loudspeakers were imbedded in the ceiling, where the foreigners couldn't reach them.
This led to a request that I, as a waibin living in Peking, add my suggestions about the voyage. 
I thanked them for having been hospitable and praised the stunning beauty of the gorges.
However, I continued, and they all nodded, I was upset to see so much trash bespoiling such a renowned river. 
Why didn't the boat install more trash baskets and mount a tidiness campaign?
The young attendant taking down all the comments scribbled furiously in her ledger and I got a flattering round of applause.
I left the meeting quite smug about my contribution. 
I leaned over the railing to watch the river I was saving when an empty soy sauce bottle flung from the crew quarters swished past my head and into the water. 
I wondered how many books of suggestions the boat had filled and where they got stored. 
AT WUHAN, THE East Is Red No. 46 ended its voyage and prepared for the trip upstream the next day. 
Travelers who wanted to continue to Nanjing or Shanghai had to go to the downtown ticket office and queue up for passage on another boat. 
My wife and I decided to stay in Wuhan because we were told that the lower Yangtze would be anticlimactic.
Wuhan, a center for heavy industry, had been a proletarian bastion for Chairman Mao, who was fond of swimming in the Yangtze. 
In July 1966, the 72-year-old leader refuted rumors of his ill health by plunging into one of history's most celebrated swims. 
For more than an hour, he floated down the Yangtze nine miles at the head of 5,000 young swimmers from Wuhan. 
Then he returned to Peking and unleashed the cruel chaos of his Cultural Revolution.
Wuhan used to re-enact Chairman Mao's swim every July, sometimes employing little red flags mounted on rubber inner tubes. 
Nobody wants to do it anymore. 
As our boat trip had suggested, revolutionary hardship is a notion whose time has come and gone in present-day China. 
The Yangtze still flows eastward to the sea, as it has throughout China's history, but now it bears peasants with baskets of baby chicks, intent on exploiting the party's latest maxim that getting rich through labor is glorious.

YESTERDAY was National Day, the 36th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China, and the Cantonese were firing off skyrockets and firecrackers, strolling and shopping, and eating up a storm.
The saying here is, ''The Cantonese will eat anything with four legs except the table.''
Or, for that matter, anything without legs. 
One of the local delicacies is called ''tiger fighting dragon.''
It is actually a combination of cat and snake.
This year the two-day National Day holiday followed a couple of days after the Moon Festival and everyone has been enjoying the long break. 
The Canton hotels are crowded, especially with many Hong Kong Chinese who have come back in droves to visit their families on the mainland. 
The stores, most of which are open, are mobbed. 
Children are having a ball racing up and down halls and corridors and through restaurants, laughing and shrieking, but apparently never crying. 
Their Chinese parents let them carry on as they please; with the one-child policy, teachers here say the children are getting spoiled.
There is a certain amount of economic pride connected with the celebration. 
Monday night the Governor of Guang Dong Province, Ye Zhen-Ping, told a large reception: ''This is the last year of the sixth five-year plan, and by the common effort of all the people, the plan we establish can be fulfilled and overfulfilled.''
China, he said, had now ''basically realized'' its aim of trying to get on an upward financial and economic trend. 
''We firmly take the economic reforms as our first priority,'' he added, ''and we will go on firmly, step by step.''
But, as though to demonstrate that the reformation of China still has a way to go before ''groupthink'' is over, the major local newspapers, Renmin Ribao, Guengzou Ribao and Nanfang Ribao, all played the leading speeches here and in Peking on page 1 and used identical pictures.
Deng Xiaoping's open door policy and four modernizations of industry, agriculture, science and technology, and national defense coexist with important remnants of old-style Marxism and what the Chinese call Mao Zedong thought, and others would call Stalinism.
In public, the fight between the two ideologies is muffled. 
Some old-style Marxists seek to push their cause by pretending there is no conflict between Dengism and Maoism. 
For instance, an editorial in Guangnung Daily states: ''In Deng Xiaoping's opinion, strengthening the second civilization'' -that is the new code word for the regime's objectives - ''requires ideological and political education as well as the development of socialist education, science and technology and culture.''
As though to scold Mr. Deng's disciples and those business types who are denounced here as ''capitalist roaders,'' the editorial says: ''We must unswervingly adhere to the four cardinal principles of leadership of the Communist Party, socialist road, people's democratic dictatorship, and upholding of Marxism, Leninism and Mao Zedong thought.''
Deng's response to the challenge is to put his own people on the Politburo and the Central Committee, and retire the old guard.
A little of the conflict at the ideological level does break into the open, however, at least symbolically. 
A new film, called ''Xiangshi Inn,'' which was previewed in Peking in July but has not yet been released, has already stirred up a storm of controversy among the politicians and intellectuals. 
It takes up the contemporary economic reforms, but without a happy ending.
The film, which was made by a leading director, Dong Kena, a 56-year-old woman, is about a young woman who is sent by the Government to take over and modernize an inn in a mountain village in southeast Hunan Province. 
But the former female manager of the inn tries every trick in the book, with the support of the county Communist Party secretary, to drive the young newcomer away. 
Finally, the new woman quits in despair and departs with her lover, an unmarried truck driver. 
(In the short story from which the film was made, her lover was married to a mad woman.) The movie critic of China Daily, Cheng Fang-Ming, who called ''Xiangshi Inn'' ''probably the best film of the year,'' drew the political-moral lesson for his readers: ''Obviously,'' he said, ''the sad ending implies that people sometimes must fight against the established order to succeed in rural economic reconstruction.''
The film's director said in an interview that ''one reason the film stirs heated response is that we produced it at the right time.''
But, here in Canton, in the midst of this holiday, the issue posed by ''Xiangshi Inn'' seems very remote. 
All day long the holiday-makers have been ogling, and buying, clothes and trinkets, refrigerators and stereos and other durable goods with which the stores are amply stocked. 
It is the consumer revolution that seems to be firmly in the saddle although, elsewhere in the country, Marxist and Maoist thought may die hard.

Nothing that a Chinese host can put on a table has more cachet than a bowl of viscous bird's nest soup. 
For centuries, it has been a delicacy throughout the Chinese world, a dish famed for its ability to keep people young and healthy.
But bird nests are becoming increasingly scarce. 
While the shortage is not yet a crisis, Chinese connoisseurs are obliged to pay more each time they bargain for nests - up to $1,000 a pound for top-quality nests.
''The price will definitely continue to increase,'' Stephen Tam, owner of the Cheong Loong Swallow's Nest store, said as he sorted the dozens of varieties of nests in his small shop here. 
''Most places the birds live have been developed into farmland or towns, and that reduces the number of birds that are left.''
In addition to the encroachment of humans on the birds' habitat, pollution is eroding some of the cliffs where they live and build their nests. 
Meanwhile, rising prices are leading the ''harvesters'' of nests to become more aggressive, sometimes snatching nests as soon as they are built, or grabbing nests that have eggs in them.
The nests used to make the soup belong to a kind of swallow, which builds on rocky cliffs or inside caves in several countries in Southeast Asia. 
Most of the nests today come from Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam or China.
The nests are not, as most Americans assume, a thatch of twigs and grass such as a robin might manufacture. 
Rather, they are made of the birds' saliva, which hardens into cementlike threads. 
When collected, the nests contain liberal amounts of feathers and even droppings, but are carefully washed and cleaned until they are white strips that look more like sponges than nests.
While swallow saliva soup may not send tingles across a Western palate, the Chinese rave over it. 
It is usually cooked with crab meat, shrimp or ham to make a gelatinous soup that is renowned principally for its healthfulness .
''The taste of the nests is nothing great,'' said Fok Kam Tong, head chef at the Man Wah Restaurant in Hong Kong's Mandarin Hotel, where a bowl of bird's nest soup ranges in price from $14 to $38. 
That is why crab and other embellishments are added, he said.
But bird's nest soup has virtues other than mere taste. 
''It's very good for you, very nourishing,'' Mr. Fok added. 
''It's good for women, for their skin, so they don't look old. 
But it's not just for women; it's good for everybody.''
Mr. Fok disputes the pessimists who say that bird's nest soup could eventually disappear. 
While scarcity of the proper nests is a concern, he and many Chinese food experts say, the resulting price increase would make it even more prized as a delicacy.
''If it becomes more expensive, it will be even more popular in Hong Kong,'' said Sunny Lan Kun Ying, a salesman at Yuen Wo Bird's Nest store near Hong Kong's business district.
Not according to the owners of the small Hong Kong shops that sell bird nests, who say most people are being priced out of the market. 
The cost of bird's nests has more than doubled in the last few years, they say, making it more difficult to afford a nest for a daughter with a skin blemish or a son who is about to take an important examination.
Some kinds of nests are becoming particularly rare, such as the red ones called ''blood nests.''
These have a reddish tinge that chefs say derives from blood in the birds' saliva. 
It is even better for one's health than regular bird nests, they say.
So, while regular bird nests sell for about $500 for a catty - a Chinese unit of weight amounting to just over a pound - the best-quality blood nests sell for nearly $1,300 a catty at the most exclusive shops.
Meanwhile, the swallows are seeking more and more remote locations to build their nests in places where humans will not intrude. 
They must avoid not only youths who scamper along the cliffs or climb bamboo scaffolding to cave ceilings, but also monkeys that have been trained to climb the rock walls and retrieve nests.
''The swallows are very careful,'' said Mr. Fok, the chef. 
''They will never build a nest where it is easy to get to.''

THE week before celebrating the Lunar New Year, which begins tomorrow, San Yan Wong, his wife, Rosanna, and his mother-in-law, Kwai Wu Chui Fung, began searching the markets of Chinatown for the appropriate foods. 
For the start of the year 4685, the Year of the Rabbit, the Wongs had decided to celebrate as they had in Shanghai.
More than 23 years have passed since Mr. Wong, a former restaurateur and now a partner in the Asian American New York Land Corporation of Flushing, had celebrated in Shanghai fashion; for Mrs. Wong it had been 16 years. 
Both had left Shanghai and married in Hong Kong before settling in New York.
''Our children had never had a true Shanghai New Year,'' Mrs. Wong said in their apartment in Chinatown's Confucius Plaza overlooking the Manhattan Bridge. 
''We wanted them to have some of the things we had.''
Their children, Lily, 14 years old, Joseph, 12, and Lisa and Lucy, their 7-year-old twins, were enlisted in the preparations.
The refrigerator holds a surfeit of seafood for the New Year's Eve dinner: two sea bass to be cooked in Shao-Hsing wine, the wine of Shanghai; two pomfret flown in from China for marinating in soy sauce and sugar in the Shanghai manner; clams for cooking in a Shao-Hsing sauce, and shrimp for stir-frying in a sweet red dressing. 
In Shanghai, fish signify plenty, clams gold and shrimp happiness, Mr. Wong said.
Mrs. Kwai, whose husband, Kwai Tak Yui, is visiting Shanghai this New Year, insisted that the apartment be swept, scoured and vacuumed in keeping with tradition, because it is bad luck to clean on New Year's Day. 
At least one new item of clothing has been bought for each child, and envelopes of ''lucky money'' have begun appearing under the children's pillows.
Tonight a New Year table for visitors is to be set up in the living room, with dishes of peanuts (symbols of birth); watermelon seeds (a wish for many sons); gold-foil wrapped chocolate coins (riches); candied lotus seeds, kumquats and dates (plenty); a pomelo, or Chinese grapefruit (abundance); oranges (life's sweetness); tangerines (good luck), and water chestnuts (many children).
On the living room wall is a picture of Chai Sun, the god of fortune, surrounded by five slogans, wishes for a successful and healthy New Year, in gold calligraphy on bright red paper.
In Shanghai, children customarily knock on doors seeking lucky money, Mrs. Wong said. 
When people answer their doors, the children cry, ''Chai Sun doh!'' and present pieces of red paper with the same words, ''The god of fortune arrives!''
This means the children are entitled to some lucky money. 
Although this tradition is not followed in New York, the Wongs plan it this year for their children, a niece and four nephews, who will come to the Wongs' door wearing red for the New Year.
The New Year's Eve dinner is to have 12 courses, ''a very good number,'' explained Mr. Wong, because it is the number of signs in the zodiac.
Â 
The family will also spend New
Year's Day together. 
''Here in New York we usually go from house to house,'' Mr. Wong said. 
''We see other people. 
It is not like that in Shanghai.
But this year we will all stay at home together as we used to in Shanghai.
We must be together for dinner and for the games - dice, dominoes and for mah-jongg.''
Preparation of the New Year's Eve dinner started early this morning with Mrs. Kwai cutting, slicing, chopping and mixing in the kitchen. 
Later she was joined by Mrs. Wong and Mrs. Leung Li Man, the mother-in-law of Mrs. Wong's second-oldest brother, - ''number 2 sister-in-law's mother,'' as Mrs. Wong puts it.
At dinner time, the dishes will begin to go to the dining room table - yueh e choi (a combination of hair seaweed, dried oysters, fried bean curd and bean sprouts), which signify togetherness and agreement; cold vegetarian ''duck'' wrapped in dried bean curd; vegetarian ''beef'' made from fermented high-gluten flour; noodle soup with Shanghai pickled cabbage, and a Shanghai New Year's dish, dried bamboo shoots and bacon.
There will be chi ma tong yuen (boiled glutinous rice dumplings filled with sweet sesame-seed paste) and a soup of egg dumplings and tiny meatballs with long bead-thread noodles symbolizing longevity. 
These dishes will be followed by boiled chicken dressed with Shao-Hsing wine, the sea bass and pomfret, the clams and the shrimp.
There will be ''gold bars'' of bean curd wrapped around pork, chives and bean sprouts; lin gau (Shanghai rice cakes) with spinach; shoots of the snow pea plant with shredded beef, and finally a sweet soup of red beans flavored with rock sugar.
Sixteen dishes are to be put on the table in the course of the meal, and offered to heaven and the family's ancestors before any are tasted.
''To our good health,'' Mrs. Kwai will say.
''Gung Shi Fat Chai,'' Mrs. Wong will say, intoning ''Happy New Year'' in the dialect of Shanghai.
''May our house be filled with gold and jade,'' Mr. Wong will say.
And then the family will eat.

text:
