Shanghai's annual crab rush begins with a frenzy in mid-September, continues unabated through October, and then subsides for another year. 
But during those six weeks virtually everyone in Shanghai, it seems, wants to eat nothing but the freshwater da zhai xie, or hairy crabs.
People line up at markets for the crabs, which are sold in the hand-woven bamboo baskets in which they are kept after being pulled from the water. 
Local people have been known to pay merchants to tell them when the first shipments of da zhai xie are to arrive. 
And after the crabs are bought, they are brought home to be steamed and eaten with shaoxing wine, the sherry-like beverage of Shanghai. 
Throughout the Shanghai region, late September and all of October are times for crab parties, time to have friends over for a feast of hairy crabs and wine.
Shanghai's crab craze is similar to the mussel madness each fall in Brussels and across Belgium, the quests for shad roe and soft-shell crabs each spring in the eastern United States, the need for crayfish each September in Finland. 
It is fascinating to watch people, mostly women, line up impatiently in Shanghai's many morning markets just to buy the crabs.
Nor will just any crabs do. 
Only the gray-blue crabs of Jiangsu Province, from the lake known as Yangcheng (west of Shanghai) are acceptable. 
And people will pay enormous prices, as much as 45 yuan (about $15) a pound for them.
Because of the demand, unscrupulous merchants have been known to place other crabs, such as those from the Yangtze River where it passes close to Anhui Province, in among the da zhai xie. 
Careful shoppers can be seen sorting through the baskets, to examine each crab individually. 
The distinguishing feature of the da zhai xie are hairlike bristles along their legs - thus their name - and the people of Shanghai know that.
So intense is the demand for the hairy crabs each fall that markets have developed in places other than Shanghai. 
In Hong Kong and the United States, immigrants from Shanghai await air shipments of the crabs, and in New York's Chinatown people will pay as much as $20 a pound for live da zhai xie.
For the markets the Chinese Government has printed brightly colored posters that show the crabs, red after being cooked, hairy legs sticking out. 
When I was in Shanghai during the crab craze last year I saw posters that read, ''Autumn is here, the chrysanthemums are blooming and the crabs are fat.''
Others read, ''This is the season to eat the crabs.''
Still others described the roe in the female crabs as ''fat and thick,'' and the meat as ''soft and tender, full of vitamins.''
It is difficult to trace historically the annual demand for da zhai xie; the three characters translate as ''big gate crab.''
The people of Shanghai say there is no religious or mythological significance to the hairy crab. 
Some suggest that it is an extreme manifestation of the appetite for crabs throughout Asia, where crustaceans are generally held in higher esteem than in other parts of the world.
In the waters of and around Thailand, Malaysia and Vietnam many species of crab exist: The so-called zebra crabs and blue swimming crabs of Thailand, the mangrove crab of Malaysia and the monkey-god crab of Vietnam are all highly prized as food.
Attention is given the hairy crab not for its history, but for its consumption, the traditions that concern how and when they should be eaten.
The body of the perfect hairy crab is ''the size of a rice bowl,'' according to the people of Shanghai, three and a half to four inches in diameter. 
The male crab has bigger claws and more bristles along its legs, and weighs about 11 ounces; the female, with smaller claws and little bristle, is about 8 ounces.
Early in the season the female crabs are much higher in demand, for they are fat with roe, their shells are softer and their meat sweeter. 
Later, as the males grow, their bodies become plump and their meat sweeter. 
The crabs are never seasoned when cooked. 
Occasionally a traditional Shanghai dipping sauce of vinegar, soy sauce and ginger will accompany them, but most often they are eaten just steamed.
The only exception to simple steaming is toward the end of October when the crabs are smaller and harder and their meat is not as tender or as sweet. 
Then they may be eaten as ''drunken crabs,'' steamed after being marinated in shaoxing wine.
Part of the art of the Shanghai table, after the crab has been consumed and all its meat plucked out, is to reconstitute the body so that it looks whole.
So much a part of Shanghai life is the hairy crab that it transcends the table. 
The way the crabs are marketed, their legs and claws bound tightly against their bodies, has meaning in the financial markets.
In Shanghai and in Hong Kong, when business dealings are most difficult, when money supplies are tight, when property transactions are moving slowly, the condition is said to be ''da zhai xie.''
I have eaten hairy crabs in the Ru Yi, a fairly new restaurant in Shanghai atop the Shanghai Friendship Store on Nanjing Road (these were steamed and accompanied by a bottle of cold Seagull Beer), and in the Lubolang Restaurant inside the mid-city enclave known as Shanghai's Old Town.
Neither of these restaurants has a listed telephone number. 
It is best to book tables through the Shanghai branch of the China International Travel Service, telephone 217200. 
The office is quite close to both restaurants. 
In both cases, the cost was about $15 to $16 each, the price of one crab the same as the normal price of a full meal for two or three people. 
But that is an indication of how greatly they are prized.
In Hong Kong, where the desire for hairy crabs increases each autumn - and where copies of the Shanghai posters are to be found in virtually every one of its Shanghai-style restaurants - the Wu Kong (27 Nathan Road, Kowloon; telephone 3-667244) is famous for da zhai xie. 
''We cook them the way they do in Shanghai,'' said the restaurant's manager, Bill Kong. 
And so they do.
Last fall, my husband and I paid about $18 each for four da zhai xie in Wu Kong, a small basement-level white marble restaurant entered from Peking Road. 
The crabs had been steamed to redness, and with them we drank glasses of shaoxing wine.
As we ate, more hairy crabs were inching about in a nearby holding tank illuminated with bright, emerald green lighting, waiting like the precious creatures they are, to give enjoyment.

text:
ï»¿
The vegetarian dishes of Japanese Zen temples are prepared in a manner that reveals and enhances the purity, simplicity and freshness of the ingredients. 
This cuisine, called shojin ryori (which means a method of cooking in which one pursues the pure way of the Buddha), has developed mainly within the Rinzai sect of Zen, with its emphasis on meditative practices and sudden enlightenment, brought to Japan from China in the 12th century. 
In Rinzai temples, preparation of the food is a kind of religious discipline, and during the meal, to which each monk brings his own utensils, one must not speak and must sit formally and adhere to various other rules.
The Tokyo restaurant Bon serves another type of shojin cooking, called fucha ryori. 
A feast to be eaten together by all the monks of a temple after a special day of meditation and discussion, fucha ryori is a product of the more recently imported Obaku sect of Zen, brought from Ming China in the mid-17th century by a Chinese monk, Yinyuan, and other refugees from the Manchus. 
The sect's headquarters are in Kyoto, at Manpukuji Temple. 
Obaku Zen incorporates elements of Pure Land Buddhism, in which salvation depends on simple faith rather than rigorous and self-denying disciplines, and this somewhat more relaxed approach to Zen is reflected in the fucha cuisine. 
In its complexity of flavor and form, the food reveals its Chinese sources.
One Chinese element traditionally associated with fucha ryori is the harmony of spirit created by each of the guests taking food from a common dish onto his own plate. 
Perhaps due to the fastidious nature of Japanese eating habits (at home each member of a family always uses his own pair of chopsticks; guests are given disposable ones) this custom is not observed at Bon.
As in other styles of Zen cooking, the meal represents a balance of the six tastes (bitter, sour, sweet, hot, salty and faint or delicate) and the five methods of food preparation (boiling, grilling, deep frying, steaming and serving raw). 
These correspond, more or less, to the five directions (east, west, north, south and center), the five colors (green, white, black, red and yellow, also represented in a Zen meal) and the five elements (wood, metal, water, fire and earth) that structure the Chinese cosmology. 
In a complete fucha meal, the selection of dishes -both the food and the ceramic, bamboo and lacquer utensils in which it is served - mirror this harmony.
On entering the serene and elegant Japanese house occupied by Bon, all of these compexities fuse into an atmosphere that is purely Japanese. 
Bon opened 14 years ago in the quiet residential district known as Hakusan. 
Twelve years before that, the mother of Furusawa Kazuaki, the proprietor, opened the original Ryusen Bon not far away, preparing food to serve at various temple functions. 
The family built the Hakusan house as their residence and there prepared temple meals to send out.
The house is a fine example of traditional Japanese domestic architecture, scarce in Tokyo since World War II, with mud-plastered walls in earth tones complementing the tatami mats. 
The sliding glass doors that form one wall of each private dining room are framed in wood, not aluminum, and look out on a luxuriant and extensive garden, unexpected in the middle of the city.
I visited Bon in one of Tokyo's rare blizzards. 
The snow, weighing down the branches of trees and shrubs in the garden, reflecting, as the sky grew dark in the late afternoon, the light of a stone lantern, made a delightful setting for the meal. 
My companions and I stepped into the room set aside for us, already warmed in preparation for our visit by a charcoal brazier and a charcoal-burning hearth with an iron tea kettle - and a hefty electric heater. 
The calligraphy scroll in the alcove, written in bold strokes by the head of the Obaku sect, extolled the pleasures of listening to the song of the boiling kettle, comparing it to the wind in the pines - a common conceit in Chinese poetry.
A full course fucha meal (about $45 to $55) is almost indescribably elaborate, consisting of the following elements: the thick foamy tea of the tea ceremony, a tiny appetizer often given the form and color of some seasonal flower or foliage, a clear soup with a few perfectly shaped pieces of mushrooms or bamboo shoots afloat, kuchi-kawari (literally a change of flavors - a vegetable dish, varying monthly in method of preparation and ingredients according to the season) and unpen (a fragment of cloud - thickened soup made with leftover vegetables).
These are followed by nimono (boiled things - a dish of seasonal vegetables cooked in a transparent but richly flavored stock), sesame tofu (a rich and silky smooth substance, similar to bean curd in texture but redolent with sesame seeds ground to a paste in a mortar), agemono (fried things - tenpura), a hearty miso soup containing vegetables and tofu, freshly made pickles, rice and fruit. 
The ingredients and preparation as well as the utensils change seasonally, however, so guests will find a different meal at different times of the year.
Among the dishes we sampled was a warm kuzu (arrowroot) jelly containing a sweetened kumquat, said to be especially good for the throat on raw winter days.
There was also sashimi made of konnyaku (a root called devil's tongue), a firm but slippery gray substance, one of many characteristically Japanese foods valued as much for its texture and consistency as for its elusive flavor. 
Then we had a dumpling made of lily root dipped in buckwheat batter and lightly fried and a shell of yuzu (citrus junos, one of the most fragrant of Japanese citrus fruits - always translated as citron but in neither appearance nor flavor resembling the heavily candied fruit we see at Christmas) in which nuts have been cooked in miso (fermented bean paste) and preserved for months until all the flavors blend. 
This was followed by a tenpura selection crowned by a fragile spray of enoki mushrooms on their long slender stems, resembling (not by coincidence) the snow-frosted branches outside.
A somewhat more limited selection, called aka-zen (red tray) because all the dishes as well as the tray on which they are brought are made of vermilion lacquer, may cost $40 to $45. 
The golden miso soup in which slices of white turnip and brilliantly colored mustard greens float must have been chosen to enhance the red lacquer bowl. 
A smaller selection, which makes a good lunch, the hangetsu fuchidaka (half-moon tray), is simplified by presenting several of the fucha courses in a partitioned half-moon shaped lacquer box (about $30).
The restaurant consists of five private rooms, which can accommodate up to 50 guests at one time. 
Each room can seat up to 10, but two rooms can be joined together to handle larger parties. 
Beer is about $3, sake $4.25. 
Only Japanese is spoken by the staff.
Bon, 4-37-19 Hakusan, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo (telephone 947-1525), open from noon to 8 P.M., closed Tuesday. 
It is best to reserve a day or two in advance, and it is customary but not essential to order when the reservation is made. 
From July 25 to the end of August, Bon moves to Karuizawa, a mountain resort in Nagano Prefecture, and the Hakusan branch closes. 
The address of the Karuizawa branch is Tsukushigaoka Building, Kariyado, Karuizawamachi, Nagano Prefecture (02674-5-4480 or locally 5-4480).

FEI LO teaches regional Chinese cooking and nutrition at the China Institute in America in New York. 
She is the author of ''The Dim Sum Book: Art of the Chinese Teahouse'' to be published in the spring.
Â 
By EILEEN YIN-FEI LO
T o the people of southeastern China, particularly those of Canton, and Hong Kong, dim sum is far more than food. 
It is a custom rooted in history and mythology. 
It is brunch with tea. 
It is the Chinese equivalent of the business lunch. 
It is the core around which families gather.
Eileen Yin-Fei Lo discusses Chinese custom of brunch with tea, called dim sum
In Cantonese the words dim sum mean ''a dot on the heart,'' or more broadly, ''the heart's delight,'' and the seemingly unending dishes of beautifully shaped dim sum that are carried or wheeled by as you sit in a teahouse sipping green or black tea do indeed bring a sense of wonder and joy.
On the mainland of China itself, dim sum is virtually unknown outside the area around Canton - and, of course, the British colony of Hong Kong that adjoins it - although in cosmopolitan Shanghai there are both dim sum teahouses and a few Shanghai-style dim sum dishes. 
In Peking there are steamed breads and small buns that are similar, but they are not consumed in the tradition of the dim sum teahouse. 
Rather, they are meals themselves or accompaniments to courses.
The atmosphere of the teahouses in which dim sum is served is often as important as the food. 
In a little teahouse such as Hing Wan on Queen's Road in Hong Kong's central district, you sit beneath a ceiling hung with bird cages. 
They belong to elderly wealthy men who cling to the tradition of carrying their birds while taking a walk before tea. 
You might prefer to indulge in a restaurant on Nathan Road in Kowloon called the International, which seats 1,500 people on each of three floors; nevertheless customers must wait for seats on Sundays.
And what is worth waiting for?
The following are perhaps the most famous of the many dim sum:
- Har gau (shrimp dumplings), crescent-shaped dumplings filled with shrimp and pork.
- Fung ngan gau (phoenix eyes), which look, as intended, like women's eyes - almond-shaped and dotted with minced shrimp and egg whites.
- Fun guor (rice noodle fruit), half-moons filled with ground pork, mushrooms and shrimp.
- Siu mai (cook-and-sell dumplings), basket-shaped dumplings that earn their name by being the first made, the first sold, the first eaten.
- Char siu bau (barbecued pork), steamed or baked buns filled with chunks of roast pork - known to many Americans.
- Siu lung bau (soup dumplings), made with gelatin, shrimp and pork so that when they are steamed, the gelatin becomes soup inside the dumpling.
- Nor mai gai (lotus leaf rice), pillow-shaped masses of glutinous rice into which have been folded mushrooms, chicken, pork, shrimp and Chinese smoked pork sausage, the whole then wrapped with dried lotus leaves and steamed. 
The leaf imparts a slightly sweet aroma and taste.
- Jook (thick rice soup), or congee, as the Cantonese call this soup, which resembles porridge because of the preserved eggs and pork, or pieces of chicken, that are usually added.
- Yeung hai kim (stuffed crab claws), claws around which chopped shrimp are mounded, then deep-fried.
- Chun guen (spring rolls), tiny log-shaped fried rolls filled with pork, shrimp, water chestnuts, bamboo shoots and scallions. 
They are not to be confused with that American invention, the larger egg roll.
- Woo gok (dumplings fashioned from mashed taro root and stuffed with pork and mushrooms) are football-shaped and deep-fried until crisp and brown.
- Lor bok goh (turnip cake), a translucent cake of turnips, ginger, shrimp and rice powder that is cut into slices and pan-fried before serving.
And there are many more, all to be discovered in serendipitous fashion. 
Waitresses traditionally wheel the dim sum in on carts in such restaurants as King Bun in Hong Kong's central district and the venerable Luk Kwok on Gloucester Road. 
You select by pointing or asking for what you want as you drink one of several varieties of tea - green, black, jasmine, chrysanthemum or oolong.
The tea has been important since the eighth century, when Lu Yu, China's historical master of the beverage, wrote his ''Classic of Tea.''
It set down for the first time how tea leaves should be grown and processed, how the product should be brewed and steeped, how it should be served. 
He wrote that tea is a drink for body and soul, a mental stimulant, perhaps even an aid toward eventual immortality.
T he beginnings of the dim sum meal go back to the Sung Dynasty, when travelers on the highways of southern China in the 10th century would stop at small roadside teahouses to refresh themselves with tea and light meals. 
It was centuries before the practice took root and the Chinese of the south devised the small bite-sized foods that became stylized into dim sum.
These days you will see businessmen discussing what is most dear to them, sales clerks around a table chattering, family groups of three or more generations clustered together for a Sunday morning reunion, all enjoying dim sum, perhaps the most inexpensive of Chinese meals.
One of the more memorable dim sum meals I have had recently was in the 1,000-seat Maxim's Palace in the new World Trade Center extension of Hong Kong's Excelsior Hotel. 
It is a huge barn of a restaurant hung with gold and red dragons supported by green-painted pillars around which curl gilded phoenixes. 
Maxim's Palace is busy and noisy and the wagons of dim sum come by at an almost breathtaking rate.
First we had har gau, those delicious moist shrimp dumplings, then bowls of jook filled with chunks of preserved eggs. 
We also had a specialty of Maxim's Palace, gum yueh gau - or golden fish - which is a dumpling sculptured in the shape of a goldfish and stuffed with shrimp and pork.
Next came slices of fried water-chestnut cake, with siu mai, those basket-shaped ''cook-and-sell'' dumplings; and another specialty, gun jing ngau yuk kau, tiny beef meatballs.
Before finishing with sweet egg custard tarts we had kim ding guen cho, pigs' feet and egg cooked with shredded ginger and black, sweet rice vinegar. 
Wonderful!
One pays for dim sum by the plate. 
Each preparation comes on a different sized and shaped plate - round, oval, deep and saucerlike, in bamboo steamers, in metal fluted pastry tins. 
And when it is time to pay the bill the waiter simply counts the plates and matches price to size and shape. 
Most dim sum cost from 50 cents to 75 cents for three or four dumplings. 
For only a few dollars a party of four can snack to their heart's content. 
Or even their heart's delight.

file: FIREWORKS AND ICE FOR CHINATOWN_S YEAR OF THE PIG.txt
text:
ï»¿
''One should rise before the cock's crow and explode firecrackers in the courtyard to ward off demons.''
So wrote Zong Lin of the New Year in the fourth-century text ''Records of Annual Festivals in Central China.''
No cock crowed yesterday. 
No demons loomed. 
Still, it began as it has for more than a century in Chinatown: A crackle here and there; slowly, one rat-a-tat-tat echoing against another. 
Then hundreds and thousands of tiny explosions collapsing into a thunderous din that resounded from the brick walls of six-story red-brick tenements. 
An odor of cordite hung in the air.
Edward A Gargan highlights Chinatown's celebration of Year of the Pig
The Year of the Pig, 4681, stumbling over snowbanks in the narrow streets, arrived in Chinatown yesterday, a neighborhood struggling with the woes of an economically depressed garment industry and troubled by recurring gang violence. 
But yesterday was a day for Chinatown to forget its difficulties and embrace the optimism brought by the year's first new moon.
At noon, a huge lion's head, trailing a paper tail in brilliant reds and blues, undulated in a small circle before a mound of exploding fireworks. 
To the thump of a large drum, the lion dancers, sponsored by the Chinatown Community Young Lions, a youth group, slowly veered up Mott Street, halting in front of restaurants and shops.
''We stop at all stores and restaurants to bring good luck,'' said Victor Soo Hoo, a director of the Young Lions, who brandished an immense ceremonial sword. 
''We usually have a wagon for the drum, but not with the snow. 
People will carry it this year.''
Â 
Pandemonium in the Snow
On the corner of Mott and Pell Streets, Lorina Lee and her sister Sandra stood on a solid mound of snow watching the semiorganized pandemonium before them.
''It's noisy, it's exciting,'' said Lorina, who was wearing a nearly luminescent blue-silk brocade jacket. 
Amid the festive cacophony of drums, cymbals and fireworks, Lorina, who works at a Chinatown branch of Citibank, said that she was worried about the area.
''I deal with owners of garment factories,'' she said. 
''Things aren't so good. 
I can't see it getting better.''
A New Year's custom in China that has endured here is giving hongbao, red envelopes that contain money, to family members. 
Shortly after midnight on New Year's Day, according to tradition, junior members of the family pay ceremonial respect to their elders and the elders, in return, give money.
To the New Year's greeting ''Gong xi fa cai'' (''Happy and prosperous times'') little children gleefully retort, ''Gei wo yige hung bao lai'' (''Give me a red envelope'').
And always there are feasts. 
The rest of the year rice is primary in Chinese meals, with cai, meat and vegetables dishes, secondary. 
But at New Year's, this custom is reversed and cai becomes primary.
''We've been eating all week,'' said Perry Hong, a camera hung around his neck. 
After taking a snapshot of a dragon swooping toward a pile of exploding firecrackers, Mr. Hong pointed to 14 family members, including uncles, cousins, brothers and sisters who came in from Brooklyn for the day. 
''Everybody likes to throw firecrackers at the dragons,'' he said.
Everywhere the dim sum restaurants, like the Silver Palace on Bowery and No. 1 on Canal Street, were teeming. 
Carts piled with duck feet, steamed shrimp balls, cold spiced pork slices and myriad other delicacies trundled past tables filled with families in their finest holiday dress. 
A special New Year's dessert, ba bao fan, a ball of sticky rice laced with sugared candies, appeared.
As the dragon from the Ho Nan Shau Lin Golden Dragon Team started down Mott Street toward Chatham Square, it paused before the Mayflower Tea Parlor, where a waiter came out to throw firecrackers. 
At Lee's Good Food, where ducks and finely barbecued chickens hung on skewers in the window, a man in an apron stood and watched the dragon bow and soar.
Not everyone on the streets of Chinatown could claim Chinese ancestry, however. 
Eleven-year-old Shay Silvestri came from Long Island wearing her own blue dragon headdress made of cardboard, Styrofoam balls, tin cans and layers of blue and green crepe paper.
''Every year I come here,'' she shouted over the rattle of fireworks. 
''I made this mask first for Halloween, and I thought I'd use it for New Year.''

text:
ï»¿
''THE food in China used to be very good, but it was set back by the Cultural Revolution,'' said Zhou Zhi Bin. 
That observation is particularly noteworthy because the man who made it is one of Shanghai's oldest master chefs. 
Western visitors to China have been saying the same thing for years.
In a period of increasing openness and contact with the West, Chinese chefs have begun to acknowledge the poor quality of the food in a country once as famous as France for its culinary heritage. 
In an effort to repair the damage, master chefs have been called out of retirement and foreign chefs have been invited to demonstrate Western cooking.
A desire to regain their culinary stature is not only a matter of national pride for the Chinese; it makes creasing number of privately owned restaurants, those owned by the state face stiff competition: as the Chinese become more affluent they demand better food. 
It is often difficult to get reservations in the best restaurants. 
And foreign visitors expect to eat equally well in dining rooms serving Chinese and Western food.
The Cultural Revolution, which extended from 1966 to 1976, is rightly blamed for the state of disrepair into which Chinese culinary artistry had fallen. 
Like so many of his peers, Mr. Zhou spent six years in that period working in a rubber factory.
But the Cultural Revolution does not bear full responsibility. 
Between 1950 and 1958, China had virtually no training program for chefs. 
As a result of these two barren periods there is a shortage today of competently trained chefs in their late 30's, 40's and even 50's. 
Most skilled chefs are in their 60's, 70's and 80's. 
In the late 1970's Mr. Zhou and other professional chefs were ''rehabilitated,'' returned from the countryside and factories to the professions for which they had been trained, but the rehabilitation was short-lived. 
These older men were soon forced to retire to make room for the young people who were coming back from ''retraining'' in the countryside. 
Speaking through an interpreter, Jie Zhi Zhong, manager of the new Sichuan restaurant in the Jinjiang Hotel, one of Shanghai's most famous old hotels, explained: ''It was the Government's policy to replace old people with young people. 
But the young people couldn't produce the best food as their fathers had done because they did not have the proper training. 
Eventually, the restaurants and hotels took things into their own hands and invited old chefs back to supervise and to teach.''
Mr. Zhou was called back to the Jinjiang, where he had begun his career 50 years before. 
This time he would train the young generation of chefs, who until a few years ago learned most of what they knew from books.
''Now, leaders of the Government at various level are giving full attention to the art,'' Mr. Zhou said, ''and we are focusing our attention on training young chefs. 
The cooking schools have improved and the chefs are going there for theoretical training. 
We understand Chinese cooking is not of the finest quality at this moment, but the food is improving.''
One of Mr. Zhou's pupils nodded in agreement. 
''Self-taught by books,'' as he put it, Lu Da Ming went to the hotel in 1974. 
''Because of Mr. Zhou,'' he said, ''I am learning the traditional dishes and I am learning much faster, especially the things you can only learn by experience. 
We all hope the old chefs will have long life and stay healthy.''
The better food in China is being cooked by chefs who have had the advantage of training under the old master chefs: Li Cheng Heng, for example, the Sichuan chef at the Golden Flower Hotel, a joint venture operated by the Chinese Government and a Scandinavian company in Xi'an.
Mr. Li, 42 years old, was also a victim of the Cultural Revolution, but he had been trained by a master chef from the age of 12. 
He gives full credit to his old teacher, who eventually became a chef at several Chinese embassies abroad, an honor accorded only to the country's best.
As evidence of the Government's renewed interest in its culinary experts, chefs like Mr. Li have been sent to Europe and America to demonstrate Chinese cooking and to work at foreign restaurants. 
The Sichuan Pavilion in New York is one of the first of these restaurants to employ its entire kitchen staff from China.
Wong Lin Chou, a gracious, sophisticated older man who speaks fluent English, was also called out of retirement, in this case to add polish to the state-run Mei Leung restaurant in Shanghai. 
At one time Mr. Wong owned an import-export business; he knows about dealing with Westerners and about the fine points of old-fashioned service. 
During the Cultural Revolution he was forced to work in a candy factory. 
In 1984, he said, the restaurant hired him to ''greet foreign guests and to teach the dining room staff how to speak English and how to conduct themselves.''
He appears to have had an effect: the service at Mei Leung was several cuts above that in many of the other restaurants visited on a recent trip to China. 
''The cooking art is picking up,'' said Ge Xian-E, vice principal of the City Restaurant and Service School in Shanghai. 
''The central Government is paying attention.''
Speaking through an interpreter, she said: ''There was a large culinary demonstration in the Great Hall of the People in Beijing in 1983, and similar demonstrations have been held throughout the country. 
The status of cooks has been raised from simple worker to master, and the system of accrediting cooks at varous grade levels, which had been stopped during the Cultural Revolution, has begun again.''
To improve the quality of middle-aged chefs, schools like the one in Shanghai are also retraining them.
Miss Ge said the quality of that training is very high: ''Most of the teachers are the creme de la creme.''
It is certainly good enough to attract some foreign students studying at Chinese universities in Shanghai.
Full-time students at the school must pass an examination to enter.
To graduate, they must design and prepare a banquet. 
The course is two years for senior high school graduates and three years for students above the junior high school level. 
American chefs are being invited to China to share their culinary secrets, among them Jasper White, chef and owner of Jasper's in Boston, and Lydia Shire, executive chef at the Four Seasons Hotel in Los Angeles.
''They want to elevate the status of the chef by having important American chefs go into the kitchens with big Chinese chefs,'' Ms. Shire said. 
''It strengthens what they are trying to do.''
The American chefs are also teaching the Chinese how to prepare Western food. 
''The Chinese have lost a whole generation of chefs and especially those who knew anything about Western food,'' Mr. White said. 
''One morning we had eggs and sausage for breakfast, and the eggs were deep-fried. 
Having us do cooking demonstrations is part of an effort to satisfy their guests, both tourists and businessmen.''

Beef and Black Beans With Noodles (From the Golden Flower Hotel)
Â 
Preparation time: 15 minutes Cooking time: 4 to 5 minutes

1/4 cup julienned green bell pepper
1/4 pound shredded beef
4 ounces cleaned bean sprouts
1 teaspoon cornstarch
4 tablespoons chicken stock
1 tablespoon salted black beans

2 tablespoons plus 2 teaspoons peanut oil
1 teaspoon grated ginger
1/2 teaspoon minced garlic

file: FOR PAO LEE, FAMILY IS THE FESTIVAL.txt
text:
ï»¿
Pao Peter Lee's satisfactory universe, not large, is his family, his restaurant and his community association, all of them circumscribed by the Chinese traditions he has stubbornly kept alive for three generations and defined by four lines from the Tang Dynasty poet Li Po, a poem he says has governed his life. 
I raise my head up To watch the bright moon, I bow my head down To think of my old home.
It gives him pleasure to recite the lines, in English and Chinese, to ink them with an old calligraphic brush, and he will tell you of the twin moons in his world, and of his ''old home.''
His first moon was his dream of coming to America from Wuhan, China, something he accomplished 30 years ago, but which still fills him with wonder because it was a happy accident. 
And then there is his family - his wife, Tsen Yee Lee, whom he married 40 years ago in Wuhan; his daughters, Jean and Karen; his son, Dickson, and his crop of grandchildren, currently numbering three.
Pao Peter Lee's satisfactory universe, not large, is his family, his restaurant and his community association, all of them circumscribed by the Chinese traditions he has stubbornly kept alive for three generations and defined by four lines from the Tang Dynasty poet Li Po, a poem he says has governed his life.
''My 'old home' is Chinese culture,'' Mr. Lee said, ''and when Li Po says to bow down it does not only mean that we must pay respect to the elders of the family, but to the elders of other families too. 
We must not only care for our family's children, but we must extend our care to the children of other families.''
It is this belief that led him to establish the Chee Yue Community Association, which helps Chinese immigrants to learn basic English and to find jobs and companionship.
His association, whose name translates into ''Freedom,'' is also devoted, because Mr. Lee thinks it proper, to maintaining Chinese customs. 
So one recent evening the extended family of Pao Peter Lee gathered at his restaurant, the Flower Drum at 856 Second Avenue, to rehearse the small family pageant with which the lunar New Year is celebrated annually.
The dances and tableaux are conducted by the Chee Yue Community Association before, during and after the New Year, which falls this Sunday. 
And Mr. Lee's children are its cast.
But his three grandchildren were there as well, as were a cousin from Wuhan newly arrived to attend college; Mr. Lee's ''uncle,'' Yi Yuen Yu; the uncle's wife, Lihua Chen, who is a ballet dancer, and the couple's two daughters. 
Although Mr. Yu is 48 years old and Mr. Lee is 61, Mr. Yu, because of convoluted family relationships, is Mr. Lee's uncle.
''In China rank counts,'' Mr. Yu said, ''not age.''
''This has always been a family thing,'' says Dickson Lee, 26, a graduate of Queens College who is being groomed by Mr. Lee to take charge of the family restaurant. 
''Our parents expect a lot from us,'' he says. 
''And we want to do it because we see how hard he and mother work and they really don't have much chance to enjoy the fruits of their labors.''
''We're basically a small family,'' says Jean Gagnon, Mr. Lee's older daughter. 
''There are still more than a hundred of us in our homeland. 
But we have always spent a lot of time together. 
He has always drawn on us as resources. 
We always come to his aid at the New Year. 
Father is old stock.''
Mr. Lee seems to be precisely that. 
He is a man who is modest about his personal accomplishments. 
Born in Peking, where his father was a court interpreter in the last days of the Ching Dynasty, he was raised in Wuhan and later moved to Chongqing.
Â 
Invited to the United States
In 1950 as the revolution moved southward Mr. Lee, who had been studying at the Central Police College in Chongqing, went first to Canton, then, like many refugees, to Taiwan. 
In 1953, because of his background, he was invited to Detroit to participate in a conference of the International Association of Police Chiefs. 
He came to America, his ''moon,'' and never left.
He became a student, studying English at Columbia University and working in a Chinatown church as a superintendent. 
He later held three jobs while at school: as a busboy in a restaurant at night, a counselor at a Bronx youth house and a weekend captain in a Queens restaurant. 
He then became an interpreter at the United Nations, but continued to work in the Bronx and Queens. 
''I saved $5,000,'' he says. 
''It was to be the beginning of my dream, my restaurant.''
Mr. Lee sent for his wife and in 1960 began work as a full-time interpreter and calligrapher for the United Nations. 
''That was my only job until 1963,'' he says, ''when my wife found Mama Goldberg East,'' the restaurant that became Flower Drum. 
The family lived over the restaurant, Mrs. Lee worked there and the children took lunch and dinner there and also helped out. 
Mr. Lee continued to work at the United Nations, but came to the restaurant lunch hours and evenings. 
In 1965 he resigned from the United Nations. 
''I made up my mind, no more part time, only overtime.''
The Flower Drum is named for a street dance native to a part of Anhui Province called Fengyang, according to Mr. Lee. The people of Fengyang are known throughout China for their dancers, who are often requested to perform at special celebrations.
He works 10 or 12 hours a day. 
''It is a tough job,'' he says, ''but I do it because my restaurant, my business has character and cultural background that must be seen to. 
It gives me satisfaction that is not of money.''
It is why, he says, he puts much effort into devising menus of classical food preparations, why he serves brown rice which he considers healthful, why he and his wife still buy the restaurant's foodstuffs, ''why the New Year festival must go on, why the family must go on.''
And so must the Chee Yue Community Association, once down on the Bowery, but now around the corner from the Flower Drum at 300 East 46th Street. 
Mr. Lee spends much of his time at the association, which he insisted had to become part of the 46th Street Block Association. 
His daughter, Mrs. Gagnon, explained, ''His old schoolmates, the people he formed Chee Yue with, still come around to talk about old times and the old country.''
Â 
A Helping Hand
''He helps everybody,'' she says. 
''He never says no. 
People come in and Dad will call a friend, a politician, a lawyer he knows. 
It's often a lot of trouble, but he insists on making the call himself. 
He gives everything. 
And still there is so much time for us.''
When asked about the cohesiveness of his family, Pao Peter Lee smiles and tells the story of a Tang Dynasty official named Chan Kung Yi, who amazed his emperor by telling him that nine generations of his family were living under the same roof. 
How, the emperor asked, could there be harmony?
Chan Kung Yi told him he would write out his secret and bring it to the emperor the following day.
''He brought in a scroll with one character of calligraphy written 100 times, Mr. Lee said. 
''It was the character for patience.''

file: FOR REMEMBERED G.I._S, THUMBS UP SIGN IN CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
Four decades ago this old city in southwest China was one of the hubs of World War II, familiar to thousands of Americans who helped Chiang Kai-shek's ''Free China'' survive invasion by Japan.
In the teahouses and free markets that enliven the city center, and in other spots where old-timers gather, fond memories linger of the Americans who helped push the ''Burma Road'' through the jungles from Kunming to Mandalay. 
Equally remembered are the men who flew lumbering transports over ''the hump'' of the Himalayas into the airfield to the west of town.
One old man with gapped teeth paused to offer his assessment while trying on a new pair of spectacles at a stall along Qingnian Street. 
''Americans?
Terrific, terrific!'' he said, shooting out an upraised thumb.
Americans visiting Kunming, China, find good will among residents, who have not forgotten how American fighter squadrons drove off Japanese bombers during World War II, ending raids that terrified city; photo; map (M)
Elsewhere, the pattern was the same. 
A 58-year-old American of Chinese origin, C. W. Kung, who grew up here during the war before leaving to make a career as a chemical engineer in the United States, told visitors to the apartment he shares with his new wife that local people still recall how American fighter squadrons drove off Japanese bombers in 1943 and 1944, ending raids that terrified the city.
Â 
Popularity Is Recalled
''Nobody has forgotten them,'' Mr. Kung said. 
''They were very popular because they actually fought the Japanese, while Chiang's air force did nothing.''
For the Americans, the good will is the only memorial. 
Local officials have no plans to mark the 40th anniversary of the Japanese defeat in August. 
There is not so much as a plaque on the wall of the four-story gray-stone building on Peking Road that was headquarters for Gen. Claire Chennault's 14th Air Force, now doing service as a hotel.
Out at Wujiaba, the wartime airfield that still serves civil and military planes, passengers looking toward the Shuimenren Mountains that hold the city like a bowl can see a cluster of dun-colored hangars and crew rooms, some of wartime vintage. 
Where General Chennault's ''Flying Tigers'' taxied in after their 700-mile journey across 15,000-foot mountains from Assam there is now a fighter base of the People's Liberation Army.
The rows of aging MIG-19's and F-5's are a reminder of the new conflict 200 miles to the south between border troops of China and Vietnam. 
Mostly, it is a war of artillery barrages and small-scale infantry skirmishes, but it is severe enough to have driven hundreds of villagers with relatives in the city to trek north for sanctuary.
Â 
'City of Eternal Spring'
Set at nearly 6,000 feet above sea level, Kunming is known as ''The City of Eternal Spring.''
Travelers reaching here from lower-lying spots elsewhere in southern China, such as Canton, celebrate the cooler air and the blossoms that linger through much of the year. 
But in other ways Americans who return to savor their wartime associations find the city transformed.
A thousand-year-old university town has grown into a bustling city of nearly two million people. 
The sinuous, cobblestoned lanes of the old days have mostly disappeared. 
As in other Chinese cities, broad avenues and rows of 12-story apartment blocks have destroyed a good deal of the old character, though much that is ancient remains.
A change that few regret is the passing of the prostitutes and opium sellers who were an insistent feature of wartime Kunming. 
Prostitutes were rounded up after 1949 and sent to re-education camps, but the opium dealers proved more persistent. 
Terraced fields outside town where poppies once grew have been given over to tea and other crops, but small-scale dealing continues.
A Deputy Governor of Yunnan Province, Zhu Kui, told Western reporters that drug abuse was a thing of the past. 
But other local residents asserted that opium was still available among the mountain tribes that live along Yunnan's 1,300-mile border with Burma, 250 miles to the west, where movement is uninhibited by fencing or effective border patrols. 
The locals said that at least six people had been shot in Kunming for opium trafficking in the past year.
Â 
Notice Confirms Execution
One of the executions was confirmed by a notice outside the Kunming Intermediate People's Court on Qingyun Street, a relic of the old city with its two-story gabled homes, its street-side merchants and its cluster of old men nursing bamboo pipes as they relaxed in the springtime sun. 
The poster announced three executions on March 30, one of them of a 54-year-old opium dealer, Qian Guanxing.
Mr. Qian had a surprisingly long career. 
Above the red check mark signifying that his sentence had been carried out, the poster said he had been imprisoned four times for opium offenses since 1955, most recently for ''entertaining'' 28 people at an ''opium den'' in Kunming in 1983. 
The poster said he was on parole from the fourth term on the ground of ill health when he resumed trafficking last year.
Outside the Kunming Hotel, the center for the city's thriving tourist trade, a retired American college professor who served as a major with a Chinese artillery unit, recalled how opium was a commonplace in the wartime days. 
''If you went out with a boatman on the lake,'' he said, referring to Lake Dian, a local beauty spot, ''he would row for a while, ship his oars, pull out his opium pipe and start puffing away.''
Like others who knew the old Kunming, the professor had little nostalgia for the uprooting of some of the old ways. 
Wartime accounts tell of hungry Chinese soldiers dying by the dozens in the streets, and of beggars at every corner. 
These days the free-enterprise markets are bursting with fresh meat, vegetables and fruit, and ''night markets'' thrive past midnight with stalls serving spicy dishes to order.
Â 
Feel of a Country Fair
So many are the merchants that a visitor passing down Qingnian Street could imagine himself in Hong Kong. 
In this the city is reverting to its old self, before the collectivist austerity of Mao Zedong extinguished enterprise. 
For a mile or more on either side of the broad avenue entrepreneurs ply selections of clothing, toys, comic books and herbal medicines, haggling over price as though Mao had never been.
Other merchants give the street the feel of a country fair. 
Men with homemade pool tables charge the equivalent of 35 cents for a quarter of an hour, with side bets for those who want them. 
An old man draws crowds with a homemade ''test your strength'' machine. 
The spirit of the place seemed to be captured when a West German reporter introduced himself to one old trader by his first name, Jurgen-Karl. 
With a grin, the man shot back: ''Karl?
Like Karl Marx?
We've no time for him around here.''
So far, there is nothing to rival Billy's, the nightclub that was a big draw among wartime G.I.'s. 
But a start has been made at the city's Peking Opera Troupe, where musicians have formed a Western-style band, rented the troupe's rehearsal hall and organized a discotheque that draws crowds of 200 to 300 at a time. 
With a repertoire that includes a reedy version of ''Home on the Range,'' the band is taking in more in a month than the opera earns in a year.

file: FREER FOOD POLICY GIVES CHINA VIGOR.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE scene at the night market along Donghuamen Street in the bustling center of Peking one recent spring evening was a grazer's paradise: Two dozen or more food stalls, some as simple as an oilcloth-covered counter, others virtual restaurants in miniature, each offering enticements.
There were hearty, filling soups; noodles with meat and vegetables, especially the tender garlic shoots popular in northern China at this time of year; fried egg rolls; dumplings steamed and fried; won tons from southeastern Anhui and mutton kebabs from Moslem Xinjiang Uygur. 
Thick rounds of Shanghai bread stuffed with chopped scallions toasted on a griddle while nearby a Peking favorite, sweet almond soup, simmered away. 
Most popular, judging by the crowds, was the Tianjin pancake maker, fat and bald like a traditional Chinese kitchen god, who deftly flipped crepes, smeared them with chili paste and stuffed them with fried eggs and chopped onions.
The lively Donghuamen night market would have been unremarkable in Taiwan, Hong Kong or Singapore. 
But only in the last few years have such night scenes become common in Peking and other Chinese cities. 
For a visitor who remembers the dispiriting look of nighttime Peking 10 years ago, the change is astonishing.
Private restaurants and so-called free or farmers' markets - outlets for food produced independent of Government quota systems - are becoming even more commonplace. 
Altogether, these are dramatic indications that after years in which farmers were often forbidden to raise even chickens and pigs for personal consumption, Government policy has been overturned and private initiative encouraged under the unlikely slogan, ''Getting Rich Through Labor Is Glorious.''
In 1984, for the first time since these changes began six years earlier, the quantity of fruits and vegetables sold in free markets exceeded that sold in state markets, according to Pang Chungmin, an economist who was formerly with the Ministry of Agriculture in Peking and is now with the International Finance Corporation of the World Bank in Washington. 
There are now some 46,000 free markets in China, Mr. Pang said. 
That figure includes only officially licensed markets, not the thousands of informal markets, the peddlers who sell fresh fish or bean curd cakes door-to-door or the older people hawking apples, oranges and homemade Popsicles outside schools and factory gates.
''It has developed much more rapidly than anyone foresaw,'' Mr. Pang said. 
''The whole thing has taken on a movement of its own. 
It's becoming quite commercial.''
So has the restaurant business. 
In 1980, Chen Yinfeng says, he became the first private restaurateur in Peking. 
With his wife, Mr. Chen now owns and operates Peking Jiale (Peking Excellent Happiness) at 5 Xiagungfu, behind the Peking Hotel.
Mr. Chen comes from a long line of restaurateurs: His grandfather opened a restaurant in Peking in 1946. 
His father and six uncles are cooks and there are seven chefs among his brothers and cousins. 
But Mr. Chen, who, like many Chinese, was sent to the countryside during the Cultural Revolution, is the only one to have a restaurant of his own.
Peking Jiale, which serves a mild version of Sichuan-style food, is his second restaurant. 
It cost 30,000 yuan (about $10,000) to open - a considerable sum in China, where the average factory or office worker earns less than 100 yuan a month. 
Mr. Chen said he borrowed about two-thirds of it from friends. 
The balance was available in profits from his earlier, smaller operation, which he closed two years ago on establishing the new place.
Business is brisk at Peking Jiale, where American country-and-western music played in the background one recent afternoon. 
Mr. Chen serves 400 to 500 customers a day. 
Unlike state-owned establishments with inflexible 7:30 P.M. closings, his restaurant is open seven days a week, 8 A.M. to 9 P.M. His cooks earn 500 yuan a month, he said, while waiters get 120 to 180 yuan, depending on their experience - excellent wages in China.
Mr. Chen's restaurant yields 20,000 to 30,000 yuan a year in profit. 
China is still China, however: Mr. Chen said he and his wife contributed much of it to ''social welfare funds.''
Recently, he said, as part of a Government campaign for people to ''learn from the heroism of China's border guards,'' he and his wife went to the Vietnamese border region. 
The trip cost 10,000 yuan, much of which was spent on presents for the guards.
Restaurants like Peking Jiale, attracting Chinese clientele as well as tourists, stand in contrast to state-owned restaurants, whose hallmarks are poor food poorly prepared, indifferent service and a breathtaking disregard for basic sanitation. 
Even a visitor who does not understand Chinese characters can quickly pick out the new, privately owned places, for, although humble in appearance, they are relatively clean, bustling and lively.
Crowded food markets, like the one along the northeastern wall of the Temple of Heaven Park in southern Peking, and another along Baiwanzhuang Street in the city's northwestern section, are other indications of far-reaching change. 
Every town, it seems, has at least one regular market where farmers and licensed peddlers hawk their wares, and prices are only slightly higher than in state markets.
In the northern industrial city of Jiamusi, in Heilongjiang Province, May Day holiday shoppers in a vast covered market thronged past stalls offering fresh cabbages, cauliflowers, cucumbers, apricot-fleshed melons from Xinjiang Uygur, Philippine bananas, eggplants, watermelons and peppers, along with live ducks and chickens, fresh and dried fish, fresh pork, spices, dried tobacco leaves, Korean-style salted and pickled vegetables, and sacks of rice, millet, corn, wheat and dried legumes.
Much of this food is lower in quality than food in American markets. 
But it is considerably better than what was available a few years ago, when northern city markets offered little more than leeks, onions, garlic and tired, often half-rotten cabbages, turnips and apples from storage cellars.
The effect of this economic activity has been spreading. 
As peasants get richer, they invest in larger and more solid houses as well as in refrigerators and televisions. 
That means more work and better wages for construction crews and factory employees. 
For example, in the county town of Fuyuan on the Amur River along the Soviet border, construction of new brick housing is so rapid that local brick factories can scarcely keep up.
All is not roses, however. 
China's 1985 grain harvest, an important indication of economic and political stabilityII here, was down 6.6 percent from the record crop in 1984. 
While the decline was attributed in part to the weather, experts say it was also caused by peasants switching from grain to more profitable crops or leaving farming to start rural industries. 
Meanwhile, city residents are experiencing inflation, a new factor with unforeseeable consequences.
For many Chinese, however, and especially for those peasants at the bottom of the heap, the new policy has meant, for the first time in modern history, money, mobility and an exciting, enticing world of possibilities.

For 17 years, Beate Gordon has been a sort of cultural detective. 
She travels to Asia each summer, ferreting out virtuoso performers of traditional arts and arranging for them to tour the United States.
The assignment, for the Asia Society,seems tailor-made for the 63-year-old Mrs. Gordon, whose background is as exotic as her work. 
Born in Vienna of Russian parents, both pianists, she was reared in Japan and studied dance, drama and music. 
She speaks six languages: German, French, Spanish, Japanese, English and Russian.
Her latest find, eight Mongolian musicians and dancers - the first such troupe ever to tour this country - will appear at the Asia Society, on Park Avenue at 70th Street, tomorrow through Friday.
They are the 34th group, from 13 countries, that she has brought over. 
Typically, they were assembled after some digging by Mrs. Gordon. The program will include khoomei - a technique in which a singer emits a long, low ''szzz sound,'' as she put it, ''with overtones'' - an art she had known about, but only glimpsed in the concert to which she was invited in Ulan Bator.
Â 
Khoomei Is Heard
''So I went to the conservatory of music,'' she recalled, ''I simply marched myself in, and talked to the receptionist. 
She was very charming. 
She ran out and came back with the man who had sung khoomei the night before!
So in the reception room he sang and I really could hear and watch how the muscles worked.''
The other artists chosen by Mrs. Gordon include players of a two-stringed fiddle, mouth harps and flutes, and an ''upper body'' dancer who performs with bowls of milk.
Mrs. Gordon, who formerly worked for the Japan Society in New York and now directs the Asia Society's department of performances, films and lectures, has many tales to tell.
There was the time a monsoon delayed her arrival in Purulia, India, and she slept on a mat in a hut until drums woke her at 2 A.M.; performers who had learned she was there were emerging from the forest to play for her.
Or her trip to the heights of Lhasa, Tibet, when she walked very slowly, as cautioned, but ignored advice not to laugh or talk - both qualities that seem natural to the impresario, whose enthusiasms break through a cordial reserve. 
So she blacked out, then had to carry around bags of oxygen while auditioning performers.
Â 
The Struggle for Authenticity
Speaking in her small office overlooking Park Avenue, Mrs. Gordon cited a pervasive problem: convincing cultural ministers and performers that she wants authentic, classical art, not tourist entertainment; genuine costumes, not glitter.
''What I often am shown,'' she said, ''are forms that have been changed to become more accessible, not just for foreigners but often even for their own audiences.''
In Tibet she heard ''La Paloma'' played by a 75-piece orchestra. 
In Burma, someone crooned with a microphone. 
They sang ''I love coffee, I love tea'' in Suzhou, China. 
And in the Chinese province of Fujian, she saw an anti-smoking puppet show.
''Can you imagine expecting this,'' she asked, showing a replica of a centuries-old Fujian hand-puppet in a glass case near her desk - a woman's figure wearing an intricately embroidered silk gown - ''and seeing a panda and a monkey?
The monkey's pipe kept growing bigger and bigger. 
They thought, 'Americans would love this.'
''
Â 
Missing the Point
Sometimes she seems to have made her point only to suffer dismay when the performers arrive in this country. 
''I have spent hours,'' she said, ''begging Indian dancers to bring their beautiful silk saris woven with gold and silver thread, only to be told that they had special costumes made for the States with hand-sewn sequins.''
Mrs. Gordon, whose research includes visits to museums and lots of questions to village elders, learned early to find a key person to put her in touch with performers. 
''You meet a patron of the arts in Madras, or a critic in Bombay who can open doors for you,'' she said.
Detecting probable anachronisms comes with experience, she said. 
For instance, she saw something amiss in South Korea when a dance that she knew originally represented the instrospective struggles of a Buddhist monk was performed by 50 people.
She spotted another alteration when dancers in Burma formed a boat with their bodies. 
There she drew on what she knew of China -that ''you might make movements of a boat, rocking side to side, or show water with a long blue scarf, but never something realistic like that.''
Â 
A War Intervenes
Mrs. Gordon, an only child, moved to Japan with her parents in 1929, when her father, Leo Sirota, played concerts there and stayed on to teach at the Imperial Academy. 
She attended a German school near Tokyo until Nazi teachers arrived, hardly the place for a Jewish child. 
She switched to an American school, and later moved to the United States to attend Mills College in Oakland, Calif.
Mrs. Gordon lost contact with her parents during World War II. 
While still a Mills student, she worked for the Federal Government, monitoring Tokyo Radio. 
Later she wrote broadcasts beamed to Japanese soldiers in the field - the counterpart, she notes, to Tokyo Rose.
After a stint as a researcher in New York for Time magazine, she became a civilian employee of the Army as a way to rejoin her parents in Japan. 
Assigned to Gen. Douglas MacArthur's headquarters in Tokyo, she wound up writing the womens' rights section of Japan's postwar Constitution.
She also met Lieut. 
Joseph Gordon, an interpreter, whom she later married. 
They have a daughter, Nicole, a lawyer, and a son, Geoffrey, a playwright. 
Mr. Gordon, who taught Chinese and Japanese, then switched to real estate, retired a couple of years ago and began accompanying his wife on what until then had been solo travels.
Pursuing old ways, Mrs. Gordon notes their swift passage. 
In the year since her first visit to Lhasa in 1985, she said, ''it changed from a sleepy village to a small town with a completely modern hotel, a new theater and even yakburgers.''
''With the inroads of Western culture,'' she added, ''it's wonderful to see that in some places, a lot of the original is left.''

text:
ï»¿
IT was lunchtime in one of this British colony's finest Chinese restaurants, a plushly carpeted aerie overlooking Victoria Harbor. 
Clear skies in the wake of the annual typhoons made for a picture-postcard view of junks and freighters and Navy frigates from the United States; behind them, grey-green mountains stretched into China.
Below, in the central district, where skyscrapers produce an aura of an Asian Manhattan, sidewalks pulsed with the energy that has turned this patch of territory into one of the world's most important financial and trading centers. 
In the restaurant, the tables were filled with Chinese and Americans and Europeans brought together by the deals in the textiles, toys and electronics that pour out of the industrial districts of Kowloon, the teeming city across the harbor.
Lunchtime talk was mostly of discounts and freight rates and currency fluctuations, but three middle-aged Chinese at a corner table paused between servings of steamed prawns and beef Szechuan-style to take up a matter that has become almost all-consuming among the colony's middle class: how to obtain foreign passports or other papers that would allow them to emigrate more easily. 
An intense-looking man with gold-rimmed spectacles explained how an acquaintance recently acquired a Fiji passport. 
The man's companions chuckled, then asked for details.
A year after Britain formally agreed to surrender sovereignty over Hong Kong to China on July 1, 1997, the mood in the business community is a mixture of confidence and caution. 
With the removal of the uncertainties that arose during the sometimes bitter negotiations between London and Peking, the economy is back to a healthy growth rate. 
This year, growth was about 4.5 percent, down from the 9 percent growth rate achieved on record export levels in 1984 but a major improvement over the early 1980's, when fears of a unilateral Chinese takeover and a recession in the United States combined to bring about a slump.
The stock market, too, has achieved a four-year high. 
Parcels of luxury real estate, which fell to a fraction of their values in 1983, are once more fetching record bids. 
A decline in exports overseas has been offset by a leap in the colony's traditional staple, trade with China.
The 1984 agreement has played a major part in this, assuring investors that they have at least a few years in which business will be played by the old rules, or by something close to them. 
For the last two decades, Hong Kong has been a place where investors could pour capital into hotels, office blocks and cross-harbor tunnels and retrieve it with a profit in as little as three to five years. 
Almost everybody agrees that there is that much time, perhaps more, before the shadows of 1997 cast a pall.
Despite the inevitable crowding in this 404-square-mile territory, most of the 5.5 million inhabitants are not likely to have any choice but to stay. 
Most potential destinations, including Britain, have made it plain they could not handle an influx of refugees. 
For these people, the handover could be a nightmare - a plunge from a freewheeling society that is relatively affluent by Asian standards into one that could mirror that of China which, despite China's recent reforms, is still considered repressive and backward by most in Hong Kong.
In the past 12 months China has been energetic in trying to calm anxieties, at least insofar as they relate to the maintenance of the colony's standard of living. 
It has worked with Britain on complex technical issues such as the establishment of an independent Hong Kong shipping registry. 
It has expanded its already substantial investments here, moving on at least two occasions to save major locally owned enterprises from collapse. 
Beyond this, it has lost no opportunity to voice its determination to keep the territory prosperous. 
The message was repeated over and over during the two-week visit here earlier this month of Ji Pengfei, the former Chinese Foreign Minister who is in charge of the Peking Government's Hong Kong Office. 
That agency has responsibility for drawing up the constitution, under which the territory will operate as a ''special administrative region'' of China after 1997. 
NEVERTHELESS, talk of eventual emigration is common among merchants, brokers and lawyers, and without them, Hong Kong could swiftly turn into an expensive drain on Peking. 
Thoughts of leaving are perhaps inevitable, since more than three-quarters of the Chinese families in Hong Kong either fled or are descended from people who fled China after the revolution succeeded in 1949. 
''Remember, most of us are refugees from Communism in the first place,'' said Martin Lee, a British-trained lawyer.
Lately, Mr. Lee, who is 47 years old, has been leading a local outcry over statements from Peking that there should be no ''democratization'' of local political processes in advance of 1997. 
The British agreement with Peking refers to an elected legislature after 1997, and to the appointment ''by election or through consultations'' of a Chinese chief executive to replace the British governor.
The apparent balking at political change has raised concerns about Peking's willingness to honor other guarantees in the 1984 accord. 
These include commitments to preserve Hong Kong's ''capitalist'' system for 50 years after 1997, along with its stock market, its convertible currency and its free port.
Nevertheless, some local executives say that arguments about prospects for the territory after 1997 obscure the fact that Hong Kong even now is moving more into China's economic orbit for reasons that have little to do with the 1984 accord. 
At the end of 1984, the territory was still the world's largest exporter of clothing, fur garments and toys, and nobody here sees much danger of those markets disappearing. 
But official figures suggest that these boom industries of the 1970's are gradually yielding their dominance and that Hong Kong is re-emphasizing its historic role as the gateway to China, but this time on a much larger scale.
Hong Kong suffered a 5 percent decline in the manufacturing work force this year, but offsetting that has been an impressive 10 percent jump in employment in the wholesale, retail and service sectors - with much of the gain in businesses that are profiting from the rapid economic growth spurred by Deng Xiaoping's ''modernization'' drive in China.
The executives here say that this basic shift in the Hong Kong economy involves more than just the slowdown in economic growth in the United States, the colony's largest export market. 
They point out that Hong Kong also faces growing competition from other Asian countries, including China, that have low-cost labor, and that the colony is having difficulty moving from low-technology industries into more sophisticated fields. 
THESE trends make the China trade increasingly important. 
In the first nine months of 1985, that trade leapt by 33 percent over 1984, to a total of 88 billion Hong Kong dollars, or $11.3 billion United States dollars, more than a quarter of the colony's total trade. 
While more than half the total was accounted for by ''re-export trade,'' goods that pass through Hong Kong on their way to and from other markets, there was also a more than 50 percent leap in Hong Kong's own exports to the mainland. 
How significant the trend is for Hong Kong can be measured from figures that show total trade with China in 1979, at the beginning of Mr. Deng's reform program, to be barely 17 billion Hong Kong dollars, roughly 15 percent of the total expected this year.
Without the increase in trade with the mainland, the territory would almost certainly have been in a mild recession this year, a point that Peking's Mr. Ji made during his visit, reminding audiences that Hong Kong was becoming increasingly dependent on China's prosperity.
China is making that point in other ways. 
At a choice site near the Hong Kong waterfront, work will begin soon on a new building designed by I.M. 
Pei as the local headquarters of the Bank of China, Peking's foreign exchange bank. 
Apart from the personal gratification involved for Mr. Pei - his father was the bank's first Hong Kong manager in the 1930's -the building's triangular glass towers and its height, at 70 stories the tallest in the colony, will make for a powerful symbol. 
The new headquarters nearby of the locally controlled Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, giant of the territory's banking industry, stands only 47 stories and has been pilloried for a skeletal appearance that one local critic compared with ''an oil-cracking plant.''
Peking has also been pumping in large amounts of money to save Conic Investment Ltd., a major manufacturer of televisions, radios and electronic components, and to prop up the failing Ka Wah Bank, which was founded by local Chinese. 
In both cases, Peking's money men consulted local experts closely before making their moves, and won plaudits for their sophistication.
''We're not dealing any longer with the baggy-suited chaps in sandals,'' one British financial official observed. 
''They still come, of course, but more and more we're seeing people who could hold their own anywhere, in tailoring or know-how.''
There are now more than 300 Chinese-owned enterprises in the territory. 
Many of these are part of China Resources Holdings Ltd., the huge trading and investment enterprise that is the mainland's answer to traditional British ''hongs,'' family-controlled conglomerates like Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd. and Swire Pacific Ltd., whose dominance of business in the territory has faded rapidly in recent years before the challenge of local Chinese entrepreneurs. 
One reason for this, critics of the British say, is that they have been slow to adjust to new circumstances - including the importance of the China market.
But lately, even the hongs have been altering their approach. 
Since Jardine's moved its legal address to Bermuda in 1984, a largely symbolic move that deeply angered Peking, the British-owned companies have shown a new sensitivity to politics and geography. 
One example came last month, when Swire's announced that it would make a public offering of up to 25 percent of the equity in Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd., a 70 percent-owned subsidiary that has been the company's most profitable holding. 
Analysts said the move was a response to the formation of a new Hong Kong-registered airline, Hongkong Dragon Airlines Ltd., in which Peking has a substantial stake.
By admitting Hong Kong investors to part-ownership of the airline, Swire's chairman, Michael Miles, evidently hopes to give the carrier a local presence that will protect it once Peking controls Hong Kong's Kai Tak Airport, where Cathay is based. 
But the view among airline industry watchers here was that the move could be a case of too little, too late.
Dragonair's chairman is Sir Yue-kong Pao, the Hong Kong shipping magnate who has been developing close ties with Peking, and its appeal to China has been enhanced by its announcement that it will train Chinese flight crews. 
Cathay Pacific has operated in Hong Kong for 39 years and has numerous Chinese employees, but none among the 500 people it employs in its cockpits.
In some ways, the airline's dilemma epitomizes the problems facing many of the British companies that once ruled the roost here. 
The sons of Britain's upper classes who have long enjoyed the fast route into the companies' executive suites have proven no match for the nimble Chinese entrepreneurs in recent years. 
Jardine's, largest of all the ''hongs,'' has seen its assets shrink by more than a quarter in the past few years.
In the meantime, the influence of American companies has risen sharply, to the point where there are now more than 15,000 Americans living here, employed by about 800 American companies with local offices, factories or joint ventures.
For the foreigners, 1997 poses less of a problem. 
Privately, many Britons say they will return home before then. 
Americans tend to be more sanguine about the prospects - but they, too, have passports that permit a relaxed view.
Â 
THE RICH FOLK GO A'COURTING IN PEKING
HONG KONG -In the year since Britain signed the agreement under which Hong Kong will revert to China in 1997, local millionaires have been conspicuously courting Peking's favor. 
One name that crops up frequently is that of Sir Yue-kong Pao, known as Sir Y. K., chairman of the Worldwide Shipping Company, whose maritime interests, real estate, and other holdings have made him one of the colony's richest men.
The shipping magnate - the ''Sir'' comes from a knighthood bestowed upon him by Queen Elizabeth - rarely gives interviews. 
But associates say that he believes that China's official guarantees will matter less than the personal relationships that leaders here can build up with the top men in China, and the degree to which they can ''educate'' the Peking elite in the things that make Hong Kong tick. 
To this end, Sir Y. K. has become a frequent visitor to Peking and his native town of Ningbo, east of Shanghai, and has more than once been a guest of China's pre-eminent leader, Deng Xiaoping, in the Great Hall of the People.
Along the way he made a major contribution to the construction costs of Peking's newest luxury hotel, the Zhao Long, whose opening last month was the occasion for one of Mr. Deng's rare appearances at a public function outside the Great Hall. 
Sir Y. K. has also pledged nearly $16 million for the establishment of a university in Ningbo.
None of this is much different from the courting of the British establishment that has been going on for decades among prominent Chinese in Hong Kong. 
What has disturbed some people here is Sir Y. K.'s political stance. 
Along with Li Kaxing, another wealthy businessman, Sir Y. K. was appointed by Peking to participate in the drafting of the basic law that will govern Hong Kong after the transition. 
It is an open secret that one of his first moves in the drafting committee was to speak against direct elections.
Few here see this as a conspiracy. 
Rather, many believe that wealthy citizens like Sir Y. K. find themselves, paradoxically, sharing Peking's anxieties about popular government. 
People like Sir Y. K., it is believed, fear that elected legislators might usher in an expensive social welfare program. 
Apart from a huge public housing program that has provided homes for more than half the population, Hong Kong currently has only a rudimentary welfare system. 
Taxes are at levels low enough to be the envy of entrepreneurs throughout Asia.

text:
