A LITHE 72-YEAR-OLD WHO still exults in his back flips, Sun Martsai is the lord of Cantonese opera.
An energetic man whose hands flutter through the air as he speaks, Mr. Sun packs theaters with his fans, who are often so overwhelmed with his grace and singing that they throw rings and necklaces and money upon the stage after a performance. 
His dominance of Cantonese opera makes Pavarotti seem like a flash in the pan.
Not everyone is so impressed, however. 
His 9-year-old daughter confesses that she does not like Cantonese opera. 
She prefers Alan Tam, the Hong Kong pop singer, whose melodies resemble rock songs everywhere. 
''She likes Cantonese opera, she likes it,'' said the father. 
''I don't like it, I don't like it,'' said the daughter.
And therein lies the challenge for Cantonese opera, and indeed for much of Chinese culture: How can traditional arts such as opera or calligraphy, which flowered with one of the world's greatest civilizations, attract today's generation of denim-clad Chinese, seduced by Western songs, films and way of life?
To a foreign ear, Cantonese opera may be a musical experience rivaled only by a classroom of second-grade maestros scratching their fingernails on a blackboard. 
Yet, if the singing is an acquired taste, the grace and subtlety of movement impress even the most callow observer.
Like its northern cousin, Peking opera, Cantonese opera combines a libretto that borders on poetry with magnificent costumes and choreography. 
The movement and makeup in Cantonese opera, however, often seem more natural than those of Peking opera. 
And of course Peking opera is performed in Mandarin Chinese instead of the Cantonese dialect spoken in Hong Kong.
Older people in Hong Kong still love Cantonese opera, and prize it as the bulwark of traditional culture. 
Its heyday, in fact, came during this century, from the 1920's to the 1950's. 
At a government-subsidized performance this month in a Hong Kong gymnasium, operagoers, many of whom could remember foot binding and Imperial China, began lining up more than an hour before the performance and filled every nook of the auditorium.
''Young people don't like to see Cantonese opera; that's left to old hags like us,'' said Siu Ngankwan, a tiny 84-year-old woman with hollow eyes and memories of the operas she saw as a girl growing up in Canton.
Young people spurn Cantonese opera partly because of its complexity and subtlety - which, to others, are its virtues. 
Every gesture, every swish of a long white sleeve, every tint in the painted faces conveys meaning. 
A whip in the hand means that the actor is riding a horse; a red face suggests righteousness and a white face, craftiness.
Therefore the dilemma for Cantonese opera is whether to maintain traditional purity, or to make opera more accessible by modifying it. 
In essence it is the same question that Western culture faces: Should Shakespeare be translated into a modern idiom, or, can an Italian opera be performed in English?
Without adaptation, traditional cultural achievements - such as Tang Dynasty poetry in China or Ovid's Metamorphoses in the West - tend to wither in influence.
The quandary may be particularly acute in the Chinese world, where conformity to artistic tradition plays a greater role than in the West. 
Chinese painters, for example, traditionally copied the exact works of their masters over and over.
In the United States, it sometimes seems as if every 25-year-old director feels obliged to interpret Sophocles in a radical new way, often a tribute more to imagination than to judgment. 
In the Chinese world, on the other hand, the artist feels obliged to follow his elders. 
Cantonese opera, which dates to the first half of the 18th century, has changed in some ways. 
Early in this century many libretti were written in colloquial language. 
Western instruments are sometimes found in the orchestras. 
Sets are more elaborate, and microphones are common. 
''It is good to change, to keep good elements while allowing others to die out,'' said Leung Puikam, an expert on Chinese opera at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. 
Cantonese opera originated with troupes who wandered from village to village, performing in the streets or in teahouses. 
Even today, Cantonese opera is more the Oriental equivalent of vaudeville than of Western opera. 
In Hong Kong, an opera is a casual evening out, to which the Chinese wear old clothes and perhaps gnaw on a chicken foot during the performance.
Western opera connotes sophistication, so people might feign enthusiasm even if they do not feel it. 
But the folding chairs, constant chatter and discarded chicken bones in the audience of Cantonese opera suggest to some young people a legacy that is more embarrassing than inspiring.
Today the greatest cultural stars in the Chinese world are pop singers like Alan Tam and Anita Mui, whose rock music is based on Western and Japanese styles; or celluloid heartthrobs like Jackie Chan, a martial arts expert who is Hong Kong's most eligible bachelor. 
Cantonese opera buffs scoff at the crooners, just as devotees of Bartok or Brahms may be put off by by Bruce Springsteen or Barbra Streisand.
For all of the obstacles facing Cantonese opera, there does seem to have been a modest revival in the last few years. 
Last year, for example, some 22,000 people attended performances in the New Territories section of Hong Kong, up from 15,000 a year earlier. 
A few new troupes have also been organized. 
But even opera singers say that the principal reason for the revival is increased support from local governments.
While some young performers study Cantonese opera, there are no sweeping attempts to reinterpret the medium. 
Few new libretti are written today, and no Arthur Miller has appeared to substitute modern themes and everyday people for the old folk tales, kings and generals that usually dominate the operas. 
Even the younger students of Cantonese opera sometimes regard it as only a sidelight.
Tin Kitwan, a 25-year-old woman who has been studying Cantonese opera for three years, said that the field did not pay well enough these days to attract her as a career, so she will pursue Cantonese opera only part time.
''I want to be a star,'' she said, ''but a part-time star.''

text:

The brooding face of Eugene O'Neill stared out from the window of the Yaxipai motorcycle dealership on Zhongshan Road. 
Farther on, his face appeared on the rough brick wall of a herbal medicine shop.
Throughout this city that hugs the south bank of the Yangtze River, huge blood-red posters, stark with a stern portrait of the American playwright, declared the arrival of the Nanjing-Shanghai O'Neill Theater Festival.
''It's a triumph for us,'' said the chairman of the English department at Nanjing University, Prof. Liu Haiping, who is the organizer of the festival and an accompanying conference on O'Neill's work in honor of the playwright's centenary.
''We were told at first that it would be impossible to have a conference on such a figure as O'Neill,'' Professor Liu said. 
''Only with someone like Tolstoy could a conference be devoted to an individual artist. 
I told them that O'Neill's influence was growing and that he had a direct relation to China.''
Â 
Discussion and Debate
Professor Liu won the day and last week on theater stages around town the Tyrone family quarreled and agonized, the Emperor Jones ruled and the Mayos were transplanted to a southern Yangtze River village. 
During the day, scholars from three continents discussed, debated and applauded O'Neill's vast dramatic work.
When Cheng Jianxun strode onto the stage of the Qianxian Drama Theater as the unshaven James Tyrone in ''A Long Day's Journey Into Night,'' the Chinese audience remained riveted to the drama, silent and attentive, a departure from the usual noisy crowds that attend Chinese theatrical performances.
The production, staged by the drama troupe of the Nanjing military command of the Chinese Army, is believed to be the first by an army theater group of an American play, and it was also the first time ''Long Day's Journey'' had played in China.
But the road to the production, indeed to the festival and conference, was not easy. 
For Professor Liu, it was an exercise in patience, stubbornness, and the conviction that it was important for China to explore the complexities of O'Neill's tragic vision.
Â 
A Year at Harvard
Mr. Liu, who was banished to work on a farm during China's Cultural Revolution, was a professor of modern English and American drama at Nanjing University but had never seen a production of the plays he taught until he spent the 1983-84 academic year at Harvard University. 
He returned to the United States in 1986 to read a paper on Taoism in O'Neill's plays at a conference on the playwright at Suffolk University in Boston.
''Actually, the idea came during a conference on O'Neill in Boston in 1984,'' Professor Liu explained in an interview. 
''One of the professors said, 'Why don't you hold a conference on O'Neill in China so we can see your country and bring O'Neill to China?'
It seemed a joke to me at the time.''
As time passed, though, the idea gripped his imagination and Professor Liu approached the administrators of the university with his project. 
Even after he persuaded the administration that O'Neill warranted the attention of Chinese scholars and dramatists, the school told the professor that without money, approval could not be granted.
''There was actually a Catch-22,'' he remembered. 
''In order for me to get money, I had to get approval from the university. 
But to get approval from the university, I had to get funding for the conference.''
This was February 1987.
''So I sat down at my typewriter and sent letters to major U.S. foundations and joint venture companies in China,'' he said. 
''One letter came back with a positive response. 
They gave us $1,000. 
But that was a start.''
Â 
Lack of Money
''We had no money in the beginning,'' he said. 
''We had to save on stamps because international postage is very expensive. 
But then the Amity Foundation in the United States provided $8,000 and another $8,000 came from the China Fund.''
As money came in, the attitude of the university changed and permission was granted for Professor Liu to go ahead. 
In the end, the more than 30 scholars from Japan, the United States, Sweden, Belgium and Britain who traveled to Nanjing were all required to pay their own way, Professor Liu said.
For Professor Liu, who has just published a book on China's treatment of O'Neill since the 1920's, the growth in interest in the playwright reflects a profound step in China's intellectual and dramatic landscape.
Â 
Alternative to Ibsen
''Eugene O'Neill was fairly popular in the 1920's,'' Professor Liu said. 
''China had established its own drama, huaju, by then. 
Although Ibsen was the most influential playwright then, people wanted someone different from Ibsen. 
O'Neill was the second most important playwright mainly because of his Expressionistic work 'The Emperor Jones.'
''When the director Hong Shen saw a performance of 'The Emperor Jones' he was impressed by the techniques and came back to China and staged a production here. 
He restaged the Emperor Jones as an army official who stole rations from his men and ran away. 
He used the drums the same way the original production did. 
It was the first introduction of Expressionism onto the Chinese stage.
''After that, Cao Yu - one of China's best-known playwrights -argued that China didn't know how to use Expressionism. 
In an influential article in the 1930's, he said that we should learn from O'Neill's one-act plays, that we should start simply.''
From the 1940's until 1979, O'Neill vanished from the Chinese stage, buried by war, revolution and political orthodoxy. 
''After 1979,'' Professor Liu said, ''he emerged as one of the most-read playwrights.''
''One reason for this revival of interest is that those of us of the younger generation see him as very modern,'' he said. 
''He has absorbed a lot of European influence: Nietzsche, Freud, Schopenhauer. 
Graduate students like to write about O'Neill because he is seen as contemporary, not a classic playwright like Shakespeare. 
And though O'Neill's Expressionism is old in the West, it is still very new here.''
''Further, there is a newly released enthusiasm about America,'' he continued.
The limits of Chinese understanding of O'Neill, however, was discussed in one of the papers delivered at the conference. 
Zhao Yu, a graduate student at Nanjing University, noted that two of the plays - ''Desire Under the Elms'' and ''Mourning Becomes Electra'' - are ''beyond the horizon of expectation of Chinese readers because of different esthetic standards.''
Â 
The Meaning of Tragedy
''As Chinese tragedians are concerned about the happiness of man in the present world, all the problems they put forward usually are solved right within the plays,'' Ms. Zhao said. 
''But this is not the case in 'Desire Under the Elms' and 'Mourning Becomes Electra.'
In China, it is a rule that tragedies, especially classical tragedies, end in happiness.''
Long Wenpei, a professor of literature at Fudan University in Shanghai, was enthusiastic about the revival of O'Neill in China, however. 
''Human nature is no longer off-limits for us,'' he exclaimed. 
''O'Neill is a real writer who looked at the meaning of life.''

text:
ï»¿
Westerners who live in China are accustomed to being told how fortunate we are. 
But for us there is a company of foreigners still more to be envied, those who journeyed here before the Communists closed the outlying reaches of the country to the world. 
One has only to read the accounts of Somerset Maugham, who visited here in 1921, or of Peter Fleming, who was here in 1935, to know the beguiling possibilities of a China where travel was less hindered.
As the Government has extended its list of ''open'' areas, this chagrin has eased. 
Most of the regions newly accessible to foreigners are in the Chinese heartland, but one of them has made possible a journey to an area remote even by the standards of those who explored the country before 1949. 
With the opening on May 1 of the Karakoram Highway, Peking licensed any foreigner to relive one of the most daunting experiences of Marco Polo, the most fabled China traveler of them all.
It was during his confinement in a Genoese prison that Polo dictated his account of his travels to a cellmate, Maestro Rusticello, a fact that has made the adventurer's precise route from Venice to Khanbalik, the modern Peking, a matter of scholarly dispute. 
But it is certain that his path, by horse and camel, led over the towering mountain passes, some more than 16,000 feet, that admit to China from what is now its western frontier with Afghanistan and Pakistan. 
It is over this terrain that the Karakoram Highway runs, a 795-mile triumph of engineering that was built over a period of 18 years before 1978 by army road crews from China and Pakistan.
The story of the Karakoram is of the road, a narrow strip of asphalt and graded gravel that runs through forbiddingly rocky lowlands, along sinuous corniches extending hundreds of feet above stony riverbeds and up into the crystal freshness of three of the world's highest ranges, the Pamirs, the Himalayas and the Karakorams. 
It is a tale, too, of Kashgar, a town of biblical simplicity that is the road's starting point on the Chinese side, of the unaffected friendliness of upland people who live much as they did in Polo's time, and of the lovely mountains and orchards of the Hunza Valley of northeast Pakistan.
On the day the highway opened the Chinese reserved the few four-wheel-drive Jeeps in Kashgar for dignitaries attending ceremonies in the Khunjerab Pass, the 16,072-foot border point with Pakistan. 
Accordingly, our party of eight - five reporters, a New York banker based in Peking, and two of our wives - resolved to spend time exploring farther east in the sprawling Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. 
This introduced us to the arid fastnesses of the Gobi and Taklimakan Deserts, nearly 2,000 miles of sand and scrub that fill most of the terrain between Kashgar and Peking.
At the searing oasis of Turpan, where summer temperatures reach 125 degrees, we measured the rigors that confronted the traders, adventurers and marauders who journeyed along the Great Silk Road, the romantic thoroughfare that linked the Mediterranean of imperial Rome to the China of the contemporaneous dynasty of the Han. 
At Gaochang, a ruined city outside Turpan, sacked by Mongols not long before Polo ventured across the Taklimakan, we gazed westward across the desert from ancient ramparts and knew how the desert got its Turkic name, meaning ''Enter, and you won't return!''
We reached Kashgar on a Saturday evening, marveling at our first aerial view of the 2,000-year-old town with its poplars, its wheat fields and its vines. 
After the biscuit-brown expanses of sand that stretch like a ruffled carpet before the Tien Shan Mountains buffering Xinjiang from Soviet Kirghizia and Kazakhstan, the greenness was like cooling air. 
Looking down on the shaded forecourts of the mosques, we understood how Peter Fleming felt - ''Few people can ever have enjoyed a bath more than we did'' -when he arrived here in a camel train after a five-month journey from Peking in 1935.
It is a safe bet that none of the 244 Chinese cities and towns now open to foreigners provides a less altered appearance to contemporary travelers than Kashgar. 
No Japanese taxis here, only donkey carts that, unsprung, carry visitors through the mud-walled back streets of Yumlakshakulbishe, heart of the old town. 
In back alleys and courtyard homes hidden behind whitewashed walls, the curious can find the unchanging rhythms of life among the Uighurs, who constitute 90 percent of Kashgar's population of 180,000 and about half of the 13 million people in Xinjiang.
In two days we were invited to a wedding, to a courtyard school where youngsters recited the Koran, and to an evening with a Uighur doctor living in the spacious home his family has owned for more than 200 years. 
Sitting beneath the stars, cross-legged on a carpeted platform over cups of thick black tea, we spoke, in Chinese, of the matters that preoccupy Uighurs' minds. 
Our host, who had doffed the Uighur's long cotton coat and boots for a dusty business suit, told us that relations with the Chinese, who established their influence here as early as the third century B.C., have improved radically since Peking scrapped the tyrannical policies of Mao Zedong.
The Uighurs, who once had an empire of their own, are essentially a trading people now, a talent displayed in Kashgar's sprawling Sunday market. 
All pretense of a collective economy is abandoned as a gigantic crowd gathers in an open area beyond the town. 
Among sellers of cart wheels and camels, we met a gregarious Uighur, Abdullah, who had learned English working with the British in India before World War II. 
He led us to the bazaar in the center of town, where a wily trader relieved us of $300 for a muted old Xinjiang carpet of the kind that graces virtually every Kashgar home.
You cannot be in Kashgar long without being drawn toward the mountains, their snowy flanks shimmering in the haze to the north and west of town. 
At noon on our third day, we paid our bills at the old Russian Consulate that does service as the Kashgar guesthouse and headed for Pakistan. 
Leaving behind our Peking interpreter, who lacked the pass necessary for Chinese entering border zones, we boarded a Toyota Landcruiser driven by an impetuous young Chinese and headed for the Pamirs. 
In the next 48 hours the driver's insistence on daredevil driving was virtually our only vexation. 
About 25 miles down the road, at the village of Upal, we came across reminders of the earthquake hazard that has plagued the area for centuries. 
In August last year a major quake hit the Keshi prefecture, leveling several villages and killing dozens of their inhabitants. 
The tomb of Mahmoud Keshgeri, the 11th-century Turkic scholar who is thought by some to have been the author of the world's first dictionary, was destroyed but has been already been rebuilt, a shimmering edifice of painted white tiles on a rise looking to the Pamirs. 
In the village, naked boys splashed in a river yards from the remains of mud-walled homes.
In the Pamir foothills, the scope of the road building began to strike home. 
Led by the Engineering Troops of the People's Liberation Army, who did the bulk of the blasting, leveling and bridge-building on both sides of the frontier, the crews spent years in regions of burning heat and numbing cold, using pack horses to carry equipment where no vehicle had ever been, menaced by avalanche, landslide or explosion. 
Often, charges had to be placed hundreds of feet up sheer cliff faces, hand-drilled into the rock by men suspended from ropes.
In all, 408 men died, many of them buried beneath simple cairns. 
Although the largest number of these were Chinese, most of the serious mishaps occurred on the Pakistan side, where the graduated plateau that carries the highway for long stretches inside China gives way to more intimidating going. 
In the Hunza and Indus River valleys, the road clings to precipitous mountainsides, with only occasional posts to keep vehicles from plunging into the riverbeds below. 
During the spring runoff, in April and May, subsidence from above is a constant threat.
In the worst cases, hundreds of tons of rock plummet down the mountainside, obliterating the highway and any bridge standing in the way. 
Road crews from Pakistan's Frontier Works Organization, which deploys 10,000 soldiers for road maintenance, are usually on the scene within an hour, but it can take days to clear the rubble, and slides can recur at any time.
Our worst moment came an hour after crossing the Pakistan frontier at Sust, above the Hunza Valley, when the American-made Willy's Jeeps we had transferred to at the border halted before a pile of rock four or five feet high that had been washed across the road by a torrent of water from a nearby glacier. 
While we dismounted and forded our way across 100 yards of rubble, our Pakistani drivers amazed us by challenging the pile with their four-wheel drive and regaining the unshattered continuation of the road. 
Two hours later a major landslide at the same spot closed the road for 48 hours.
A lesser worry was altitude sickness. 
Of the total of 36 hours of driving between Kashgar and Islamabad, nine are spent at altitudes above 10,000 feet, and those, either side of a night stop at Taxkorgan, 250 miles from Kashgar, are spread over the better part of a day. 
We traveled with an amateur dispensary that included tablets for altitude sickness prescribed by an Australian doctor in Peking. 
But none of us took the pills, and perhaps as a result each of us suffered to some degree from heavy limbs, headaches and labored breathing.
Between myself and my wife, Jane, a smoker, the odds for trouble seemed to lie with her. 
But it fell to me, a 41-year-old nonsmoker, to suffer most. 
The trouble started over lunch by a lake in the lee of Muztagata, one of a number of peaks along the highway that hover around 25,000 feet. 
While Jane prepared a meal - canned baked beans and sausages brought from Peking, supplemented by chocolate - I set out to photograph a passing camel. 
We had risen 8,000 feet in five hours since leaving Kashgar, and now, at 12,500 feet, I began feeling dizzy. 
But the symptoms eased overnight in Taxkorgan, at 14,000 feet, and when we reached the peak, 2,000 feet higher, I felt no more than listlessness and a minor headache. 
We were amply rewarded for the physical discomfort. 
Although there are long stretches of nearly barren road, even they offer unexpected relief. 
In a rocky section two hours out of Kashgar, where the road crossed a bridge over an icy brook, a heavily laden camel stood tied to a lean-to made of rocks. 
Smoke curled upward from a chimney, and beside the door stood a weather-beaten old man, white beard falling to his chest, in ankle-length coat and boots. 
This was a trader taking a rest on the way to Kashgar, much as Polo and his caravan must have paused on their journey through this region in 1275.
Elsewhere, habitation took the form of felt-lined yurts, the circular tents favored by the armies of Genghis Khan. 
The Uighur and Kirghiz herders of these uplands, mostly nomads, migrated more than 1,000 years ago from areas to the northeast, near Mongolia, but little in their customs has changed. 
Unlike ethnic Chinese, who are often wary of admitting strangers to their homes, herders' families came forward in greeting when our Landcruiser pulled up, inviting us into the rug-lined comfort of the yurts and offering mugs of fermented yak's milk or tea.
Our stop in Taxkorgan offered another reminder of the ethnic tides that have swept across the old Silk Road. 
After hours of rough driving the road emerged into a landscape of green pasture stretching to the mountains, reminiscent of Ireland's County Galway. 
By a river of crystal-clear water, a group of herders' children were taking the last rays of the sun, dangling their feet over the bank. 
Turning smiling faces to the camera, they were a revelation - blue eyes, proud noses, features wholly European.
This was our first glimpse of the Tadzhiks, a people of Persian origin said to have migrated at about the time that the armies of Alexander the Great pushed eastward from Greece. 
Contemporary Taxkorgan, a few streets of whitewashed homes with an army barracks and blaring loudspeakers, is no more than a century old. 
But closer to the Soviet frontier, 20 miles distant at this point, lie the ruins of an earlier town of the same name, leveled by earthquakes, that was mentioned as the ''gateway'' to China by the mathematician and geographer Ptolemy when writing in the second century.
China demurred for several years before acceding to Pakistan's suggestion that the highway be opened, and one reason was probably the proximity of the road to Afghanistan. 
The Wakhan Corridor, the eastern finger of Afghanistan, meets the Chinese frontier about 50 miles southwest of Taxkorgan. 
The corridor has been occupied by a heavy concentration of Soviet troops since 1979, and it is a fair assumption that the Chinese have fortified their own defenses. 
The only clue we saw was the unsignposted road that breaks westward toward the Wakhan, its surface rutted by trucks.
Another reason for the Chinese to demur was obvious at the Pamir guesthouse in Taxkorgan, used until recently by the Pakistani and Chinese travelers who were the only permitted users of the road. 
Although an effort had been made to upgrade the 160-bed hotel, its washing facilities consisted of an outhouse and a galvanized steel tank with ice-cold water outside each room. 
When one of our party opened a door off his room and spied a bath, the Tadzhik room attendant swiftly locked it. 
The baths are to be activated when running water is available, but nobody was sure just when.
The road, hitherto washboard gravel, turns to asphalt shortly before the Chinese border post at Pirali, and is paved thenceforth all the way to Islamabad. 
In our case, the relief from the gravel was offset quickly by a bureaucratic snafu at the Chinese border post, when our banker friend was found to have an invalid exit visa. 
As usual with foreigners in China, a lengthy discussion and expressions of good will were enough to surmount the problem, and we were soon under way for the final stretch to the frontier proper, at the pinnacle of the Khunjerab Pass.
There, beside a stone plinth recording the official commissioning of the road, we gathered for a group photograph. 
The heavy winter clothing we had brought with us proved superfluous in the brilliant sunshine but the altitude made itself felt in other ways, mainly on our breathing. 
Two days later, overnighting between Gilgit and Islamabad, we could only marvel when a party of British mountaineers enroute to K2, at 28,250 feet the world's second highest mountain, told us that they planned to ascend the mountain's unconquered northwest ridge without oxygen.
In the Kirghiz language Khunjerab means ''Valley of Blood,'' a name the pass earned centuries ago from the activities of the Khanjut brigands who made a livelihood attacking caravans. 
The worst dangers to be faced in our passage, and thereafter through 500 miles of driving to Islamabad, came not from brigands, though even 20 years ago they had not entirely disappeared, nor even from landslides, but from a still more deadly hazard, the Pakistani driver. 
Times beyond number, we stiffened as our Jeep approached a blind corner on the highway to find the entire roadway filled by a careering truck or bus.
The heavy vehicles are mostly British Bedfords with custom-made superstructures that have been extravagantly painted and filigreed, a popular Pakistani folk art. 
Designs include wrestling lions, iridescent peacocks, mountainscapes and mosques. 
High above the Indus, on our fourth day out from Kashgar, we followed a lavishly decorated truck with a rhyming Moslem couplet inscribed in Urdu on its rear door. 
''Oh God, protect me and those who travel with me,'' it began. 
On the Karakoram Highway, with an 800-foot drop beside us, we too felt the need of Allah on our side. 
Three weeks after our journey, a Bedford truck carrying 47 people swerved off the highway near Chilas, south of Gilgit, killing 11 in its plunge into the Indus.
Fortunately, we had fortified ourselves for this last, most taxing part of the journey with a day's rest at Karimabad, in the heart of the Hunza Valley. 
It was a tossup between Kashgar and the Hunza for the highlight of the trip, for in the lee of 25,550-foot Mount Rakaposhi we found what must be one of the loveliest spots in Asia. 
Viewed from Baltit, a medieval village situated hundreds of feet above the valley floor, the Hunza in spring is a carpet of pink and white blossoms, rising to the green of terraced fields on the mountains' lower slopes, and above all the pristine whiteness of the peaks. 
Here, two hours' drive from the bleakness of the Khunjerab, is a vast orchard of apricots, peaches and plums, nurtured by a people renowned for their longevity and their gentle hospitality. 
For at least 1,000 years this has been a stronghold of the Ismailis, the Moslems of Persian origin whose spiritual leader is the Aga Khan, and it was among Ismailis that we relaxed at the $7-a-night Tourist Park Hotel. 
We felt we had found much that was best among them in our young guide, Irfanullah Baig, who charmed us with his chiseled good looks, his porcelain blue eyes and his intense loyalty to the race-horse-owning multimillionaire who is the sect's current leader, Prince Karim Aga Khan. 
''He has his faults, of course,'' he said. 
''But he is ours, and we love him.''
At Baltit, we found traces of the ''great game'' played out between Russia and England for a century and a half after 1800 for dominance in the strategic fastnesses of Central Asia. 
At the 600-year-old Baltit fort, home until 1948 of the mir of Hunza, traditional ruler of the valley, the aging caretaker scurried forward to a dusty mantelpiece and snapped to attention as he displayed the item that seemed to delight him most of all - a sepia-colored photograph, duly autographed, of Field Marshal Lord Roberts of Kandahar, hero of the Indian Mutiny of 1857, who visited the fort after British-led troops marched up the valley in 1891 in furtherance of Britain's policy of controlling the Himalayan passes.
Lower down the valley, at Gilgit, there were reminders of the price that great powers have paid for their efforts to entrench their influence in the region. 
Outside the town, in a shaded grove, stands a granite monolith surrounded by 88 concrete tombs, each containing one of the Chinese who died in building the Karakoram Highway. 
A mile or two away, near the bazaar on the northern side of town, protected by barbed wire, are the crumbling remains of the old British cemetery. 
There, on tablets shattered by vandals or overgrown with weeds, are inscriptions to pioneers ''most cruelly murdered'' in the Pamirs, to missionaries who fell victims to typhus, and to mountaineers killed while tackling Himalayan peaks.
As we drove southward toward Islamabad, rarely losing sight of the torrents of the Indus, one tablet in particular kept coming to mind. 
It was simple in its grief, yet a powerful reminder of how the harshness of geography in these parts has so often triumphed over man. 
''In loving memory of our only son, Harold S. Eldred,'' the inscription read, ''Captain, Sikh Pioneers, Kashmir Infantry, accidentally drowned while fording the Indus, Dec. 
1, 1929, aged 33. 
'Until the day breaks and the shadows flee away.'
''
Â 
THROUGH THE KHUNJERAB PASS -
Planning Few trips in China fall easily into place, but this is one where careful preparation can be especially important. 
Particularly on the Chinese section of the highway, limited hotel space, Jeeps and air service create potential bottlenecks. 
Although Pakistan, too, has only recently begun to develop the route for tourism, matters there are somewhat easier.
The journey can begin from either end of the highway, in Kashgar or Islamabad, but uncertainties of transport on the Chinese side make it easier, for the time being, to begin in Kashgar. 
Barring serious landslides, the entire 795-mile distance from Kashgar to Islamabad can be covered in approximately 36 hours of driving. 
In our case, with a day's rest stop in Karimabad, in the Hunza Valley, and an afternoon's layover in Gilgit, the journey took five full days, with eight to 12 hours' driving on each of four days.
Travel arrangements must be made separately for each side of the border, since Chinese and Pakistani vehicles are currently permitted to serve only their own section of the highway.
Â 
When to Go
For now, the highway is open to travel by nationals of countries other than China and Pakistan from May 1 to Oct. 
31 each year for group travel and from May 1 to Nov. 
30 for individuals. 
Eventually both countries hope to keep the route open year round, but currently problems with snow clearance and general road maintenance dictate the limited season.
Â 
Visa Requirements
A standard Chinese tourist visa is accepted for entry and exit at the frontier post at Pirali. 
In the first weeks after the highway's opening, Pakistan required special visas for those making the journey, but this has now been dropped for all but two categories of traveler - journalists and nationals of countries that do not enjoy 30-day visa-free entry to Pakistan for tourist reasons. 
In the case of Americans and most Westerners, no visas will be required by Pakistan regardless of whether your trip begins in Kashgar or Islamabad.
Â 
Group Tours
A number of American companies specializing in China are offering Karakoram Highway trips. 
Mountain Travel (1398 Solano Avenue, Albany, Calif. 
94706; 415-527-8100 or 800-227-2384) is offering two 23-day group tours departing June 14 and 22 next year that are priced at $3,575 a person, based on double occupancy, not including round-trip air fare from the United States. 
However, the price for the trip does include extensive travel inside China, besides the Karakoram Highway. 
Lindblad Travel is planning to include the highway on its trips to the region next year (1 Sylvan Road North, Westport, Conn. 
06881; 203-226-8531 or 800-243-5657).
Â 
Independent Travel
Costs can be considerably lowered by making arrangements yourself, but where the Chinese side of the journey is concerned this may be difficult to arrange from outside China, and commitments made by the China International Travel Service can be infuriatingly unreliable. 
The large numbers of backpackers making the journey in May in both directions proved, too, that for those willing to accept delays of days at a time - and to entrust themselves to the public buses that run on either side of the frontier - the journey can be made with practically no advance preparation.
Agencies to contact in China include the Peking branch of the China International Travel Service (domestic bookings, 755272) and the branch in Urumqi, capital of Xinjiang (25794). 
In all probability, direct contact with Urumqi through the international operator will be more effective. 
The Urumqi branch can make bookings on the five weekly flights between Urumqi and Kashgar, a three-hour leg on a twin-engine Antonov-24 that is one of the major potential bottlenecks; if sandstorms ground flights, a common occurrence, the only other means of covering the Urumqi-Kashgar leg is by public bus or minibus, a three-day journey across the desert. 
By minibus, the cost is about $600.
Jeep or minibus bookings from Kashgar to Sust, on the Pakistan frontier, are another potential bottleneck, since there are fewer than 20 vehicles available for the journey in Kashgar. 
The standard rate for a Toyota Landcruiser between Kashgar and Sust, where the highway crosses into Pakistan, is about $350. 
Here again, the best contact is the Urumqi office of C.I.T.S., which will seek reservations by telephone through the travel service's Kashgar branch. 
Most C.I.T.S. officials answering the telephone in Urumqi speak English.
For arrangements on the Pakistan side, the easiest course is to contact one of Pakistan's best-known travel agencies, Travel Walji's Ltd. 
(Walji's Building, 10 Khayaban Suhrawardy, Box 1088, Islamabad; 828324 and 826621, telex 5769 WALJI PK or 5836 WALJI PK). 
Arrangements can be made for a Jeep or minibus for all or part of the journey on the Pakistan side, including having a vehicle waiting at the Pakistan frontier on your arrival from Kashgar. 
The company will also book hotel rooms and air flights, including the crucial Islamabad-Gilgit leg, which cuts 15 hours of driving off the journey for those who decide to forego the journey through the Indus Valley. 
Walji's drivers are excellent, and the company's other services impeccable. 
Costs vary according to vehicle and distance, but for a jeep journey over the entire length of the highway on the Pakistan side will run about $325, regardless of the number traveling.J.

THEY call it ''From Mao to Mozart - Isaac Stern in China,'' and the title of this delightful film that opens today for a five-day run at the Symphony Space gets the general idea across.
Our American violin virtuoso, a remarkable, cheerful and cherubiclooking man, visited that calisthenics-smitten nation, marveled at the extraordinary nimbleness of mind and body, shrugged his shoulders and observed, ''On the other hand, they can't play Mozart.''
Mr. Stern by no means deprecates his hosts in this account of his visit to China in June 1979. 
Indeed, he marvels at the talent developing there, and his love for the musicians and students he met overflows in his singularly expressive and good-humored way. 
This is a film that will teach you something about China but more about Mr. Stern. For those who have not met the man behind the violin before, it offers insights into his deeply humanistic approach to music.
He took something to China that is not prevalent there: the realization that the music must come from the heart and soul rather than from the instruments alone. 
The director of a conservatory of music in Shanghai - an older man who suffered during the Cultural Revolution - explains how young Chinese set great store by technical skill. 
They want hard pieces, loud and fast, to demonstrate how well they can use instruments. 
And in so doing, they miss the point of the music itself.
Mr. Stern and David Golub, the pianist who often appears with him, are seen in performance; negotiating for a piano to replace the unusable one they found in Shanghai; getting a tourist's-eye view of China.
The film, which has been nominated for an Academy Award in the best-documentary category, produced and directed by Murray Lerner, with Allan Miller as artistic supervisor. 
It is a beautifully made documentary that does not presume to tell all about China or Mr. Stern but does give us a most enjoyable record of a productive visit.
From Mao to Mozart - Isaac Stern in China (Movie)

text:
ï»¿
''Gung Hay Fat Choy!''
400 pupils roared yesterday at the Edward Hart Elementary School in Flushing, Queens.
Perhaps a third of the students were Chinese. 
Most of the others, though, were for the first time hearing and saying ''Happy New Year'' in Cantonese, one of the dialects used by a fifth of the planet's population.
The pupils who were able to get through the snow to the school, also known as Public School 21, gathered to hear Chinese stories, watch Chinese dances and learn a little Chinese history.
Â 
A Time for Ethnic Sharing
The idea behind the event was ''to encourage ethnic sharing at a very early age,'' said Teresa Ying Hsu, executive director of Asian-American Communications, which organized the event. 
The group, based at Teachers College of Columbia University, visits schools from time to time in its role as a liaison between Asian communities and others.
Yesterday's event was one of the first celebrations of the Year of the Rabbit, which, on the lunar calendar, begins on Thursday. 
For Chinese, Koreans and other Asians, the 60th day of the Gregorian calendar used in the West is the first day of year 4685.
The Rabbit is one of 12 animals whose names are given successively to each year. 
As the Year of the Tiger dwindles to its final courageous days, people born in the Year of the Rabbit can begin to take comfort in the positive nature of the traits said to be possessed by them.
Rabbit people are talented, affectionate, seekers of tranquility and get on swimmingly with Sheep people and Boar people. 
Rabbit years are said to be good for world peace.
Â 
Proclamation by Koch
The New Year's doings began Friday when Mayor Koch proclaimed the week beginning yesterday Chinese Heritage and Cultural Week. 
The celebration continued last night with a dinner at the Flower Drum restaurant given by the Chinese Chee Yue Community Association, an organization dedicated to helping new immigrants.
Today at P.S. 
130 in Chinatown, students who six months ago were in mainland China will perform the Silk Ribbon and other dances.
The big event comes about 10 P.M. Thursday, New Year's Day, when thousands of people will pour into Chinatown's Mott Street amid long, bright-red dragons, lion dancers and the snap of firecrackers. 
On Saturday the drum and bugle band of the New York Chinese School will march in Mott Street.
Â 
Classical Dances Performed
In Flushing, at P.S. 
21's celebration of the year of the Rabbit, a high point was two Chinese classical dances, adeptly performed by 29 dancers chosen from 120 who had auditioned. 
The first featured a giant bok choy plant, a Chinese cabbage, as a cardboard prop.
The star of the performance was clearly Damian Williams, an 11-year-old sixth grader who switched parts to replace a dancer absent because of the snow. 
Damian and his compatriots said his prowess at Chinese dancing was only to be expected: he is the school's most accomplished break dancer.
But the real high point for most students was discovering what has always been the most pleasant part of the holiday for Chinese youngsters -gifts of red envelopes containing money. 
Ms. Hsu passed them out for such feats as guessing in which of three years the first Chinese immigrants arrived in the United States. 
(The answer is 1848.) In the shower of coins, the students' enthusiasm was such that the principal kept jumping up to remind the students where they were and exactly what they were not going to get away with.

OPERA STAR IN ENGLEWOOD
Montserrat Caballe, soprano and international opera superstar, will perform at the John Harms Center for the Arts in Englewood next Sunday afternoon.
The concert, which begins at 3, will include Rossini arias and works by the Spanish composers Obradors and Chapi. 
''Trois melodies hebraiques'' will honor the 50th anniversary of the death of Maurice Ravel.
Ms. Caballe, born in Barcelona, performed at Carnegie Hall for the first time on April 20, 1965, in a concert version of Donizetti's ''Lucrezia Borgia.''
She later made her debut at the Metropolitan Opera as Marguerite in Gounod's ''Faust.''
Tickets for the John Harms concert are $16.50, $19.50 and $22.50.
The center is at 30 North Van Brunt Street in downtown Englewood.
Information: (201) 567-5797.

text:

THERE is the shock of ''deja vu'' about the the Guangdong Yue Opera Troupe of China, which gave its first performance in the Beacon Theater on Saturday night. 
The opera troupe, which is performing 10 operas in Chinese until July 18, is presenting a style of musical theater that developed only recently in Chinese history - a mere 200 years or so ago, which makes it a bit younger than European opera and a bit older than grand opera.
As in a deja vu, the opera ''Searching the School,'' seemed intimately familiar. 
There was the young woman, unjustly condemned; the sensitive man, unwittingly causing her harm; vaudeville pieces of comedic dialogue between a folksy man and a mannered scholar; mime out of a silent movie; a woman disguised as a man.
THERE is the shock of ''deja vu'' about the the Guangdong Yue Opera Troupe of China, which gave its first performance in the Beacon Theater on Saturday night.
The shock was that, as in a deja vu, there was something strange, as if the scene were watched from the outside: and so it was. 
It derived from folk traditions in the south of China, and used folk instruments - including the erxian, a two-string guitar - and an elegant microtonal folk-song style, a heightened speech, in which pitch and duration extend the expressive sounds of words. 
It was also created with formalized gestures: the placing of fingers in the air, the motion of hand against face and the explicit darting of eyes were used, along with the stock situations, to express an inner life.
Then, too, there were the costumes, peach, lime and violet robes and headgear; the women's hairpieces, long black locks divided into parts and adorned with shells and beads; and the sets, gauzy drapes, ocean backdrops and eloquently simple light effects.
And if the plot unfolded familiarly, it was also always surprising, taking place in a different realm: A woman is flying her kite; the string breaks. 
A man finds it and writes a poem upon it; when the kite is returned, the poem seems incriminating; she is beaten and imprisoned. 
In 19th-century opera she would have to have an illegitimate son to be so condemned; instead a gust of wind and a poem carries her to her fate.
The opera, then, fascinated, even while long stretches of dialogue could be understood only by the largely Chinese audience, which could also read the Chinese script flashed on a small screen near the stage.
Hong Xiannu, as the woman, Chilian, created a minutely detailed performance that at times made her transformation into a man and her shifting emotions seem uncanny. 
Now in her 50's, she is reportedly a classic actress in this form. 
She was abused by the Cultural Revolution, rehabilitated, abused because of her connection with the Gang of Four and rehabilitated again. 
With such experience must have come some knowledge of incriminating poems and wind gusts.
Her daughter, Hong Hong, played the same role in some scenes, giving the uncanny another twist. 
Huang Zhiming, as the schoolmaster Xie Bao, was also a theatrical master, mixing seriousness with exaggeration. 
Chen Xiaofeng was the stolid yet sensitive scholar Zhang Yimin. 
Ye Weixiong was Qiong Tai.
The operas scheduled vary from the fantastical to the military and, judging from the first, the Guangdong Yue Opera might well provide a fascinating experience - at least once.

text:
ï»¿
Each time I have been entertained in a Vietnamese home it has been a typical summer night in Washington - hot and humid. 
The hostess's choice of food has always seemed especially felicitous. 
The marvelous variety of unusual dishes and the lightness of the cuisine, with its finely tuned use of gentle seasonings, have been particularly appropriate for hot weather. 
So it is no wonder that such fare is especially appropriate for, and becoming increasingly popular at, stylish pool parties across the country.
As I was to find out later, the food is not at all difficult to prepare. 
That is, once you have mastered the use of a few ingredients that are unfamiliar to most Westerners, such as rice paper and lemon grass. 
Rice paper is the edible translucent paper used for making Vietnamese spring rolls, a specialty far more delicate than Chinese egg rolls, to which they are often compared. 
Lemon grass, sometimes called citronella root, imparts a distinctive lemony taste and fragrance to the food.
Salads, vegetables, fish, sprightly sauces -all conspire to tempt the palate of the diner who, given a choice on a summer's eve, might ordinarily opt for cold roast chicken and jellied consomme. 
But not if shrimp salad with mint or brochettes of beef scented and spiced with galangal, an unusually piquant form of ginger, are offered as alternatives.
With the first exposure to the subtle refinements of the Vietnamese kitchen, the uninitiated American quickly puts aside any preconceptions of the food as being the same as Chinese. 
These cuisines do have many ingredients in common and both are properly eaten with chopsticks, but the similarity ends there. 
Despite 1,000 years of Chinese rule, ending in the 10th century, the Vietnamese maintained their identity not only in their own language and customs but in their own culinary sophistication.
Other cultures have had more of an influence. 
There is an easily definable French presence in the Vietnamese kitchen, and traces of Indian cooking also can be found. 
The resulting cuisine is a rather sophisticated one that reflects the richly varied history and geography of the country.
The food is almost always light. 
Uncooked vegetables and salads are an integral part of Vietnamese meals, which makes them especially appropriate for warm-weather entertaining. 
Shallots, Maggi seasoning, white potatoes and asparagus commonly are used. 
There is much less emphasis on stir-frying and thick sauces than is found in the Chinese kitchen, and lemon grass, unknown in China, is a hallmark of Vietnamese cooking. lthough Vietnam is quite small, about the size of New Mexico, its cooking is divided into regions. 
In the south, with its hot, humid climate, the French influence is the most pronounced. 
Indian curries are particularly strong there. 
Because sugar cane is grown in the region, dishes in the south tend to be sweeter than those elsewhere.
In the central region, where Hue, the ancient capital, is located, the food is rather decorative and very spicy. 
Hot chilies and shrimp sauce frequently are used.
To the north, with its colder weather, there are fewer ingredients and the food tends to be lighter and less heavily spiced. 
Black pepper is widely used, and stir-fried dishes are common.
It is not only the ingredients but the names given to some Vietnamese dishes that reflect the French influence, although the name is often as far as the Western influence goes. 
From the French the Vietnamese learned to make exquisite pates, but they often are seasoned with their famous sauce, nuoc mam, an anchovy-based mixture that is as popular as soy sauce is in China. 
The Vietnamese also have a chicken pate that is deep-fried.
Asparagus, which the Vietnamese call ''Western bamboo,'' is an essential ingredient in crab soup, a dish enjoyed all over the country and equally popular among Americans. 
Typical of the food of the country, it is both light and extremely savory. he recipes for this summer repast are creations of Bach-Yen Boun, chef at Indochine in New York City. 
Part Cambodian and part Vietnamese, she learned to cook at home in Cambodia. 
Her sister runs a Vietnamese restaurant they own in Paris called Au Coin des Gourmets. 
Despite its simplicity, Boun's food is not picnic fare. 
It is, however, especially appropriate for summer because it satisfies without leaving you stuffed.
These dishes - such as the Vietnamese spring rolls (called pates imperiaux in France); shrimp with mint rolled in rice paper (or rouleau de printemps); beef brochettes marinated in lemon grass paste, skewered with red peppers and onions; even the small, greaseless spareribs - will provide a dinner your guests are likely to remember for a long time. 
The cook will be happy because most of the dishes can be prepared and cooked in advance. 
And even those that require last-minute cooking can be prepared ahead almost completely.
Serve this food lukewarm or at room temperature, not steaming hot.

1.In a small saucepan, bring three cups of water to a boil.

Drain and let cool.

Remove the pot from the heat. 
Add the rice sticks and let stand for five minutes, or until they are soft. 
Drain them, run under cold water and drain again. 
Cut into three-inch strips. 
Set aside. 
#3.Dip the rice-paper wrappers in cold water and lay them on a clean towel or between paper towels for about five minutes to soften. 
Rice-paper wrappers should be handled carefully; they break easily. 
#4.Separate the leaves of the lettuce, discarding the tough ones. 
#5.Place a rice-paper wrapper on a work surface. 
On the lower half of the rice paper, layer a lettuce leaf, some bean sprouts, rice sticks and four to five mint leaves. 
Fold the sides of the rice paper to cover the filling. 
#6.About four inches from the top of the rice paper, arrange a row of four shrimp halves, placed vertically. 
Starting from the bottom, roll tightly to enclose the filling and the shrimps. 
Repeat with the remaining ingredients. 
#7.Cover the rolls with a damp cloth until ready to serve.

Stir and let stand until the sugar is dissolved. 
This sauce can be kept for several days in the refrigerator. 
When ready to serve, add the carrots and peanuts.
Yield:Two and three-quarter cups.
Note:Nuoc mam is a fish sauce available in most Oriental specialty stores.

1.In a small bowl, combine the lemon grass paste, nuoc mam, sugar, salt and oil. 
Mix well. 
#2.Cut one onion into julienne strips. 
Cut the remaining onions into one-inch cubes. 
#3.Place the strips of beef on a work surface and rub the marinade over them. 
Place a strip of onion across each strip of beef and roll it to enclose the onion.

#5.Preheat the broiler or barbecue grill.

1.Place the fish on a heat-proof plate on the rack of a steamer over simmering water and cook, covered, for 30 to 40 minutes, or until the fish is no longer pink at the bone.

#2.In a large bowl, combine the bean threads, pork, onion, carrot, bean sprouts, sugar, salt, pepper and one egg yolk, and mix well. 
#3.For each roll, use two layers of triangles.

Rice-paper triangles should be handled carefully; they break easily. 
#4.Mix the remaining egg yolk with one teaspoon of water.

text:

New Cardin Beachhead
The largely untapped Chinese market is the target of a new venture linking Pierre Cardin, the French designer, and Gruppo GFT, an Italian manufacturer and distributor of ready-to-wear. 
The plan is to manufacture and to sell in China Mr. Cardin's clothing and accessories for men, women and children, his home furnishings and his leather goods.
Mr. Cardin's name is already known in China. 
He showed his haute-couture collection there in 1979 and opened Maxim's restaurant in Beijing in 1983. 
He has also manufactured some apparel there, as has Gruppo GFT.
But just how much of a market for high fashion does China represent?
''The Chinese people like to dress,'' Mr. Cardin said by telephone from his Paris office. 
''They have rejected the Mao suits. 
They don't like classique. 
They like high fashion. 
The clothes we will sell there will be the same as what I show in Paris. 
We are expecting to open 40,000 stores in China. 
It's a very big deal.''
Â 
Spring Hats Sprout
''This is a hat season,'' said Patricia Underwood, a millinery designer. 
''We're making them as fast as we possibly can. 
What we've shipped for spring is selling, and we're already getting reorders.''
With just seven employees, her small business may reach $700,000 in sales this year, she said, up from $150,000 five years ago.
''The hat business started going for me when I got into Bergdorf Goodman about six years ago,'' she said. 
''They took 10 hats. 
This year there were 500 in the initial spring order.
''When we started in business in 1974, the hat industry was very hand to mouth,'' Ms. Underwood added. 
''Only dyed-in-the-wool hat wearers were buying hats. 
But making hats was the only thing I knew how to do, and it was a very easy business to go into on a small scale because you need very little equipment: a sewing machine and hat blocks. 
I had a partner and we each put in $500.''
Millinery is still a business that requires only a modest investment to start: a few thousand dollars, say. 
But the growing market has generated increased competition. 
And it is wide-brimmed straw hats lavished with flowers that are giving the millinery business a boost right now.
Bonnie Pressman, fashion director of Barneys New York, said women are responding to the romance and fantasy of such hats. 
Jane Tuma, vice president and fashion director for accessories at Saks Fifth Avenue, said it may be the femininity of the styles. 
And there is no doubt that many women were captivated by the flower-bedecked hats Christian Lacroix showed with his clothes.
Philippe Model, a French milliner, brought two dozen brimmed straws covered with brilliant silk roses -very much in the Lacroix mood - to Bloomingdale's in January. 
The store has sold more than half, priced from $400 to $525.
Â 
Enter German Tailoring
Hugo Boss, a West German men's-wear company known for quality fabrics and tailoring, is making a serious pitch for the United States market. 
An American subsidiary, Hugo Boss Fashions, was formed last November with Barry Wishnow, an American, as its president. 
Previously, the line was handled by sales agents here, but that didn't allow the company to compete successfully.
''Hugo Boss was very involved in Europe,'' Mr. Wishnow explained recently. 
''We will begin to expand the position of Hugo Boss in this country, not by selling to every store that exists, but by developing all parts of our business with each store we sell to. 
We want to do as much business in one store as someone else might do in 10 stores. 
We want to sell each store men's clothing and furnishings, sportswear, rain wear, outer wear and our new women's collection.''
The women's clothes (suits average $650), will be sold only in the United States. 
The target market includes stores like Saks Fifth Avenue, Barneys New York, Charivari, Bullock's and I. Magnin.

file: PEKING_S FASHION CODE LEANS TOWARD THE DON_T_S.txt
text:
ï»¿
Young employees of the Peking municipality were told recently to avoid ''bizarre dress'' or be turned away from the office.
Men must also cut their hair and shave off sideburns and mustaches, and women may not have hair longer than to their shoulders or wear heavy makeup or earrings or other ''unhealthy ornaments.''
''We must preserve our habits of simplicity and bitter struggle,'' Peking Daily explained in publishing the new regulations, which took effect this month. 
''Hats and clothing must be clean and simple and bizarre dress is forbidden.''
Peking issues new dress code; although Chinese are no longer confined to baggy jackets and trousers, there are still many restrictions on dress and appearance; photos (M)
The dress code is a barometer of today's ideological climate, in which there have been many warnings that decadent bourgeois tastes and values are infiltrating China under the country's open-door economic policy. 
The distrust of long hair and modish attire echoes the generation gap in the West, but here the old guard can invoke Communist Party dogma to apply the brakes.
Â 
Better Dress Encouraged
Chinese are no longer confined to the baggy jackets and trousers that passed for fashion under Chairman Mao Zedong. 
Last spring, Hao Jianxiu, a member of the party secretariat, said that people should not be afraid to dress better. 
Miss Hao even managed a good word for the ''qipao,'' the traditional tight-fitting women's dress with the slit up the side.
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang and the party chief, Hu Yaobang, have appeared in Western suit and tie at official functions. 
But most officials, including China's paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, stick to the familiar high-collared tunic popularized by Sun Yat-sen, father of the Chinese Republic.
Last summer, many young women blossomed in bright print dresses and some young men wore pastel T-shirts like one from Shanghai that proclaimed its owner a ''vigorous, graceful sportsman.''
But fashion is very much seasonal in China. 
As the willow trees shed their leaves and harvested cabbages pile up on the roadsides, the Chinese are reverting to monotonous blue and olive drab work clothes padded out with layers of long underwear.
When it was warmer, some young people took to fashion with a zest that disconcerted their elders. 
Last May, 700,000 visitors jammed a monthlong exhibition here of Western-style clothing made in China and bought nearly a million garments. 
Scalpers sold the restricted tickets at up to 50 times the nominal cost of 5 cents each.
Â 
Modern Apparel Made for Export
Better clothing has become available because China is making modern apparel for export. 
After the United States imposed a limit on textile imports from China when the two sides failed to agree on a new pact, clothes intended for the United States began spilling out onto the sidewalks of Peking. 
Plaid flannel shirts with an American label and $11 price tag were being sold for the equivalent of $2 apiece. 
The supply has dried up since a new textile agreement was reached.
Bolder Western styles, including blue jeans, are smuggled up from Hong Kong by way of Canton and sold by black-market peddlers. 
A pair of sunglasses with a foreign label still pasted on one lens remains the most prestigious accessory. 
A few youths so flaunt the Hong Kong look that they have been nicknamed ''spare-time overseas Chinese.''
Â 
New Trends Stir Concern
Conservative Chinese feel that the trend is going too far. 
''Go down to Wangfujing,'' said one older man, speaking of a major shopping street in Peking. 
''You'll see young girls walking around in suggestive clothes trying to catch the attention of the boys. 
And the boys go to the barber shop and have their hair curled so you can't tell them from the girls.''
The scene looked tame by Western standards. 
But the authorities, sensing a distinction between bourgeois unisex and proletarian unisex, are trying to draw the line.
The Xidan Department Store reported a few weeks ago that it had required more than 70 of its young salesmen to shear off ''strange'' hair styles and more than 20 saleswomen to give up their earrings, eyebrow pencil and lipstick.
Â 
French Fashions Shown
Peking Daily quoted store officials as saying that such ''unhealthy beauty'' not only was distasteful but also ''enticed certain customers with unhealthy thoughts to tease the employees and distract them from working well.''
The debate over fashion has not been limited to Peking. 
In the southern province of Hunan, a television series on ''the beauty of clothing'' considered the propriety of items like bell-bottomed trousers.
Chinese men can get away with wearing floppy white sleeveless undershirts in the summer, but any bare flesh on a woman causes clucks of disapproval.
When the French designer Pierre Cardin recently held a fashion show here to promote his line of apparel being turned out for export by 14 Chinese textile factories, some plunging necklines and backs on the models were demurely hiked up with safety pins.
Afterward, Mr. Cardin thanked the models by presenting them with sets of delicate underwear and shoes, which were thereafter confiscated by the authorities, according to one informant.
The interest in fashion seems largely confined to urban young people who already have a job or are waiting for one. 
University students tend to dress down in the familiar baggy blue, though some women at Peking University have cut their pigtails and treated themselves to home permanents.
The university look is based on conformity, not rebellion. 
With less than 4 percent of Chinese youth able to get a higher education, those who make it hew to the proverb here that ''the gun shoots the bird that sticks its neck out.''

FOR several months following its opening in July, the Sichuan Pavilion exhibited a marked unevenness, both in service and cooking. 
But based on about eight visits in the last five or six weeks, the 10 chefs from China have certainly hit their stride, and so has the dining room staff.
The food served now at this North Chinese restaurant is exceptional, with only a few disappointments, and if the management would add the requested amount of spicy seasonings to the appropriate dishes, this rating would be four stars instead of three. 
On a menu as large as the Sichuan Pavilion's, there are bound to be a few offerings that do not measure up to the kitchen's most successful efforts, but for the most part, this is the best Chinese food we have ever had in New York when ordering from a standard menu. 
The quality and intricacies of the dishes have been exceeded elsewhere only when we were known and had ordered meals in advance.
Comfortably laid out in the premises formerly occupied by Ho's Pavilion on 44th Street between First and Second Avenues, the two dining rooms with their cheerful paintings of pandas, their meloncolored napkins, their carnations, comfortable lighting and a decent noise level are far more felicitous than most of their Chinese counterparts in the city.
Mimi Sheraton reviews North Chinese restaurant, Sichuan Pavilian
The array of recommended dishes is dazzling and the appetizers alone could add up to a marvelous meal. 
Among the hot first courses were fragrant and soothing turnip patties studded with ham and black sesame seeds, silky little dumplings in a sauce that needed a more generous lacing of chili oil - as did all other hot dishes - and, most unusual, meltingly tender spareribs in rice flour, served in small metal steamers. 
Similar containers held moist and aromatic beef strips. 
The petite, crisp spring rolls were heady with minced scallions, giving new meaning to this standard specialty.
Two dishes that had the proper sting of dried chilies were cold marinated Sichuan cabbage and cold, tangy coriander-scented chicken, which came close to matching the spiciness of the cabbage.
Our cold appetizer selection was completed by chewy slivers of dried and sweetly mellow marinated beef, crunchy with sesame seeds, tender and gently smoked fillets of fish and shredded rabbit meat in a rich sesame dressing. 
All this went beautifully with a tall, cool scotch and soda. 
Tsingtao beer could be ordered as an alternate, as could Chinese and European wines, but to us scotch has always seemed more astringently refreshing.
Soups lacked the interest of other first courses. 
Most disappointing of all was the hot and sour soup, which was pink, bland and vaguely sweet. 
Better choices were Sichuan-style wonton soup in a light and flavorful chicken broth and chef's special soup, a brew perfumed with sesame oil and steamed in a ceramic jar with pork and vegetables. 
But unless you consider soup essential to the success of a Chinese meal, skip it.
Three exquisite seafood dishes include Chengdu fish - a whole sea bass braised with minced vegetables and spices in a darkly rich hot sauce, a crispy whole bass, scored in diamond cuts and deep fried to parchment fragility, and a steamed bass prepared Cantonese style with black beans, scallions and ginger. 
One captain assured us that such Cantonese preparations are preferable because the gossamer sauce does not mask the fresh and fugitive flavor of the fish itself.
A pink and spicy garlic sauce can be served on satiny chunks of chicken, on slender, moist shreds of pork, on sliced large shrimps or on filmy strips of eggplant. 
Savory toasted peanuts, also in a sesame-and-chili-oil sauce, did as much for the diced chicken or rabbit meat as they did for the large snowy sea scallops. 
And the hot and spicy sauces on lobster chunks or bean curd are also delicious, even though too mildly seasoned. 
Dollops of slightly sticky, soothingly bland rice, or the chewy double side golden-fried noodles with shrimp and vegetables, or the pan-fried beans can bridge the gap between the heavier fish and meat dishes.
The duck is lean, meaty and filled with the earthy essence that American-style duck dishes generally lack. 
Whether smoked, crispfried or braised to melting tenderness with vegetables (Buddha's duck), all proved to be masterpieces. 
Tinkling bells with sliced pork sizzled musically as meat and vegetables were poured onto a hot metal platter in the dining room and garnished with curlicues of crisply fried Sichuan dumplings.
Disappointments included the rather tasteless crispy rabbit meat loaf, flat and somewhat stale lamb ''quick-fry'' with brown sauce, Napa cabbage with dried shrimp, scallops overpowered by enormous and ordinary white mushrooms and a simmered combination of vegetables made up of broccoli, white mushrooms, frozen peas and similar banalities.
There is a lovely, soul-satisfying dessert - puree nuts that is really a warm, pudding-like creamed froth of walnuts lightened by a pearly meringue. 
For more exotic tastes there are slippery sweet rice cakes steamed in bamboo leaves and for the less adventurous, melon balls and canned lichee nuts.
In addition to all of the above, which appear regularly on the menu, some special meals are available. 
On Saturday and Sunday from noon to 3 P.M. there is a small dim sum tea lunch, and though the waiter at first said it was served only to Chinese, we were able to order it. 
Wonton soup, the round dumplings, deeper pastry puffs filled with pork, and a number of the regular appetizers and desserts are included. 
Each small dish is enough to serve three or four and prices range from $1 to $4.25 a dish. 
Four is the perfect number, allowing a sampling of all dishes, and as is customary, wind up with some of the pan fried noodles to fill empty corners of your stomach.
Two banquets are offered as standards and must be ordered several days in advance. 
It is possible to substitute dishes to suit individual preferences. 
One is $30 a person, the other $50. 
At each a minimum of 8 guests is required. 
These banquets are especially popular with Chinese and United Nations officials. 
Our banquet, at $50, was perhaps the single most extraordinary Chinese meal any of us have had in this country. 
Some of the menu's regular appetizers were served along with a lavish butterfly composed of various fancy-cut cold meats, vegetables, bean curd and fish. 
A domed aspic encased shrimp and vegetables, and two kinds of pickled cabbage lent their cold, clear bite to the course. 
Stir-fried spicy lobster and a fried roll of chicken and walnuts were followed by ''gold fish at play with lotus soup'' - a steamy, diamond-clear chicken broth with tiny quenelle-like fish studded with corn and peas. 
This was accompanied by a round beef cake not unlike a piroshky. 
Rabbit in both a spicy and an orange sauce preceded pandas at play - the pandas being sculpted of pureed fish with a sort of dried black-green vegetable marking off arms, ears and eyes, all leaning agains an Alpine peak formed of fish whipped and steamed with egg white and flecked with smoky, nut-flavored ham. 
Sharks fins mingled with chicken and ham, squares of rather tough fried abalone and dried scallops lending their briny zest to verdant hearts of cabbage, and a spicy crisp fish rounded out the meal. 
Dessert was a silken dish of almond gelatin in a cool sweet broth and a round pastry that could almost have been Viennese, with its candied fruits and cinammon sugar overtones. 
Garnishing was exquisite, with intricate floral mosaics of cut vegetables.
Prices for the regular meals are moderately high and run to about $35 a person, tips included, for a generous meal with drinks. 
Food at Sichuan Pavilion can be portioned for you, or you can dip into it family style, by far the better way. 
Most of the time service is cordial, helpful and patient. 
Only once were we told we would have to hurry because there were many reservations.
Â 
Sichuan Pavilion ***
322 East 44th Street (between First and Second Avenues), 986-3775. 
Atmosphere: Bright and attractive modern dining room with comfortable lighting and decent noise level. 
Excellent service that is only occasionally rushed. 
Recommended dishes: All hot and cold appetizers, wonton soup, chef's special soup, double side golden-fried noodles, Chengdu-style whole fish, steamed bass Cantonese style, crispy whole fish, hot spiced lobster, diced rabbit, shrimp, scallops or chicken with peanuts; chicken chunks, sliced shrimp or shredded pork in garlic sauce; Buddha's duck, smoked duck, hot and spicy bean curd, pan-fried string beans, eggplant strips in garlic sauce, puree nuts, sweet rice cake in bamboo leaves; all dishes in special banquet priced at $50 a person, Saturday and Sunday dim sum lunch. 
Prices: Lunch and dinner, a la carte, with main courses from $9 to $24. 
Dim sum from $1 to $4.25. 
Credit cards: All major cards. 
Hours: Noon to 11 P.M. daily. 
Reservations: Recommended.
