text:
ï»¿
Joao Rodriguez, a Portuguese missionary, wrote of finding a varnish of unsurpassed quality, like ''smooth shiny ivory,'' applied to everything from jewelry to armor in an island kingdom east of China during the 16th century. 
Early traders, dazzled by this rare lustrous coating that was produced from the sap of an indigenous tree of the sumac family, christened it with the name of the land of its origin -Japan.
Today fine lacquerware can be seen in shops all over Japan and in museum collections in Tokyo. 
It's also possible, and rewarding, to visit the handful of rural towns, like Wajima on Japan's western coast, where old networks of small factories and craftsmen survive.
In an age of plastic, few younger Japanese use wooden lacquerware in daily life. 
But among older and wealthier Japanese - for whom the warmth and glow of a simple soup bowl can evoke deep cultural values - the mystique lives on.
One connoisseur is Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone, whose gift to the visiting President Reagan in 1983 was a lacquer chest of drawers embossed with a powdered gold maki-e, or sprinkled painting, of butterflies. 
It was produced in Wajima, a small town on the Sea of Japan and the home of Japan's most renowned regional variety of lacquer.
When he returned from his mission to open trade with Japan in 1854, Commodore Matthew C. Perry brought lacquer gifts for another President, Millard Fillmore, and noted in his report that it was ''one art in which they excel the world.''
Perry added, ''It is said, however, that the best specimens are never sent out of the kingdom.''
The oldest known Japanese lacquer, found on wooden implements excavated near Fukui on the coast of the Sea of Japan, dates from 2400 B.C. Buddhist and feudal artisans began producing sophisticated decorative styles around A.D. 500, copying Chinese and Korean masters at first, then inventing their own techniques, most notably gold and silver maki-e.
By the time the priest Rodriguez arrived in Japan, lacquer was ''the most universal art in the kingdom,'' applied to tableware, helmets, beaded armor, chopsticks, temple art, furniture and miniature boxes, called inryo, which were hung from sashes.
The coating adhered to wood, metal, rock, bamboo and even stiffened linen to produce feather-light teacups. 
The aging of milky crude lacquer produced a black tint. 
Chemicals were added to make other colors - red, yellow, green and Prussian blue. 
Embossing, etching and inlays of ivory, shell, metal and stone evolved.
When exported, gaudy Japanese lacquer became the rage in the salons of Europe and America. 
Marie Antoinette, for one, amassed a huge collection.
The industrial revolution and the end of feudalism in the mid-19th century brought an end to the golden age of lacquer. 
Export markets were soon flooded with cheap mass-produced lacquer products.
Today the industry is segmented. 
Lacquered plastic, said to account for $20 million worth of the lacquer business a year, has replaced wooden lacquerware on most Japanese tables.
As for traditional lacquer, there are still some masters, like Gonroku Matsuda, 89 and deemed a living national treasure, who create works rarely seen in public for an elite clientele. 
Mr. Matsuda, who lives in Tokyo, combines the skills of woodworker, embellisher and painter to fashion decorations and furniture fit for the Imperial household. 
His powdered gold maki-e and glossy gold-flecked nashi-ji, or pear-skin, surfaces are extraordinary.
A walk through the National Museum of Modern Art in Tokyo provides a primer on the tradition Mr. Matsuda represents. 
A Matsuda crane poised on gold foil legs seems to rise from a shimmering thicket of willow leaves on a decorative box. 
Its wings are formed of bits of varnished quail eggshell. 
On a glossy black table large molten birds swirl in a golden sun.
''Properly made,'' Mr. Matsuda has said, ''a lacquer article will last almost forever.''
Other craftsmen, found mostly in remote areas of northern and central Japan and along the Sea of Japan, produce traditional lacquer art - on a more modest scale - that can be used as well as admired. 
The best known of these towns is Wajima, which produces a durable red and black lacquer called Wajimanuri as well as fine designs of maki-e and chinkin, etchings usually filled with gold powder or foil. 
Kazuo Yamagishi, 30, one of a younger generation of Wajima craftsmen, compares the patina of the lacquer process to the effect of severe weather on the people and landscape of the Noto Peninsula, a curl of land in the turbulent Sea of Japan where Wajima sits. 
He doubts whether outsiders can fully appreciate his art's subtlety.
''The most common question Westerners ask is why do you have to paint it so much?''
Mr. Yamagishi said recently. 
''You must live in Japan and experience the seasons to understand the art of lacquer,'' he added.
Mr. Yamagishi makes boxes and tea containers with chinkin designs in the home of his father, Mori, a bowl latherer, whose shop is near the churning Sea of Japan. 
In winter, snow drifts surround it. 
During the typhoon season, waves splash over the sea wall across the street.
For Mr. Yamagishi, the difficult technique and muted beauty of fine lacquer embody traditional values that are still a way of life in this wind-buffeted region. 
He etches common road-side grasses and flowers with steel styluses on polished lacquer. 
It's a modern touch that sets his chinkin work apart from more traditional depictions of cherry, plum and pine. 
Once tamped with crushed gold, the patterns resemble negative images of sumie (ink paintings).
The Omukai Kokudo Company, which produced the chest given to President Reagan, operates two of the dozens of small lacquerware factories in Wajima. 
Modern technology has done little to speed up the process. 
Companies employ craftsmen and contract with others to work at home.
After cutting and shaping the wood, latherers dry it and smoke it in ovens for as long as five years. 
Zelkova wood is used for round objects, warp-resistant cypress for flat ones.
The tough finish of the typical wan, or soup bowl, results from about eight coats of lacquer, some laced with baked clay, which are each slowly hardened and buffed with ash, whetstones and water. 
Strips of cloth, glued underneath the primer coats, strengthen fragile edges. 
Finer pieces may have as many as 60 coats of lacquer and take a year to complete.
The lacquer hardens by slow chemical oxidation of the varnish in damp rooms or compartments. 
The hardening takes from about eight hours for thin primer coats to four days for the finishing layer of lacquer.
Traditionally, Japanese lacquer -which contains from 40 to 90 percent more of the main hardening ingredient, urushiol, than other Asian lacquers - was favored. 
But an imported Chinese variety is now used.
Leveled during World War II to make more room for food crops, most of the lacquer trees were never replaced, according to Masato Nakayama, the director of a cooperative representing 8,000 manufacturers.
The cheaper Chinese product remains the choice of all but a few artists, like Mr. Matsuda, who represent a small percentage of Japan's annual $40 million wood lacquer industry, Mr. Nakagawa said.
The cultivation of a lacquer tree is itself painstaking. 
A tree takes 15 years to reach maturation and then produces small amounts of top grade sap in the summer and early fall for about six years before it must be cut down to start again.
In the Omukai workshop, painters wearing nylon clothing apply the last coats of lacquer in glass-encased rooms. 
A piece of lint can destroy months of work.
In two adjoining tatami rooms, craftsmen paint shimmery designs on finished pieces with various brushes. 
Hair from the forelegs of mice is said to be best for fine detail work. 
Maki-e specialists sprinkle gold dust from pencil-thin bamboo tubes on wet lacquer drawings. 
Others use gold-laced paint. 
A chest similar to the one made for President Reagan would cost about $2,000, according to company officials.
During a visit to the small shop, next to the plant, which sits on a narrow lane a few blocks from the sea, the company's president, Mitsugu Omukai, 66, the mayor of Wajima, or his son, Minoru, may appear, and guests may be treated to Japanese tea and rice jelly sweets while browsing. 
Mr. Yamagishi has some works on display.
Now visitors can also observe the lacquer process at the company's new factory and showroom near City Hall across town.
Besides Wajima, the Ministry of Industry and Trade recognizes 16 towns where the lacquer tradition survives. 
Yamanaka, for example, produces a clear lacquer that highlights the wavy grain of native zelkova wood and cherry. 
Kamakura and Murakami specialize in Chinese-influenced carved vermilion lacquer on chestnut wood.
Some varieties of multihued, mottled or pitted lacquers resemble swirls of latex, tortoise shell and bark. 
Among other places noted for lacquer are Tsugaru, Kyoto, Kanazawa, Kiso and Hida, which makes a caramel-like lacquer.
In Tokyo, Wajimanuri and other varieties of regional lacquer are sold at the Japan Traditional Crafts Center in Minami Aoyama. 
The center employs staff members who speak English and will show, on request, videotapes on lacquer and other folk arts, some of which have English narratives. 
Two tapes focus on the work of Mr. Matsuda, who was trained in Kanazawa, and Taiho Mae, a chinkin master from Wajima who died in 1977.
The Omukai company has a shop on the first floor of the same building, where prices are the same as in Wajima.
Yujiro Sahara, an adviser at the traditional craft center, which is run by an association that promotes crafts, suggests visiting smaller shops in Tokyo where, because of special arrangements with craftsmen and smaller commissions, prices are apt to be lower than in large department stores. 
The cost of top-quality lacquer in shops like Omukai and the crafts center in Tokyo can range from about $30 for a black or red soup bowl with matching cover to more than $1,000 for a large low table with an ornate gold-embossed design. 
A decorative tray costs about $100, and boxes range from $150 for a small gold-etched one to about $200 for a larger, gold-embossed one that can be used to store documents. 
A set of five small tea coasters sells for about $20, a vase for about $190.
Neither shop ships to the United States, and the craft center warns that fragile lacquer can be damaged in transit. 
The Omukai factory in Wajima and larger department stores like Takashimaya and Mitsukoshi, both in Tokyo's Nihombashi district, will, however, arrange shipping on request.
Dealers say that lacquerware should be kept in the shade away from dry air and wrapped loosely if stored. 
In museums, lacquer pieces are displayed next to a glass of water. 
During the winter, lacquer shops use humidifiers to keep the air moist. 
The traditional crafts center has an expert in the repair of scratched or damaged lacquer on its staff. 
Where to see lacquerware Museums The National Museum of Modern Art (in the Takebashi district of Tokyo) is open from 9:30 A.M. to 5 P.M. every day but Monday. 
Modern lacquerware is normally exhibited in the museum's traditional crafts building. 
Entry fee: $1.20. 
The National Science Museum (in the Ueno district) is open from 9 A.M. to 4:30 P.M. every day but Monday. 
An exhibit of the lacquer-making process and finished pieces are on permanent display. 
Entry fee: $1.20. 
Shopping Tokyo: The Japan Traditional Craft Center (Minami Aoyama district) is open from 10 A.M. to 6 P.M. every day but Thursday. 
The center sells a wide variety of folk crafts and sponsors daily demonstrations and exhibits. 
With a $10 membership, you can receive a 10-percent discount on purchases. 
Free admission. 
Dial 403-2460. 
The Omukai Kokudo Company shop on the first floor of the same building as the craft center is open from 11 A.M. to 7 P.M. every day but Thursday. 
Dial 479-1313. 
Kuroeya (Nihombashi district), a shop carrying many regional lacquers, is open from 9 A.M. to 5 P.M. every day but Saturday. 
Dial 271-3356.
Wajima: A visit to the Omukai factory can be arranged by calling the company's shop in Tokyo or the plant directly for an appointment with an English-speaking guide. 
The local phone number is 2-1313. 
The factory is open from 8 A.M to 5 P.M. every day but Sunday.
The showroom of another Wajima lacquer company, Wajimaya, is open from 9 A.M. to 5 P.M. every day. 
An adjoining coffee shop displays a new line of modern lacquerware - tables with curved chromium steel legs, saucer-shaped lacquer-on-steel lampshades and monochrome tableware in a rainbow of colors. 
A lunch of Japanese buckwheat noodles and wild vegetables served with lacquer tableware costs about $4. 
At 7 o'clock each night, the shop reopens, and there is a free performance of the thunderous music of taiko, hide-covered wooden drums, by a nationally known troupe, Gojinjo Daiko (the drums of the gods).A K. O.

file: SHOPPER_S WORLD_VINTAGE TEAS IN A TAIPEI SHOP.txt
text:
ï»¿
TERRY TRUCCO is a Tokyo-based writer.
Di Yung-zu may be the most hospitable merchant in Taipei. 
Dressed in an old T-shirt, Bermuda shorts and sandals, he greets his customers warmly, bowing, smiling, offering a cigarette and patting a chair.
Briefly he disappears to fuss with his teapots. 
But within moments he returns to present his visitor with a thimble-size china cup filled with a flowery jasmine brew.
Shopper's World describes tea merchant in Taipei
The customer is admonished to savor the tea, hold the warm liquid in the mouth, then swallow it slowly, allowing it to caress the throat. 
''Tea is very, very healthy,'' he says, sipping from a cup of his own. 
''It improves the blood circulation, settles the stomach and helps you sleep.''
When the last jasmine drops are gone, Mr. Di produces a pot of oolong, the blend for which Taiwan is famous. 
Then just as his guest thinks it is time to leave, out comes a sampling of Chinese green tea, rich and tangy. 
All are delicious and making a selection is difficult. 
The customer leaves laden with three large tins.
For more than 40 years Di Yung-zu has held impromptu tea parties each day at his humble shop, the Hua Yei Tea Company. 
Tea is the staple drink for this country's 18 million people, and Taiwan's capital supports an estimated 1,000 tea establishments, old and new, large and small.
What distinguishes Mr. Di's enterprise is its appearance, which immediately marks it as a traditional Chinese tea shop. 
A neat, handpainted sign labels the place, and with no front windows or doors, customers enter by walking past an old-fashioned wood-framed display case of tea jars and tins.
The place, Mr. Di says proudly, has changed little since the day it opened in 1939. 
Even then he made no attempt to be up to date, equipping the shop with the dim lighting, bright-colored tins and traditional wooden tea crates used for decades.
''Many young people think tea has to be displayed in a more modern style,'' Mr. Di says, holding a worn, rust-colored teapot, which is more than 200 years old and still in daily use. 
''But I've kept my store this way for historical reasons, for the same reason some people collect antiques.''
Styles of clothes may change, he adds, ''but the tea doesn't change.''
For someone with an eye for tradition Di Yung-zu made a brilliant real estate decision. 
Though Taiwan's brisk economy has replaced many older buildings with gleaming skyscrapers, Di Yung-zu's part of town has stubbornly remained the same. 
According to one longtime resident, the area has changed little since the days of the Japanese occupation, which lasted from 1895 to the end of World War II.
The business pace is also in harmony with that of old Taipei. 
Hours are long, stretching from 8:30 A.M. to 7 7 P.M. every day except Sunday. 
But the pace is unhurried and informal, leaving Mr. Di ample time to discuss tea with his customers.
A slender, white-haired man with tea-stained teeth, Mr. Di has spent all of his adult life in the tea trade. 
Though he was not born to the business, at the age of 15 left his family's farm for Taipei, where he was apprenticed to a tea merchant.
When Mr. Di was 29 he bought his present shop and a few years back unofficially retired, turning the business over to his daughter-inlaw, an efficient-looking woman with a grown daughter. 
He still lives above the shop, and every day he comes down to chat with customers, read the newspapers and play with the neighborhood children.
He also purchases his own tea, patronizing farmers in Taiwan's northern and central regions. 
''I never owned my own mountain like some tea merchants, because this way I could select the tea I thought was best. 
Even when it all comes from the same mountain, the quality can differ, he says.''
The tea drunk in Taiwan today has a provenance as distinguished as its flavor. 
As Mr. Di says, tea cultivation in China is believed to date back to prehistoric times. 
The first of these leafy evergreen tea plants grown in the Taiwan mountains were originally imported from the China mainland, probably by the vast waves of immigrants who arrived during the Ming and Manchu dynasties.
W ith its balmy climate, ample rainfall and mountainous terrain, Taiwan proved a rich breeding ground for tea. 
Last year the island produced more than 25,000 metric tons, a 3 percent increase over the previous year.
Tea plants, which are related to the camellia family, can grow to a height of 30 feet, though when cultivated they are usually pruned to three to five feet. 
More importand than climate is site. 
The finest tea comes from the upper mountain reaches, with the quality dipping as one moves down the hill. 
At the top, tea receives the proper amounts of sun and dew, Mr. Di says, while tea grown on flatlands often suffers from too much of both.
The harvest season is vital for a quality brew, too. 
For most teas, the finest is harvested in the spring, though choice oolong tea is gathered in the summer. 
Additional caches of tea are cut in early autumn and November.
All these factors help determine the tea's price, and good tea can be expensive. 
Di Yung-zu's tea sells by the gram; 600 grams -a bit more than a pound - of the finest can cost as much as $80. 
The same amount of a lesser grade can sell for as little as $5. 
Tins cost about 50 cents extra.
If the tea is not packed in tins, it is measured into thick paper bags, never plastic, says Mr. Di. He has weighed tea for years on the type of iron scale seen in small shops all over Taipei. 
It is important to keep the tea away from light and heat, which is why the Hua Yei Tea Company's leaves are stored in old metal-lined pine boxes. 
Mr. Di has more than 50 of these brown trunk-size crates. 
''Wood keeps the temperature moderate so the tea's color won't turn,'' he says.
There are hundreds of teas, but the basic types in Taiwan are jasmine, tiehkuanyin, assam, oolong, daffodil, green tea and yen tea. 
The tea's color depends on the method used to process it. 
Black teas, such as assam, are fermented before firing. 
Oolongs are partially fermented, and green teas not at all. 
Even within a broad category like green tea, which the Chinese call bao chung, dozens of varieties exist.
The shop also sells what is best described as old tea. 
Tucked away in some of those wooden crates is tea dating back to the days when Mr. Di opened the shop. 
It is quite costly: 600 grams for $770. 
It hasn't much flavor. 
But many people believe in its medicinal effects - calming nerves, cleansing the system and releasing excess body heat. 
There is also an old myth that it can treat cancer.
How can a customer identify choice tea?
A hearty sniff helps. 
''The better teas all smell good,'' says Mr. Di. Still, the smell won't tell you if the tea comes from the mountaintop.
Almost as he spoke, two middle-aged women entered the shop, headed for the yen tea bin, scooped up a handful and held it to their noses. 
And how is the best tea brewed?
Mr. Di says you simply cover the bottom of your teapot with leaves, add boiling water and let the brew steep for two or three minutes. 
The leaves can be used again the same day and should yield almost as much flavor, provided the second brew is allowed to steep six or seven minutes.
Technically, any tea brought into the United States has to be submitted to a Food and Drug Administration examiner, but travelers have reported that Customs officials have allowed them to bring in a tin without question.
Â 
If you go
The Hua Yei Tea Company is at 96, Section One, Kai Fang Street in the northern section of Taipei. 
The phone number is 3114918. 
The shop willingly accepts both United States dollars and Japanese yen. 
If he is there, the retired owner, Di Yung-zu, a seasoned businessman, quickly looks up the exchange rate in the day's newspaper as a courtesy to customers. 
T.T.

text:
ï»¿
Sotheby's auctioneers recorded nearly $500,000 in sales today at their first auction in China, and the organizers said the profits would go to renovate half a mile of the Great Wall.
''It's super,'' Julian Thompson, an auctioneer and chairman of Sotheby's International, said after 73 Chinese and Western works of modern art and rare objects brought a total of 1.76 million yuan, or about $475,850.
After auction costs of about $100,000, half the remaining money is to go toward renovating the crumbling Great Wall and half toward saving the Italian city of Venice, which is sinking beneath the waters of the Lagoon of Venice.
Danial Vial, a Parisian public relations agent, who organized the auction as part of four days of events to benefit the Great Wall and Venice, said enough money was raised to rebuild a kilometer of the wall.
Parts of the wall were built more than 2,200 years ago, and many sections have been reduced to rubble by time and warfare.
Some bids were made by telephone from New York and Los Angeles, but most of the purchasers were among more than 200 wealthy foreigners who paid $4,300 each to attend the benefit.
The auction was held in the former imperial palace in a 15th-century hall where Chinese emperors once worshipped their ancestors.
Some participants said their purchases would be souvenirs of the unusual benefit, which included a caviar luncheon on the Great Wall, boating at an imperial palace and a gala performance by opera and ballet stars at the Great Hall of the People.
The painting that had been expected to bring the highest price -''China Proverb'' by Robert Rauschenberg - went for only $40,387, half its presale estimate.
A painted pottery jug by Picasso sold for $14,808, also well below its presale estimate.
The cheapest item was a Sevres porcelain cup that went for 500 yuan, or $135, about half the annual salary of the average Chinese factory worker.

file: SPEAKING PERSONALLY_A FRIEND FROM CHINA FINDS SIMPLE PLEASURE.txt
text:
ï»¿
I REMEMBER thinking, as I stood on the platform waiting for my Chinese guest, that there wasn't a single bench to sit on in the whole station, and I was tired. 
I hadn't stopped rushing for hours, what with dusting my entire collection of Chinese spoons and rice bowls, making up the guest bed, hiding the grandchild's toys and preparing to act nonchalant once Hu Shiguang arrived. 
I had it all worked out to join our mutual Chinese friends for dinner out in our own special restaurant, so I wouldn't have to spend hours in the kitchen. 
My aim was to return his hospitality in Beijing, and give him a day in the countryside at peace with the world.
I searched for the train's headlight, checked my watch a dozen times, and I think I worried that train into view around the curve. 
Shiguang bounced out of the open door with a shout of, ''Hello, Penny!'' and I knew he meant his big smile. 
He was carrying a backpack and a bunch of carnations. 
We really did throw our arms around each other, he, the diminutive Chinese, I, the overstuffed American. 
''How have you been, Da Jie?'' he asked - he has always called me ''Big Sister'' because I am older than he - and we got to talking about everything that had happened to us since we had last met, as I drove us home.
''I have a dog, a big, black dog my neighbor threw away!'' he said. 
It is unheard of for a Chinese on the mainland to have a dog. 
''I called him Reagan, so everybody knows he is mine,'' he chuckled. 
''And I am learning to drive. 
My roommate bought a car for $150, and he is teaching me. 
I need a driver's license as proof of address, so I will be permitted to have a library card.''
I thought to myself, what extraordinary process of logic brought him to that conclusion?
New York University had brought him to the United States to teach Chinese poetry for one year. 
''But the students clamored for language lessons instead of poetry, and so I was drafted into a new vocation,'' he said, smiling wistfully. 
''They are all A.B.C.'s (American-Born Chinese) and they don't know the language. 
It's a difficult job for me.''
I knew that Shiguang was almost prevented from coming here, because he was the only person in Beijing who could translate the ancient poets into modern Chinese.
My husband, Jimmie, came outside to greet us and we all migrated to the backyard where Jim was whip-cutting the edge of the vegetable garden. 
Shiguang automatically squatted and proceeded to pull weeds. 
There he was, smack in the middle of all those vegetables - Chinese, of course - bok choy, snow peas, long beans - in his pin-striped pants and shiny black shoes.
''You enjoy weeding, Shiguang, a city boy like you?''
''Of course!'' he answered. 
''I am a human being.''
''Would you harvest the snow peas, if I get you a bucket?''
I asked.
''Of course!'' he said again. 
So I set about fixing the raspberries and we worked in silent rapport. 
Then we recalled his months of forced labor on a farm, during the Cultural Revolution.
''Is it true, Shiguang, that the farmers would steal your crops if you didn't post a lookout?''
He laughed. 
''They would steal anything you turned your back on, even a little piece of wire!''
''But you were all one people - why would they do that?''
''The peasants were very intolerant of the mass of intellectuals that got dumped in their midst. 
They told us, 'You have money to buy food!
Why should you be growing it?'
We were torn from our homes and families, separated from our work, but we were rich in their eyes, and envy makes a dangerous bedfellow.''
I eventually found the courage to ask him a question:
''Shiguang, I am giving a barbecue in late August for my father's 85th birthday, and I don't dare attempt to plant the back wall like I used to, because of my surgery. 
Would it appeal to you to stick in a few plants for me?''
''Of course!''
His ever-faithful reply. 
We took off in the car for the best nursery around, knowing it was late in the season for such a project, and he was delighted to see shed after shed of impatiens and begonias of so many colors.
Shiguang hand-picked 36 six-packs of coordinated colors and I watched him tenderly place them in the car. 
He unloaded everything in the shade, to await the next morning for planting.
During dinner, our friends' college-age niece volunteered to help, so we picked her up bright and early the next day. 
I had a surprise in mind for both of them and took them to the Scarsdale Women's Club Book Drop, where they thumbed through the stacks like bees checking blossoms. 
She emerged with a handful of books on shells, gems and household pets, all subjects for her art classes; he took an armful on contemporary American literature, necessary for his forthcoming book in Chinese.
In three hours the whole job was done, and marvelously, too. 
Shiguang organized the work. 
He dug the holes, and Zhen Rong planted the flowers, everything by color.
After I had fixed my favorite Chinese dinner - shredded chicken and zucchini with fish flavor - we relaxed with two symphony orchestras on television. 
Then Jimmie asked Shiguang if he had ever played computer games, to which he replied excitedly that he had wandered into an arcade once, and would like to try again. 
So my ''Little Brother'' and my giant husband banged mercilessly at the computer keyboard - forgotten was the culture gap, the exhaustion from the garden work, even the hour of the night, for they played until 1 A.M., like young boys.
The next day Hu Shiguang made ready to leave and pumped both our hands by way of ''thank you.''
''It's friendship across the oceans once again, Da Jie, isn't it?'' he said. 
I hugged him goodbye so no one could see the tear caught in my eyelash. 
Penny Stamm of Scarsdale is a member of the Westchester Chapter of United States-China Peoples' Friendship Association.

text:
ï»¿
THE stuffed dumpling, humble as it may seem, is a dish with a fascinating history, going back many centuries and interwoven into the cuisines of a number of countries.
The story has often been told of Marco Polo arriving in China during the 13th century and discovering with delight that the Chinese were producing a variety of stuffed noodles that included won ton. 
So impressed was he that he brought the secrets back to Italy. 
That tale is considered apocryphal by both the Chinese and Italians, but wouldn't it be fascinating to know how the two cuisines are related?
Similarly, what about the pelmeni of Russia?
These are delectable Siberian dumplings filled with meat or mushrooms or potatoes or cabbage. 
What cook traveled the roads from Canton, or wherever, to the Irtysh River in the cold plateaus of Siberia, bringing with him the goodness of filled pasta?
Craig Claiborne comment discusses recipes for fillings of variations of stuffed dumplings
Or consider the kreplach, the filled dumpling held in such high esteem in the Jewish kitchen. 
The migrations of the Jews, carrying with them a culinary heritage from various parts of the world, are well known, as is the fact that many Jewish specialties are borrowings from the Russian. 
At what point did the pelmeni turn into kreplach, with its economical use of ground cooked beef as the filling?
That use of cooked meat, probably from a soup or stew, is also characteristic of dumplings. 
The lack of kosher meat in medieval ghettos dictated that there be ways to stretch a meager supply from one meal to another.
The uses to which dumplings are put are intriguing as well. 
They are probably most often used in soups, and yet a wide array of sauces may also be served with them.
Won tons, for example, go deliciously with a blend of soy sauce, garlic, vinegar, grated ginger, hot chilies and the like, a combination that would seem odd to an Italian chef thinking of ravioli. 
For ravioli there is nothing like a tomato sauce with freshly grated cheese or alla panna - a reduction of heavy cream and cheese. 
Or (as they do in Rapallo when they serve pansotti, a form of ravioli) a salsa di noce made with walnuts and a form of ricotta cheese.
Â 
Curiously, however, the Siberians and those who prepare pelmeni arenot averse to serving them with a sauce somew hat akin to the Chinese soy sauce, vinegar and herb combination.
Pelmeni are often served with a mustard sauce, sour cream and chopped dill. 
Kreplach, like the Chinese dumplings, are often fried in fat (butter or chicken fat, for example) rather than served in soup.
What follow are our versions of these stuffed dumplings. 
It is difficult to pinpoint the exact yield of filled dumplings because it depends on the thickness to which the noodle dough is rolled out, the amount of filling allotted to each dumpling and the caution exercised by the cook in cutting out the dough to be filled.
Â 
Won Ton
From ''The Chinese Cookbook'' by Craig Claiborne and Virginia Lee (J.B. 
Lippincott,
Â 
1972).
Â 
1 pound lean pork, ground 1 bunch watercress 1 egg 2 tablespoons light soy sauce 1 tablespoon dry sherry or @Shaoxing wine 1/2 pound raw shrimp, peeled, deveined and chopped fine 1/2 teaspoon monosodium glutamate, optional 1 tablespoon cornstarch 2 tablespoons water Salt to taste, if desired Freshly ground pepper to taste 1 package won ton skins (see note) Chicken broth (1 cup per serving).
1. Place pork in mixing bowl. 
2. Pick over watercress to remove tough stems. 
Drop watercress into boiling water and let stand about 30 seconds. 
Drain immediately and run under cold water. 
Press to extract excess water. 
Chop until fine, then add to pork.
3. Add all remaining ingredients except pepper, won ton skins and chicken broth and stir. 
4. If thin won tons are desired, roll each skin with rolling pin or put through noodle machine, or they may be stuffed just as they are. 
Fill each skin with teaspoon of filling. 
Keep stack of won ton skins covered with damp cloth so they do not dry out.
5. To fold, bring up two sides of won ton skin and pinch all around to seal in filling. 
Dampen edges with a little water if necessary to make them stick. 
Pull two bottom edges together and pinch firmly to seal.
6. Continue until all filling is used. 
As you work, cover finished won tons with damp cloth to prevent drying out. 
7. Bring several quarts of water to boil in large kettle and add won tons. 
When water returns to boil, add half cup of cold water and let water come to boil again. 
Won tons are done when they float to top.
8. Heat chicken broth. 
Put a little salt and pepper into bottom of individual serving bowls and pour in hot broth. 
Ladle few cooked won tons into each bowl and serve immediately.
Yield: 90 to 100 won tons. 
NOTE: Won ton skins are available in Chinese markets.
Â 
Ravioli
Â 
Noodle dough made with 2 cups of flour (see recipe) 1 tablespoon butter 1 1/2 teaspoons finely minced garlic 3/4 pound ground beef Salt to taste, if desired Freshly ground pepper to taste 1/2 teaspoon dried basil 1/2 teaspoon dried marjoram 1 egg, lightly beaten 3 tablespoons heavy cream 3 tablespoons bread crumbs 3 tablespoons freshly grated Parmesan or Pecorina cheese 2 tablespoons finely chopped parsley Meat sauce (see recipe).
1. Prepare noodle dough and set aside. 
2. Heat butter in saucepan and add garlic. 
Cook briefly and add beef. 
Cook, stirring and chopping down with the side of a heavy metal spoon to break up lumps, about 5 minutes. 
Add salt and pepper and stir. 
Remove from heat. 
Let cool.
3. Add basil, marjoram, egg, cream, bread crumbs, cheese and parsley. 
Blend well. 
4. Roll out pasta. 
5. If a ra violi maker is used, cover utens il with thin sheet of pasta, add about 1 1/2 t easpoons of filling for each ravio li. 
Cover with second sheet of pasta and press between fillings to e xclude air.Use rolling pin to seal pasta and to cut them as you roll.
6. Remove ravioli to a rack. 
Let dry for 1 1/2 hours before cooking. 
To cook, drop ravioli into boiling water without crowding. 
Let boil about 7 minutes or to desired degree of doneness. 
Drain and serve with meat sauce (see recipe).
Yield: About 48 ravioli.

Siberian Pelmeni (Russian ravioli)
Adapted from ''The Russian Tea Room Cookbook'' by Faith Stewart-Gordon and Nika
Â 
Hazelton (Richard Marek, 1981).

Noodle dough made with 1 cup of flour (see recipe but divide ingredients in half) 1 tablespoon butter 1 cup finely chopped onion 1 teaspoon finely minced garlic 1/4 pound twice-ground beef, preferably top round 1/4 pound twice-ground lean veal Salt to taste, if desired Freshly ground pepper to taste Dash of Tabasco sauce 6 cups rich beef broth or consomme (see recipe), optional Melted butter, optional 1 cup sour cream 1/4 cup prepared mustard 1/2 cup vinegar, such as malt vinegar.
1. Prepare dough as directed. 
2. Heat tablespoon of butter in small skillet, add onion and garlic. 
Cook, stirring, until wilted and scrape into mixing bowl. 
3. Add ground beef and veal, salt, pepper and Tabasco sauce. 
Blend well by hand. 
4. Roll out dough and fill in desired fashion into 48 or more pelmeni. 
5. Drop pelmeni into rapidly boiling water and cook to desired degree of doneness, 5 minutes or longer. 
6. Serve pelmeni in soup bowls with hot consomme, or serve with melted butter with sour cream, mustard and vinegar on the side. 
The usual serving of pelmeni as a main course is 12 to 16.
Yield: About 48 pelmeni.
Kreplach
Â 
Noodle dough made with 2 cups of flour (see recipe) 1 pound boiled beef (see recipe) 2 tablespoons onion juice (see note) 1 egg, lightly beaten Salt to taste, if desired Freshly ground pepper to taste.
1. Prepare the dough as directed. 
2. Shred or chop the meat fine (may be done in food processor). 
There should be about two cups. 
3. Put meat into mixing bowl. 
Add onion juice, egg, salt and pepper. 
Blend by hand. 
4. Divide dough into quarters. 
Roll as thin as possible by hand or in pasta machine. 
A preferred method for filling kreplach is to cut the sheet of dough into 2 1/2- or 3-inch squares. 
Fold over and seal.
5. Drop kreplach into boiling water and cover. 
Cook 15 to 20 minutes. 
6. Serve kreplach in well-seasoned hot chicken broth - 4 to 8 kreplach apiece. 
Yield: About 36 kreplach.
Â 
Boiled Beef for Kreplach

1 pound lean chuck steak in one piece 1 small leek, trimmed and rinsed well 1/2 cup coarsely chopped onion 1/2 cup coarsely chopped celery 1/2 cup coarsely chopped carrot Salt to taste, if desired 12 peppercorns.
Combine ingredients in small kettle or large saucepan. 
Add water to cover and bring to simmer. 
Simmer 1 1/2 hours until fork tender. 
Drain.
Yield: 1 pound of beef.

Noodle Dough

2 cups flour Salt to taste , if desired 2 large eggs ( 1/2 cup) 1 to 2 tablespoons cold water.
1. This dough may be made with food processor or by hand. 
With processor, combine all ingredients in container and blend thoroughly. 
Shape dough into a ball.
2. If done by hand, put flour on flat surface and make well in center.

Knead well for 10 minutes or longer. 
Add more water as necessary to make smooth dough.
3. Place dough in clean cloth and wrap neatly to enclose. 
Let stand 30 minutes before using. 
Yield: Slightly less than 1 pound.
Â 
Sugo di Carne (Meat sauce)
Â 
1 ounce dried mushrooms, preferably Italian (funghi secchi or porcini) 1 tablespoon olive oil 2 tablespoons butter 3/4 cup finely chopped onion 1/4 cup finely chopped celery 1 teaspoon finely minced garlic 1/3 cup finely chopped carrot 1/4 pound ground lean pork 1/2 pound ground veal 2 cups dry red wine 2 cups imported canned tomatoes 3 tablespoons tomato paste Salt to taste, if desired Freshly ground pepper to taste 1 cup beef broth or consomme (see recipe).
1. Put mushrooms in bowl and add slightly hot water to cover. 
Let stand 30 minutes. 
2. Heat oil and butter in skillet. 
Add onion, celery, garlic and carrot. 
Cook, stirring, until wilted. 
3. Add pork and veal. 
Cook, stirring and chopping down with the side of a heavy metal spoon to break up lumps, until meats lose raw look.
4. Drain mushrooms and chop coarsely. 
Add mushrooms to meat mixture. 
Add wine, tomatoes, tomato paste, salt and pepper. 
Bring to boil and cook uncovered 1 hour.
5. Pour sauce into saucepan. 
Bring to boil and skim fat from surface. 
Add broth and continue cooking 1 hour. 
Yield: About 6 cups.
Â 
Consomme
Â 
8 pounds meaty beef bones 6 quarts water 40 black peppercorns 2 cups coarsely chopped carrots 4 cups coarsely chopped, well-rinsed leeks 2 cups coarsely chopped celery 2 whole cloves 4 sprigs parsley 2 sprigs fresh thyme or 1 teaspoon dried 2 bay leaves.
1. Put bones in kettle and add cold water to cover. 
Bring to boil and simmer 1 minute. 
Drain well. 
Rinse bones under cold water and when thoroughly chilled, return to clean kettle.
2. Add six quarts of water, peppercorns, carrots, leeks and celery. 
3. Tie cloves, parsley, thyme sprigs and bay leaves into bundle and add. 
Bring to boil and simmer uncovered for 5 hours. 
4. Strain, discard solids and skim off fat. 
Yield: About 10 cups. 
NOTE: Leftover consomme can be frozen.

text:

Only in Newport, where the social arts function with the force of great money, could the event planned for today transpire: at the behest of the First National Bank of Chicago, China's Ambassador to the United States has consented to come here to honor the restoration of a teahouse built almost 70 years ago for Alva Vanderbilt Belmont.
As the teahouse glows in stained and lacquered shades of jade green and red in the afternoon light, a United States Navy band is to play, with Deputy Secretary of State Walter J. Stoessel Jr. and Claiborne Pell, the senior United States Senator from Rhode Island, in attendance. 
A uniformed squadron of the Newport Artillery Company will aim its cannon to sea and fire 19 times from the lawn of Marble House, the Vanderbilt mansion built for $11 million in 1892. 
His Excellency Chai Zemin, the Chinese Ambassador, is to cut a ribbon opening the teahouse to the public. 
And a troupe of balloons will float off on the ocean breeze.
NEWPORT, R.I. 
- Only in Newport, where the social arts function with the force of great money, could the event planned for today transpire: at the behest of the First National Bank of Chicago, China's Ambassador to the United States has consented to come here to honor the restoration of a teahouse built almost 70 years ago for Alva Vanderbilt Belmont.
Thus is an extraordinary restoration of a singular little building to come to its official end. 
It is thought to be the only structure of its kind east of San Francisco. 
Almost $500,000 and a year and a half of work by craftsmen in 15 specialties has gone into the restoration by the Preservation Society of Newport County.
A sad and coincidental footnote is that the society's director, Paul E. Molitor Jr., will not be on hand to celebrate the completion of the project he supervised. 
After an interview at the site on Sunday and a dinner party that night at Bailey's Beach, the 36-yearold Mr. Molitor apparently drove to the top of the Newport Bridge over Narragansett Bay. 
His car was found there just before midnight with its lights on, according to Detective Sgt. William E. Eckert Jr. of the Rhode Island State Police. 
Mr. Molitor's body was pulled from the bay on Monday afternoon, Sergeant Eckert said.
''I think he was just despondent,'' said John G. Winslow, president of the society. 
''It was a personal thing. 
He was very enthusiastic about the teahouse. 
He devoted most of his time the last two or three years to it.''
Compared with the piles of brick, stone and marble that the money barons of the 19th century built here as summer ''cottages,'' the teahouse is as bright and fanciful as a cut jewel. 
Mrs. Belmont, who was divorced from William K. Vanderbilt and married O.H.P. 
Belmont, may, in fact, have intended it as a temporary adornment for the lawn of Marble House, which became hers by the divorce.
The architects and researchers in the restoration project cannot be sure of her intent in the year 1913. 
But in the same way that mansions such as Marble House have been saved for the public by donations from the rich, a fond memory has interceded to preserve the teahouse, which had been boarded up and left to the vandals and the salt air for decades.
It happened this way, Mr. Winslow said: The late Frederick H. Prince of Chicago, whose fortune came from railroads and Armour & Company, owned the Marble House after the Vanderbilts did. 
When Harold S. Vanderbilt, a son of Mrs. Belmont, provided the funds for the preservation society to purchase the estate from the Prince family in 1963, the society restored the mansion but had no money for the teahouse.
But William Wood-Prince, Mr. Prince's stepson and heir and a director of the First National Bank of Chicago, remembered courting his wife in the teahouse. 
He gave $50,000 toward restoring it. 
Other money was raised. 
And when the project neared completion, the First National Bank of Chicago, which has business interests in China, prevailed on Mr. Chai to lend his office to the occasion.
That is how things work on that level in Newport. 
But on another level, at the teahouse, the work of restoring the obliterated Chinese calligraphy, the paintings of 12th- and 15th-century Chinese garden scenes, the chopped-off copper figures of dragons, lions and dogs on the roof, the broken terra-cotta roof tiles, the crumbled plaster of paris moldings, all proceeded by hand, tediously and inch by inch.
The teahouse had been designed for Mrs. Belmont by the New York architectural firm of Richard Howland Hunt and Joseph Howland Hunt. 
Documents in the firm's archives indicate that someone from the firm went to China to study and sketch pavilions there, and the resulting design, according to Mark Weber, a consultant hired by the society to research the history of the teahouse, ''is a composite image,'' and perhaps ''the most significant example of American chinoiserie architecture in America.''
''The French term chinoiserie,'' Mr. Weber added, ''can only properly be used to mean European decoration whimsically applied in the Chinese manner, not to Oriental work or strict copies of it.''
Mrs. Belmont called her little building ''the Teahouse,'' he said, but it was actually an imitation of Chinese temple architecture.
Many of the original architectural drawings, along with records of the pavilion's cost and the number and identity of the original craftsmen, were lost. 
The restoration had to proceed from old photographs, from intuition, from copying existing parts to reproduce missing pieces.
Jeffrey L. Staats, the supervising architect for Donal Simpson Associates of Newport, discovered that Mrs. Belmont had cut corners. 
Spruce and pine had been used instead of the mahogany and teak called for in the original specifications. 
Instead of elaborate lacquer work and varnish, only a single coat of paint was used. 
The teahouse was built with ungalvanized nails. 
And the paintings inside were done on plywood.
Before restoring the paintings, Christy Cunningham, who specializes in frescoes on wooden panels, had to restore the surface of the vandalized and peeling plywood. 
She had to make such carved inscriptions as ''L.S.D.'' and ''Joey Loves Sarah'' disappear. 
It took her a year.
Arnold Cyr, the coppersmith who hand-hammered a new dragon's head and parts for a lion and a dog for the roof, discovered to his amazement that the coppersmith who had originally done such beautiful work had not scratched his name inside the copper sheeting. 
On the new work, Mr. Cyr said, ''I put my name inside.''
Only one defect now remains in the teahouse. 
Should the Chinese Ambassador look up, he will see that the characters on the bottom of the bronze lanterns tell of the reign of the emperor in which the lanterns were made. 
But the characters are Japanese, as was the emperor. 
The lanterns were made in Japan.

text:

Thanksgiving, in our house, is a changeable feast. 
It is American to the extent that it is observed on the day set aside for it, occasionally Italian in flavor simply because that is the ancestry of my husband and old feasts die hard, and quite often Chinese in taste because that is what I know and what I cook.
It wasn't always so. 
Thanksgiving, American Thanksgiving, came upon me in 1959, the year we were married and I came to New York to live. 
That November my husband told me we were going to his mother's for Thanksgiving dinner and I asked what Thanksgiving was.
Eileen Yin-Fei Lo discusses meeting of Italian and Chinese cuisines for Thanksgiving feast
He told me about the pilgrims and the Indians and corn and turkeys and how the day originally had been a day of thanks on the part of the pilgrims for their continued well-being.
''Oh,'' I remember saying, ''that is like the 24th day of the 12th month in China, when my mother used to say thank you to Tsao Chun.''
''Oh?''
I remember him answering. 
That day, the culmination of the New Year celebration, which is China's most important holiday, was our traditional day of thanksgiving for a year enjoyed, for harvests that were successful. 
During the year a picture of Tsao Chun, also known as the Kitchen God, drawn on rice paper, was tacked above our kitchen stove, a vantage point from which he observed our family at table, which as we all know is when truth comes out. 
At any rate, on that 24th day of the 12th month his job is to report to the Jade Emperor on the family he has been living with.
So we would smear honey on Tsao Chun's lips and put him on a tiny bamboo throne, then join him in a thanksgiving feast of sweet cakes, candied fruit and sweetened glutinous rice before setting fire to his picture so that, through the wisps of smoke, he would rise upward and say only sweet things about us. 
That was our thanksgiving.
''Ours is a bit different,'' said my husband, and as he described it I thought to myself that it certainly was. 
He mentioned that we would certainly have turkey, but that there would be important Italian additions to the feast. 
To wit, an antipasto of such things as freshly smoked salami, peppers that had been roasted atop the oven that morning and dressed with olive oil, and chunks of hard cheese called locatelli; a thick chicken broth with chicken; a green salad; followed by the roast turkey and everything that would go with it, including dressing; followed by cold celery and fennel to cool the palate, then dates and nuts. 
Dessert would come a few hours later, after Uncle Frank's accordion music and the penny poker game.
That, I thought, was certainly more elaborate than what we did for the Kitchen God. 
My goodness!
It was also the first turkey I had ever eaten. 
I had never even seen a turkey until I went to Hong Kong from Canton, where I was born, and those that had been imported for the Christmas holidays of the British in the crown colony always looked so skinny and stringy that I refused even to taste them. 
Did I wish white meat or dark?
I was asked. 
Well, everybody knew that white meat is essentially tasteless, so I chose dark. 
And it was pleasant, I remember, but not at all special, and frankly I guess I couldn't understand what all the fuss was about.
The roasted peppers were, however, utterly wonderful, and I told my mother-in-law so, which made her feel a little better than she had when I suggested that turkey was dull. 
She also liked it when I told her I liked the chicken broth.
We did make the Thanksgiving Day dinners for years later, watching it move from in-law to in-law. 
And then my husband's family scattered and soon Thanksgiving Day was a day for my immediate family. 
We had turkey for a couple of years mainly because I enjoyed figuring out ways to creatively use the leftover turkey meat. 
I curried it, made Shanghai-style pastries with turkey as the filling, stir-fried it with celery, carrots, scallions and onions, all of which tasted better than the roasted turkey, I thought.
Thanksgiving kept meaning turkey because my husband and my three children said that at Thanksgiving you had to have turkey. 
That of course was nonsense and one year I listened to them ask for a turkey as they always did but I gave them a duck.
And a very special duck it was, a classical Chinese preparation called Tea-Smoked Duck. 
First I steamed it whole with ginger, eightstar anise and cinnamon sticks, then I smoked it with Dragon Well tea, that magnificent green tea from Hangzhou, roasted it briefly in the oven, then deep-fried it, whole, to give the skin the texture of parchment. 
Instant success!
And from then on there was no longer talk of Thanksgiving turkeys simply because tea-smoked duck tasted better.
After that came a couple of years of roasted fresh ham, a huge ham into which I slipped slices of garlic and basted with soy sauce and sugar for about nine hours, and with which I served snow peas and black mushrooms. 
It was also successful and wonderful as a leftover stir-fried with vegetables. 
Then, a couple of years ago, we started going to the home of our friends, the Perlines, for Thanksgiving. 
And the culinary character of our Thanksgiving changed still again. 
It was back to turkey, but before the turkey there was always a matzoh ball soup, and later on a flan, because Irving makes the best there is, and a wonderful chocolate sponge, cherries and whipped cream Black Forest Cake made by Frieda, the lady from Germany who came in to help the Perlines out. 
Now what sort of traditional Thanksgiving Day feast is that?
We do enjoy it very much, however, as much for the company as for the food, because Thanksgiving for the Perlines is sort of an open house and each year, it seems, there are others joining the regulars for dinner - students, relatives, friends who have dropped by. 
And that is a fine Thanksgiving too. 
Do I contribute?
Not really, except to say a few quiet and private words to Tsao Chun about the Perlines' very nice kitchen, so he can mention it upstairs.
Eileen Yin-Fei Lo teaches Chinese cooking and nutrition at the China Institute in America, in New York, and is the author of the forthcoming, ''The Dim Sum Book: Art of the Chinese Teahouse,'' Crown Publishers.

file: THE BEST OF HONG KONG_Four Hotels in the Grandest Manner. . .And Food Fit for Emperors.txt
text:
ï»¿
There are nearly 20,000 restaurants in Hong Kong, a city where it may seem that every resident is a self-styled gourmet and that everyone eats out as often as possible. 
The result is some of the very best cooking in the world, be it French, Italian or Vietnamese.
But why go to Hong Kong to eat foreign dishes when the territory's five million Chinese are mostly from Canton (Guangdong)?
Although Americans associate Cantonese food with thick, saccharine, orange-red sauces, it is considered by many the best Chinese food in the world. 
The key culinary words are harmony and simplicity: the subtle and the delicate play off the rich and spicy.
Hong Kong chefs, however, do equally well with food from other Chinese regions, so whether you choose to sample their talents in the hundreds of simple restaurants throughout the city or in the hotel dining rooms that you will love despite their amazing pretentiousness, you will be forever spoiled for most Chinese food in the United States, particularly what passes here for Cantonese.
From the jade and silver of Lai Ching Heen in the Regent Hotel, to the glazed tile walls and tile floors of the Hoi Tin Garden Restaurant in the fishing village of Lei Yue Mun, from the red lacquer and gold at the Shang Palace in the Shangri-La Hotel to the less than spotless tablecloths in the second floor Tin Fat Restaurant, Hong Kong food will astonish your senses.
Some of the most expensive meals are in restaurant hotels, but unlike the United States, most of the diners in them are local people. 
Hong Kong is a rich territory and, as the promotional literature for it says: ''Money is something of which most Chinese are proud and much of it is spent on lavish dining and entertaining.''
Meals in some of the most elaborate settings are easily more expensive than the costliest meals in New York. 
The great delicacy is anything made with sharks' fin and it is not unusual for a single dish to cost $200.
First-time visitors should not be put off by tales of dinner checks fit for an emperor. 
On a four-day eating tour that covered eight restaurants, there were meals that cost only $10 a person as well as one that was $60.
If, however, you are put off by less than impeccable linens you may have to confine yourself to the most expensive restaurants, where Western fastidiousness is practiced. 
But be prepared to pay for the jade and silver serving pieces.
A few words of practical advice: napkins are offered in some restaurants, but damp terrycloth washcloths before the meal are more common. 
A 10 percent service charge is added to bills; if the service warrants it, add another 3 to 5 percent. 
Don't hesitate to ask your waiter for advice. 
By the same token don't let him intimidate you into ordering dishes that cost more than you want to spend. 
But be sure to let him know that you don't want ''safe'' choices like sweet and sour pork. 
Chinese beer, particularly Tsing Tao, is usually the most appropriate accompaniment to the food. 
Most restaurants are open every day for lunch and dinner, closed only for Chinese New Year and public holidays.
Â 
SHANG PALACE
It is difficult to say where we ate the best food: different restaurants excelled at different dishes. 
And certainly if price is no object and conspicuous consumption is your cup of tea, you cannot go wrong at the aptly named Shang Palace.
Don't let the ornate decoration fool you. 
Despite copious quantities of imperial red lacquer and 22-carat gold leaf, carved lacquered elephants, gold tableware, impeccable linens and personalized matches for all who have made reservations, the food is exceptionally well prepared.
The meal began with a small whole suckling pig, the most succulent I have ever eaten. 
The usual maraschino cherry eyes were replaced by tiny lighted red bulbs. 
Served in the style of moo shi pork, scallop-edged steamed breads are used instead of wraplings, each to be spread with a delightful sweet and slightly spicy plum sauce, the scallion bundles wrapped with strips of hot red pepper.
Every dish was a picture, all of it served under silver domes in the French fashion.
A dish of crab and bamboo fungus, which has a texture not unlike a mushroom, had that subtle, delicate flavor for which Cantonese food is famous.
Pan-fried chicken with soybean and chili, though a simple mixture of green pepper, scallions, garlic and chicken, rose above the ordinary with a bit of hot red chili and black bean paste. 
Cantonese food has its own hot peppers.
Seasonal vegetables were an exotic mixture of hairy seaweed, black fungus with the rich taste of earthy wild mushrooms served in soybean skin. 
I am an unabashed fan of Chinese sweets and I thought the coconut cream soup with tapioca was delightfully refreshing.
For two, this superb dinner cost $75. 
The restaurant also offers a dim sum lunch.
Â 
(Shang Palace, Shangri-La Hotel, 64 Mody Road, Kowloon, Hong Kong; telephone 3-7212111. 
Lunch and dinner seven days. 
American Express, Diners, MasterCard, VISA.)
Â 
LAI CHING HEEN
If Shang Palace is exuberantly ostentatious, Lai Ching Heen is subtly ostentatious. 
Instead of imperial red and gold, it is jade and silver. 
The chopsticks are ivory and silver. 
The setting spells money. 
Like the Shang Palace, the service is flawless and instantaneous.
This was our first meal in Hong Kong and thus my first encounter with the much touted and very expensive sharks' fin soup. 
Although it is adored by the Chinese because of its texture, Westerners are not always taken with it, because it is bland and slippery. 
But if, like me, you are wild about the tapioca pudding you will love the soup with its extremely delicate flavor.
Topping off the well-prepared food is a glorious view of the harbor. 
Dinner for two is about $100.
Â 
9Lai Ching Heen, the Regent, Salisbury Road, Hong Kong; 3-7211211. 
Open for lunch and dinner seven days. 
Visa, American Express, Diners.)
Â 
FOOK LAM MOON
To veteran visitors the name Fook Lam Moon conjures up expensive meals, and if you insist on having abalone you can ring up a bill that will make the Four Seasons or the Quilted Giraffe in New York look like bargain basements. 
One abalone dish is more than $300; there is an entire page of abalone. 
There's another page of shark's fin dishes, which start at $180. 
But there is also exquisite golden deep-fried chicken for $18.
Garoupa, a fish with pristine white flesh that is extremely popular in Hong Kong, had just come out of the pond. 
Served with spring onions, it was very moist and delicate, as was the lobster in garlic sauce.
The food at Fook Lam Moon is quite sophisticated and while the setting is not as glamorous as the hotel restaurants it is attractive with a newly redone pale pink and green color scheme. 
As in so many Chinese restaurants, the lighting is far brighter than you would expect.
Dinner for two was $120.
Â 
(Fook Lam Moon, 31 Mody Road, Shop A Tsimshatsui, Kowloon, Hong Kong; 3-688755. 
Open seven days for lunch and dinner.
Â 
American Express, Visa, Diners
Club, MasterCard.)
Â 
YUNG KEE
If you want to see what restaurants were like in Hong Kong 40 years ago, a trip to Yung Kee is a must. 
Crowded and noisy, done up in gold and red, with less than spotless tablecloths, it is still an especially good choice for lunch, though there is less of a crush before noon or after 2.
The specialty is thousand-year-old eggs, exceedingly good with pickled ginger. 
But all the Cantonese food is an example of how light such cooking can be, even when it is as rich as golden-skinned roast goose with a delicate plum sauce. 
Here is the place to try fried rice as it should taste, flavored with salted fish rather than barbecued pork.
Judging from what we tried, you probably cannot go wrong with anything you order. 
Lunch for two wasIt was enough for a dinner.
Â 
(Yung Kee Restaurant, Yung Kee Building, 32 Wellington Street, Hong Kong; 5-221624.
Open seven days for lunch and dinner. 
Visa, American Express, Diners.)
Â 
HOI TIN GARDEN
If really fresh fish is your passion, be sure to take a trip to Lei Yue Mun, a tiny fishing village just a four- or five-minute ferry ride from Hong Kong. 
About 30 fish stalls line your route to about 14 restaurants. 
You choose from a vast assortment of exotic fin fish and shellfish and they are delivered to the restaurant of your choice, where your order is cooked in the simplest fashion in the plainest surroundings.
The preparation of the food is sublime: abalone steamed with soy sauce and ginger; clams steamed with spring onions, soy and oil; scallops with their roe in black bean sauce. 
Dinner for two was $45.
Â 
(Hoi Tin Garden Restaurant, 53-59 Praya Road, Lei Yue Mun.
Open seven days for lunch and dinner. 
No credit cards.)
Â 
TIN FAT
After hearing so much about Chiu Chow cooking, I had to taste it before leaving Hong Kong. 
In this country it is the least known of all Chinese food. 
Chiu Chow is in Guangdong Province, but the food is much gutsier than Cantonese. 
It is distinguished by its use of large quantitites of garlic and oil, and fish sauce in place of soy sauce.
The Chiu Chow restaurant I visited is nothing to look at. 
The menus are in Chinese. 
The staff speaks no English. 
Find someone who speaks Chinese to take you. 
It's worth it.
Sharks' fin soup was much richer and thicker than the Cantonese version and was served with dark vinegar that provided an appealing tang. 
Steamed lobster with Mandarin-flavored honey, stir-fried whelk with garlic, chili and black beans were very savory. 
Rice congee instead of steamed rice was served with the meal. 
Dinner for two was about $45. 
Menus do not show prices.
Â 
(Tin Fat Restaurant, 9 Des Voeux Road, West, Hong Kong; 5-481739. 
Open seven days for lunch and dinner. 
No credit cards.)
Â 
LUK YU
Everyone who has been to Hong Kong will tell you to go to Luk Yu for dim sum. 
People who live there will tell you not to bother. 
But because we were tourists we went.
We made sure, however, to go when the regulars were not around because we had been told that when the restaurant is busy no one pays attention to strangers.
Luk Yu, which opened in 1925, looks like an old English restaurant in the colonies with its overhead fans and highly varnished wood wainscotting, its wooden-backed booths, enormous stained-glass windows, marble floors and spitoons at each booth. 
There are glass tops on each white tablecloth. 
The present location is not the original.
This is a place where you are expected to wash out your cup and the tips of your chopsticks in a basin of tea, just as they still do in China for sanitary reasons. 
It is a place where the waiters shuffle along on slippered feet, and the women who carry the dim sum dishes sing out their wares as they pass.
Dim sum are not much different from what you will find in a good dim sum parlor in the United States: pork buns, sui mai filled with pork, har gao with shrimp, steamed beef rolls made with rice flour.
You don't have to speak Chinese to come here in the morning because you can motion to the women carrying the food and look at what is being served. 
In the afternoon, however, you must order from a menu, which is in Chinese without translations. 
Dim sum are $1 or less apiece.
Â 
(Luk Yu, 24 Stanley Street, Central Hong Kong; 5-232973.)

text:
ï»¿
THE TSAI FUNG DANCE COMPANY was founded in 1982 with the aim of expressing Chinese tradition in modern dance and music. 
Some of the dances performed by the company on April 25 at Pace College's Schimmel Center had the look of uneasy hybrids. 
But there was also authentic theater, much of which tended to occur when Jiang Qi was on the stage.
A former member of China's Central Song and Dance Company who is now dancing with the Joffrey II, Mr. Jiang moves with the kind of magnetic exuberance and strong, clear focus that one would expect from a dancer who has performed in such new Chinese dance operas as ''The Red Detachment of Women'' and ''The White-Haired Girl.''
But the neatness of his dancing and the quietness of his charm insured that the occasional acrobatics in Mr. Jiang's ''Yellow River'' never looked like audience-pleasing tricks. 
Instead, the solo impressively evoked the river in all its pounding grandeur and playfulness, as well as depicting the swimmers who live along its banks, as it was intended to do. 
Named after the waterway considered the cradle of Chinese civilization and the symbol of the nation, ''Yellow River'' is set to Ying Chong-Jong's comparably refined Yellow River Concerto.
Based on the legend of the origins of face-painting in the Peking Opera, Mai Mei-Jiun's ''Double Image'' tells the story of a king who is so handsome that he has to wear a ferocious mask when he goes to war. 
Miss Mai, artistic director of the company, works in bold, strong images that can be seen as vibrant, stylized abstractions and traditional narrative elements.
Lu Yu was superb as Lan Ling, the handsome king, projecting smiling serenity and a ritual fierceness. 
The cast was completed by Xue Wei-Xin, as his warrior spirit, David Foresman and Wayne Williams as his soldiers, and Tobi Arrington, Naoko Katakami, Dyane Neiman and Susan Richardson as his enemies. 
''Double Image'' is set to a score by Tan Dun.
Miss Mai's ''Awakening'' was a similar piece of narrative, though it had good performances from Miss Katakami, Mr. Lu and, in particular, Mr. Jiang. The program was completed by Miss Mai's ''The Cicada Speaks,'' set to an evocative score by William Bolcom, and ''Ocean Series,'' by Mr. Xue, the company's resident choreographer. 
Unlike ''Yellow River'' and ''Double Image,'' these interminable impressionistic group works seemed to have been choreographed out of a compulsion to create rather than to express.

text:
