21, plus July 4, at Stern Grove, 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard, featuring artists ranging from the San Francisco Symphony, San Francisco Ballet and Lola Montez Dancers to Turk Murphy, the jazz trombonist, and the Preservation Hall Jazz Band. 
Organ recitals will be given on June 26, July 10, July 24, and Aug. 
7, at 5 P.M. each day, at Grace Episcopal Cathedral, California and Taylor (415-776-6611). 
The Joffrey Ballet will be at the Opera House (415-864-3330) July 6-16.
''Master Harold and the Boys'' with James Earl Jones plays June 29-July 24 at the Curran Theater, 445 Geary Street (415-673-4400). 
''Zorba,'' with Anthony Quinn, plays July 20-Aug. 
20 at the Golden Gate Theater, Taylor and Market (415-775-8800). 
''Hello, Dolly!'' with Carol Channing will be at the Orpheum Theater, 1192 Market Street (415-474-3800), July 26-Aug. 
14.
San Francisco's 207th birthday will be celebrated June 26-29 with Spanish and Mexican music and dance in the Bandshell at Golden Gate Park, with mass at Mission Dolores and lunch at the Presidio Officers Club. 
Reservations: 415-282-8502.
''Crossroads of the Ancient World: Israel's Archaeological Heritage'' will continue through Sept. 
5 at the California Academy of Sciences, Golden Gate Park (415-221-8268).
Â 
Hotels
Even though new hotels seem to sprout every month and the variety is great, one is well advised to have a reservation. 
Of course, there usually is a vacant room a few miles north or south or east, even if locating it by telephone and then getting there cause a few gray hairs. 
But it isn't like being in the city.
The famous hotels deserve their imposing reputations. 
The Fairmont (415-772-5000), the Stanford Court (415-989-3500), the Four Seasons Clift (415-775-4700), the Hyatt Regency (415-788-1234), the Mark Hopkins (415-392-3434), the Huntington (415-474-5400) and others provide luxury that anyone could grow to love. 
Prices run about $65 for the least expensive single room to $190 for a room with twin beds.
A step down is still luxurious. 
Rooms at the San Franciscan (800-227-3050) are $95 top for two. 
The Westin Miyako (800-228-3000), with a Japanese flavor, has a $115 top. 
The Chancellor (415-362-2004) has a maximum rate of $55, and the El Cortez (800-223-5695) has kitchenettes at $50. 
There are even less expensive places. 
Bed and Breakfast International (415-525-4569) specializes in referrals.
Anyone planning to a visit cannot go wrong by writing the San Francisco Convention & Visitors Bureau, P.O. 
Box 6977, San Francisco 94010, and asking for the ''San Francisco Lodging Guide.''
Â 
Restaurants
First, let us understand the dark side of many San Francisco restaurants. 
Some close on Sunday. 
Outside of that I can think of nothing about them to criticize, except that a few will not take reservations.
Ernie's, 847 Montgomery Street (415-397-5969), is a truly splendid place where the captains and waiters come from central casting and the food comes from heaven. 
Others in this category are the Blue Fox, 659 Merchant Street (415-981-1177), La Bourgogne, 330 Mason Street (415-362-7352), L'Etoile, 1075 California Street (415-771-1529), or the Carnelian Room, atop the Bank of America World Headquarters at 555 California Street (415-433-7500). 
This is by no means the full list of top-drawer French and Continental restaurants where two people can scarcely feed themselves decently for under $75.
At Bardelli's, 243 O'Farrell Street (415-982-0243), and Alfred's, a steakhouse at 886 Broadway (415-781-7058), and similar places, two can dine well for $50 or $60. 
The Convention & Visitors Bureau will give you a copy of ''Restaurant and Night Life Guide.''
On those occasions when you have a group of eight or 10 - they will want to talk across and down the table during dinner - I always call on Jack's, a French restaurant, 615 Sacramento Street (415-986-9854), which has upstairs rooms of different sizes. 
You can order off the menu, and escape the fixed menu that you get saddled with even at Ernie's or the Blue Fox, both of which have basement rooms for large parties.
There are any number of Chinese restaurants, ranging in style from a half-dozen stools at a counter to places seating a hundred or so. 
The Chinese cuisine comes from all across Asia, a development of the last 20 years as Chinese from many nations have come into San Francisco. 
My favorite Cantonese restaurant is the Imperial Palace, Tommy Toy proprietor, at 919 Grant Avenue, (415-982-4440). 
The bill for four of us a month ago was $135. 
Hunan Village, 839 Kearny Street (415-956-7868), is less expensive. 
The Mandarin, at 900 North Point in Ghirardelli Square, offers excellent North China cuisine, and it takes reservations (415-673-8812), which Hunan Village does not.
There are several Japanese places, such as Yamato, 717 California Street (415-397-3456), and Nikko, 1450 Van Ness Avenue (415-474-7722).
There are Italian restaurants all around San Francisco, because the city has a big population descended from the fishermen and farmers who came from Italy a century ago. 
North Beach Restaurant, 1512 Stockton Street (415-392-1700), is northern Italian. 
Two people can eat for $40 to $50. 
Original Joe's, 144 Taylor Street (415-775-4877), is less expensive, and in the tomato sauce style.
Seafood is something special in San Francisco and generally I go to Fisherman's Wharf, straight to Castagnola's, 286 Jefferson Street (415-776-5015). 
Sometimes the sea lions will come into the Wharf, and if you have a window table you can watch them beg for scrap fish at the fish buyer's dock. 
There are other great places at the Wharf - Alioto's No. 8 Wharf (415-673-0183), and Scoma's on Pier 47 (415-771-4383), which is behind Castagnola's. 
Downtown, one of the best is Tadich Grill, 240 California (415-391-2373). 
Another is Sam's Grill, 374 Bush (415-421-0594).
Â 
Transportation
The cable cars are closed this year, to reopen in the summer of 1984 at the earliest. 
The system was about to fall apart from pure exhaustion.
However, San Francisco has an excellent system of buses, electric trolley coaches and streetcars called the San Francisco Municipal Railway. 
The fare is 60 cents, 25 cents for children under 17, five cents for the disabled or people over 65, who should be prepared to show a passport or drivers license or some other document, if the driver asks proof of age. 
The information telephone for the Muni, as the system is called, is 415-673-6864. 
It is attended 24 hours, seven days a week.
Even more good news is the weekend and holiday operation of 10 vintage streetcars on Market Street, beginning June 24 and running through Sept. 
26. The old cars have been gathered from Portugal, England, Melbourne, Milwaukee, Portland, Ore., and from the Muni's own back lot, which produced cars dating from 1912. 
During the week, the regular streetcars operate in a subway, but the old tracks and trolley wires have never been taken down from the surface and the San Francisco Chamber of Commerce helped the Muni put the streetcar package together as an answer to the loss of the cable cars.
Regional public transit is good, too. 
For Oakland, Berkeley, Richmond, San Leandro, Newark and Fremont, all across the Bay, you may use Bay Area Rapid Transit's trains (BART), or the AC Transit buses. 
BART schedules can be had by calling 415-788-2278, or AC Transit at 415-653-3535. 
Cities north of the Golden Gate Bridge in Marin and Sonoma county are served by the Golden Gate Bus system. 
The district also operates ferries to Sausalito and Larkspur. 
Information on all this can be obtained by calling 415-453-2100.
To go south down the San Francisco Peninsula to Burlingame, San Mateo, Palo Alto, or San Jose, call the Southern Pacific Railroad's commute schedule number, 415-495-4546, or the San Mateo County Transit District bus lines at 415-761-7000.
Â 
Tours
You can go on a tour to see or do almost anything around San Francisco, running typically around $20 a person. 
There are luncheon cruises (415-861-2165, China Basin Charter) and cocktail-dinner cruises (415-540-8352, San Francisco's Love Boat). 
There are helicopter tours (415-495-3333, China Basin tours) and you may trudge along in the steps of one of the great mystery writers by paying $4 to go on the Dashiell Hammett Tours (415-564-7021). 
Someone will even lead you through the War Memorial Opera House, the Louise M. Davies Symphony Hall and the Herbst Theatre on Monday from 10 A.M. to 2:30 P.M. or Wednesday at 1:30 and 2:30 P.M., all for $3.
There are horse-drawn buggies in Golden Gate Park (415-761-8272) or on Pier 39 (415-398-0857). 
There are city tours for an hour or so or all day. 
Gray Line (415-771-4000) and Dolphin Tours (415-441-6810) offer a broad range, with Gray Line ready to supply a Bay cruise and double decker bus, while Dolphin will take you to Muir Woods redwood grove and Sausalito. 
Lorrie's Travel & Tours (415-826-5950) offers Alcatraz Island, the long-vacant federal prison.
Upward of 20 percent of San Francisco's population is Oriental, which gives special meaning to the Chinatown and Japantown offerings of Dragon Tours (415-392-0244) and the Chinese Cultural Center (415-986-1822). 
Ding How Tours (415-981-8399) will take you through Chinatown and serve you dinner.
To the north, south and east of San Francisco Bay are the vineyards and wineries that produce the nation's premier vintages. 
There is an immense variety of wine tours, and the best way to pick the one you want is to get a copy of ''Visitors Guide to the Wine Country'' from the San Francisco Convention & Visitors Bureau (415-974-6900). 
The bureau maintains an office at Halliday Plaza, that sunken area where Powell Street runs into Market and where the Muni and BART trains stop.

file: WHAT_S DOING IN VANCOUVER.txt
text:
ï»¿
Fresh flowers and firecrackers will brighten February in Vancouver, British Columbia, when the city's Chinese community throws a party. 
The event is called Spring Festival, and its highlight is the celebration of the Chinese New Year, Feb. 
17, with a lion dance and costume parade through one of the largest Chinese communities in North America.
The Chinese first came to western Canada in 1858 in search of gold. 
Today there are more than 100,000 Chinese-Canadians living in or around the Pacific Coast city. 
In recent years the long-established Chinese community has been boosted by many new arrivals from Hong Kong, who are leaving in anticipation of the transfer of the British territory to China in 1997.
Spring Festival, which runs from Feb. 
6 to 28, will include a flower market and children's art show. 
The New Year celebration (call 604-687-0729 for details) marks the start of the Year of the Dragon, and the streets of Chinatown will explode with firecrackers to scare away evil spirits.
Antique light fixtures, widened sidewalks and pagoda-style telephone booths have helped in recent years to give Chinatown a special setting. 
The Chinese have done the rest. 
Vegetable stores spill out onto the sidewalk laden with bok choy (cabbage) and dung gwa (winter melon). 
Herb shops are crammed with jars of unidentifiable substances alleged to cure any ailment under the sun. 
And the vivid reds and yellows of store canopies alongside flashing neon signs make a kaleidoscope on the darkest winter day. 
But that bustling street scene is not the heart of the district. 
That label has now been placed, with great pride, on a garden of serene beauty that opened last year on the edge of Chinatown.
The Sun Yat-sen Garden, behind high white walls, is the first, full-size classical Chinese garden to be built outside China. 
Named for the revolutionary who led the overthrow of the imperial system in 1911 and who helped to establish the Chinese Republic, the garden was built with donations from individuals, corporations and governments. 
Construction was done by 52 workmen from Suzhou who used traditional methods and tools. 
Even in the rain, it's a lovely place. 
A waterfall splashes, wind rustles the bamboo, and its tranquility defies the traffic outside the walls. 
The garden unfolds like a landscape painting scroll of rockeries, evergreens, pebblestone paving and pools of jade green water teeming with goldfish.
The garden (578 Carrall Street; 604-689-7133) is open daily from 10 A.M. to 4:30 P.M. during the winter. 
Admission is $2.25, $1.50 for older people, students and children. 
And there's a gift shop where you can buy anything from a silk rug for $1,500 to a bar of sandalwood soap for 45 cents. 
(Prices throughout are given in United States dollars.) Also unique to Chinatown is what is claimed to be the narrowest commercial building in the world. 
Only six feet wide, the Sam Kee building, 8 West Pender Street, was recently fronted by a 100-foot-long lighted sidewalk of glass blocks; it has become a magnet for tourist cameras.
Â 
THE MOUNTAINS
The glory of the city of 1.2 million is its setting: the 4,000-foot peaks of the Coast Mountains drop steeply to a natural harbor. 
Ten sandy beaches are within easy reach - some by foot, others by bus or car - of the city center, and they are a playground for sailors and windsurfers almost year round.
The city's mild, wet winter has an average low temperature of around 35 degrees in January, but skiers should not abandon hope. 
The mountains that tower over the city, Grouse and Seymour, provide good skiing only a 20-minute drive from downtown. 
At Grouse (604-986-6262 for snow report) a daily lift ticket is about $17, at Seymour (604-986-3444 for snow report) about $12.
And 80 miles north is a two-mountain ski resort rapidly making an international name. 
Whistler and Blackcomb mountains (604-932-4191 for snow alongside an Alpine-style village, offer 10,000 vertical feet of skiing on 180 marked runs with 26 lifts. 
A day pass on either peak costs $24 and, with luck, skiing lasts well into spring. 
For accommodations, contact Central Reservations Service, Whistler, British Columbia V0N 1B0 (604-932-4222).
Blackcomb invested $25 million in new facilities this year, including three express lifts that whisk skiers to the mountaintop in 14 minutes rather than 45 on the old lifts. 
A transfer to the Seventh Heaven Express then takes a mere six minutes to reach powder country.
With 22 hotels and condominiums in the village and more under construction, the resort is turning into a year-round destination with a golf course, tennis courts, hiking trails, fishing and windsurfing.
Â 
CITY SIGHTS
In Vancouver the first-time visitor might head to Stanley Park, a five-minute cab ride a mile west of the downtown area. 
The park, a 1,000-acre-peninsula, combines near-wilderness forest, beaches, formal rose gardens, a waterlily lake and an excellent aquarium. 
The park is circled by an eight-mile seawall walk and one can rent a bike ($3.50 to $4.50 an hour) at the park entrance.
Granville Island, also a peninsula, is beside the inner city lagoon of False Creek. 
The island is a mixture of art and industry with a waterfront food market, theaters, restaurants and boats. 
For a good, inexpensive lunch one can buy a bagel with smoked salmon and cheese, and sit in the sun watching the jugglers and waving at the passing yachts.
Â 
NIGHT LIFE
At night, Vancouver's affluent young people converge at Pelican Bay, a waterfront club inside the Granville Island Hotel (604-683-7373). 
This is where California North - as Vancouver likes to think of itself -dances the night away (the night begins around 9:30; a cover charge of about $2 is charged weekends.) And long a night life favorite is Richard's on Richards (1036 Richards Street; 604-687-6794). 
There nearly always seems to be a well-turned-out lineup on the sidewalk waiting to get in to Richard's, where guests' cars are handed over to tuxedoed valets. 
(Cover charges vary under $5, depending on the night of the week.)
Â 
EVENTS
Five buildings stuffed with 341 cars from the world's leading manufacturers will make up the Pacific International Automobile Show Jan. 
15 to 24 at Exhibition Park in the east end of the city. 
For those who prefer floating to driving, there's the Vancouver International Boat Show from Feb. 
3 to 7 at the B. C. Place Stadium (604-669-2300). 
Everything from a rowboat to a 50-foot yacht will be on view.
The Vancouver Opera Association (604-682-2871) will present three operas in English at the Queen Elizabeth Theater (Hamilton and Georgia). 
Leos Janacek's ''Cunning Little Vixen'' will be performed Jan. 
30, Feb. 
2, 4 and 6; Benjamin Britten's ''Turn of the Screw'' March 12, 15, 17 and 19, and Johann Strauss's ''Fledermaus'' April 30, May 3, 5 and 7. 
Tickets range from $13 to $39.
The Vancouver Symphony (604-684-9100) will be conducted for the first time by a woman, French-born Catherine Comet, now music director of the Grand Rapids Symphony, March 13, 14 and 15 at the Orpheum (601 Smithe Street). 
On the program: Beethoven's Piano Concerto No. 1 in C Major, Debussy's ''Afternoon of a Faun'' and Hindemith's ''Mathis der Maler'' The Hungarian pianist Annie Fischer will be soloist. 
Tickets range from $6 to $19.
Â 
HOTELS
With Expo 86's millions of visitors now a memory, Vancouver's hotels have been suffering. 
But the tourist wins because competition is fierce, making for moderate prices and excellent service.
In the luxury class, the venerable Hotel Vancouver (900 West Georgia Street; 604-684-3131 or 800-268-9143) will always be a survivor. 
Its green copper roof is a city landmark and its central location is great. 
Recently an indoor pool was added to give the elegant, old hotel all the essentials of contemporary life. 
Doubles range from about $50 to $90.
More moderately priced but lacking in nothing is O'Doul's Hotel (1300 Robson Street; 604-684-8461 or 800-663-5491). 
Set on a street of boutiques and specialty stores, O'Doul's is only a short walk from Stanley Park. 
Rooms include writing desks and three telephones. 
Doubles are about $60 to $85.
There are studio suites with queen-size beds and kitchenettes in the Pagebrook Hotel (1234 Hornby Street; 604-688-1234 or 800-663-1234). 
Suite rates go up from about $60 a night; children under 16 are free.
A 12-minute ride across the harbor by SeaBus ferry is the Lonsdale Quay Hotel (123 Carrie Cates Court, North Vancouver; 604-986-6111). 
The small waterfront hotel has gorgeous views; double rooms are about $70 to $95.
Visitors on a budget will get good value at the Greenbrier Apartment Hotel (1393 Robson Street; 604-683-4558), which lacks decor but has a location as good as O'Doul's. 
Doubles start at $30.
For tourist information and more accommodation possibilities, including bed and breakfast's, contact the Travel InfoCenter (562 Burrard Street; 604-683-2000).
Â 
RESTAURANTS
A fine new restaurant called the Prow may now have the best view in the city. 
The restaurant is in the northern end of Canada Place, a striking building topped with white sails that juts into the harbor like a sailing ship. 
It was Canada's pavilion at Expo; now it houses a trade and convention center. 
At the Prow (604-684-1339) dinner for two with wine costs about $50. 
The menu is likely to include mussel cream soup with Pernod and grilled swordfish in pink peppercorn and orange sauce.
Not quite so pricey and very lively is Joe Fortes (777 Thurlow Street; 604-669-1940). 
Situated in a neighborhood of boutiques, Joe Fortes is named for a long-dead local character and is known for its oyster bar and live piano music. 
Dinner and wine for two costs about $45; among recent menu choices have been roast boneless duck with pear sauce and a cheesecake made with sour cream.
Well within budget range is the fine Japanese food at Kibune Restaurant (1508 Yew; 604-734-5216). 
The tiny place, which is decorated with lots of wood, has miso-shiru soup for 75 cents, and a house specialty called yosenabe that contains everything from seafood and tofu to chicken and bamboo shoots ($5.25).
The range of Chinese food is wide. 
Downtown there's the elegant black and white decor at the Beijing (865 Hornby Street; 604-688-7788), where a meal for two with wine costs $45 to $65; among the dishes might be a soup of bird's nest and crabmeat ($19) or spicy Szechuan chicken hot pot ($7).
For bargain hunters in the midst of Chinatown, there is Hon's Wun-Tun House (524 Main Street; 604-688-7018). 
An order of the quick-fried steamed dumplings, which come in a tangy sauce, costs only a bit more than $2. 
There's no liquor license but for $8 two people can eat their fill.

text:
ï»¿
''CINEMA IN CHINA'' surveys, respectfully, some 50 years of Chinese film making. 
Are the films any good?
It's hard to tell. 
Most of what we see looks wooden, although perhaps Western standards shouldn't apply. 
Chinese films, the documentary tells us, have been ''inextricably involved with the political and social changes'' in China. 
The documentary will be seen on Channel 13 at 9 o'clock tonight.
Tony Rayns, the host, narrator and writer of the program, which was originally produced for Britain's Channel Four, says that China has a ''very rich film heritage,'' and that something like 80 million Chinese go to the movies each week. 
The film industry, still recovering from the depredations of the Gang of Four, Mr. Rayns says, produces more than 100 features each year.
In an interview, we see Sun Yu, who studied at Columbia University in the 1920's, and became, Mr. Rayns says, ''one of the first leftist intellectuals'' to make movies in China. 
''Cinema in China'' shows excerpts from his 1931 ''The Highway.''
A crew of road builders give their lives to defend China against invaders, presumably the Japanese.
What's interesting here are the exhortations. 
In subtitles, the road builders sing: ''Pull the roller!
Don't slacken your efforts!
/ All together!
Make light the weight of the roller!''
Then the refrain: ''Let all work hard!
Go forward together.''
The English subtitles may not be absolutely accurate, although presumably they catch the general flavor. 
Most of the film excerpts, no matter what the decade, are intent on sending messages. 
This doesn't mean they are all without charm; a 1962 film on women's equality looks promising. 
We do, however, get an impression that Chinese films aren't much for frivolity.
Mr. Rayns, meanwhile, has some difficulty in describing the state of film making now. 
The excesses of the Cultural Revolution, he says, have disappeared: ''China's studios are now free to make whatever films they want.''
Then, almost in the same breath, he says that ''if a studio chooses to tackle a controversial subject, it runs the risk of having the Film Bureau refuse to release the film.''
And does the Film Bureau ever refuse to release films?
We're not told, although Mr. Rayns does say that Chinese studios now make movies on ''controversial'' subjects. 
He doesn't identify the subjects, however, and one wishes he did. 
By the documentary's own evidence, film making in China seems to be a very cautious affair.
Thus we get the head of a studio script department. 
His job, he says, is ''to guide the group properly so that it follows the right path.''
Meanwhile, an actor describes a 1949 film about a man who supposedly loved both his country and money. 
In the old days, the actor says seriously, ''such two-faced people really existed.''
We also see an excerpt from the 1982 ''The Herdsman.''
The ingenue says it doesn't matter if her fiance is a teacher or a goatherd, ''as long he isn't a rightist.''
''Cinema on Cinema,'' part of Channel 13's ''Film on Film'' series, is solemn about this. 
Mr. Rayns is an enthusiast, not a critic, and he is reluctant to say that Chinese films are Government instruments. 
It would be a better documentary if he were a shade more judgmental.

text:
ï»¿
THERE'S a little slice of China in Chester. 
Free public lessons in tai chi, the ancient Chinese system of exercises, are being offered by the National Theater of the Deaf, which is based in the Connecticut River Valley town.
Three mornings each week, 70 to 100 people assemble on the green by the 1793 Chester Meetinghouse to learn the traditional routines aimed at promoting harmony of mind and body.
The theater, made up of deaf and hearing actors, is known for its performances that combine sign language with the spoken word. 
Over the years, several members have practiced tai chi, according to David Hays, founder and artistic director of the company. 
But actors in the troupe became particularly interested in the exercises last year when they toured China with two plays.
One actor, wandering through the streets of Beijing, met an 80-year-old man who knew some English and taught tai chi. 
Soon the actor rounded up others from the theater to attend his new acquaintance's classes.
Mr. Hays had tried tai chi before and knew his level of ability. 
''I'm enormously unskillful at it,'' he said. 
Nonetheless, he joined the Beijing classes and attends those in Chester when his schedule permits.
Shanny Mow, a deaf actor with the troupe, attended the classes in Beijing and now leads those in Chester. 
He said he began practicing tai chi several years ago after receiving several bloody noses while learning karate.
''I decided there had to be something more gentle,'' Mr. Mow said through a sign language interpreter. 
Tai chi, he said, ''tones your nerves.''
''If you do it first thing every morning, you start the day feeling good,'' he added.
When members of the theater decided to make tai chi routines part of their summer schedule, they sought a spot large enough to accommodate actors, staff members, students from the National Theater of the Deaf's summer school for deaf theater personnel, and any friends, neighbors or others who might be interested. 
They settled on the tree-shaded green.
Tai chi on the green is not the same as tai chi in Beijing. 
For one thing, the Beijing exercises took place at 5 A.M., while the sessions on the green are conducted at the more acceptable 7:30 A.M. For another, many Chinese brought their pet birds in cages to the Beijing exercises, and although the theater has invited its tai chi students to bring birds, nobody has yet done so.
''But I'm still hopeful,'' said Germaine Schumacher, a copy editor and proofreader from Middletown who attends the classes and thinks birds would be a fine addition.
The lack of birds has apparently not discouraged attendance.Mrs. 
Schumacher and dozens of others have shown up faithfully for the lessons, undaunted even on a recent morning when rain had fallen most of the night, the skies were gray and the green was so wet that the class had to be conducted in the adjoining gravel parking lot.
That day, as usual, the participants carefully followed Mr. Mow, stretching their arms, raising their legs and bending their bodies in the slow, balanced, flowing movements of tai chi.
Only occasionally did Mr. Mow issue instructions through the interpreter.
''Please remember to keep your back straight; don't lean over,'' he reminded his followers at one point. 
Then he added, ''But don't worry if you don't get it right.''
The followers - encompassing teen-agers to the elderly - looked intent, but not worried. 
Some, like Rosemary Bleyer, a clinical psychologist from Middletown, were attending on their way to work.
A few, like Ruth Thayer, a retired newspaper photographer from Old Saybrook, were trying the routines for the first time. 
''They seem to exercise every muscle,'' Mrs. Thayer said.
Among those going through the paces set by Mr. Mow were five students from China who are attending the theater's summer school. 
These students were hardly more familiar with the tai chi routines than the other participants, noted Andrew Vasnick, director of the summer school.
In China, Mr. Vasnick explained, most of the practitioners of tai chi are older people. 
The theater invited foreign students to its summer school as part of its effort to encourage the formation of theaters of the deaf in other countries, he added.
Mr. Mow's students seemed to agree with him that tai chi was a good way to start the day. 
''I'm a terrible person in the morning,'' said Cathleen Riddley, a hearing actor with the theater. 
''I need a slow, pleasant way to get the body moving.''
''The exercises are so beautiful and graceful, and there's no strain on the body,'' said Mrs. Schumacher.
Robert Scheifer, a theater summer school student who lives in Chicago, said, ''I feel balanced; it helps my mind.''
Mr. Mow said that he had taught his students about a dozen moves. 
He uses a tai chi textbook in which photographs of the moves have titles like ''Moving Hands Softly Like Clouds'' and ''Stork Beginning to Spread Wings,'' but he said it was not important to memorize such romantic names.
What is important, he said, is to learn the movements well enough to ''concentrate on what you're doing, not on what you should be doing.''
''It's gratifying to see so many people want to learn,'' he added.
The classes will continue on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday mornings through July 11. 
Soon after that the actors are to begin rehearsals for their 1987-88 production, ''The Dybbuk'' by S. Ansky.
